summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 in the Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal, (I) the Public Analyst reported that the sample contained adulterated food due to insect infested pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and I am of the opinion that the same is adulterated due to mismatch infestation by insect in infested articles of Kajuus to its extent of 20%. The Food Inspector reported that " Date of analysis: 10 1 1969 Insect infestation, including infestation even by dead insects, the further point to be considered is whether mere insect f infestation without more, would be sufficient to hold the article to be 'adulterated ' within the meaning of sub clause (f) of section 2 of the Act. The Food inspector reported that on 10 11969 Insect in the municipal Corporation of the Delhi vsKacherooMal, (1) the public analyst had reported that date of analysis was 10 1 1970 and that the percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, disgusting rotten or insectinfested, it would be deemed to be unfit for human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section2(1)(f). The respondent was tried for an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the ( Act) on the ground that the Food Inspector had reported the fact of analysis of the sample in question as "No. 1" and that he had not given any reason for his opinion. The trial court acquitted the respondent holding that the report of the Public analyst did not support the prosecution case and that it was not necessary to prove further that the article of food was unfit for ' human consumption ' within section 2(1) (f). In appeal, the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish by any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section 3(2)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and that there was no proof that the lal mirchi powder was adulterated. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The true meaning of section '2(ia)(f) has been brought out in Municipal Corporation Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, (supra). [473B] 2.1 In the instant case, the true meaning and effect of section 1(1), (f), has been put out in the said Municipal Corporation. The conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove additional evidence is a correct statement of the law. [473C D] 2:2 It is well settled that where two views are possible, one pointing to the other and the other pointing to another should be preferred. If the view taken by the High court is accepted, then the Court would not interfere with the findings of fact unless it is shown that the conclusions arrived at by the trial court were perverse or based on no evidence or that they were based on such misreading of evidence or were based upon no evidence. [474E F] 2(i) The true interpretation of section l(1 ) (f)(f), as given in the context of sub clauses (a) and (b) is that if the article is unfit for consumption on account of (a), its consisting wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid disgunting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insectable, (b), or on account Of any other cause, and (c) or on accounts of any other causes. [475E F; 475A] 2.(ii) The word "insect" has been used in the sense of "adulteration".

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. HELD : The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. [901 B] It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a 'dealer and that is the essence of the Order. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. The total circumstances in the case show that the appellant was in fact carrying on agricultural operationsoperations.

The respondent was a monthly tenant in respect of the land described in Schedule to the plaint. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the property on the allegation that the defendant was a a monthly tenancy in respect thereof and that the tenancy was determina tion by a valid notice to terminate the tenancy. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had made a Persuliyat before the High 'Court to establish that as the Patta of 1913 as well as the Kabuliyat were both invalid and inoperative, he was never a tenant in the land by prescription or otherwise; (ii) the tenancy created by payment and acceptance of rent in the year 1925 was from the beginning a tenancy from month to month under the provision of section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. HELD: (i)(a) The High Court rightly held that the respondent 's tenancy was one from monthto month since its inception in 1924. [277 E] (b) The question whether payment to the Receiver amounted to payment to payment of rent to the appellant was a mixed question of fact and law which could not be decided by this Court in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution. [278 G] (c) The respondent ' s tenancy created in 1924 was from month, to month since it had no authority to receive them. It was not the case of the respondent at any stage of the suit that because one year 's rent was paid a tenancy for one year was brought into existence. [279 C D] (d) The appellant 's claim based substantially on the terms of the Kabiuliyat executed by him on 24th December, 1924, and the suit was, in fact, one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease.

The appellant assessee, a firm carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of cotton yarn. The assessee filed its return for the assessment years 1964 65 to 1965 66. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of privilege under section 138(1)(b) of the 1961 Act holding that the documents produced by the assessee were immune from production in a court of law. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that the document produced by an assessee was immune from disclosure under section 137(1) (b) and that the finality attached to an order of Commissioner with regard to claim of privileges under Section 138(i)(b), had no relationship to the power of the court to summon that record. The High Court, however allowed the appeal holding that after the repeal of section 137 by Act V of 1964 there was no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summoned the production of documents filed by an assesee during the assessment proceedings before an Income Tax Officers after 1.4.1964 in respect of assessment years 1965 65 onwards, and that, the finality attaching to an earlier order of assessment with regard thereto had no relevance to the exercise of powers by a court to summoning the production or disclosure of any information therefrom to it, in a case pending before the Court when the court, by a judicial order, requires the production Of the record, considered relevant by it for decision of a case filed pending before it. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finality attached under section137(i) (a) of 1961 Act is, thus restricted to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for by any person other than a court in law by a Judicial order. [563F] 1.2 In the instant case, the documents filed before the Income tax authorities even after April 1, 1964 were immunefrom production in the court of the Commissioner of Income Tax. The finality which has been attached to the order under section138(1), is thus restricted only to the case where theinformation etc. are called for from any person, other than the Court of law by judicial order. The jurisdiction which has already been attached with the order passed by the IncomeTax authorities under Section 139(1). [563B] 1:3 In the present case, there was nothing on record to show that the assessee had produced any evidence before the income tax authorities in respect thereof. Therefore, the finding of the Tribunal that the information furnished by the assesee was immune for production in court of a judicial decision on summons for their production being issued by the Court and that it was open to the Incometax Authorities to summon the production from the income Tax authorities after April I 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65 onwards is not correct. [564C D] 1 :4 The finality attaching under section 139(i), (b), has no relevance in the exercise Of powers by the courts to require the productionof documents from the Income lax Authorities after April l, 1964 relating thereto to assessment years1964 65 onwards and that such an order can be called in question in any court of Law. [565D] 1 5. The effect which has 564 been attached under the order dated April 1. 1964 is, restricted to cases where information etc., as contemplated under the section is called "for by any other person,other than a Court of Law by ajudicial order". The finality that has been attaching to the earlier order is, therefore, restricted only in respect to the matters which are pending before them.

The appellants were the minor children of a Hindu female. They made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotty died on May 3, 1946 without any issue. The first appellant and her mother accepted the gift on behalf of their minor wife. On February 25, 1947, Mammatty was put up for trial before the Sub Judge who held that the gift was valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor or by the grand father or 'quasi guardian ' provided there was a real and bona fide intention on the donor 's part to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift to the donee and that even a change in the mode of enjoyment was sufficient evidence of such an intention. The Sub Judge further held that even if the gift actually made was not the gift, actually made, and that there was no legal guardian for property in existence, the gift could be completed by delivery of the property to and acceptance by any person in whose control the minor is at the time. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the appellants were entitled to succeed to the properties on the ground that they had failed to prove their case beyond reasonable doubt. The question whether possession can be given to the wife 's mother when the gift is from the husband to his minor wife and when the minor 's father and father are not alive and there is no executor of the one or the other. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gifts for his benefit is the sole consideration. Mamman vs Kadar Bux, (1918) L.R. 43 I.A. 4, p. 484, followed. Nabi Sab vs Papiah and ors., ; , referred to.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951 was enacted to provide for better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides that every religious institution, the annual income of which, for the fasli year immediately preceding as calculated for the purposes of the levy of contribution under sub section (1), is not less than one thousand rupees shall pay to the Commissioner annually such contribution not exceeding five per centum of its income as may be prescribed. The Act did not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution was to be levied. The High Court held that under the Act the Government had to make under section 100 rules applicable to each temple separately and prescribing the method for determining contribution found no support in the provisions of the Act or its scheme. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Under section 76(2) of the Madras Act 19, audit fee is not to be prescribed by rules. The Commissioner has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than the maximum prescribed) for meeting the cost of audit of the institution. That im.plies that the Commissioner has not determined the audit fee under section 76 (2). [920 E] H. M. Abdul Rahim vs The State of Mysore, ; , followed. (ii) Under the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 19 of 1950, audit fees is not a fee and is not beyond the legislative competence of the State Legislature. [921 B] H, M. Abdulla & Ors. vs The Commissioner of Income tax, Madras, ; and H. C. Abdul Rahman vs The District Board, Palghat, ; followed.

The appellant, a practising advocate, filed a complaint against the respondents under section 19(1) of the (Act), alleging that he had committed contempt of Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no appeal lies to this Court under section19 of the Act from an order issuing notice as nothing yet has been decided by the High Court. In appeal to this court, it was contended on behalf of the respondents that no appeals lay to this Courts under section 20 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The preliminary objection raised on behalf 'the respondents is well founded and must be accepted as correct. Section 19(i) says "No Court shall initiate any proceedings for contempt either on its own motion or otherwise after the expiry of a period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed". The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High court affecting their right, the mere order issuing the notice does not decide any question. This Court, while deciding an appeal under section 18 of the , cannot be asked in such an appeal to decide whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt. [508 H] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, ; and Baradkanta Mishra 's case, ; referred to. In the instant case, the order or decision must have been such that the proceeding was not barred, it may well be that an appeal would lie to this Supreme Court under s 19 from such an order although the proceeding has remained pending in the High Courts.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 4(1A) of that Act on the ground that he had failed to prove that the offence was committed by him within the meaning of section 6 (1 A). On appeal, the High Court held that the amendment made in 1949 did not affect the continuance of the earlier amendment made by the amending Act of 1949. Held, that the words "in any other enactment" in section 4 of the 1952 Act were comprehensive enough to take in wireless telegraphy transmitter and this Court gave leave limited to the question of sentence only. The words "any enactment shall not affect any other law in which the repealed enactment has been applied, incorporated or referred to". Section 20 of the Indian Wireless Telegraphy The whole (Amendment) Act, 1949, did not prevent the possession of a wireless apparatus. Therefore, it cannot be said that section 6 of the 1947 Act continued to be on the statute book even after the amending Acts of 1949 were repealed by Act XLVIII of 1952, and that it was in force when the offence committed by the appellant was committed. The amendment made to the Indian Telegraphy Act, 1933 did not effect the continuance or continuation of the original amendment made under the amending provisions of the repealed Act. Section 20 (1A), inserted in the Act of 1933 by the Amending Act of 1948, was either covered by the provisions Of the , or a surplusage not serving any definite purpose.

The appellant, who was the wife of a son of one Adwaita, executed two decrees in favour of the respondent and his wife. The decree holders filed two applications under section 36(6) (a)(ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned above and passing of new instalment decrees in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The trial court dismissed both the applications but on appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and restored that of the first appellate court. In appeal to this Court by special leave: Held, that the object of restoring possession of the properties sold in execution of the decree to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled, and in case of default in payment of any of the instalments, the properties are returned to the decreeholder purchaser. The sale itself was not annulled and in cases of default, the property is returned to him. In other words, the object is restoring possession to the Judgment debtor under clause (c) of section 36 (2). Under clause (d), the court has to order the payment of the decretal amount in such instalments as it thinks proper, and cl.(e) further imposes a duty on the Court to give a direction in such cases that if there is default in the payment Of any one of the instalment instalments, he properties restored to the judgement debtor under cl. (e) would be put back into the possession of 'the decreeholder. It is quite true that the purpose of restoring the possession is to enabling the latter, to pay out of the proceeds of the sale and so far as it is necessary to give relief to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the . The sale must remain with the appellant.

The appellant company was incorporated in the erstwhile State of Bombay. The company had a building at Bombay and its buildings were situated within the limits of the City of Bombay, but the building was let out to the respondents by the appellant company on lease for 99 years. The respondents filed a suit against the appellant Company for specific performance of an agreement to transfer the decree in favour of the respondents. The appellant contended that the deed of assignment in favour Of the respondents was not executed by Habib & Sons and (2) that the assignee of the subject matter of the suit and not of the decree itself was not entitled to apply for leave under Order XXI, r. 16. Held, that the provisions of Order XXI rule 16 contemplate the actual transfer by an assignment in writing of a decree after it is passed and that while a transfer of or an agree ment to transfer a decree that may be passed in future may, in equity, entitle the intending transferee to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after he has passed such an order. The provisions of 0. XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure contemplate the exact transfer by assignment in words and phrases which are not defined in the Code but are intended to be used as a guide to interpretation of statutes. The normal rule is that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and rule 10 enables him to do so, while rule 16 enables the transferee of the judgment to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution made by the decree holder. It seems to me, therefore, that there must be a decree in existence which is transferred before the transferee can benefit from the provisions Of rule 16. The respondent cannot claim to be a transferee of a suit by an assignee of his decree by an assign ment in writing within the meaning of Order 21, r . 16.
