" The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineers, Ajmer, its tender for providing, and fixing 'S. H ' W 'C ' Type" "E ', "S".H ' Type", "t", "D 'H" and "Motor bus being one for sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for this service. The Deputy Commissioner, Excise & Taxation in appeal held that from the acceptance of the tender two contracts resulted : one for providing doors and windows and another for "fixing" those doors and window leaves in a specified building, and thus partly liable to sales tax. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the contract was one of service in the execution of which some movable property passed : it was not a contract for sale but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts, one for the supply or the sale of articles for consideration, and that the price of, the supplied but not charge for service, was taxable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the contracts were one of 'service in the executing of which certain movable property passing : it could not be said that ultimately the property was to pass to the War Office under the head contract. [507 C] (ii) The contract may be for work to be done for remuneration and for supply of materials used in the construction of the works for a price; it may be a contract of sale though work and labour are involved in the making and fixing of these windows. If the windows were not properly fixed, the contracts would not be complete, and in the case of a building contract the property in materials used does not pass to tho other party to the contract as movable property. [511 E F] (iii) The test in each case is whether the object of the party sought to be taxed is that the chattelas passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection therewith are under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution thereof of the work; or it may not be a 'fix" the windows. [ 512 B] (iv) The tests in each ease are whether the objects of the parties sought to he taxed are that the goods supplied by the manufacturer, and, if so, whether the contract is in substance one for work and Labour or one for ' sale of a chatttel.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B Indian Penal code read with Section 120 B Indian Penal. The prosecution case is that on November 8, 1967 Shankerlal, who was a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar Prasad complainant and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. On November 16, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to Ram L. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report lodged by Ram Avtar and the accused were discharged. The appellant contended that he was not a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. There is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. [279E] 2. It is well settled that in criminal cases where there are two offences one under section 420 and other under sections 120B and 109 Indian Penal, the court has to consider the evidence adduced by the prosecution and decide whether it should be held that the accused was a party or not. In the present case, the part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the first report. The part which relates to Raj kumar is that when the latter brought washer plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the washer plate plates from Ram Avtar.[279F G] 3. There are no cogent grounds for interference.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways he has alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 and claims reliefs of mandamus to the Union of India for implementing the reports of the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees appointed by the Railway Administration. The petitioner contended that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. The quality of the service should improve. [741C] 1.2 In the instant case, Government have limitations, both of resources and capacity, yet we hope that the Government and the Administration would rise to the necessity of the occasion and take it as a challenge to improve this great public utility in an effective way and with an adequate sense of urgency. Giving directions in a matter like this where availability of resources has a material bearing, policy regarding priorities is involved, expertise is very much in issue, is not prudent and we do not, therefore, propose to issue directions. [779E F] 1:3 The common citizen 's method of transport through the Railways should be maintained. It is true that Government have constraints, both in resources and ability, but this means that accidents have to be avoided, attack on the persons of the passengers, and prying on their property has to stop. [780E F; 780A] 1 :4 The responsibility cast by the railways Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It cannot be said that the common man "s mode" of transport carefully connected with free play is not proper and we did not, however, propose it to issue any directions. The Railways Act and Rules under them must be comply with. [781C] 2:5 The responsibility imposed by the railway Act and rules under it should be complied within a reasonable time. [783E] 3:1 The obligation cast by this Act and Rule thereunder must be strictly complied with, and the Railways are bound to provide adequate facilities and create an environment in which the right to move freely and carry on any business or profession would both be practicable and feasible. [784G H] 2.6 In the present case, the Railway has not denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ petition. The Government and Administration would have rise to this necessity of tile occasion and taking it as the challenge to improved this greatpublic utility in a effective way, and with adequate sense Of urgency. [ 784E] 2 :7 The common law man ' s mode of transportation closely connected With the free exercise play of the fundamental right must not be allowed to be abused by private individuals or groups of persons or associations of persons. It may be that this power must be lodged somewhere and under our Constitution and laws, it has been lodged in the Judges and if they have to fulfil their function as Judges, it would hardly be lodged elsewhere. [ 786B] 2(a) The common method of transportation through the Railway is not just a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the State but there is no iota of hesitation in this Court to say that the Common man 'S mode of road closely connectedwith the free trade of this Article should not he.

The appellants were the owners of certain lands in Bombay. The lands were resumed by the Collector under section 13(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act, 1952. The appellants filed applications for restoration of their lands on the ground that they had been prevented from appearing in the appeals before the Revenue Tribunal and that the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations. The application was dismissed by the Revenue Appellate Tribunal but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there is default in appearance of the appellant and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal; and (2) the words "decide it on merits" used in Regulation 21 are wide enough to include within their scope and ambit an application for restoration. HELD: (1)(a) The Tribunal has no power either to dismiss a appeal for default but it was obligatory on the part of the Tribunal to decide whether the appellant had notice of the date of hearing or that be was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the appeal or application was called for hearing, and to recording its decision even though the default on the face of it is not wilful. [143 E] (b) The words " Decide it" in Regulation 19(1), are wide and include within its scope and amplitude an application made under regulation 20 shall be filed within 30 day from the date when the order for resto ration of the appeals or application is made. If the view that the Tribunal has committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases was correct, it follows that Regulation 21 applies to the present case and the period of limitation prescribed by that Regulation being 30 days from the day of receipt of order of dismiss ment of the Appeal, the applications for restoring the appeal filed by the appellant in all four cases were well within the period prescribed by Regulation 21. [144 H] (2)(a). The Tribunal committed an erroneous error of fact in dismissing all the appeals. [145 A B] (3) The orders of the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal dismissing the appellants ' applications for restitution made by them in all these four cases are well within its terms and do not call for any interference.

The appellant was the manager of a temple where the idols of Shri Ramchandra, Sita, Laxman Bharat, Satrughan and Hanumanji had been worshipped for several years. The appellant 's case in the plaint was that Telibandha was dedicated to the deity of Shri Ramachandraji as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later on in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath Sao of this village of Telibari but also dedicated the village Telivancore to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The Trial Court held that the dedication of the village was not proved but disagreeing with the Trial Court, it held that there was no absolute dedication of that village for the purpose of the temple by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 and no trust was created thereby. On appeal to the High Court, Held: (i) The document (the Panch Fairsala) clearly and unambiguously shows anabsolute dedication of a village to Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple, set aside the judgment and decree of the High court and send it back to the trial court for disposal in accordance with law. (ii) The fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. On the contrary, the document (he Panch Faima Hasia Award of 1796) clearly shows an abso lute dedication of ' the village to the temple of Shri Ram Ramchandra Swamy Temple, set up by Dinath Sao and Teli Oriya in the partition the Panchayat caused the same to be given to Ramsaran Lal absolutely with only a charge on it for the expenses of the deity.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Oudh Bar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. The first charge was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The second charge was with respect to the contumacious conduct of the appellants individually. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associ ated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of contempt as contemner Nos. 1 & 2 were guilty of contumacious behaviour; (2) the High Court committed an error in discharging the notices; and (3) the appellants were responsible for the passing thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (i) The language used by them was unfortunate. It is true that the High court referred to the Gratification 's case but the High Courts did not wish to proceed against the appellant. [603E] (ii) The words "in the discharge of his duties" in the resolution were unfortunate. The matter becomes clear when the High ' Court said "we do not propose to punish contemners Nos. I & 2 for the contumami mious conduct of which we have adjudged them guilty though they did express their strong disapproval. [ 603F] (iii) The High Courts committed an errato ry error in treating the appellants guilty of criminal contempt. It was a matter of regret that the contem ners who are prominent members of the Assembly did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. The language employed by them is unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into a partnership with the fourth appellant in respect of partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators; namely, three appellants Nos 5, 6 and 7 herein. On or about 11th of June, 1977 an unregistered deed of agreement between the four brothers being the appellants Nos., 5,6 and 7 was entered into regarding partition of their joint family property and the said was referred to 3 arbitrators. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge for registration but on 2nd September, 1978 the learned Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for registration. On 2nd Sept., 1983 the arbitrators made a reference to the arbitrators and made and signed the award. The appellants Nos 1 to 3 filed an application on 25th November, 1983 for return of the award on 6th March, 1981 setting aside the aforesaid order of the Sub judge holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration and that the limitation for the registration of the arbitrator had already expired. The Sub Judge rejected the application and did not direct return of award holding that the period for registration of award had already elapsed. On appeal, the High Court ordered that the arbitrators should be returned back to the sub court for presentation of the same after the expiry of four months from 28th November 1977. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the order made by the court directing the arbitrators not to take back their award for presentation to the Sub Registrar was wrong and without jurisdiction; (ii) the award was presented within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely 28th January, 1978 to 24th November 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section 15 of the . Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The order made on 24th June, 1985 is restored. [121C] 2.1 In the instant case admittedly the award had been presented within four months of 28th February, 1978 till the return of 'the award to the arbitrator on 24 th November,1983 and before the expiry Of the four months period from 28st November, 1977, the award is filed in the court pursuant to the order of this Court. The award was made on 28th of January,1978 and before that date the award Was presented for registration to the office of the sub Judge on 25 th November 1983. Therefore, this period, that is to say from 28nd January 1978 to24th November,, 1983 the award, was the date of the order directing maintenance of status quo and 20th December 1982 was the day when the interim stay was vacated, but still the award has been in the custody of the court and there is ample evidence as it would appear from the narration of events hereinbefore made that the arbitrator has tried to obtain the custody from the court to take any further steps for its registration then it cannot be said that he has failed to get the award registered as the law required. [122D E] 2:2 The Sub Registrar pursuant to order of High Court on 24.6.1985 found that the award in the Court was presented before the office pursuant to an order of court and this was manifest from the order in Misc. Furthermore, as noted before the award being made on 25.11.1983 the award could not be said to have been presented before 28th Feb., 1978 to the court subsequent to the expiry period of four weeks from 28.11 1977.

The appellant was the tenant of a sub tenant in respect of certain premises. The respondent gave notice to the appellant terminating his tenancy and asked him to vacate the premises on the ground that he had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub letting. The appellant refused to do so. The suit for ejectment was brought under section 13(1)(e) which provided that " notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in this Act, a tenant may sublet any portion of his premises to a subtenant provided he is forthwith intimates in writing to his landlord (i) that the tenant has since the coming into operation of this Act sub let the whole or part of the premises or assigned or transferred in any other manner his interest therein ; and (ii) that if the Court was satisfied (a) that there was a breach of the agreement, it would be lawful for the landlord to eject the tenant under section 14(1) (e); and (b) that he has waived his rights in regard thereto. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decree. Held, that the right of the respondent to sue for ejectment on the grounds of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 12(1). The right of eviction which flows directly from an infraction of a provision of the Act is a personal one and cannot be parted with or renounced by the landlord. In the present case, the question was not merely of waiver but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the contract which section 15 of the Contract Act declares to be illegal. The right to sue on the basis of sub letting being a statutory right for the benefit of one of the parties and which he may waive must be regarded as inserted in the interest of the public also In that case there was no provision made by the Legislature that disputes mentioned in the section of the , were to be determined by an Expert nominated by the Board of Trade and it was contended that section 13 (1)(a) had to be read separately and not in conjunction with section 15 Of the Act. Held further, that a statutory provision inserted in public interest cannot be said to have the same effect as a provision in an agreement which is for the protection of private rights enacted for the welfare of the tenants and which they may waive. The prohibition contained in section 13 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and of section 15 being a provision for the enforcement of the agreements would produce the (1) A.I.R. 1950 Bom. 871.

The respondent Board, a recognised institution, conducted the examinations and dealing with the use of unfair means at the final examination. The Divisional Board, after examining the evidence, found that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or parents or the guardians to their advantage. The Board, therefore, issued a notification dated August 31, 1990, directing that the examinees/parents/guardians should be allowed to appear at the S.S.C. examination in March, 1991 by the Board. The respondent Board challenged the said notification before the High Court and contended that the decision of the Divisional Board to which they were members and the decision was on behalf of the State Board, was on its behalf. The High Court rejected the contention of the Board that the findings reached by the authorities that the fabricated fabrication was made at the instance of either of the candidates or parents was based on records. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant Board: (1) that the finding of the authorities was based upon no evidence and the conclusions reached were based on facts, and therefore, they were not sitting Committees; (2) that in any event the findings arrived at by the authority that the forgery was done was based solely on the basis of admission made by the examinee. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conclusion reached by a Divisional Board that fabrication ofrieved candidates ' mark sheets was done after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the state board at Bombay and before the moderators ' mark sheet were taken out to Pune to feed the computer is supported from the record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [799C D] 1.2 The conclusion arrived at in the present case was based entirely on the admission made to the respondent Board. Therefore, when the evidence justified the examination Standing Committee to record the finding that the forging was done in the behest or the parent or guardian is based on the evidence on record. The fabrication of the moderators "mark sheets" was done before the scrutiny of the concerned officers in the Office of the District Board at Bombay, and before tile wherefor contacted the respondent No. 1, it was incumbent upon the respondent to produce the original records relating to the fabrication of their mark sheets. [788E F] 1:3 The conclusion that the fabric was done by either the examinors or their parents or guardians is amply borne out from the Record. It depended on the type and gravity and seriousness of the offence to be charged. [789F G] 1 :4 In the instant case, the fabrication and fabrication of tile moderators 'mark sheets was undertaken after the examination by the officials in their office at Bombay. The foundation of the wherefor 'mark sheet ' was done without the scrutiny and scrutiny by concerned officials. It is, therefore clear that the conclusion reached was based mainly on the admissions made by respondents. Ltd.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 to be committed by Madan Lal one of the prosecution witnesses. The trial court acquitted all the accused but convicted them on the ground that they had not been able to account satisfactorily their pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the offence as defined in section 5 of the Act did not come with within the meaning of bribery as defined by section 21 of the . The object of the section was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it could come into play only when there was no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. The offence as described in cl. (d)(i) did not fall within the mischief of section 5. The object was to make a person liable for criminal misconduct under section 161 of the Code. The words "any other person on his behalf" in section 21 were wide enough to include persons who had been found guilty of criminal conspiracy and to commit criminal misconduct. The charge of criminal offence under section 165A of the Penal Code did not therefore fail within the scope of that section. Gian Chand vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to. The appellants were rightly convicted by the trial court on the basis of the evidence adduced in the case. The conviction was based on the testimony of Labhu Ram that Gian Chand came along with the appellants to him when the talk about the bribe took place.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,36804 P. from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor Harilal Parmanaddas Adatia and his surety original defendant 2 Chitranjan Rangnath Raja. The surety endorsed in favour of the Bank, Ext. 81, and another by the principal debtor in favour thereof, all on September 16, 1957, constituted one composite transaction and they evidence that the principal creditor had offered two securities, one the pledge of oil tins and another personal guarantee of the surety. The appellant bank filed an application for restitution of the security amount. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the bank with regard to the safe custody of the pledged oil ties but as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge, of goods given by the creditor in favour and also the bond executed by the Principal debtor in his favour, all On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal amount and that as in this case the entire security was lost, the surety was wholly discharged. Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the creditor having lost one security, namely, the pledged goods, the bail would not be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of guarantee. [922D] 2.1 In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the debtor had taken more than one security from the principal borrower at the time when the contract was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the latter, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the sureties parts with the security, the sureties is discharged to the extent of the value of thesecurity. [936E] 2:2 In order that section 141 would be attracted and an application under restitution will have to be made to the Court of first instance, i.e., the Court Of first instance i. the Court where the suit in favour was decreed by the trial court, i .the Court of second instance and this decree has been reversed by the High court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction. [948E F] 2 :3 The surety is entitled to restitution. The present one is the simplest case where the plaintiff Bank lost onesecurity on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the clear understanding that the Principal creditor had offer security by way of pledge of goods and the goods were to be in the custody of creditor Bank. In any event, if it is held proved that security of pledged goods was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor bank, yet the surety would not he discharged from his obligation undertaken tinder the letter Of guarantee. It is difficult to entertain a contention that section 142 would not apply and the sureties would not discharge even if it was found that a creditor has taken more or one security on the ground that a debtor had offered another security. [947G H] 2(a) The surety himself agreed to give personal guarantee in the specific understanding and with the full knowledge of the Court that the main debtor was offering another security, viz., pledge of certain goods and that the goods are to be kept under the lock and key of the respondent Bank. The bail bond executed on September 15, 1957 by the appellant bank was therefore a valid document. [946C D] 2 (b) The High court was right. It held that in view of combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, the guarantor was discharged to that extent of value of security and that he would not therefore be discharged even if the surety is discharged from its obligation undertaken by the letter OF guarantee.

The appellant was the son of a member of the family. The patelki inam lands were divided and the lands in suit were allotted to the share of the appellant. As a result of these enquiries it was held that the appellant was not entitled to hold the "patelki Inam" lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family. On this part of the case the Government excluded the " patelka inam " lands from the resumption proceedings relating to the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir. The appellant 's suit for possession was dismissed by the trial court but in second appeal the High Court held that (1) the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume and regrant the lands. Held, that the grant made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag was not a service grant and no question of title by adverse possession arises against Government even though the lands are shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866. Amrit worked as patel till he died in 1920, and even though he got possession by partition in 1923 it was not open to Government to resume the same. The grant was not made by way Of remuneration or wages for services rendered by a member or members of the joint family burdened with service and so long as the service is performed by any member of family, the lands arc joint family properties subject to partition etc. among the members of family.

The appellant was a Cutchi Memon, and belonged to the same family as the other persons who had been made insolvents. He filed an application under section 64(1) of the , claiming that he was entitled to succeed to the estate of his father in view of the provisions of the . The trial court held that the appellant 's claim was barred by limitation and dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that as there was only one solitary decision of the High 'Court of Madras which limited the application of Hindu law to matters of succession and inheritance, the Bombay view was the correct one. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the rule of Hindu Law applicable to Cutchi memons governed matters of inheritance only; (2) the rules of Hindu laws were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi, Memon and therefore when a Cutch Memon widow dies issueless her property would be governed by the Hindu law as to stridhan. HELD : (i) The rule of succession applicable to Rattingchi Memons is not inconsistent with Hindu Law but is consistent with Hindu law. [234 E] (ii) In the matter of inheritance, it would appear from the fact that barring one or two stray deci sions, the general trend of judicial opinion in Bombay was that both the Khoias and the Cutchi were subject by custom to Hindu law of succession, and succession, including rules as to joint family property. The Act came into force as from November 1, provided that all Cutchi Moons shall in matters of devolution and inheritance be governed under the Mahomedan law. Therefore when a cutch Memons had been settled down and where they had lived in Hindu Kingdoms with Hindu surroundings and traditions, there was nothing surprising that they retained the rules Of Hindu Law in general not only in matters relating to succession but also in matters other than succession and succession. [235 E H] (iii) The High Court 's view that the accountable persons having been born lone before 1948 had already acquired a right by birth in the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the Act.

The appellants are manufacturers of cotton yarn. The fabrics were obtained at an intermediate stage and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to payment of excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the retrospective effect given by section S I of the Finance Act, 1982. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the retrospective operation given by Section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act ') and that the yarn which is produced at an intermediary stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected thereto to the integral process of manufacture of another commodity, is liable to pay excise duty. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Collector had to specify the place of manufacture and also any premises appurtenant thereto, and therefore, the provision of deemed removal with regard to the commodity produced at intermediate stage, and consumed or utilised in the continuous process of manufacturing the end product, is inapplicable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Explanation to rule 9 and rule 49 contemplate the collection of duty levied on the production of a commodity at an earlier stage of an integrated process. It does not, in any manner indicate that it is only when the goods are removed from the factory premises it will be removal and when the excisable goods manufactured within the factory is removed from one plant to another it will not be a case of removal. [707C] 2. The definition of 'place of removal ' in Rule 9 and Rule 49 do not contain any definition of "place of manufacture or production of the excisable Goods". In the instant case, the appellants are liable to excise duty on the yarn after it is sized for the purpose of weaving it into fabrics. [700D] 3. The explanation to rule9 and rule49 contemplate the recovery of duty paid on the raw material used in the manufacture of a product at an end stage of the integrated activity of manufacture. It is not required to be made of the place where the goods were produced, cured or manufactured but any premises ancillary thereto. [607E] 4. The specification that has to be given by the Collector is of any premises adjacent to the place or premises appurtenant to such place in that case, it will also be a question of removal for the purposes of payment of duty. [625F G] 5. The Explanations to rule 49 and rule 50 contemplate collection of excise duties levied on production of an commodity at intermediate stages to be removal from such place or Premises of manufacture.[607C D] 6. Under the definition "place" may be a factory or any other place or places of production or manufacture of the dutiable goods etc. The Note to Rule 9 does not contain anything about the kind of manufacture, but provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or at an inter state stage and consumed/ utilised for the manufacture thereof. [650E] 7. The exclusion of the Explanation to Rule 49 and Rule 50 is not applicable because the commodity which is obtained at a intermediate stage of manufacture in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such factory premises, it would be removal, but rule 9 does, in no manner indicate the place for manufacture or Production of the finished product.

The petitioner filed a suit for an injunction restraining the Hearing Authority appointed under section 68 D of the (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act ') from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme. The Civil Judge, Bulandshahr allowed the application holding that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. In revision, the Additional District Judge held that the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit as the jurisdiction was impliedly bar and that the Civil Courts had no power to issue an order of injunction restraining it from proceeding further with the trial of the suit till disposal of a special leave petition before this Court since the question relating to the maintainability of suits of similar nature involved in the said special leave petitions was involved in that special leave Petition. The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for staying the hearing of the case till the disposal of the special leave peti tion and for stay of the trial till the pendency of a Special Leave Petition before this court since the questions relating to maintainability of suit of similar type were involved in this special leave writ petition. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a State Government (the hearing Authority under section68 D of tho Act) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue any order of interim injunction restraining a Hearing Authority from proceeding With the hearing or final disposal of an appeal under section 69 D of that Act. [545C] 2. The power of the State Government under section 66 D of U.P. Act, 1950 is exclusive and in character. It is not disputed that the scheme had been duly published under section 67 C of the Act by an authority which had the power to publish it and that it was for the Hearing Authorities to consider such objections and representations and to pass appropriate orders thereon. The rules also provide for the particulars to be incorporated in the scheme published under Section 68 C of tho U. P. Act. From the above provisions it is clear that on the publication of the scheme under section 1968 C of Act any person who is aggrieved by the proposed introduction of the Scheme is entitled to file his representations and objections and to appear before the Hearing authority under section 64 D of Act and make his submissions in support of his objections or representations. [544C E] 3. The civil court was right in declining to stay further proceedings in the suit. This is a suit which should have been rejected at the threshold under order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that it did not disclose a cause of action. [543D] 4. Section 68 D empowers the State Transport Undertaking to prepare a scheme giving particulars of the nature of service proposed to be rendered, the area or route proposed to he covered by the scheme lies, may within thirty days from the date of its publication in the official Gazette file objections to it before the State Govt. [542E] 5. The procedure laid down for the preparation of the schemes is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D. Section 69 D empowers a State Transport undertaking to prepare and approve a scheme either with or without modification. When the scheme is approved or modified under section 71 D of Chapter IVA of the U. Pradesh Act, the transport authorities concerned can issue permits only in accordance with the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IV A of the . [542F] 6. The right to file objections and appeals against the orders of the High Court is a creature of statute. It has been conferred on the State by section 68D of the , which authorises the State Road Transport Undertaking (the Hearing Authority) to prepare or approve a Scheme either with modifications or not.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on August 29, 1963 at about 9.30 p.m. the appellant went to the house of his sister 's husband in police uniform and accused Russel Niel and his wife expressed their reluctance to send Miss Eylene with him to the police station and therefore the appellant asked Russel to pay something to him. The appellant then compelled Russel L.R. Wadeen, a Police Officer to make arrangement for the bringing up of the child. On being questioned the appellant told the D.S.P. that he never asked for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 161, Indian Penal code and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 4(1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act. The High Court maintained the conviction of the appellant on each count. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal Act or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel Khennaniel and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal, it cannot be said that the appellant has obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act, or for showing or forbir ing to show, in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The order of sanction in the present case fulfils the requirements of section 6 of the Act. [755 E] (2) The appellant grossly abused his position as a police officer and extorted money from him. He proved facts that there was a gross abuse of his office as a Police officer and that he had obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section is established. [700 G] (3) The conviction of appellant under s 5(1) (d) is not excessive. For the reasons expressed we affirm the judgment of the High Court.

The appellant was a railway employee. He was prosecuted under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for showing favour towers in respect of the claim cases filed against him. The Special Judge rejected this contention and convicted him. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the sanction accorded was not a valid sanction and that it was not necessary to examine the witnesses who were examined before him. Held, that the sanctioning authority had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction granted was not valid in law. The sanction was not for the prosecution of the appellant but for the offence of criminal misconduct for the corrupt and illegal use of his official position to obtain pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, , applied. Gokul Chand Dwarkadash Morarikka vs King, A.I.R. 1943 Cal. 971 and Gokulchand Parshotam Lal Dhingra vs The Union of India, ; , referred to. Held further, that sanction accorded by the authority was not invalid in law as it did not disclose a valid sanctioning authority for the same. Gokul Chandra Bhusan Chatterjee vs The State of West Bengal, A I. R. , distinguished.

The respondents were the tenants of a building in which the appellant was the holder of life interest. The tenancy under the landlord is admitted by the tenants there is also no question with regard to validity of the notice of eviction. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of the tenants. The High Court, however, allowed the revision petition filed by the respondents holding that the appellant had no right to evict the tenants on the ground of demolition and reconstruction. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) A dispute as regards the two different tenancies though in the same premises, one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purposes is outside the ken of this Act. Even a possible dispute, imaginary or real, between the landlord and the remainder man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the landlord against his tenants under the provisions of the Act. Such questions as are raised in this appeal by the tenant are, therefore, irrelevant in a litigation between the landlords and tenants when a suit for eviction is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the Act.[275 H] M/s Raval and Co. vs K. Thus, a controversy that may arise between a landlord and others who are not his tenants tinder the Act, is outside this Act and cannot affect adjudicated of the claims of the 'landlord against his tenant under the Rent Control Act. [275 C D] (2) The Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of the rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/S Raval & Co.v. K. B. Desai, ; M/O. Raval and Company vs K B. Natesan, , referred to.

The respondent decree holder filed a execution application in the executing court for recovery of certain trees, which were included in 34 grove land. The executing court held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(a) (i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950, the respondent 's right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary free from all encumbrances. The decree holder then filed an execution application before the executing Court for recovery. The Executing Court dismissed the execution application holding that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in the trees of "rove land" as defined under section 3(13) of Act read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. The High Court dismissed this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The definition of 'intermediary ' in section 3 (13) is wide enough to include grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such. [811B] (2) The contention that trees before they were cut form parts of "land" cannot be accepted. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the "land". Section 18(1)(a) of U. P. Zamindari Act provides that an "intermediaries 's grove" is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari rights.

The appellants were charged with an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The prosecution case was that on 9.3.1992 when the deceased along with his two sons, went to the house of one V, the accused No. 1, armed with chopper, and the other three with choppers, attacked him with choppas and sticks causing injuries to several persons including the deceased. On hearing the hue and cry of the deceased, the appellant No. 2, who was armed with a chopper and the others, rushed towards them and tried to run away. The deceased succumbed to his injuries on the spot. The accused Nos. 1 and 3 were charged for an offence under Section 326/149 IPC and convicted for an offences punishable under section 302 read with section 149 IPC. On appeal, the High Court acquitted all the six accused persons but convicted him for an other offence under section 325 IPC and awarded them a sentence of rigorous imprisonment. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An assembly of less than five members is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 and cannot, therefore, form the basis for conviction for an accused with the aid of section 149. [89F] 1.2 The intention to cause death of a person so as to hold him guilty of an offence of murder under Section 300 IPC since the injuries inflicted by him were not found to be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. [90G] 1:3 In the instant case, none of the accused persons individually had been charged for the substantive offence of murders punishable under Sections 302/149 I.P.C. even the trial court, which tried the six appellants was not justified in recording a conviction against him for the procedural offence of killing the deceased and convicting him for other offences with the help of Section 149 IPC also. [91H; 92A] 1 :4 The intention of causing death of the person so charged as to holding him guilty under section 326/34 I. P.C., could not be attributed to him and the medical evidence also shows that the injuries caused were cumulatively sufficient to cause the death of his person. From the ocular evidence read with the medical evidences, it stands established that the injury on the deceased had been caused by all the four appellants and that the death had occurred due to multiple injuries which were found sufficient in ordinary course to cause such death. The intention was to cause murder of the said person so that he can certainly be cloathed with the liability of causing culpable homicide not amounting to murder. [92B C] 1;5 In view of the sentences recorded for offence under Sections 304 Part I against the first appellant Subran, Section 325 IPC against appellants 2 and 3, Rajan and Preman, for an incident under section 307/149, I.L.R. [93A B] 1,6 Subran had not been charged with the substantive offences of murder punishable under sections 302/34 IPC even the Trial Court, which trying the six persons was not unjustified in recording conviction against them for the said offence after framing a charge against him. The High Court, therefore rightly convicted each of the two appellants for an alleged offence under [Section 326/ 149] I.

The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1969 70. The assessee company had credited to the assessee in its accounts for the relevant accounting years (accounting year for the Indian Company) a sum of Rs. 1,10,000/ representing royalty received by it from the Indian company. In the returns relating to the assessment year 1967 68 and 1968 69, it stated that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax was payable by it. The Income Tax Officer rejected the assessee 's contention and assessed the assessee company for the said three assessment years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal to the Tribunal, it took the stand that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assess year 196768 and 196869, it has been maintaining accounts on Cash basis and hence since it does rot actually received any income from all these three years, there is no receipt until it was received by the assessee firm in U.K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own books at Coventry. The High Court answered the reference against the Revenue. Hence these appeals by the asses see. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the circumstances of the case, the method of accounting adopted by the assesses for the various accounting years is really irrelevant. [106E] 1.2 In the instant case, it must be held that in the circumstances, the mode of accounting adopt by the Income tax Officer for the respective accounting years was really irrelevant and that Section 5(2)(b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts or mercantile basis. [107F] 1:3 The method of account adopted by assessee for the purposes of assessment year 1968 69 is really relevant. In this view of the matter, it cannot be said that the assessee has received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U .K. In these circumstances, it is immaterial whether it maintained its accounts with respect thereto. [108G] 1 :4 The High court was right in holding that the royalty amounts should be assessed to Income tax only on its actual receipt under Section 5 (2)(a) of the Act on the ground that it maintains their accounts on mercantile basis and does not amount to receipt of income by the assessees. [109H; 109A] 1 .5 The method adopted by an assessee is really immaterial. In other words, it can be said to have received the amount only if it receives it in UK. [110B] 1 6.1 It must be presumed that the entries relating to royalty amount are correct and that they are correct. [111C] 2.2 The method for accounting adopted is really decisive. In order to determine whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between Section 5 and Section 145 of the Indian Income Tax Act, it should be shown that the method adopted is binding upon the department; on that basis it was argued that if the assessee is proved to have maintained its account with respect lo royalty amount on cash receipt basis, then there isno receipt until the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. He appealed to the High Court which confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. The High Court, however, reduced the punishment to one already undergone. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there should be corroboration of the approver in material particulars and qua each accused. Held: (i) The statement of the appellant is no corroboration of his accomplice 's story because the knife was got prepared by him by accused No. 1, and the time gap between the preparation of the knife and murder is great and it is possible in such circumstances that the appellant might have cemented and not proceeded with the commission of the offence. The fact that the knife had been got prepared from accused No, 1 does not affect his case because under that section a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice may not be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes (1) as follows "There is Do doubt that the uncoroborated evidence of an approver is admissible in law (R. v Attwood; , But it has been Ion(,, a rule of practice at common law for the judge to warn the jury of the danger of convicting a prisoner on the scribing him on the unceremned testimony of a accomplice, and in the discre tion of the Judge, to advise them not to convict upon such evidence, but the judge should point out to the jury that it is within their legal province to convict on such unconfirmed evidence (R v Stubbs, Dears 556 In re Heunier, ; , referred to. (ii) The rule of law in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King (I) as well as R. vs Baskerville (I), is not applicable to the present case because there was no corroboration by the approver 's evidence and it was not sufficient that there was evidence to corroborate the participation of the first accused in the murder.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on or about December 11, 1962 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the argument was put forward that upon the findings recorded by the High court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. The trial Magistrate acquitted the accused and convicted him under section 161, Indian Penal code. On appeal to the Sessions Judge, the High, Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1 ) the words "public servants" in el. (12) of section 21 were wide enough to include officers who were appointed to some office for the performance of certain public duties; (2) the word "public" in cl. (13) of article 311 of the Constitution was not used in the sense in which it was used in that clause and therefore the appellant was a "person" within section 5, (1), (2), Prevention of corruption Act, and (3) the prosecution was barred by limitation. HELD: (i) The appellant could be deemed to be a public servant within the definition of section 2(12) because he had not been acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of that Act. [690 B] (ii) The words "any other law" in cls. (a), (b) and (c) of el. 12 of section21, are wide enough in their amplitude and they cannot be limited only to officers who are appointed to certain office for performance of some public duty. [681 E F] State of Maharashtra vs Jagatsing Charansingh, ; , followed. (iii) The word "person ' used in cl.(12) is wide enough not to include a person who was appointed to any office for that office but also to persons who were employed as a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops and were working under the Works Manager who was an officer of the Government and the duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to those of the Works manager who was the lead of the office. [683 G H] (iv) The expression "public officer" in section 21, cl. 12 is wide and includes officers who have been appointed to that office for performing some public duties. [684 B] State vs Jagarsing Charlesingh, A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 971, followed.

The appellant was convicted for contravening the provisions of section 3(1) of the Maharashtra Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1962. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) of Defence of India Rules, 1962 is ultra vires the Defence of india Act because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: The High court having set aside tho conviction and sentenced in respect Of contravention of el. 3, it was illegal to maintain the order regarding forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appellant because, he says, the Maharashtra Jowar (Restrictions on Purchase) Order, 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order 1965, did not contain any provision authorising the Court to forfeit the juari. [273 D] The fact that the rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the Defence Of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act". The fact, that the Rule is contrary ly to an earlier act does no matter because s. 43 of Defence Of india Rules provides that if in the course of any judicial proceedings a question arises whether a person was duly informed of an order made in pursuance of these rules, compliance with sub rule (1 ), or where the order was notified, the notification of the Order shall be conclusive proof that he was so informed.

The appellant and the deceased were tried by the Additional District Magistrate, who convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the evidence of the eye witnesses showed that the appellant fired a shot from his gun as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down and died within half an hour, and (2) the High Court ought not to have interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PW 3 is not sufficient to sustain the conviction of the accused. [10E] 2. The fact that the deceased was a colleague of the deceased and his companions could themselves have detected the presence of Kunwar Singh more easily and with lesser ado. The circumstance that Shri Ram had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified, in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour. [11F] 3. The circumstances that Shri 's men were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [12G] 4. The mere fact that he had a standing of but 2 years in the District when he is supposed to have appeared for the complainant in the particular case, would not make any difference. It is unrealistic to assume that he was so flooded with work that he could remember no details of an important murder trial. [13G] 5. The question whether the only inference which arises from the fact that violet gave the particular shout is that by so doing, she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar singh. [14H; 15A] 6. The court which acquitted Shri Ram was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held, That is not the only point in favour of Shri Ram. [15B C] 7. The Court which acquitted the appellant was justifiably justified by his evidence.

The appellant was charged under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for committing murder of his wife in furtherance of their common intention. The prosecution case was that on the day of occurrence, the deceased and four others were murdered by some people. The trial court acquitted accused 1, 3 and 4 but convicted accused 2 under section 304 Part I of the Penal Code. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD : (i) It is well settled that in a case where two or more persons are charged under sections 302 read together with section 149 and section 147 of the said Code, it should come to a definite conclusion that the said person had a prior concert with one or more other persons named or unnamed for committing the offence. [682 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the evidence did not establish that the accused were guilty of murder under section 300 read with s 34, of the Code. [683 E F] (iii) It was well settled by a long line of decisions of this Court that where two persons are acquitted either on the ground that the prosecution witnesses named only the said accused and unnamed, they acted conjointly along with one of the accused charged. The effect of acquittal of accused 1 3, and 4 is that they did not conjointly act with accused 2 in committing the murder. Realizing this mutually destructive findings of the High Court, learned counsel for the State attempted to sustain the findings of fact by persuading us to hold that if the said finding was read in the context of the whole judgment, it would be clear that the learned judges meant to hold otherwise, they did conjointly acts with accused 1 in committing murder.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of Metalic metal Indus tries, was granted licence for import of certain goods. The licensing authority issued import licence No. 2959845 for Rs.20, 12729 in favour of M/s Metalic Metal Indus tried. The petitioner filed an application under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April,1988 this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective sheets/coils" which have arrived at Bombay Port per S.S. It is contended on behalf of the respondents that for the payment of duty, the liability of the petitioner to pay the duty is the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 32 guarantees the right to a constitutional remedy and relates only to the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 111 of the Constitu tion. Unless a question of the enforcement or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any recourse to the provisions of the Act, it does not automatically involve breach of fundamental right for the enforcement Of which alone Article 32 is attracted. Article 226 does not apply. There can be no question of enforcement of a fundamental fight if the order challenged is a valid and legal order, in spite of the allegation that it is appreci ously suited to any particular question of law without taking recourse to any provisions of tho Act, It does not necessarily involve breach or infringement of fundamental rights for the protection of which alone article 32 of The Constitution is attracted [626D E] 2. Article 31 guarantees the rights to a legal remedy and relate only to enforcement of those rights conferred under Part 111. Unless such a question arises, article 32 does not application. There cannot be any question of enforcing the fundamental right if the Order challenged is valid and pub lished legal order in spite Of the allegation of that it was apprecia ous. [627E F] 3. Article 33 guarantees the Right to a statutory remedy and pertains only to its enforcement. Unless the question of infringement of a constitutional right arises, Article 32 does no apply. [625B C] 4. The relief under Article 226 is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. It has further to be reiterated that for enforce ment of fundamental fight which is dependent upon adjudica tion or determination Of questions of fact as well without taking resort to the provi sions of the statute, it is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of the fundamental rights. [ 625C D] 5. Article 30 guarantees the fundamental freedom to a person who has been granted licence in accordance with the provisions contained in Part 111 and provides for an appeal against the order of the licensing authority. The right to obtain possession of goods from the warehouse is dependent on the interpretation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of tile Act would breach fundamental right which entitle a citizen to seek recourse to Article 32. [ 626D E; 626A] 6. The petition is not maintainable. [643E F].

The appellants were the sons of one V. V. N. Nani who was a managing director of a company and had been receiving a monthly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore the sale in execution of the payment order could not be challenged as the sons were under pious obligation under the Hindu Law to discharge the debts of their father. The appellants contended that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the share of the sons did not pass to the auction purchaser; that the sale could only be challenged on proof of the debt of defendant No. 1 which were characterised as misfeasance " and that the suit for possession by partition was barred by limitation under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, because it was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of defendant Nos. 2 4 and 5; Held, that the liability of the appellants to discharge debts of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the son which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the mother and which does not come to an end as a result of partition of the joint family property. The liability of a father, who is a managing agent and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a consequence of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avy avarika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals".

The petitioners who were seven in number challenged the constitutional validity of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, and a notification issued under R. 8(i) of the Act by which the tax was imposed on passengers and goods transported by road or inland waterways to their respective States. The contention of the petitioners was that the Act in the guise of taxing passengers and Goods, taxes really the income of the petitioner, or at any rate, fares and freights, and is thus unconstitutional. Held, that the tax levied under R 8(1) of Act is a tax on passengers but it does not cease to be a tax merely because the amount of fare or freight charged is measured by the fares and fares and charges. The tax is still on passengers, and goods, though what it is to be is determined by the amount Of fare or fares or freights. The Act and the Rules must be read harmoniously and reading them so that it is plain that the apparent mandatory language of the Rules and the notification still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount must be, if lump sum payment is made in lieu of payment of the tax calculated on actual fares and/or freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory even though the journey starts. The words "in respect of all passengers carried and goods" are not used in the Act as meaning "in connection with any passenger or goods transported". The word "tax" is not defined in the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act but it is a taxing statute. It is the cost of construction and maintenance which makes the difference in the tax, and no case of discrimination can be said to be made out.

The appellant was retrenched from service by the respondent management on the ground that they had not been paid retrenchment compensation. The Labour Court directed reinstatement of the workmen with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to them as back wages. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The award is modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the amount paid to them and pay able. [567B] 1.2 In appropriate cases the Court may, in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry direct scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. [568C] 1:3 The question in controversy which fairly often is raised in this Court is whether even where reinstatement is found to be an appro priate relief, what should be the guiding considerations for awarding full or partial back wages is the guiding factors for awarding compensation to the extent of full wages or a Part of it ? [568D] 1 :4 The question is whether the Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back wage. It is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. [569D] In appropriate case, the Court might, in its spirit of Labour and management having being partners, direct scaling up of back wage with some sacrific on management part too, and it may well be that in appropriate cases, the court may, if in the course of labour or management being partner in the Industry direct scaling over of back Wages with some erosion on management. [570E] 1;5 The question whether the workmen who were retrenched were entitled to the relief of reinstatement effective from the day on which A they were sought to be retried is no longer open to challenge. It confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia, against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. Though Article 136 is couched in widest terms, it is necessary for this Court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where Awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman) (1) The question In controversy which is fairly often raised in the Supreme court is whether, even where reinstate is found not to be bona fide and that the workman continued to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to he raised(l. Pai, learned counsel for the appellant in his attempt to persuade us to give something less than full back Wages, attempted to re open the controversy concluded by the order of this court while granting limited leave that the retrenchment was inevitable in view of the mounting losses and falling production for want OF raw material and persistent power shedding.

The prosecution case was that the accused and his wife were married to Churi deceased near about 1958. At the suggestion of Nagju, Churi, Joginder and Nagju came to the house of the accused in village Shilaroo which is at a distance of 1 1/2 mile from Gani. The accused stated that he was with Churi in the house during the day but at 6 p.m. he left for Kotkhai leaving his wife alone at the house. He also made the following statement "I had cordial relations with my wife for the fast 14 years. According to the prosecution case, the injuries found on the body of Churi were caused by the accused. The confession was recorded during investigation and as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the same is inadmissible in evidence. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing the murder of his wife Churl (26) and sentenced him to death. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the statement recorded during the investigation of a case by a second class magistrate not specially empowered was admissible in evidence; (2) the accused having been born to her as a result of adulterous conduct, the confession could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD : (i) The statement recorded by the Magistrate and signed by the witnesses is inadmissible under section 164 Cr. P.C. [14 F] (ii) It was the accused who and none else who was responsible for the murder, of Chur luri deceased as a consequence of which she died. The fact that the relations of the parties with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. [15 F] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Singhara Singh and Others ; , followed. (iii) It is not correct to say that the statement was recorded by a Magistrate under section 161 Cr. The statements recorded during such investigation are admissible under sections 73 and 74 of the Evidence Act and can be used in evidence against an accused person. [16 G] State Of Uttar Pradesh v Singhara singh and Others, ; , referred to. (iv) It would be unsafe to rely on the statement made by the witness before the Magistrate under sections 164 Cr P. C., for the purpose of corroboration of his testimony. The statement was not admissible in law because it was recorded after the accused had visited the house or the deceased and the fact that he alone was with the Churi did not make any difference to his innocence. [17 G H] (v) It could not therefore be said that the confession was inadmissible under sections 77 and 74 Cr. A. No. 10 of 1970.

The appellants were appointed as Asstt. Engineers (Civil) and (Mech.) for the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment by Selection) Rules 1973. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [494C] 1.2 The selections are made according to the rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation with the dictum laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., J.T. [1988] Sup. S.C R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, J. T. Devaramier & Ors , J.J. Merchant & Ors vs State & Ors ; , Jt. Director, Public Works De partment & Anr. vs M/s. B.S .N. Sinha & Ors [1988], Sup. C.A. No. 2101/1989 dated 24th May, 1990 and Mohinder Singh Gill & Anr vs State o. Haryana & Anr., J .T.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on 11th April, 1983, the Collector 's car was parked in the verandah of the Collectorate and after he finished his work, both the accused persons had supplied the bomb to him. On the same day, the police recovered a bomb from the house of the deceased. The deceased was taken into custody following the raid on the Ashram. The police arrested the appellants and sent them to Gopalganj Police Station. The investigation revealed that the deceased was a Member of the Bihar Administrative Service and was posted as Collec tor and District Magistrate in the State of Bihar on 11.4.1983. On 11th July, 1982, the Superintendent of Police, who was attracted to the scene by the sound of the bomb burst recorded the first information given by P.W.62, arrested Yadav and sent him to Gopalpur Police Station, which was followed by a raid on that Ashram. On 12th July 1983, at about 9 p.m., the police seized the bombs from the place of occurrence. The accused persons were put up for trial before the Sessions Judge, Gopalganj who convicted them under section 120B read with Section 120 B and sentenced each to death under section 201 read with s.120 B of IPC. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed on the appellants. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. In the case involving the killing of the District Magistrate, in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law.
