[437C D] 1.2 The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [414E F] 1:3 In the instant case, the prosecution has relied upon the confession but later conceded that apart from what the High court has observed with regard to the confession, it appeared to be exculpatory in nature and, therefore, would not be admissible against the co accused. The conviction of the appellants is not sustainable. [416F G] 1 :4 In a case involving murder of the State Government in hisoffice, better investigations were expected and, the State must have taken considerable care to ensuring that every tallhole was plugted at the right time in accordance with law.[414G H] Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State ofBihar, ; , followed.

The appellants were employed as clerical and subordinate staff in the respondent 's concern. The dispute between them related to the fixation of wages and dearness allowance, and the Tribunal held that the appellants were entitled to the minimum wage scale applicable to the employees of the respondent company. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and Dearness Allowance and had made comparison with concerns which are not comparable, and that the tribunal should have taken into account comparable concerns in the same industry and provided wage scales on the same lines so that, far as manufacturing concerns in these appeals are concerned there will be equality in the matter of competition. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages or dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done; but considering that wage scales fixed are less than the highest in comparable concerns, it cannot be said that the total Wage packet fixed is abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total wages packet in other comparable concerns. [375 C] (ii) The principle of 'equal pay for equal work ' has been evolved by this Court in several decisions and it has been consistently held that in applying industry cum unit formula for fixing wage scales the Tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the formula if there are a large number of concerns in that region carrying on the similar industry. [376 E] (iii) The dearness allowance is not a bounty but a payment made to an individual worker and it is a valuable consideration for the purpose of fixing his wages. It is a part of a social welfare legislation which has to be interpreted strictly. In the present case, the Tribunal has relied on a number of cases in which the maximum is higher than fifteen months wages. The Tribunal had not specifically consider what the minimum wages would be applicable to employees of comparable concerns and therefore it should not have adopted this pattern. [423 F G] (iv) The contention that the principle of "equal pay" has been introduced by the Central Government in 1957 cannot be accepted. It was a case where the company was already paying the highest wages in the particular line of business and therefore comparison had to be made with respect to the exemplars filed before it, but the way in which it had made compared for clerical and other subordinate staff.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, filed a suit against the respondents for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances. The trial court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddhappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that the plaintiffs were agriculturists, that they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. On appeal the District Court held that by the Raj inama, Shiddappappa 's share was concerned, the Rajnama was a complete relinquishment of his interest, but as regards Annappa 's half share in the mortgage property on payment of one half of the amount due under the two mortgages, it held that he could not bind Annaappa 'S share by the said Rajinamama and in this view of the matter he dismissed both the appeals. Held, that though an unregistered occupant may be in favour of more persons than one, the notice of relinquishment must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the registered occupant, or that the registered occupants has the right to give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest in the occupancy. The words "in whose favour an occupancy is relinquished" in section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as they stood prior to its amendment by Act XLV of 1948, indicate that relinquishment may be made in favour or against more persons but it does not mean, in the absence of any specific pleading and cogent proof, that a notice of transfer given by the registered owner must necessarily include a notice. The word "in" used in section 76(1) of the Act means "in his own name". In the present case, there were more occupants than one. The notice of relinquished on behalf or against any occupant was not a notice under section 74.

The respondent, a dealer in carbon paper, was assessed to sales tax at the point and at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The Sales Tax Officer did not accede to the conten tions of the respondent and holding that carbon paper re mained paper even after going through certain chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to the end of March 1967 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to levy of tax on carbon paper at 6%, and ribbonat ed at 10% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of aero plane nor diesel is a part o f the type writer though it may not be possible to type out any matter without it. [838 B] (2) The use of the word "paper" in the Notification makes it clear that Carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification. Just as aviation petrol is not a part or of a vehicle in the same way, ribbon is not an essen tial part of any type writer although it may be possible for type out some matter without there.

The appellant Mills was running a sugar mill at Amroha. It was not an express term of the contract of service between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant had the right to transfer them to any of its concerns in any place and the respondent, therefore, was entitled to be transferred from one concern to another of his in the circumstances of this case. The workmen were employed by the owners of the sugar mills at the Sugar Mills at Amroha and they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mill at Bulandshahr. It is also not suggested that even if the appellant bad such an intention, the respondents I to 4 had knowledge of the same. In the words of the Appellate Tribunal, the only connection between the two was in th identity of ownership and, but for it, one has nothing to do with the other. The question raised was one of law, namely, whether the appellant 's right to be so transferred must be deemed to be an implied condition of service. Held, that the employer in the present case had no such right. The employer in this case had not such right and the question that arose was whether in the facts of each case the transfer from one branch to another was valid or amounted to victimization. The appellant Mills had no right to the transfer of an employee if he has the right of transfer to him under the contract Of service or under any statutory provisions. Held further, that it was not a condition of employment of the respondents either express or implied that the respondent had the inherent right to transferred them to a new concern stared by him subsequent to the date of their employment. The fact that the appellant Mills did not employ any person in the sugar mill did not prevent the employer to transfer an employee when he chooses to start (4) 923 the question raised as one of fact was a substantial question of law involved between the parties and that it could be well within the powers of the Labour Appellate Tribunal to entertain the appeal.

The appellant company was a public limited company carrying on business as manufacture and sale of goods. It had its factory at Ahmedabad in the State of Gujarat. The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the case of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provisions for certain other matters in relation thereto. Section 28 lists the purposes for which the Fund may be expended and it includes among other items, (i) payment of benefits and provision of medical treatment and attendance to insured persons and where the medical benefit is extended to their families. The provisions of Chapter V A were introduced by section 20 of Act 53 of 1951. The appellant company claimed that the contribution payable under Chapter VA was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The respondents contended that the payment of contribution directed to be made by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. Both Parliament and the Legislature of any State, subject to conditions with which we are not concerned, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List llI It is pursuant to the power entrusted in respect of entries 23 and 24 of List III that Parliament has enacted the . In understanding, entries 23 & 24 of list III, their own force, empower Parliament or the legislature of a State to direct the payment by an employer of contributions of the nature of those contemplated by the for the benefit of the employees. The cost of these benefits will` not be met from the general revenues of the state, but will be borne entirely from the aforesaid fund only. the employers ' contribution under the Act constitutes only a fee, and not a tax. The Government cannot go on levying employers ' contributions under section 28(4) of the Act with reference to the very benefit itself and its connection with the levy. Corporation(4), have upheld the levy of special contribution as a Tax. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant Company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The payment of special contributions directed to he made by an employee under the , or other allied payment or benefits under various other social welfare legislation must eitherbe labelled as tax or fee in Order to attain paternity or not and at all; both Parliament and State Legislature have power, therefore, to make law with respect respect to matters enumerated In List lllI. [1088C D] 2. The scheme of the Chapter V is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the cases of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the ease of employers, who straightaway receives the benefits under the scheme, Their rate of contributions is lower. [1188E F] 3. The Act does not contemplate rendering of services or the conferring of any benefits to the employees as conse quently for the grant of insurance schemes. When the whole Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. The employers ' liability under the provisions of section 28 is a tax and its levied is illegal as it does not involve the rendering or conferment of benefits to an employee as quid pra quo for payment. [1108G H] 4. The levy of Special contribution by the respondent company constitutes only one fee and not any tax. [109C D; 110A B] 5. The contribution under section 2(4)(IV) is a fee.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as regular workers. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there is no work for them; and as such, there isno question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a short time. The respondents are also running heavy losses during the last three years and it is not possible to absorb the petitioners immediately as regular workmen. In spite of this conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at the hearing before the High Court, the High court rejected the petitioners ' claim for and came to the following conclusion: "The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific job to do, they are surplus to the establish ment and merely kept on the roll on humanitarian ground. The Respondents are also operating in heavy losses due to the last 3 years and there being a vacancy available for them, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely on humanitarian reasons so far. Further facts have been stated in support of their contention. It has also been stated that a voluntary Retirement Scheme offering considerable amount to these daily rated workers has been framed, which is Annexure R VI to the counter affi davit. This document shows the amount of retrenchment com pensation and the ex gratia payment offered to the 63 daily rated employees under this scheme. The 54 petitioners are included therein. It was stated at the time of hearing before this Court that 9 out of these 63 daily wages mentioned in Annexure R IV have accepted this Scheme of voluntary retirement and respondent No 2 is prepared to give benefit of the same even to those who may not have agitated their claim. On the clear findings in this case, this is not the position. This petition must, therefore, fail.

The appellants purchased the property in execution of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The suit was brought by the appellants claiming title to and recovery of possession of a property known as the Azambad Tea Estate which comprised about 378 acres of land in Touzi No. Ltd. claim to have purchased the entire 16 as interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a mortgage decree obtained on that basis against Kazia Ismail, who was no party to the mortgage, and the sale thereunder passed to it no title except to the extent of 2 1/2 as share belonging to Mohd. No doubt, if this transaction were made out and was real, it would stand on the same footing as the 8 pies share in regard to which a decree was granted in favour of the plaintiffs by the judgment now under appeal. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed that decision. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the 8 annas share decreed to them by the High court. [213 E] (ii) The appellants ' contention that when a sale was effected and Pir Baksh who was examined as a witness admitted this fact, it could not be accepted as frivolous. It is common ground that if the transaction were true and intended to pass title to PirBaksh, the appellants would be enti tled in addition, to the eight pies share decreed by the trial Court, to a further 2 as 13 gondas share belonging lo PW 1, the mortgagee of the property.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under sections 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case against him was that on the day of occurrence, P.W. 1, who was a police officer, had gone to the village and when he reached the village he saw the appellant 's person in the company of another person in his hand. He also stated that he had seen the appellant going out from the village after taking him away. The Sessions Judge found that the evidence showed that P.Ws. 1 and 2 were not present at the time of occurrence and that they were not examined by the prosecution. On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) had not been complied with and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. Held, that the omission on the part of the police officers concerned or of the magistrate before whom the committal proceedings had fended, has caused prejudice to the accused in the interest of justice, and the irregularity is curable by reference to section 537 of the Code as no case of prejudice has been made out. The word "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 173 and sub section(3), of section 207A is not mandatory but only directory. The words "shall". in the amended section, are not mandatory and merely directory. It is not necessary that the accused should be given an opportunity to explain his case before the Magistrate who was holding his inquiries under section 207 A(3). The word 'shall" used both in section 173(1) and sub s.(3) of s.207A(4), is not directory but only mandatory, because an omission by a police Officer to fully comply with the provisions Of section 173, should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court of Session wholly ineffective. Gurbachan Singh vs The State of Punjab ([1952] S.C.R. 869), referred to.

The appellant Municipality issued a notice to the respondent Municipality under section 153A of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888 for the discharge of effluents in the area specified in the notice. The respondent Municipality filed objections and contended that the provisions of section 153 A were not violated as the respondent had failed to comply with the requisition within the fixed period. The Special Officer held that the appellant was guilty of a nuisance under section 3(3) of the Act and ordered the removal of the nuisance from the premises. On appeal, the Special Judge set aside the order of the Special Officer and directed the removal. The Municipality appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The scheme under section 154A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence of a " nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned. It is plain that before the appellant could be called upon to comply, with the direction of the respondent municipality involving several lakhs of rupees as expenditure the Special officer ought to have decided and report only as to whether a nuisance existed or not. The order of refusal to go into the question whether the nuisance in question exists was one which ought to be set aside. (ii)The appellant rightly contends that the provision of section 3 (3) is violative of article 19 of the Constitution because it would be reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right under article 19(1)(C) to prevent a nuisance which would affect the public health and fertility of the soil. The provisions of sections 153A and 153A do not offend article 19 or article 19. (iii)The order of dismissal passed by the Special Magistrate declining to go on into the questions whether the appellant had established a nuisance was one that ought to he set aside; and (iv)the direction as to manner in which the discharge should be made. The special officer ought not to have gone into the matter because the person to whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence or of the problem in question and is prepared to comply therewith without any objection. If the existence was assumed because that was a matter for the subjective opinion of the municipality, then it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire and report merely as to how the nuisance existed.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which were seized by the Railway Administration. The prosecution produced evidence to show that the articles were being actually used or were intended to be used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The trial court convicted him under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove that the goods belonged to any particular railway administration but only those which were used or intended to been used for such construction, operations or maintenance as in the case where they have become unserviceable or outmoded no person can be charged with an offence under section 2 of the Act. HELD: (i) The prosecution must first adduce evidence to establish that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. [189 G] (ii) In the case of goods which had not been put to use evidence would have to be led to establish the identity marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to he led to the effect that the said goods were being lawfully used by a railway administration and that the Railway articles were mixed with other goods in the bags. [188 C] (iii) The onus of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on goods or any some, _ peculiarity or of the articles not to he found in case of non Railway goods. In most cases the burden of proof is discharged on proof of the identifying mark on the articles or some , peculiarityof the goods Not to be established in cases where non railway property has been discarded or rejected for further use would have been outside the definition of railway Stores.

The appellants had leased out the demised premises to the respondent on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 1,000 per month. The action for ejectment was initiated by the respond ent on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing sub clause (vii), thus: "tenant" means (a) The person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and (b) In the event of death of such person as is referred to in sub clause(a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the Case of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally carrying on business with him in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The appellants ' mother died on September 30, 1966 leaving behind her widow and two daughters. On October 29, 1967 the respondent filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised shops in Jaipur. The defence was that the tenancy had been terminated by the appellants without notice to them and that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court decreed the suit but the first appellate court reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. In second appeal, the High Court held that the amendment Act did not apply to the facts of the case and did not have the effect of divesting their vested rights in the lease hold right in the tenancy held by the tenant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Amending Act does not apply in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. But the appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the leased premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to t he rights in favour of the respond ploy created under section 13(1) (a), to (k) and other provi sions of the Act. [9F] 2. The mere fact that in the Act no provision has been made with regard to the heirs of tenants in respect of commercial tenancies on the termination of the tenancy, as has been done in the ease of heirs of the tenants of residential premises, does not indicate that the legislature intended that the heirs Of the tenant will cease to enjoy the protection afforded to the tenant under the Rent Acts. [10G] 3. The amendment Act does no apply to a case where the tenant continues to remain in possession even after the termination o f the tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or Decree for possession specified in the statute is established. [11F] 4. The heirs of a contractual tenant even after determination of his contractual tenancy till a decree of eviction against him is passed, continue to have an estate or inter est in the tenanted premises and tenancy rights in respect thereof are heritable. Therefore, despite the termination by the tenancy the tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs are entitled to enjoy t he protection of the Rent Act. The widow succeeds to the inherited interest in tho lease hold rights in tho leased premises held by her son. [12G H] 5.

The appellant Board was a financier of the respondent company. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The employees also contended that the services of the workmen of their Board are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under tho Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. The Employees ' Provident Fund Tribunal held that all the workmen were entitled to the benefit of the Contributory Provident fund scheme and that there should have been no distinction in between the appellant Board 'S Contributory Provident Funds Scheme and the Scheme under the provisions of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the employees of the appellant company should have their same and identical benefits and therefore there could be no difference between the Boards ' Contributory Provident Scheme and that the scheme tinder the Employees ' Insurance Fund Act was applicable to all workmen other than those who were covered by it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The financial capacity of the employer is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the company. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [47C D] 2. The contribution to the provident fund reserve is a Statutory obligation and it is a specific proportion whereas, it is not open to any ordinary commercial concerns to credit an amount to a depreciation reserve.[48E F] 3. Payment towards provident fund and gratuity is expense to be met by an employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of payment of gratuity and Provident Fund does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden Of wage structure in the interest of social justice. Even so it was noticed that the stability of the industry as well as the fact that the onus of provident fund & gratuity did not result, in loss, to the employers that burden would have to he borne by them like the onus, of wage structure In the absence, of a specific detailed examination, the finances could not be properly considered. [48F G] 4. The contributions to the development reserve are a statutory obligations and is an definite proportion. It is open open to the ordinary commercial Concern to creditany amount to be the depreciation Reserve. These matters cannot also be properly determined in the presence of a proper examination of financial finances of a company. [49E F; 50A] 5.

The respondent wife filed a petition for maintenance against the appellant husband and his father. The Magistrate dismissed the application of the respondent for maintenance. Thereafter, the matter was taken up in revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the various authorities of the High Courts seem to have overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of Section 125 of the Code of 1973 under which a wife could refuse to reside with her deceased husband if there was a just reason for doing so. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decisions referred to above in the judgment taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are hereby overruled. [707G] 1.2 In the instant case, it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a husband is impotable and is unable to discharge his marital obligation, this would not be a proper ground for refusing to live With her husband when it seems to us that the ground of impotence which had been held by a number of authorities under the civil law to be a good ground not only for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. [ 705A] 1:3 The decisions in Arunachala Anandayammal vs Babu Lal Dixit, J. sounded a very pragmatic note on this aspect of the matter and in this connection pointed out the scope of the Amendment of 1949 observed thus: "The second proviso is a very different thing from holding that no evidence of cruelty can be admitted in a proceeding under the section to prove not indeed cruelty as a ground for separate maintenance, but the conduct and acts of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refusal to maintain the wife. [700C D] 1 :4 The Courts cannot compel the wife merely because she is implient and unable to perform his marital obligations, this will not be just ground as contemplated by the aforesaid proviso for the husband 's refusal to livewith her husband if the husband has contracted marriage with another wife or taken a mistress before the amendment made in Section 488. [807E] 1;5 In the present case, the conduct of the wife from which she Court may drawn the inference that where a wife refuses to live alongwith her husband, if the wife has contracted marriages with another woman or keeps a mistook this would be deemed to be just grounds within the meaning of the first proviso so as to make the refusal of the spouse to live separately justified and entitled to maintenance.

The plaintiff was the owner of a plot of land in village Rasala Lines, District Bhavnagar. The suit property was originally owned by the State of Saurashtra and later transferred to the Defence Ministry of Home Affairs. In 1949, the Government of India recognised the aforesaid Resolutions dated 19th January, 1948 and 29th February, 1948. The plaintiff 's case was that by virtue of these orders the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint had: vested in the defendant who entered into and remained in possession thereof till recently. The defendants were the Union of India and the State Government. The State of Gujarat contested the suit on the ground that by reason of these Orders the entire land including the suit lands had vested in it, there was nothing on record to show that the Municipality was formally handed over the land in question, that its right over the suit property had never recognised by the Union or the State and that the various documents filed in this case would go to show: that as early as July, 1950 these lands and other properties which were in occupation of the erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Department. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff had not shown possession of the suit building within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, the suit being barred by limitation. The High Court also held that since the plaintiff 'had not shown posses sion of the land within 12 year prior to March,1964 when the Suit was filed the suit had been also liable to be dismissed as barred by time. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the vesting that was contem plated in the Resolution 37 dated 19nd January,1948 and Resolution 77 dated 29th Febu ary, 1948 was not intended to be vesting in its full amplitude but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the lands. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that since there was no evidence to show actual possession with the plaintiff, it was necessary for the Court to give a finding on title of the plaintiff even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse posses tion. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Resolution No. 37 dated19th January 1948 by the Government recognised the said Resolutions dated ly 19th Janu arry, 1948, and 29st February,1948. [225F] 2.1 In the suit notice the plaintiff has also not claimed that they "en tered into and remain in possession" of the property as stated in the suit para 5. The resolution No. 36 dated l9th August 1965 by the state Government recognised this Resolution only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the title itself in the Municipality. [226B] 2:2 In the instant case, there is evidence to indicate that physical possession was with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with th e plaintiff as the title to the land is not vested in them. The finding of the High Court that possession of land was also not taken by the Municipali ty at any time. [227C] 2 :3 In this case, not only there is no evidence on record that physical possesion was with tho defendant but further there could be no legal possession without the plaintiff as it the title in the land was not vested therein.

The appellant was employed in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was performing the duty of a metal examiner known as Chaser in the railway Carriage Workshop. He was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence under section 161 I.P.C., read with section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, by the Judicial Commissioner, Ajmer, on the ground that he did not fall within the terms of the last portion of cl. (9) of section 21 of the Act and was therefore not an "officer" within the meaning of that term as used in section 21(9), Indian Penal code. The Judicial Commissioner held that the appellant was an officer within the definition of a public servant contained in section 2 of the Prevention of corruption Act, but on appeal by the State Government, the Judicial Com missioner granted certificate of fitness for appeal to the Judicial commissioner. Held, that the decision of the Judicial Commissioners of the Lahore High Court in Ahad Shah vs Emperor (I.L.R. , was correct and must be affirmed. The appellant was not an officer of the Government but was merely a labourer employed by the Government and was thus performing a public duty. He had been appointed to some office for the performance of some pulice duty. The fact that he was in service or pay of the government did not make him a public Servant within the expression "officer". The appellant, therefore, rightly convicted under section 165(2) Of the Indian Railways Act and as such a public officer within section 21 (9), I. P.C. was not entitled to be convicted of the offence under that section.

The Respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The Excise and Taxation Department of the State of Punjab, Patiala Division, in respect of which they had to pay a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ . A suit was filed by the Respondent against the Appellants for recovery of the said share of the Respondent in the said property. The appellants contended that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, inserted in the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 by a State amendment. The Respondent also filed 847 an appeal before the District Judge, Patiala being Civil Appeal No. 554 of 5.9.79 and the learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the said second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exempt from sale under Clause (cc) of proviso to Section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached, and accordingly issued a permanent injunction with regard to the portion in whose favour the Respondent was residing and dismissed the suit so far as it related to the portions of the property in which liquor shop is situated. In second appeal, the learned single Judge of High Court held that the part of the premises used for his residence was exempted from attachment under clause(ccc)(cc) and that the half share of Respondent in that property was exempt under Clause(cc)(ccc). The Letters Patent Appeal filed by them before this Court was also dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The words "such attachment or sale" in the proviso refer to the attachment and sales mentioned in sub section(1) thereof. [848C] 1.2 The words 'such attachment ' or sale ' in the aforesaid proviso refer only to the execution of the decrees of civil courts and declares what properties are liable to attachment and sold in execution of such a decree and the proviso thereto to sub Section (1), of section 60 sets out the properties which are not liable to such attachment or sales, and the said clause (c) provides as follows: "The expression 'such attach ' or ' sale ' refers to the attached property and 'the said property is liable to ' attachment and ' sale in execution ' of a decree. [884D E] 1:3 The words used in the opening words of sub section 2 of Section 59 are "shall not be liable to any attachment or auction sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto". The attachment levied on, and, the auction sale notified in respect thereof were also under the provisions of the Punjab Act. [874E] 1 :4 The words of the aforesaid 848 proviso are 'Provided that the following particulars shall not be exempt from such attachment, or sale, namely." The expression "such attach" refers to attachment & sale mentioned in subsection (1). On a plain reading of the section 60, it is clear that Section has no application to attachment, and sale in any proceedings other than execution of a decrees of Civil Courts. [877D] 1 5. The attachment imposed on, or the auction sales notified in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the said Act for recovery recovery of revenue due to the State. There is no provision in the Act which makes the provisions Of section 60 applicable to attachment or 'sale for recovery and sale of revenue under the aforesaid Act. The properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sale, in revenue recovery proceedings under that Act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said said Act.

The respondent, a displaced person, was assessed to duty under the Land Acquisition Act on the basis of his total income at Rs.1,000/ . The Special Deputy Collector in his award dated January 9, 1970 determined the compensation payable by the respondent for the lands acquired by him. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of assessment and remanded the case back to the Special Deputy Commissioner for fresh disposal on merits. In the meantime, the respondent filed a writ petition before the High court challenging the validity of the notice dated January 8, 1970 issued under section 61(a) of the Act on two grounds: (1) that the reassessment made pursuant to the impugned notice was illegal and unsustainable in law inasmuch as the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in the original assessment had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court, and the High 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on the wrong basis was liable to be set aside; (2) that for purposes of section 61 the land acquisition proceedings and Land References in the Civil Courts could not be regarded as part of the assessment record and he so called mistake discovered by reference to such other record was not a mistake apparent from the record and as such the impugned notification was liable tO be quashed. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the notice issued under s.61(a), which was issued on a wrong basis and with the aforesaid objective and the subsequent reassessment made in pursuance thereof would be clearly illegal and void inasmuch as it had been issued on the erroneous assumption that the acquired lands still formed part of his estate, that the valuation for those lands adopted on the earlier occasion which was on the footing that the value for those land adopted on earlier occasion was on a basis different footing than that of the respondent. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the notice was dismissed by the High COurt holding that it had not been issued in accordance with law and that the impugned notices were liable to quashed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts ' decision upholding issuance of a notice under section61(A) would be wholly unsustainable inasmuch as there was no mistake apparent on the record which could have been discovered by referring to such relevant record and that in any event the impugned order was liable lO set aside. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the respondent having merely accepted the value of the acquired land as determined by the Special Assistant Collector in its award and the accountable person had no objection to this course and, therefore, the notice under s 61(A), which would otherwise be applicable to a notice issued on wrong basis, was liable 'to be quashed; (3) that in the reassessment which was made pursuant thereto, the quantum of extra compensation decreed by the civil court was included in the principal value of his Estate by undertaking the rectification proceedings and brought to duty. It was further submitted that since in the instant case the wards made by the special Deputy Collector were not accepted by the heirs of the deceased and Land references were sought by them and the same were pending in Civil Court at the relevant date (being the date of death), the notice could not have been issued under Section 61(1) with a view to get over the bar of limitation under section 73A, which would be otherwise applicable to such a notice. On the other hand it was urged on behalf respondent that the decision in P.V. Ramanan Chettiar vs The State of Madras and Anr., ; , relied upon by the appellant had been overruled by this Court in PV.

The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the Bank from the Brewery Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur, issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of Bank as per the provisions of section 73FF(2) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960 a person committing defaults ceased to be the Executive Committee (member) or Director. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the validity of the said notice was dismissed by the High Court on 30.8 .89 holding that the appellant was defaulter under section 73F(1)(b) of Act and rejected the appellant ' s contention that section 73 F(2), became applicable from 6.81986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.86, and since he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21.10.1986 when he was declared elected as Director, he was still not eligible to contest the election. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 78F(2)(b), did not envisage setting aside of an election as has been done by the impugned order; that the mere making of payment on 21 10 1986 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 886 to 21.11.1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and that even assuming that the disqual on account was common both for election and for continuation as a Director in the Committee, the special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply, Mr. Patil, the learned counsel for the respondent Bank submitted that the impugned notice under section 80 F(1), was issued without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant his election as Director of the bank and that procedure having not been followed the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 79(2). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The notice of the Deputy Registrar was in effect to say that the appellants had already ceased to hold office as Director and his seat already fell vacant. This has to be interpreted in the context of the provisions in the section. [680C] 2.1 Section 78F (2) says that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section(1, shall cease to be a member of the committee and his seats shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. The fact that he repaid the loan before the notice was issued would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section 84. [679D] 2:2 Section 78 F (2), which is an exception to the generalia Specialibus non vacant general word, does not derogate with special, and would apply if there is apparent conflict in the two or the maxim Generalia specialius non derogants general words are read together. The maxim generalibus non abrogant general Words do not differ from special. [677E] 2(a) The disqualification as defaulter continued after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant having continued to be in a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that the he repaid loan before tho notice was issue would not make material for taking action against him under section 83.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. On the conclusion of the enquiry the State Government issued orders reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders reducing his pension by 50% permanently under rule 188 of tho Bombay Civil Service Rules. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The reduction of pension by 100 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the respondent. [34B] 2. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable ' to a Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service, provided that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note I to Rule 33 of the Rules. [35D] 3. The State Government had power to reduce the amount by taking proceedings against a Government Servant even after his retirement was expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. This rule further provides that before an order reducing, or withdrawing of any part pension is made, the procedure referred to in Note 1 to Rule 34 of the said Rules shall be followed. [36E] 4. The validity of Rule 189 was not challenged either before the trial court or before this Court. In this view, the Government has power to reduced the amount. of pension paid to a government servant. This reduction is too harsh. It would seriously affect his living. Therefore, the reduction of the respondent 's pension by 25 per cent would seriously prejudice his living.[36E F] 5. The High Court committed serious error in holding that the State had no authority to initiate any proceedings against the Respondent.

The appellants were the tenants of certain premises in U.P. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground that the appellants had committed default in payment of rent and that the suit was not maintainable as the appellants were not the landlords under section 3(4) of the U. P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947. The trial court dismissed the suit but the first appellate court allowed the appeal holding that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 2(3) of Act was invalid in law. On second appeal the High Court held that the order granting permission to sue the appellants was not a nullity as it was passed without notice to the tenant and so, he came to the conclusion that the appellant 's suit was incompetent. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The words "any order passed by the State Government under section 7 F of the Act" in section 3 (4) are clear and unambiguous and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the civil courts is completely excluded in relation to the question as to whether permission has been properly or validly granted or refused by the appropriate authorities exercising their powers under the relevant provisions of the . [563 D] (ii) The High Court was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the width of the revisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3. That is why it must be held that in a given case, an order has been passed without hearing the party affected by such order, it would be open to the said party to contend that an order passed in violation of the principles of natural justice is a nullity and it existence should be ignored by the civil court. [563 F G] (iii) The amendment in question has been introduced by Act 17 of 1954.

The petitioner was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission. He was convicted by the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, on the ground that he had committed an offence under section 302 IPC and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The appeal filed against his conviction was dismissed by the Sessions Judge. In the revision petition before this Court it was contended that before making this Reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. Dismissing the Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference under Article 317(1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that, subject to clause (3), the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Com Commission can only be removed from his office on the grounds of misbehaviour and (ii) the order of removal can be passed after the Supreme Court has on inquiry reported to the President that the Chairman/or such other person ought to be removed on any such ground. [640C D] 2. The recording of evidence will be over by September 30, 1983. In case it is not over by that date, the learned Judge may write to the Registrar of the Supreme court for extension of time. The evidence will he transmitted to the Registry of this Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded. [643E F] 3. The record of evidence would be limited to the cross examination of witnesses who have filed affidavits before this court. In other words, no person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court will be examined or cross examined as a witness except with the leave of this court.] [642C D; 647A B] 4. The mere fact that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned Judges will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. [641E] 5. The Court will, therefore, record the evidence which the parties lead before him within the constraints of the following guidelines: (i) The affidavits filed in this court will be treated as the examination in chief of the respective witnesses; (ii). The mere circumstance that the witness has not produced an affidavit does not conclude that the issue is of such a nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his Office. If a full opportunity is given to the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial, it is an idle complaint that the witnesses have filed affidavit in the Supreme Courts may be summoned or requested by the Judge to attend his Court for the purpose of cross examination; (iii) The evidence to be recorded by a learned Judge will be limited only to the examination of the witnesses who had filed affidavits. [651C D, F] 6. In cases where the allegations are of assault and murder, the Court may take judicial notice of such incidents as in the present case. [631G] 7. The inquiry which this Court is required to hold is not into the limited question whether, on a consideration of facts found by the President, the charge of misbehaviour is made out and whether the misbehaviour is ofsuch a nature that to warrant removal from the office of Member of the Public Service commission. If such a full opportu nity is given, it will be an idle allegation that the Evidence has been examined and found upon by the Supreme and not by a court of first instance. [661H; 63A] 8.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. Chatterjee, for short). The respondent pleaded that the approach made by the High Court was wholly incorrect and it has misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the endowment was a private one and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the dedication was of a public nature and the endowment had been of a private character and it had misconstrued the documents and documents brought on record in the proceeding before the High court. In appeal, the High COurt held that the institution was purely one of private endowments and the temple installed in a temple was merely a family idol having nothingto do with its public. It further held that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family temple, it is a private and not a public endowment as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the deity can only be the members of the family and that is an ascertained group of individuals. In this appeal by certificate under article 133(1)(c) of Constitution, it was contended on behalf of the appellants plaintiffs that the High Courts were in error in holding that a private endowment or a private trust is unknown to English law where all trusts are public trusts of a purely charitable and religious nature; (2) Extensive private properties belonging to the Pani family alone were dedicated for maintenance of the temple and the idol was merely for the benefit of the members thereof and there was nothing to show in the deed to show if any contribution was called for from members of public or strangers which is a clear proof of the intention to dedicate the temple to public and not to the members or their descendants; (3) Ext expeditious private properties belong to the deity and there is nothing to indicate that any contribution had been called for by members of tho public nor was there any averment in the document to show what was the nature of the endowment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has misconstrued and mis appreciated the oral evidence led in the proceedings before the trial court which runs counter to the conclusions arrived at by the trial Court. [830E] 2.1 In a public charitable endowment the dedication is for the use or benefit of public. If however, it be proved that the worship by the members was as of right that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the endowments was of private nature. [889G] 2:2 The mere fact that members of a community used to come to the temple with out any hindrance also does not necessarily mean that the temple is a public temple, for members of family do attend private temples. It is manifest that whenever a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed therein in a Temple, the worship is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the idol, and therefore, the mere factum of worship would not determine the nature or character of the endowments. [879G H] 2 :3 The mere factum that members are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that they were a circumstancewhich may in most cases conclusively prove that the trust was of such a nature. It may be that a document is available to prove the nature and origin of the dedication and the recitals of the document show that there was no stipulation for taking offerings from the members by way of a Public endowment, clause 15 would have clearly provided that in cast the family became extinct the members Of the public or of the brotherhood or the Government could have taken over the management.

The appellant Bank entered into an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys have agreed to finance contracts and to advance moneys to Malhotra against his bills for payments to be received by us under the contracts issued by the Government In various departments, and have entering into certain other contracts. Whereas an agreement was made between the appellant and the respondent Bank in pursuance thereof, the power of the attorney recited: (1) that we are functioning as contractors; (2) that the debt owing shall be paid out of a specific fund coming to the debtor or an order given by a debtor to his creditor upon a person owing money or holding funds belonging to the giver of the order directing such person to pay such funds to the creditor, will create a valid equitable charge upon such fund in other words, wfll operate as an equitable assignment of the debts or fund to which the order refers; and (3) that on a proper construction of the document the conclusion is irresistible that there was an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the appellant debt owing to the respondent would be paidout of a particular fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the power attorney dated July 13 was irrevocable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The power to attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 created an interest in a specific Fund and was irrevocable; there was no equitable assignment. [766 E] (ii) The document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. As the lender had an interest of the fundS the power to Attorney was expressed to be irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment by the appellant to the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill and amounted to an equitable assignmen of the Fund by way of security. [777 E F] (iii) The High Court was in error in holding that there were no equitable assignments. In the last case, the Court held that there wag an agreement by which the power was expressedto be irrevocable; but the endorsement was sent to and acknowledged by the military authorities. Read in the light of the power power of power attorney the endorsement of on the Bill created an Interest in a particular specific fund and was unconditional. There is thus a clear distinction between a debtor and creditor that the debts owing to him are paid out Of a specific funds coming to his debtor or any order givenby a debtor directing such persons to pay the moneys to the creditors will create an equitable charge on such fund, in other terms, wlth operate as a equitable assignmentof the debt or fund by way o security. security. In Loonkaran Sethiya vs State Bank of Jaipur, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 777, followed.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., The said company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not recognised by the Income tax Officer as his salary, the same was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. On further appeal to the Tribunal by the assessee, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the said income was his income as defined under section 17 Of the Income ' tax Act, 1922 (to he Act); the same having not been assessed as his ' salary, it was his own contribution to the fund. The High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: 1. The meaning of section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any rule of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [440 D] 2. The expression "profits in lieu of pay" in section17 has nothing to do either with deductions or with exemptions. As the income in question is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on the securities; income from house property pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. it has to be considered as "income from other sources" and brought to tax under section 56. [441 E] 3. The receipt of Rs. 27,948 by the appellant in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered ' income ' because the said amount is not an income. [442 G] 4. The respondent was not represented before this Court. He was not present at the time of hearing of the appeal.

The Bihar Legislature passed the Bihar Act, in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of she buffaloes, male and female, but that it is constitutionally valid in so insofar as it imposes a total ban on the slaughter Of her buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness. The Bihar Act was passed with a view to preventing the spread of cattle therein and for matters connected therewith. It was enacted by Parliament in exercise of its powers under Entry 54 List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, to provide for the control of trade, commerce and intercourse among the States and for the establishment of industries and for securing the equitable distribution of water supply and electricity. The Act was amended by the Bihar Legislature with a further object to prevent the spread over of cattle in the State of Bihar. It also provided that no person shall slaughter any animal except under a licence issued by the appropriate authority. Section 3(1) of the Act empowered the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the , and for giving effect to such rules, the Central Govt. may make rules consistent with this Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned Acts on the grounds (i) that the Bihar legislature was incompetent to enact the impugned Act as it infringed a fundamental right under article 19(1)(g) of Constitution; (ii) that it violated articles 14 and 19(2) of Part III of the Constitution inasmuch as it imposed a total prohibition on the slaughtering of cows, buffaloes and sheep, and therefore void no question can arise, even in the Bihar State Legislature 's case, in view of the fact that the impugned legislation was passed by the Parliament with a clear intention to prevent such spread over; (iii) that a total restriction on the slaughtered of all cattle would not be in the best interests of the country as it is merely a negative and not a positive approach to the problem. HELD: The Bihar Legislature had no power under Entry 53 List I, read with Entry 54, List II, to make laws for regulating the slaughter or trade of any animal. [655 C] (i)(a) The impugned Acts were passed by Parliament with the object of preventing the slaughter and of buffaloes, including bulls and bullocks, and it was not possible to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on slaughter of she buffalo, breeding bull, bullocks or heifers and the slaughter. [660 D] (b) The Bihar State Act in so much as it prohibited the slaughter by any person other than a citizen of India and that it was constitutionally valid was valid in law. [661 F] (ii)(a). The impugned Act was not passed by a competent authority within the meaning of article 19 of the Constitu tion inasmuch as the Parliament had no competence to enact it. It is, therefore, not possible, to apply this doctrine of excluding the operation of article 14 and uphold it.

The respondent was a public limited company having its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh. Its Manager, and Assistant Manager were the employees of the Company. The respondent filed a suit for damages against the appellants who were the workmen of the company on the ground that the relationship between them was contractual and not statutory and the remedy of the respondent was to sue the Company in damages for wrongful dismissal; and (3) as for amendment of Standing Orders so as to include the respondent and persons in his category, the only remedy open to the respondent, was to take action under the relevant Act by approaching a recognised union to move in the matter. The High Court held that the inclusion of the name and ticket number in the departmental muster was an essential characteristic of an 'employee ' as defined for the purpose of the Standing Orders, and the mere fact of employment in the office, Mains Department Stores, Power House or Receiving Station of the Companies was not enough to make a, 471 person so employed an ' employee ' within the meaning of the said Standing Orders. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the word "employee" in section 2(1) of the , means such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen by the management and Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order NO. (a) of standing order No. 1 of 1948, which was applicable to the appellant company, and an 'workman ' as contemplated in the Standing Order was not an "employee". The definition of an employee is employment in a Office, Main Branch or Office of the Government either at Nagpur or Wardha, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order Nos. 1 and 2 of 1948.

The appellant, a company owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company, was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in the years 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1967 68 when this Project went into manufacture. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this project went into the production. The Tribunal held that alloy steel Project could not be treated as a separate Establishment because, under the Act, a Company is itself an establishment and so, all units of a company like Hindustan Steel Ltd. will constitute one establishment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the proviso to section 3(2) of the Payment Of Bonus Act did not stand in the way of this claim because there was no evidence at all that in any year, after Alloy steel project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units; (ii) the Explanation to section 16(1) only came into play when the Act itself was inapplicable in view of the provision contained in section 1, sub section (2), and that the proviso could not apply in such a case. HELD: (i). The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that simply because Alloy was owned controlled and controlled by Hindustan Steel Company Ltd., it has to be treated to be a separate unit because, there is no evidence of at all, that in some year, before Alloy 's Project was set into production bonus was given to the workmen of all those units on that basis. [633 C] (ii). The proviso to sub section(2), only comes in the manner it bonus is paid in any one year to the employee of all of the units. Therefore, no bonus could be payable, to the workers of this undertaking for the year 1966 66 in view Of the provisions contained in sections 1, 3 and 4 of the Act.

The appellant, a sugar manufacturing company, was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of sugar from sugar cane. The cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column II thereof as the Central Govern ment may by notification specify. The Cess was payable on every person who carried on any industry and Every local authority, and is computed on the principle of water consumption. The appellant challenged the cess on the ground that it fell within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 14 as "processing vegetable products industry". In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the word 'vegetable ' in Item (6) of Schedule 1 to the cess Act must be construed as understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense meaning. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The definition of "manufacture" in section 2(g) of the is wide enough to include all kinds of products which are produced or made of or out of vegetable. [514C] 2. The word 'manufacture ' has been used in Entry 15 and a fortio ri t the manufacture of alcohol from molasses could not be considered to be an industry within the meaning of Entry 15. [525D E] 3. The expression "manufacture ' is defined in section 3(a) of . It includes any process incidental or ancillary to the completion of, or addition to, or otherwise of, a manufactured product. [511F G] 4. The term "process ing vegetable products" has been employed in Entry 14 and a wide amplitude. It cannot be said that the expression "manu facture" is used in common sense and it includes all kinds which are capable of being converted into articles or things. [500C D] 5. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within the Entry 15 as " processing vegetable products". [501D E; 526A B] 6. The levy of cess on sugar is a well known process and has to be judged by the predominant purpose and process and not by any ancillary or incidental process carried on by a particular industry in running its business. [446C D, F] 7. In order to bring an industry under any of these entries it has to he seen what is the end product produced by that industry. If the botanic meaning of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule I like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry No 15. The words "manufac ture" in the context does not attract the botsanic or meaning. [347E] 8. The Sugar manufacturing industry does not, however, come under Entry 15 on Schedule I of the Cess Rules. [50F G; 526G] 9. The industry manufacturing sugar itself is not an industry for certain purposes and vegetables are products of that industry.[545C D]. 10. The use of word "vegetables" in Entry 12 does not bring within the bowanic and meaning. The said expression has been interpreted by this Court in State of West Bengal & Ors. vs Washi Ahmed etc.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a) (iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of appellant on the grounds that he requires the premises bona fide for carrying out his profession. In revision, the High Court held that the respondent bona fide required the building for the purpose of carrying on profession as a lawyer and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'business ' in Section 10 (3) (a)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice which had nothing commercial about it was not ' business within that meaning in Section 2(1)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. [14G] 1.2 The word 'business" has been defined in section 2(11) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease Rent and eviction) Control act, 1960 as including the practice that of a liberal profession like that of an Advocate or a Doctor which had no nothing commercial relation about it. In Stuchbery & Ors. vs General Accident Fire and Life Assurance Corporation Ltd., ; , it was observed that the carrying on of a Solicitor 's business was the carrying of a profession and was not the carrying out of a trade or business within Section 10 of the Act. [15A B] 1:3 The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the sense in which other statutes or in a manner alien to the context in which they occur. In the instant case, the practice was 'business within the expression ' business ' in section 10( 3)(a)(ii) of Act, 1927. The word "business" must be construed in the light of the context and the statute concerned. [16B C] 1 :4 The word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. In a sense different from that in which the expression is used cannot be given a wide meaning so as not to include any profession. It is right to ascribe to the word ' business" occurring in the Andhra pradesh Buildings (lease, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1959, the same meaning that the word may has when it occurred in other Statutory provisions. The words must be understood in the background of the Statute in which its language occurs and cannot be extended to include all the provisions of the Acts including Section 4 which provide for the determination of fair rent and Section 10 which provides for the eviction by a tenant where the landlord of a residential building requires it for his own occupation. [17C D] Stuchield & Ors vs General Fire and L Assurance Corporation, Ltd., , referred to.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that the use of the word ' depositing by itself occurring either in the roznamcha or in the letter dated 29 September 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not be decisive of the question whether it was a case of deposit of the sum of Rs 4,00,000 by the respondent with the appellant under an agreement that the same would be paid on demand. Held, that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before the limitation can star in case of demand for return of the amount deposited. The payment of money is not a condition precedent to the making of the award.
