It is also important to bear in mind that a demand in the year 1943 for a part of the money would not have sufficed the needs of the appellant who were then unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. The transaction was between the appellant and the respondent and the appellant was not a case where the respondent giving loan to the appellant had made any advances to all or any of them or their moneys which may be in deposit with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course. The fact that the money was debited to India Supplies as deposit is clear from the letter of credit dated 29th September 1942, shows that there were advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award, and were therefore not covered either by the Award.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were served on him in the criminal case and he was remanded to judicial custody. He was taken into custody. A charge sheet had not been submitted against him in that criminal case, but he was already in custody. The detaining authority did not accept the same and passed an order of detention under sub section (1) thereof. The petitioner challenged the order of his detention by a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same on the ground that the period of parole from May 15, 1986 to February 28, 1987 could not be added to the maximum period of deten tion of the detenu for one year as specified in the impugned order of detenment passed under sub s (1). The petitioner has filed this petition after obtaining special leave. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is al ready in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that tho detaining authority was aware of the fact that he was earlier in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of preventive detention became necessary. [845C D] 2. The question whether a person accused of certain offences whereunder he is undergoing trial or has been acquitted, does not depend upon the facts of each case. In the instant case there is suffi cient material to show that the detaining author ity was aware that the petitioner was in custody when the order was made, yet he had been satisfied that the preventive detention was necessary. The mere fact that a detenu is in jail for at the most one day does not detract from the order being passed for preventive deten tion. [884D E] 3. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, it would not be proper to hold that summons under section 108 of the Customs Act was in existence. By the time the order came to be made the petitioner Was in jail custody for at least one day. [864C D; 845A] 4. The facts of the present case there are suffi fient material on record to show the fact of the petitioner being in custody, yet the detaining au thority was aware thereof that the peti tioner was in detention when the impugned orders were made, but still he was satisfied that he preventive detention had become necessary. In such circumstances it would be not proper to conclude that summons could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authorities were satisfied that there is sufficient ground for making an Order of preventive Detention. [874D] Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate, Etah, ; , referred to.

The petitioners were working as 'Daily Rated Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They were engaged on daily wages basis. The casual labourers were paid wages at the rates equivalent to the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled (Rs.210 270) skilled ( Rs.260 350 as the case may be, plus DA/ADA admissible thereon. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court contending that even though they belonged to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they were not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government agencies in particular should not allow 610 workers to remain as casual labourers or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep persons as casual labourer for years as is being done in the Postal and Telegraph Department. [617C D] 1.2 In respect of categories (ii) and (iii) i.e. for those who have completed 720/1200 days in 3/5 years, the revision is done as and when DA/DA. 302 of 1986 was filed on 5.2.1986 for the issue of a writ in the nature of mandamus to the Union of India to direct it to pay to the petitioners same salary and allowances and other benefits as are being paid to the regular and permanent employees of the Union Government in the corresponding cadres and to direct the Union to regularise the service of the casual labour who had been continuously working for more than one year in the Post and Telegraph department. [ 608D E] 1:3 The petitioners belong to the class of casual labourers and are therefore not being paid regularly employed. They are, therefore, not entitled for the same benefits which the ordinary employees are enjoyed. [ 609F G] 2.1 In respect Of categories (i) and(ii) i, viz., for those whose cases the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period of more than six months, the Revision is done in as much as the casual labourers who strictly conform to the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210270 and Rs. 260 350 as tho case may he and that there should not be any variation in the respective job con tent. [ 610A B] 2:2 The benefit of increased rates of daily wages will not be admissible to casual semi skilled/skilled labour in whose case the continuous spell of duty is intervened by period of less than six month. These enhanced rates of monthly wages are applicable to the semi skilled and unskilled labour who strictly comply with the job conditions content ofcorresponding regular posts In scales of pay Rs. 210 270 and Rs260 350, as the cases may be and that they there should have not been any variation or variation in their respective job conditions. [ 611C D; 612A B C] 2 :3 The benefit Of increased rates will not he admissible to the casual semikilled/s skilled labour in whom case the continuously spells of duties are intervened By a period Of more than 6 months, these enhanced rates will be without prejudice to absorption of casual semi skill/s unskilled labour against regular vacancies as and whenever they occur.

The assessee, a non taxable income, filed a return showing a total world income and total world incomes during that year. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Indian Income tax Act on January 5, 1950, to the assessee calling upon him to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days a return. The assessee contended that he was entitled under section 23(3) to make a " voluntary " return on the date he did, and with a voluntary return before the Income tax officer there was no scope for the issuance of a notice tinder section 34. Held, that the notice issued by the Income Tax Officer was not in accordance with law and the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the extended period of limitation under section 24(1) of that Act. The notice was therefore valid. The question whether a return filed in compliance with a notice unders. 22(3), if filed belatedly, could not be treated as a return under section24(1)(a) of Income tax. Commissioner of Income Tax vs Shaw Wallace & Co., , relied on. Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay City vs Shaw skil, (1932) L.R. 59 I.A. 206 and Commissioner of Incometax, Madras vs M/s. Shaw Wallace and Co., (1930) L,.R. 58 I. A. 206, referred to. The view of the Calcutta High Court was that a " voluntarily " return showing an income below the taxable minimum was filed could not possibly be ' treated as such a return made under section 34(1), or a return called for under that section but filed under section 25(3).

The petitioners in the Transfer Case No. 219/88 and C.M.P. 8572 of 1989 were employees of the Reserve Bank of India, a nationalised bank. The Central Government by its circular dated 23.8.1982 directed that the existing Board of Directors should be constituted for the purpose of constituting the Board of directors so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. The petitioners in C.A. No. 1657/89 were employees in the nationalised bank, who had furnished their representative Union. The Reserve Bank by its Circular dated 23 8.1982 provided that the Board shall include representatives from the employees of nationalised bank who are not workmen, to be appointed by the Central Government after consultation with the Reserve bank; and the Central Govern ment was also directed to make a scheme for the constitution of the Board in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Board by its letter dated 23 9 1982 informed the petitioners that the scheme would be implemented only if the representatives of employees had been appointed as per the procedure prescribed under the Act, and that the guidelines issued by the Reserve Board were not followed. The respondents in CAs Nos. 1659/89 and 1660/89 challenged the said circular by filing writ petitions before the High Court which allowed the same holding that the Circular dated 3.8.,1982 was ultra vires the Act and that it was, therefore, null and void. In the appeals to this Court on behalf of the petitioners it was contended that (1) the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the board of Directors and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Gov ernment; (2) the method of election or nomination must, therefore be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking industry and the choose ment of the mode is generally a matter for decision by the central Government; (3) the scheme should not be even more defective if sub clause (c) were to receive the same construction as sub clause(b); (4) the Board has been constituted in accordance ly with the procedure laid down under the statute and that, therefore the Circular was ultra rites of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act, he says speaks of election and nominations, and if election were to be construed to be the appropriate mode of choosing the representatives o f the employees, appointment by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election. [561F] 1.2 The Act speaks of elec tation of election to the Board and it is, therefore. open to the central Govern ment to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. It is incumbent upon it, until any such amend ment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. That means, it would be perfectly in order for the Central Govt. to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employ ees, and, if necessary, to amend t he Scheme suitably so as, to appoint the true representatives of tho concerned employees, and to hold re election of their respective representatives. [562G H] 1:3 The Circular dated March 23, 1982 (Annexure A) is ultra vires and void and of no effect. [563C D] 1 :4 The circular dated March 3, 1982 is ultra ly the Act as it has been issued in exercise of powers conferred by sub clause 2 of Article 162 of the Constitution.

The respondent was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1,000 on an assessee during the pendency of an appeal before it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the penalty but reduced the amount to Rs. 2,000. In appeal by the Revenue to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of the penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power in granting stay as incidental or ancillary to it 's appellate jurisdiction, [69D] (2) The power of stay by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It can well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction it impliedly grants the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [69E] (3) The Tribunal must have the discretion to grant stay as ancillary or incidental to its original jurisdiction. This is particularly so when section 220(6) deals expressly with a situation when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Assistant commissioner, but the Act is silent in that behalf when an 'appeal is pending against the Appellate Tribunal. It could well be contended that when the Income tax Officer grants the necessary relief to an assessee, he can grant time for the payment of the tax.

The respondent was charged with having committed offences under section 7 of the Police Act, 1861. The enquiry ended in his dismissal and on August 18, 1953, he was placed under suspension and on September 8, 1953 he was charged under section 13(1) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, with a view to preventing him from acting as Sub Inspector of Police. On July 28, 1953 the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal and for quashing his dismissal. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereof the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage, and that as no prejudice was caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said regulations would not affect the validity of the order dismissing. Held, that the departmental trial was only one further step and the enquiry ended into the dismissal of the Respondent. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect tho question, if substantially the subject matter of the mag judicial inquiry and the departmental Trial is the same. In such cases, and in other cases until and unless a magisterial enquiry is ordered, inquiry will be made under the direction of the Superintendent of Police in accordance with the following rules; Paragraph 489: "A police officer may be departmentally tried under section7 of the police Act (1) after he has been tried judicially; In this case the departmental enquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the Magisterial inquiry and therefore it falls within the express terms of para. 486 of the Indian Police Regulations.

The appellant was a Professor in the Department of Health and Family Welfare. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. The post of Director of Health Services was abolished by conversion of one post from amongst unspecified specialists ' Grade posts in supertime Grade II. In the year 1966, the Central Government converted one post into a specified post and transferred Dr. Sen to the newly created post of Professor in Medical Education at Willingdon Hospital and transferred him to the post created at Willingsdon hospital. The appellant challenged the promotion on the ground that he was not qualified for being promoted to Supertime grade I because he had put in 8 years of service in the category of Specialists ' grade posts in Supertime Grade I and that when a post in Ophthalmology at Willesingdom Hospital was created on February 1, 1971 by conversion, of one posts from amongst the unspecified Specialists Grade posts into different specialities and were filled in by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists Grade I, that post could only have been filled in from amongst persons who were qualified to be promoted in the respective speciality in which the post was created. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that when the post in question was converted into a Specialist ' grade and that as it was assigned to Ophpadmology, he being the seniormost and otherwise qualified, he should have been promoted from that date. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended: (1) that when an unspecified post is converted into an unified post which means specified in the speciality in Which a need has been felt from amongst these persons in the specialists grade belonging to that speciality and in order of their inter se seniority a promotion could be given; (2) that as these 28 posts were in Specialists " grade" and the strength of Specialist Grade posts was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to super time grade II is required to be filled in, it can only be filled by promotion and he should be promoted and the posting of Dr. P.S. Jain was not made; (3) that the promotion of the aforesaid four respondents should be set aside had no merit in it; (4) that there was violation of the rule inasmuch as the appellant was not a qualified and, therefore, he must be considered eligible for promotion from the date on which Dr. Sharma was promoted; and (5) that in refusing promotion to him when some posts were converted into unspecifiedspecialists ' posts into separate specialities, posts were treated as being found qualified for the same and for the post to which each one of them was promoted he should not have been considered for promotion to superftime grade 11. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. When a post from among unspecified persons is converted to a specified cadre post it can be filled only in by promotions from amongst such persons who are qualified to he appointed to that cadre and not some one who is on top of the general seniority list in Specialist " grade or general duty officers" grade from which promotion is to be made. [53E] 2. When an unsspecified specialists" post is conversion into a specific post it cannot be said that there is any violation of rule. If this contention were to prevail, apart from anything else, appellant himself would not have got the benefit of promotion to Super Time grade II in February 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for promotional promotion to the supertime scale 11. [54F G] 3.

The appellant, a small holder of land in excess of the permissible limit, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19 B of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the gift to the son or wife was not hit either by section tenA or section 19(1)(i) of the Land Reforms Act, 1950 and that section 19A had no application as the land in question was not a surplus area and so he sought harbourage by moving the High court under article 226 where he urged that the lands inherited by his father and later transfer to his son and wife are not hit By section 10 A and section19B of Act, he succeded in the Court in view of a certain strict construction adopted by the Court and the State has come up in appeal challenging the soundness of the High 'Court 's approach. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The gift to son or daughter is not hit under section 10(a) of Act. [637C] 2. Section 19 B directs the owner who, by inheritance, comes to own an excess area, to make a declaration of his lands within a prescribed time. What is intended is to give some time to the heir to ascertain the assets he has inherited, make the choice of his 'reserved area which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. [643E] 3. The scheme of the provisions of the statute according to the learned Judges, was to see that no one held in excess Of the permissible area and since by the gift the son had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. This reasoning is repugnant to the basic scheme because the surplus pool will be adversely affected if gifts and other transfers which will skim off surplus were to be allowed. [641C D] 4. The drafting of the saving clause is cumbersome but the sense is and having regard to the conspectus, can only be that although in the hands of the propositus, it is surplus land, if among the heirs it is not, then their transfers will not be affected by the interdict of section 10. [651C] 5. The language of the provision makes it clear that the intention was to give certain time to a heir to determine the assets He has inherited and make necessary declaration.[637E] 6. Section 20 B directs that the owner shall, within a specified time furnish to the Collector a return indicating the permissible areas he desires to retain.

The plaintiffs, who were the eldest member of a joint Hindu family, filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain lands on the ground that they had been granted to them by the Government under the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951. The trial court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to the Zamindari on the death of one Amarshah upon his death and that the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of proprietary rights (Estate, Mahal or Alienated Land) Act, 1951 had become binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof. The High Court held that on the date of the vesting of the Zamindari in the State of Madhya Pradesh, the Zamindari was impar tible and was governed by the rule of primogeniture and Pratapshah father of the plaintiffs being the eldest son of Amarshih as an impartible estate devolving by the Rule of primimiture. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decision in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the ' death of Amtshah was not binding and therefore the decree passed by the trial court could not be reopened; (ii) the order of the Governor recognising Dayaram as Zamindar was not a binding and con tended right or title upon the defendants because no action had been taken in respect of Malgu zari lands; and (iii) the will set up by the plaintiffs represented true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah. HELD: The High court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awardable to the plaintiffs. [328 C] In the present case, the order dated August 30, 1951 set up a wholly false and fictitious will. It did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. The order of compensation Officer under sub section (1) shall not be subject to any appeal or revision but any party may, within two month from the day of such order institute a suit in the civil court to have the order set aside, and the decision must be binding on the Compensation officer, but subject to the result of such suit if any, the compensation Officer shall be final and conclusive. Section 14 was enacted with a view to put an end to disputes with regard to claims to proprietary rights which by virtue of the notification issued under section 3 are extinguished.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the tenant had committed default in payment of rent. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court took the view that the provisions contained in section 12 (3) (a) of the Act do not apply to the suit, but that the suit was governed by the provisions of section 12(3)(b) of tho Act and that the tenancy could be raised only within one month from the service of the notice on the tenant. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The Bombay High Court in Ambalal 's case held that in order to attract the applicability of section12 (3), there must be non existence of the dispute at the date of the service and such non existence must continue right up to the expiration of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2) of section 11. [630 E] Ambalals ' case, ; , followed. The Bombay view is that the dispute in section12(3) is not limited only to a dispute raised within one months of the date when the notice terminating the tenancy by raising a dispute as to standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act. The Gujarat High Court was right in taking the view it took. Amballal Nagindas took the contrary view and held that the question whether the tenant can raise a dispute is not restricted only to the dispute raised at one month of the tenancy but also to a claim for possession of premises.

The respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent company. The appointment was made by a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondents company, the Aluminium Company appointed three temporary directors on board of Directors of the Respondent company. L. G. Lit. G., L.G. L., G. Bash who was then the appellant before the Tribunal, was a director of the Company nominated by the Aluminium Co. Ltd. to vote and/or from time to time appoint a special general or general panel to vote on behalf for and On behalf of Aluminium Ltd., it was appointed as a special and general proxy. L, G.L. G Bash who had been appointed to vote, and L filed a return of its income for the assessment year 1939 50. The Income tax Officer held that the directors of respondent company had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, and that the shares held by them were registered in the name of Aluminium Company Ltd., and that they could not be said to have "a controlling interest" in the respondent ' company. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but on further reference the High Court answered in favour of the assessee. The question for consideration was whether in the facts and circumstances of these cases, the Income Tax Officer was right in holding that the Directors of respondent Company had a control in it. Held: (i) In order to have 'a controlling interests" the person or persons who hold the majority of shares as trustees and may even be accountable to their beneficiaries and may be brought to book for exercising their votes in breach of trust, nevertheless as between them as shareholders and the company they are the shareholders, and as such, have " a controlling interests". The controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium company and is at no time vested in Mr. L . G. K. Lang who was appointed to act as an agent of the aluminium Company attends a general meeting of the shareholders of the company he has to produce the resolution of his principals authorising him to cast the votes of his principal. In such a situation, in the eye of the law, the controlling interest remained vested in 'the Aluminium Ltd.; and is, at no point vested in Mrs. Lob G. Shah who was the managing director of respondent No. 1 company and although he may be bound to cast his vote according to the directions of his Principals, the aluminium Ltd., attends the general meeting and as between him as shareholders, the beneficial interest is vested in them, though as between themselves as shareholders. The controlling interests remained vested with the Aluminium Limited and is therefore, at any time vested In Mr. Kang vs Commissioner of Income tax, , followed. (ii)The respondent Company must pay the costs of the appellant in this Court as well as in the High Courts.

The respondent was an employee of the appellant Electricity Board. He opted to the service under the Board and ceased to be an employee with effect from that date. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their passing the S .A. Examination while promotion was denied to the respond ent as he had not passed the examination. The appellant Board by its Resolution dated 19th May 1969 directed that the respondent should pass the S.,A.T.S examination. Part I & Part II. On 1st October, 1957, some person junior to him were promoted as Accounts Superin tendent on their being found fit for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendent as before be in sisted ' the court held that the allotment was not justified and allowed the writ petition. The respondent thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Board dated 19st May 1969. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ application holding that the resolution dated 19nd May, 1969 was no longer open to the respon dents to rely on the Resolution dated19th May,1969 and therefore allowed the Writ Petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant Board: (1) that the High court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that passing of the Resolution was not relaxed by amending the Regulations; (2) that in view of the later resolution of the board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no more open to it to the appellant to rely upon the Resolution of 19th t May 1969; (3) that even if the respondent had not obtained the examination he could not be denied promotion on the ground of inordinate delay and laches. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in wrong in construing relevant provisions in the Regulations passed by the Board under section 79(c) of the Act. [505C] 2.1 In any event the plea of the respondent will have to fail on the grounds that the regulations framed under section79(c), had not been relaxed by amend ment of the Regulation. The passing of a Resolution by the board cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by it in the exercise of the powers conferred by the statute. Apart from this circumstance by a subsequent Resolution the Board itself considered the ques tion in all its aspects and resolved that passing the resolution by the earlier Resolution had resolved on insisting on the passing of examination. Examination for promotion, to the Cadre of Accounts superintendent as before being insisted. Whatever might have been the purport of the resolution of 19 th May 1969, the Board by a later Resolution had decided on insist on the pass ing of the examination and the examination for promotion for promotion. It was not possible to infer from the Resolution that the allottees were exempted from passing the Departmental Examination I and the inference that the allotees were exempt ed from passing it. The conclusion of the High ' Court cannot be upheld as binding nature of the regulations passed by Board under s 79(C) has not been taken due note of.

The petitioner, a minor, was taken to the police custody in connection with an alleged escape of his son Suman Behera from a railway compartment. The said Suman Behra was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, Bisra, Distt. The petitioner 's mother was taken into custody and the petitioner was taken in police remand to police custody. On 1.1.1987, the petitioner made an application before the Chief Judicial Magistrate for payment of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of Suman Behara, for contravention of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Chief Judicial Magis trate rejected the said application on the ground that the petitioner ' s son was a " custodial death" within the meaning of Section 2(c) of the . The petitioner filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of rejection of his claim for compensation to be awarded to him consequent upon, the death of his father. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the decision of Dr. It may be mentioned straightaway that award of compensation in a proceeding under Article 32 by this court or by the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitu tion is a remedy available in public law and is based on the strict liability for contravention thereof of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private law in an action based on tort. The decision of this Court in Rudul Sah vs State of Bihar and Anr., ; granted monetary relief to the victims for deprivation of their fundamental rights in proceedings through petitions filed under Article32 or 226 of tho Constitution of India, notwithstanding the rights available under the civil law to the aggrieved party where the courts found that grant of such relief was warranted. The payment of compensa tion in such cases is not to be understood as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental rights of the citizen. The compensation is in the nature of exempellary damages awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public law duty and is independent of the rights of citizens. Therefore when the court molds the relief by granting "compensation" in proceedings under Article 30 or 226, the seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental right, it does so under the Public Law by way of penalising the wrongdoer and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental Rights of the citizens. The award of monetary compensation is not a measure of damages but an amount of exemplary damages, in proceedings instituted under Article 31 or 226 would be granted only once it is established that there has been an infringement of the right of the petitioner and no other form of appropriate redressal by the court in the facts and circumstances of the case, is possible. The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of money compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only mode of redress available. The amount of monetary compensa tation awarded against wrong doers for the violation of their human rights in an illegal manner or in a public law, would be a just and equitable relief to victims for loss of their right to life under Article 19(1)(f) of our Constitution.

The petitioner, a prisoner of the Hindustan Times, was sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by him to the President of India for commutation of her sentence to imprisonment for life were reported to have been rejected by the President recently. The petitioner 's petition under article 32 of the Constitution was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court on the ground that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the constitution, which includes the freedom of Press is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. The writ petition filed by the petitioner was dismissed in limine. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the constitutional rights to freedom and expression are not an arbitrary right, and (ii) the right to express any particular view or opinion is not a absolute right, nor indeed did it confer an right on him to have a unrestricted access of means of knowledge. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The right claimed by the petitioners is not the right of express any specific view or opinions but the right claimed is not that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. [1187C] 2. The constitutional right under article 19 (1)(b) of Constitution, which include freedom of press, is not absolute right but indeed does not confer any rights on the Press to have any unrestricted access or to means information. [1286D] 3. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for the petitioner to say that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be interviewed and, indeed, if it were to appear that the petitioners themselves did not desire not to be interview, it would have been impossible for him to pass an order directing that the petitioner should be allowed to interview them. [1386E] 4. The presence of a freedom Press does imply or spells out any enforceable obligation on citizens to supplying information to Press, Such for example as there was under section 162(2), Criminal Procedure code, and no data has also been made in respect of that position. [1487F G] 5. It is not necessary that the newspapermen who can broadly and we suppose without great fear of contradiction be termed as friends of the society be denied to the right. [1586G] 6. The fact that for example rule 552A provides for a search of the person who wants to interview an prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. [1787H; 1588A B] 7. Rule 549A also provides that all reasonable indulgence should be granted to a condemned detenu in the matter of interviews with relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. But it does not provide that no newspapermen will be allowed.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950 the appellant bank applied for the appointment of a Receiver. The District Judge transferred the mortgage suit to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Agartala. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he also allowed the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22 of 1956 filed by the Receiver against that order was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner, Tripura on December 18, 1959. On October 4, 1961 the appellant filed an application for the execution of the bond and the appellant prayed that the damages awarded to him be recovered from the appellant. The respondent resisted the application contending that the surety bond executed by the appellant as he is neither the successor nor the assign of the District Judge; and (2) Under the terms of the agreement, the appellant was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. The trial court decreed the respondent suit on the ground that the bond can be enforced only by or at the instance of the presiding officer of the Court. On appeal the Subordinate judge held that the bail bond could be enforced even by or under the Court and that the appellant is not liable for the losses caused to it by the fire. In second appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal on the view that the respondent was not liable to make good the loss sustained by the respondent in respect of the tea gardens. On further appeal by special leave: HELD : (1) The order for the recovery of damages obtained by the Respondent against the Receiver can be executed against the appellant to the effect that it rendered itself liable under the terms Of the bond. [360 C] (2)(a) The surety bond is a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the subordinate Judge. Therefore, by virtue of section 150, the Subordinate Judges was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of the enforcement of the bonds as the District Magistrate himself. [361 D E] (b) The appellant is liable for making good the losses occasioned to the Tea garden due to the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. [362 G] (c) The bond would cover the loss occasioned to tea garden due by the receiver 's default. It is impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect thereof. He was put in possession of the Tea Plant in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea plantation was managed by the Trust economically and efficiently. The surety bonds would therefore cover the losses incurred to the factory due to him 's fault. [363 D] (d) The respondent is liable to pay damages for the damage caused to tea gardens due to his negligence.

The appellants who were dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U .P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller but to the controller. In appeal the Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the Act and therefore the sales were not exigible to tax. The Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales tax referred the following questions to the High Court of Allahabad for opinion (1) Whether the sales made to the appellants by the dealers were sales within the definition of 'sale ' under section 2(h) of the . (2) Whether in the circumstances of the case, the assesses are liable to pay sales tax on the sales effected to the State Government under cl. 5 of the Order and not pursuant to the directions issued under cl.(5) of that order. The High Court answered the questions against the appellants. In appeals by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (1 ) the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax, because steel products were supplied pursuant to directions of the Iron and Steel Controller made under cl 5 of that Order; (2 ) the supplies of sugar; pursuant to a direction issued by the Controller, did not resulting in sales, and therefore no tax was exigible on such transactions. HELD : (1)(a) The levy of tax is a liability to deliver half the quantity of wheat purchased or purchased by the dealer every day beginning with the date of commencement of the order until such time as the State Govern ment otherwise directs. Delivery of the wheat has to be given by the licensed dealer to the specified quantities of the goods on hand, and he had also to supply to the state Government 50% of the quantity, of wheat procured or purchased. [50 E] (b) The tax payer was under the Control Order compelled to carry out the directions of tho Controller and it had no volition in the matter. The tax payee was under a control order compelled to do so. The State Government had no option but to accept the direction of the Controller. [51 C D] (c) The sales were on the same footing as supply of goods pursuant to orders issued under a Con trol Order. The levy was therefore not exigible on the transactions. [52 E F] (2)(a). The taxees contended that the transactions did not resulted in sales or were on account not exposing to sales Tax, because they were supplied pursuance to directions issued by him under cl . 5 of order and not Pursuant to the direction issued under el. 5 was, it said, not to dispose of or agree to dispose or export any iron or steel except in accordance with the conditions contained or incorporated in the order of the controller and that since there is liberty of contract between the parties but subject to restrictions, the transaction could be regarded as a sale. [53 E F]. (b). The levy did not involve any element of volition. It was therefore a liability for payment of tax on goods supplied pursuant thereto. [54 G] (3) The Sales were not sales within section 2 (h) and were therefore liable to tax under section 3(1)(d) of Act. [55 E F; 56 A B] (4) The High court erred in holding that the sales did not amount to sale within the purview of section 2 of the , because the supply was pursuant to an directions issued tinder a Conservation Order.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. Though acquitted he was not straightaway released from prison. The reasons are not clear to us from the record. Presumably he was required in connection with some other case. He had been due for release from prison on June 23, 1986 and since then he was under detention. The mandate of article 22(4) is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been, or were qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. In the instant case, on the date when the detention order was made, there was no Advisory Board in existence to which a reference could be made under section 11 of the Act and whose report of its opinion regarding suffi cient cause for the detention was required to be obtained within three months of the detention under article 22 (4) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was sufficient cause to justify the detention. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. An order of detention should have been made, knowing full well that there were no fresh facts, the maximum period within which the detaining authority can on its own satisfaction detain a person is three months. [206E] 2. The observation of the court to the extent that they go to support the contention of the appellant, but we must say that in that case, the Court was not confronted with the present situation at all. This implies that the question to which the Advisory Board has to apply its mind is whether on the dates of its report there is sufficient cause or not. If the report of the advisory Board is to be obtain ed within three weeks, it is no answer to say that the report though not made within three days, was disposed of before the hearing of the case. [205B C] 3. The observations of the Court to the effect that in a habeas corpus proceeding, it was not a sufficient answer to saying that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date of hearing and therefore, the detention should be upheld. If a reference to an Advisory board is to he made within 3 weeks, then it is not answer to the say that tho reference though not not made in three weeks was made before the hear ing of the cases. If such report is obtained within 3 months, it would be no answer t to say, that the representation, though not ac quired of within three yea rs. 15(2) of Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 which provides for the making of successive order of deten tion so as to bring it in conformity with article 22.(4)of the Constitution, is no answers to say whether the procedural provi sions of the Constitu tion and the statutes have been comply ed before the expiry of three ye ars. [207E F] 4. The facts that the Report of such an Advisory Boards has to be obtaining within three month, are not in any way different from those mentioned in section 11(4). If the representation made by the detenu is required to he disposed of within a stipulated period, it will not answer the say whether tho reference, though made within two weeks, was made within the hearing o f the case and if the report is sought to be received as required by the Constitution.[207E] 5. The order of the High Court quashing the detention dated August 7, 1986 is set aside.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, filed an application for setting aside the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act ') on the ground that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the petitioner had agreed to such entrustment. The arbitrator made a decree in terms of the award. The petitioner preferred a civil revision application against the judgment and order passed by the Civil Judge raising practically all the disputes which had been raised by the petitioner in this civil revision petition. The main objection to the award was that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the dispute to arbitration, and that the arbitrator had not signed the award, and therefore, the award could not be set aside under section 30 and (4) that the award being not remitted under section 16(5), the award is not liable to be setaside under section 18. The High Court dismissed the revision application holding that the Civil Court had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the arbitration award under sections 14 and 17 of Act, and directed the trial Judge to dispose of the suit in terms thereof. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the conduct of the parties that there were an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed agreed to refer both the disputes in writing to the arbitrator. [532C] 1.2 The conduct of parties that the matter was wholly foreign to its jurisdiction or that the defendant was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some such other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the Suit or over the parties thereto. [540D] 1:3 In the instant case, both the petitioner and respondent had re affirmed the acceptance of the Award. The award was signed by two parties, about which there is no factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the party had agreed not to refer any dispute to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. This, in our opinion, cannot be said to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms Of section 2(a) of the Act. [541E F] Seth Hira Lal Patni vs Shri Kali Nath, ; , followed. Seth Hira lal Patni v Shri Kali Charan, ; ; Seth Hiralal Patni and Anr. vs Shri Ludh Budh Prakash, ; and Seth Hira Lai Patni, vs Shri K.S. Vaidya, ; referred to.

The appellants filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under a mortgage executed by them. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was not an assignee within the meaning of sub section (5) of section 36 and therefore, he could not be said to have received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub s.(1) of sec tion 36. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the suit was barred by limitation because the respondent had not received the notices referred to under cl. (a), and as such, he was not entitled to any exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section(1) Of section 36. HELD : The words "all the rights of the mortgagee" used in clause(a) are wide enough to include assignment of debts" and that the interest taken by the respondent 's mortgagee was not a "proceeding in execution within the definition of section 2 (22) of the Act. [118 E] Promode Kumar Roy vs Nikhil Bhusan Mukhopadhya, , followed. Promode Chandra Roy vs Mona Kumar Mukhopada Mukhopadhaya, A.I.R. 1939 Cal. 971, approved. Promod Kumar Roy 's case, and S.K. Das vs Debabrata Roy, A I. R. 1940 Calcutta, approved; Promode Ranjan Roy vs Sashi Bhusan, A 1. R , distinguished.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. A 1 and A 2 were brothers. In 1947 he transferred to the appellant certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1948 he executed exhibit A 1 in favour of the appellant for a consideration of Rs. 45 lakhs. He also undertook to give his services only and not his properties. The respondents contended that the transfers were made by way of gifts and not in consideration of past cohabitation, and that the two deeds though ostensibly sale deeds were in reality gift deeds. were invalid and the subsequent severance of joint status in 1947 could not validate them. Held, that the alienations were without consideration and were valid. The alienation was without consideration. The transfers were without considerations and were by way Of gifts. The alienations were not hit by sec. 6(h) of the . In the alternative, the respondents contend that assuming that the transfer was made in consideration for past cohabitations, they were hit by section 6(g). The properties gifted under exhibit A I and A2 were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which Venkatacharyulu was governed he had no power to make a gift of his own property to his concordine. The invalid gifts were not validated by the disruption of the joint Hindu family in 1947. Balo vs Parbati, (1923) L.R. 43 I.A. 206, referred to.

The respondent, a Life Insurance Corporation, had taken a policy of insur ance policy from the appellant for the period from 1.4.1975 to 31.3.1976. The policy was to be operative from 5.12.75 and the premium was to commence on 30.6.76. The respondent paid the premium in advance. The L.I.C. made the requisite statement on oath under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 raising an objection that no part of the amount was due to G.V. Ranade and it was the duty of the L. I.C., to promptly make the requisite statements on oath. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the validity of the notice under clause (vii) of sub section (3) was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object and purpose of the provision are to ensure that the assessee is not deprived of his money on account of any act which he has done or omitted to do. [114G] 1.2 The object of section 226 is to prevent abuse of process of law by the Income tax authorities in the discharge of their statutory duties. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that where there is an express provision in the statute, it should be construed strictly and not in any other way. [115C D] 1:3 The object underlying section 226 of the Act is to ensure expeditious payment of interest on the amount due under the policies to the assessee. It does not contemplate a contingency of such a contingency. It only requires that the amount should be paid within a reasonable time and not beyond a period of two years from the date of accrual of the cause of action. [116E F] 1 :4 The object is to avoid multiplicity of proceedings in respect of amounts which are due under policies to an assessee. The object being to prevent evasion of tax, it is necessary that the interest should be calculated on the basis of the value of the goods sold by the assessee and not on the ground that the price of the products sold by him is less than the market value. [117F] 1 5.1 In the instant case, the L .I. C. itself has taken the stand throughout that the sum demanded by the notice issued under section226(3)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961 by the I.T.O. did not belong to the appellant inasmuch as it was payable only to the assignee, Smt. Kamalabai G. Ranale and not the defaulter. The action of the I .T.o. being the only reason given by the LI.I.,C. to justify the inordinate delay in making the requisite declaration under section 227(3), the amounts of the matured policies within the time given by it, instead of in doing so. [118G H] 1;4 The inordinate delay on the part of L.l. C., in making this statement on solemn affirmation by the appellant, was the result of misconstruction of the provisions and misappreciation of its liability thereunder. performance of this statutory obligation by the l.T., in the present case, being after inordinate delay, award of interest to the respondent, it was unnecessary to persue that writ petition when the I 'T. O. had made the order withdrawing the notice u/s 226( 3) of I. T.O., had been made the necessary statement on affidavit.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of possession of certain lands. The respondent contended that the suit was barred by limitation under section 29(2) (a) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time and therefore it was governed by section 29 (2) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that for invoking sub s.(2) Of section 29 of the Limitation Act the necessary condition is that the First Schedule thereto shall prescribe a period of limitation for an appeal and that as in the present case the First schedule had not prescribed any period of Limitation for an application under section 12(2), the requirement was that the first schedule thereto shall be prescribe a time limit of three years for an appeals and that therefore cl. (a), which provides a period Of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first Schedule, would apply even to a case where the First Sch. had not been prescribed any such period of limitations for an Appeal. Held:(i) The words "where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application" in section 29 are wide enough to include suits or appeals preferred under special or general laws and therefore they would be governed by that section. (ii)The word "suit" in the first limb of sub section (2), is not restricted to proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special, local or special law for which a period prescribed in the First Scheduled is provided in the Second Schedule. The words 'proceedings under special and local law" in cl. 2(a) are wide and include proceedings under Special or local laws for which periods of limitation are provided in tho first schedule. (iii)The words "in any suit" in sub section 2(b) mean suits or applications made by the parties to a suit, appeals or application under a particular local or Special law for such suits, appeals, applications or proceedings. The word 'suit ' is not defined in the Code of Civil Procedure but it is wide enough if the words are wide in their amplitude and include all proceedings which may be taken under special laws for the time being in force. (iv)The first limb Of sub section(2)(a) is concerned with proceedings of a kind similar to one for which period of time is provided for in the second Schedule because it is enough if special law prescribes a period which is different from any period prescribed therein in the Third Schedule.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 702 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage vehicles in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986, which was filed against the order of District Magis trate declaring the old bus stand of T.A. Section 68(2)(r) of the Act containing the provisions relating to 'control of transport vehicles ' confers the power on the State Government to make rules for the purposes of the said chapter. The appellant challenged the vires of section 76 of the , contending that the District Magi trate had no power to appoint any area as a Bus stand under section 76, of the . It was further contended that the power to fix any area was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. The High Court held that section 76 conferred wide powers on the District Commis sioner to fix the places for bus stand and that could be done only under section 68(1)(r), of the ' Act. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 76 of tho Act confers wide powers upon the State Govern ment to make Rules for the pur pose of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specifi c provision in section 68 (2)(s) of . The Municipal Council is not empowered to fix a bus stands under section76 of the. [717C D] 2. Section 78 of the provides for the appointment of the Regional transport Authority, having jurisdiction in the area, and therefore, the rules could be framed by the State Gov ernment regarding the said subject under section68(2) (r) for that purpose. The Municipal Corporation is not a 'State Transport Undertaking ' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. [617D E] 3. Section 77 of the empowers the Regional Authori ties to fix places for the bus stand orhalting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional . Transport Authority, as held by this Court in T.B. Shah vs State of Maharashtra & Ors., ; , followed. The power under section 78(2), however, could be exercised only by the Central Government having jurisdiction to determine the location or places within the Town area of Baldev (odar) as also by the appropriate Government regarding the same subject under s 68(3)(r). [618E F] 4. Section 79(1) empowers the State Govt. to make a rule for the proper control and regulation of the transport vehicles in the town. The Regional Transport Authori ty can fix any particular place or places at which the bus stands orhalt may be required by the owner or other person in charge of motor buses to stop their buses at the bus Stand. There is no provision in the Act for fixing a particular place. [613C D, G] 5. The District Magit trate could not exercise the power of fixing a bus Stand under section 77 of tho . [619D E; 613A B] 6. Section 80(2 ) empowers the appropriate Govt.to make rules regarding the conditions of service of persons in charge or other persons in respect of motor vehicles to stop only at certain places for that pur pose. The State Government has no power under the Act to fix or alter any particular area or place within the town area of the town, as a ' bus stand '

The appellants were convicted of an offence under section 7 read with section 8(1) (a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of the appellants and acquitted them. In revision to this Court it was contended that there was no attempt on the part of the appellant to commit the offence of export; that there had been an attempt on their part to export paddy outside the State of Punjab in this case, and so there was an attempt to commit an offence of sale; that the appellants were not guilty of any offence under the Act. HELD: (i) There has been no export of paddy within the meaning of para 2(a) or para 2 (b). [669 C] (ii) The fact that the Delhi Punjab boundary was, at the relevant point of time, at about the 18th mile from Delhi, and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to export or abet the export of rice. It follows therefore that there has been an export of the paddy outside this State in this ease. [669 D] (iii) There was no export or attempt on part of appellants to commit export. The fact, however, that the goods were not exported within the State is not a ground for holding that there could be an attempt at export. It was merely a preparation on the parts of the accused and as such a preparation would amount to an attempt in committing it.

The Sassoons entered into an agreement with the appellant company for the purchase of certain machinery and plant and machinery. The agreement provided that the Managing Agency Agreement would be effective from 1st April, 1948, and that the Company would pay to the Sassoon the entire remuneration received by it during the chargeable accounting period. Clause 10 provided that if the Sassoon was not paid within a period of one year from the date of assignment, the company would be liable to pay tax on the entire amount of remuneration received during the previous year and the Sasasons would be entitled to deduct the said sum as income from business profits. The Sassoors were also required to pay interest at 6% per annum on the balance of the remuneration received till the date it became payable. The Income tax Officer treated the Sascoons as a separate entity for the purpose of computing the taxable income of the assignee and taxed them in respect of the same. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but the Tribunal, on reference, held that the Sas couons had not earned any part of the Managing agency commission which had been paid by the companies to the transferees and were not liable to tax in respect thereof. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the agreement between the Sasiffors and the Company showed that the assignor and the assignee were to be treated as one entity and that on assignment the assignee became the Managing Agent as if his name had been inserted in the Managing Agents Agreement from the beginning, and the continuity of the managing Agency was preserved thereby and that whoever satisfies the description of the said Managing Agent at the time when the commission for the year becomes due, is also the person entitled to the amount by way of remuneration not as per this argument by virtue of any mutual arrangement between the assignors and assignee but by the very terms of the agreement which is the source of income. The right of the assignee to receive the entire sum did not depend on any specific term between the parties, but on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that falls due after the date Of assignment. It may be mentioned in this context that clause 10 of the Agreement showed that while it may be, that in the normal run of events the contract for remuneration under the Managing Agencies Agreement is an indivisible contract for a whole year 's remuneration on the completion of a whole years ' work, this clause necessarily implied divisibility of contract and of the consideration in the year of assignment since the assignment necessarily took place with the consent of the principal Mill Company. The mere fact that the assignment was made by the Sasiverors to the respective transferees did not affect the right of assignee to receive any part or the remuneration of the year, such a right may arise by virtue Of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee either as part of his deed of transfer or independent thereof. The fact that it may also be that in this case the Sasessee had been referred to as service and the commission therefor as remuneration for purposes of convenience, the true nature of the functioning of a Managing Agent, where it is, a firm or a Company, which so functions, has been recently held by this Court in Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son, Ltd. vs The Government of Hyderabad, ; , followed.

The appellant was a resident of the District of Gonda. He lost his wife years ago. His eldest son, Kirpa Shanker, a lad of about 8 years, was employed in Lucknow and his wife was residing with his father. It is said that he had to be persuaded through the influence of their neighbors, Mohammed Abdullah and his womenfolk, to go back to the house of the accused. The only other inmate of the house was the appellant 's second son, who lost his widow years ago, and his mother in law, and thereby finished the daily quarrels. The evidence showed that communication to another was not a necessary ingredient of the concept of "confession". The trial court convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) A statement made by an accused admitting his guilt is a confession of guilt. The Evidence Act places them in the category of relevant evidence, presumably on the ground that, as they are declarations against the interest of the person making them, they are probably true. [959 D] (2) It is implicit in the concept Of "confinement" that it shall be communicated to another. This raises an interesting point, which fails to be decided on a consideration of the relevant provisions of the Evidence Act. [963 E] (3) The probative value of an admission or a confession does not depend upon its communication to the other, though just like any other piece of evidence, it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. This proof in the case of oral admission or confession can be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or the confession, as the case may be. Even if so much was established, prudence and justice demand that such evidence cannot be made the sole ground of conviction.

The appellant, an employee of the respondent company, was appointed as a driver in the appellant 's General Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. on April 29, 1976. The terms and conditions of service were duly altered by the Central Government under section 7 of the Act. The appellant was asked to retire from service on completion of 55th year 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. On his failure to do so, he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said rule. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Board of Directors had no power to terminate the services of a permanent employee by giving one month 's salary in lieu of notice and also a direction to pay all the allowances upto that date including the period of his suspension. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "in the event of the Society not having any further need of any employee" occurring in section 7(1) of the , means permanent or temporary and that the word "may" in section 2(g) of Act means a period of one month and not a period exceeding 30 days. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The Board of Management did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of the employee occupying couched in Rule 5 also. [225F] 2.1 The expression "may", in section 3(g), means a notice or salary in addition to any notice or wage in lieu thereto. It is thus manifest that an employee, whether permanent or permanent, has an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days ' notice in writing of his intention to do it. Equally in the event, of the society not having no further need for the employee 's service, whether Permanent or temporary which shall be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days notice in written writing for termination of his service or in lieu whereof pay such employee a sum equivalent to his one month salary including allowances upto the period during which he was on duty. [226H 227A] 2:2 The expression 'in the case of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance business, immediately before the appointed day, shall become an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co. in which the undertaking of the insurer to which the service relates has vested and would hold his office on the same terms and Conditions and with the same rights to pension, gratuity and other matters as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such vesting and shall continue to do things unless and until his appointment is terminated. [227C] 2 :3 The expression `in the ease of the existing insurer ' in section 4(1)(g) means a service which is not permanent or Temporary but has an alternative employment. It does not mean that the services can be terminated by giving notice in terms of the provisions of law or the rule. [228D] 2(a) The expression used in section 6(1), means permanent, temporary or officiating and does not include a period which is capable of being terminated by one month notice or wages in lieu therefor. It may mean that it may be terminated at any time without giving one months 's pay in addition or salary. [229E] 2.(b) The word `may ' in the context means permanent temporary, temporary, or officiating. It has not been defined in the Act but its dictionary meaning is that a person can have no option to either permanently or temporarily to continue in service for any reason whatsoever and he may be required to serve in any other manner. [230F] 3.1 In the instant case, the Board did not abolishing the post nor put an rest to the services.

The appellants were the successful bidders for a licence under section 6 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act 1915. The Collector issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to show cause why the license should not be cancelled for failure to comply with the provisions of the amended section 29(2) of the Act. The appellants submitted their explanation and the Collector called upon them by his letter dated April 15, 1970 to submit their reply within two weeks from the date of receipt of the notice failing which they were liable to pay a penalty of Rs. 1,000/ . The appellants did not accept the said explanation and proceeded to auction the shops on the basis that the licence was granted for a period of five years. The appellant challenged the validity of the order by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court quashed the direction of the State Government dated April 18, 1970 for reauctioning the license and declared that rule 103(1) of Bihar and Or Orissa Excise (Amendment) Ordinance 1970 was ultra vires the Act and directed the Collector to call for tenders in accordance with that order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 6(a) of Amending Ordinance, 1970 was not made retrospective in operation and that the High court erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the grant of an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sellliquor. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The State has the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor. It has the "power to hold a public auction for the granting of such a right or privilege and to accept payment of a sum therefor. The power to hold an auction for grant of such right or privileges is not conferred on the Board of Revenue. [785C] 2. Section 6(1)(a) does not make any distinction between a "privilege" and a "public auction". It merely provides that the State may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare its intention to do so. The expression "public auctions" is used in contradistinction to a "procurement of country liquor". [786D] 3. Section 2(a)(i) of Act 17 of 1970 was amended by the Amending Ordinance No. 17 of 1971 which came into force on April 1, 1972. It does not deal with the grant or renewal of licences for manufacture and sale of liquor. The words "public tenders" are wide enough to include all public auctions held in pursuance of a notification issued under section 4(1). [787E] 4. Section 3 of the Amending Act of 1970 is a provision which provides that no person shall be entitled to any licence or permit for the manufacture and selling of liquor except under the authority of a licence granted by the State Excise Commissioner. The amended section 6 was not retrospective in nature. It merely provided that the Board may, after giving the appellant an opportunity of being heard, issue a fresh notice to him requiring him to showcause why he should not pay the penalty imposed on him. [777F] 5. Section 4(2)(a)(ii) of amended section 30 of the by Act 17 Of 1970 is not retrospective and it does not affect the power of the Board to grant or renew licences for manufacturing and sale "liquor". The High ' Court was therefore right in holding the sale notification issued by Collector was invalid and the writ petition No. 2091 of 1972 is allowed, the impugned judgment of the High 'Court dated April 16, 1971 is set aside and the Writ Petition No. 1855 1863 of 1972 are restored.

The appellant was charged with the offence of murder under section 302 read with section 120B, I.P.C., and section 302, I P.C. The prosecution case against him was that he had purchased the silver material from accused No. 2 and on 27 12 1967 the deceased went to the bungalow of Dr. Nanavati and asked him to take out the key of the godown which he had seen. On 27 12 67 the deceased took out all the goods from the house of Dr, Nanavati. The appellant was convicted under section 304 Part I, I,.P. C., and sentenced to death. The High Court reduced the sentence of accused No 2 to one of life imprisonment. In appeal by special leave it was contended that there was corroboration in regard to accused No 3 in material particulars in regard lo the connection of the appellant with the crime and in regard thereto the common intention was not lost sight of. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The High court rightly came to the conclusion that there were sufficient corroboration of the evidence which connected accused No, 3 and were guilty of the offence. [621 B] (2) There was no infirmity in the evidence as to whether there was any infirmity in evidence or not. The discovery of articles in the godown of Takalkar was as a result of a statement by accused No 1. The name of accused 2 was found in the note book of Taknkar. The relationship of father and son between accused No., 3 and accused No 4 is not to be lost sight. Accused No. 3 went together for the sale of cycle carrier to Rupvate. The evidence of the tailor was that those articles were given by accused Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 who afterwards returned the key and gave it to accused 1. There was also a piece of hand writing with the signature of accused NO. 2 at the foot of it and that was the list of the articles sold to Gadekar. [625 E F] (3) The evidence regarding the nature of the transaction is not sufficient to connect accused No; 3 with murder.
