The fact that there is capital sentence of Accused No, 2 and 3 is not a ground for interference by this Court in appeal against acquittal.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the final scheme. The Town Planning Officer under section 32(1)(iii) of the Bombay City Municipal Act, 1888 framed a scheme for the area 87 in respect of which the declaration had been made and published it in the prescribed manner. Under section 64(1) (f), the amount by which the total value of the plots in the provisional scheme with all the buildings and works thereon allotted to a person falls short of or exceeds the total amount to be deducted therefrom under any of the provisions of this Act, the net amount of his loss shall be payable to him by the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. The appellant 's case was that the Town Planning officer had a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect thereof from the local authorities and partly from such person as the Town planning Officer may in each case determine. The respondent contended that the Act specifies a principle of compensation, it is observed in Shantilal 's Case at page 357 of the report: "It is true that under the Act the market value of land at the date of declaration of intention to make a scheme determines the amount to he adjusted, and that is the guiding rule in respect for all lands covered by the scheme. (v) estimate the portion of the sums payable as compensation on each plot used, allotted or reserved for a public purpose or purpose of the local Authority which is beneficial partly to the owners or residents within the area of the scheme and partly to general public, which shall be included in the costs of the Scheme; The Town planning officer under section 33(1), (iii) has to find out the market Value of each of the original plots at the time of declaration. Under clause (xiii) the Town Development Officer is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner in cash and in such manner as may, in each ease determine." The respondent 's contention was that since the appellant had not been provided with a plot, he could not claim compensation under section 64. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Under the Act, it would be the value of a reconstituted plot or not; compensation is payable on the basis of the market price of the land at that date. [876B] 2. The principle for determining the compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted Plot or not and compensation is paid on the footing of the value at the the date on which the declared intention to makes a scheme. In the instant case, the Town development officer under Section 32(i)(iii), has to estimate and determine the amount of compensation to he paid to him. The owner of an original plot who is not provided with the plot in his final scheme gets his right to compensation from section 71 of the Act which says that the net value of such property or right shall be determined on the principles of market value at that place. [888C D] 3. Under cl. (xiii), the Town Improvement Officer is empowered to estimate a sum to be fixed by him in cash, or in any other way, as may he agreed upon between the parties and not according to the final plot. The proviso to this clause states that the amount payable as compensa tion on each plots included in a final scheme shall be deducted from or added to, as the case may be, the contributions leviable from such persons. [898E F] 4. Under Clause (xiii)(a) the town planning officer is required under section 68 to estimate compensation to the extent to which the value has been determined by him.

The appellant, who was the third son of the deceased, had a brother Seetharama Iyer who died in 1934. He left two daughters surviving him who were minors at the time of his death. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties and for possession of the same. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right to choose in such circumstances applies also to India also, and had further held that on the construction of the will it was for Seetharams or in the legatees, and that on construction of a will it took effect. Held, that the words "he shall deliver possession of all the remaining properties to my son" show that it was Seetharamas who was to make the selection and give the devised land to the two daughters and stress was laid on the words 'he shall give to the female children". The intention of the testator was clearly to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legateees making the selection in the order in which they were named in the will. The words " he shall deliver Possession of the remaining property to his son" showed that it meant that the daughters would get their lands after taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. The gift cannot be said to be void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, for it can be made certain by the selection of the daughters and is not so uncertain that it is impossible to make it certain.

The plaintiff and the defendants were in joint possession of plots in dispute. The plaintiff and defendants were co sharers of the plots in question, being co bhumidars, because after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. After the abolition, the Zamindari was abolished and the Zamindari vested in the State. In the consolidation proceedings, separate plots were carved out and she was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants or by anyone else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. The suit was contested by the defendant mainly on the ground that the defendants had practised fraud on her by giving an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. The trial court accepted the allegations of the defendants and dismissed the suit of the appellant. The District Judge, however, found that on the admitted facts even after the Abolition of Zamindari, the position was that in 1357 Fasli the plaintiff 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants, and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. In second appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the District Judge and dismissed her suit for joint possession as far as plots Nos. 201 and 274 are concerned and restored that judgment of the trial court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The findings of fact recorded by the courts below are not sustainable in law and the judgment of High Court cannot be allowed to stand. [867C] 2.1 In view of the clear decision of this Court referred to above, the question whether a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the respondents or by somebody else as the result of Which the rights were sought could not be extinguished is not correct. The High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the defendant assured the plaintiff that her name shall be entered in the record during the Consolidation proceedings. [889D E] 2:2 In view Of the clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraudulent fraud was made to drop the appellant 's names from the revenue records and full advantage was taken of the consolidation operations in the village by the Respondents, it is not open to the High court to interfere with this finding of facts in second appeal. [879E] 2 :3 The High court erred in holding the present Suit was barred under section 49 Of the U .P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1952 or that of the defendant.

The petitioner was appointed as Deputy Prime Minister of India in the year 1950. He was later transferred to Haryana and his appointment was challenged by Respondent No. 1 on the ground that he was still functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. The High Court dismissed the petition for the reasons indicated above. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: (1) In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Chief Minister but the description of him as Deputy Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Minister along with his other submis sions, this court is of the view that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to it, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. [319D E] Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , referred to. (2) The requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [340B] Virjibhai Ram Sutari vs Natulal Premanji Bhavadia, & Ors.

The appellant, a public utility undertaking, put up a notice that the stoppage of work on the 1st November did amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the Factories Act. The management put up the notice that it was not entitled to holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Act because they would not have completed a period of 12 months ' continuous service in the factory, and that the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounted to a strike. Held, that the action of the appellant on the night of 1st 11 1948 fell within the definition of the word "strike" as given in section 2(q) of ' the and it was an illegal strikes and the workers thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The fact that a very large number of leave applications were put in for various reasons pointed to the concerted action and that appli cation given by the workers and their representatives also indicated that they were acting in combination both in striking and refusing to go back to work on that day would not be treated as depriving them of the holidays under the Rules. The decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal on this point was set aside and it directed that the holidays at full rates as provided for in section 49 A of the , will have to be calculated in respect of the operatives concerned on the footing that there was no break in the continuity of their service by the stoppage or of work.

The appellant, a film producer, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1 lakh in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case against him was that he had given the certificate 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings, and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censorors. The High Court dismissed the petition, ignoring the contention that the film had been given 'A certificate by Central Board Of Film Carnors and found in the Prosecution nothing frivolous nor vexatious nor anything to quash any proceedings. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 5A of the Act is exculpatory when read with section 5A, of the Penal Code and Part II of the , relating to certification of films. If, as here, the Board certifies a film as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292 l.P.,C. prescribes. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 exonerates them at least in view of their bona fide belief that the certificate is justificatory. [517 B C] 2. The offence under section 293 I. P.C., is exculpatory, when read alongwith section 5 A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and the certificate issued thereunder. If the offender can irrefutably establish that he is actually justified by law in doing it, then also, the exception operates and the bona fide believe, though mistaken, eliminates the culpability. If a person can irreliably establishthat he is really justified by Law in doing the act or, alternatively, that he entertained a mistake of fact and in good faith believed that he was justified bylaw in committing the act, then, the weapon of section 79 demolishes the prosecution. [525 E F] 3. The Board under section 5B has to consider, before certification, all the points section 292 1.P .C. prescribe. At best as a matters of interpretation section 79 I.p.C.; resolves the apparent conflict between section 292 and Part 11 of the . If, As here,the Board of Civilensors acting within their jurisdiction and on an application made and pursued in good bonafide faith, sanctions the public exhibition, the producer and connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 79 exonerated them at almost all. [511 F G] 4. The trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under the Act and, in the light of our observations, it fills the bill under section 79 it is right for the Court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. [ 511 E F; 512 A B] 5. Section 79 is exculpatory while read with Section 5 A, of I.T. Act. The certificate issued under section l0(1A) of the Indian Penal Code by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under s 292 I P. C. driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the Certificate of the Board notwithstanding, the films was offensive ? The Board is right in discharging the accused, as the charges are groundless.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an agent of the State Government in all the civil cases. He was later promoted as an Advocate by the High Court and continued to hold office till he attained the age of superannuation. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the Bihar Land Reforms (Fixation of Ceiling on Land) Act, 1961, which came into force with effect from 1st April, 1962. In the writ petition filed in this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution, it was contended that his client 's claim as the sole representative of the Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. Dismissing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The duties of the Govern ment Pleader, Madras are duties of a public nature. (36) The duties and functions of the Public Prosecutor, Madras, are duties which are of an independent and responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [763E] 2.1 In every suit or proceeding to which the Government is a party or a public officer acting in his official capacity is a Party, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [764G H] 2:2 The duties or functions of Government pleader are duties and of a Public nature. [774A B] 3.1 The duties, of the public servants are duties as of a private character. (37) The State Government Pleader is only an agent to the Government who are his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of aPublic office. [777C] 3:3 In a sense every member of the legal profession, has a higher dedication to the people. The time has come to examine the quality of the product or service, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the persons who are the third world clients, and practise internal distributive justice oriented on basic social justice so that the profession may flourish without wholly hitching the calling to the star of material amassment immunised by law from the liabilities of other occupations. [779E] 3 :4 The learned Attorney General appearing for the State was critical of a lawyer asking for or cling to briefs and counsel for the petitioner (a former High Court Chief Justice) rightly slurred over the pecuniary part of the petition and veneered his submissions with the law of the High office of government pleadership. But before we come to that, let it be bluntly stated that if Government does an act offending the public office filled by a Government pleader what becomes the incumbent in the land of Gandhi is a dignified renunciation of office not a chase for the lost briefs through the 'writ ' route.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of it in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by them in this company. At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the bank held on May 6, 1948 a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the Mills and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the ratio of 1:1. The face value of the new shares was to be Rs. 100 for acquiring the new share. The mills as the holder of 5,00,000 share became entitled to receive 1,66,62 shares of this company at the rate of Rs. 200 per share. 50 as premium per each share and it is considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said Bank the funds of this Company to the extent of 66 shares only and to distribute the right of this shareholders to the remaining 1,600 shares of that company in the manner specified in section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act. The appellants held that the distribution amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Income tax Act and as such liable to be set aside under section 66(1)(a). The Tribunal, however, held that it was not necessary for the Mills to distribute any dividend. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the distributed right to apply for and obtain two shares of a Bank of Indian company amounted to distribution of dividend within the ambit of section 1(6 A) of Income tax ' Act. It did not take into account both the normal and the extended meaning of that expression in section 2 (6A). The High Court had rightly held that distribution of the right to applied for and obtained two shares amounted to transfer of the rights. The form of the resolution sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the Resolution could not be altered. It took the form of distribution of a right which had a monetary value.

The appellant was declared elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly from the State of Haryana. The election petitioner filed an Election Petition challenging the election of the returned candidate on various grounds, namely (1) that the respondent had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951; and (2) that he was not entitled to be declared elected as a member of the Legislative Assembly. The High Court rejected both the contentions and dismissed the Election Petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1 ) the requirement of sub rule (1A) of Rule 1 of order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the court is necessary; and that the failure to mention the name of a witness in the list envisaged by sub rule(1) of rule 1 would enable the Court to decline to examine such witness, and (ii) the omission to mention his name in the List contemplated by sub Rule (1), would not have omitted to mention that only those witnesses kept present could be examined whose names are mentioned in the lists envisaged by Sub rule (I) of r. 1. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule is in relation to the witnesses to procuring whose presence assistance of court is t necessary. If mere omission to specify the name or the gist of evidence in the form envisaged by Rule 1A would enable Court to refuse to examine the witness who is present in the Court without the assistance, of the Court, it was not necessary to provide in Rule 1 A that the party may bring any witness to give evidence or to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1. [532C D] (b) The only jurisdiction the Court has to decline the examination of the witness is the one set out in proviso to Section 87 of the 1951 Act which enables the court for reasons to be recorded in writing to refuse examination any witness or witnesses if it is of the opinion that the evidence of such witness or witness is not material for the decision of the petition or that the Party tendering such witness and witnesses is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. [525E F] (c) The failure to specify in the order XVI Rule 1(A) would enable it to decline examination of such a witness, if it was of the view that the name was not mentioned in sub rule.(1) and who can be produced without the aid of the party, and kept present when the evidence is being recorded and is not closed, and the Court had no jurisdiction to refuse examine the witnesses who are called to produce document under Rule lA. [455H; 526A] (d) The omission to include the name in a list envisaged under sub Rule(1), by itself would not enable the court to decline its examination on the short ground that the names of the witnesses and the gist thereof have not been set out In the list prepared under sub clause (2). [530B C] (e) The requirement of Sub rule(3) of Order XVI is that the person who has to produce a document should be examined by the Court on the sole ground that he has sufficient cause for the omission, to mention in the notice issued under Rule I. But where the party wants assistance of Court to procure presence of a person on being summoned through the court, it is obligatory on the party to file the list with the gist and of evidence of witness in Court as directed by sub clause(1).

The appellant was appointed as Principal of a College in the year 1981. He was later transferred to another college where he was working as Principal. The Committee of Management of the College issued an appointment order on April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of management had suspended or withdrawn its power. The appellant challenged the said order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which held that the radiogram dated April 7, 1981 contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee was not competent to make any appointment and therefore it had no power to set up a selection committee nor the selection committee had any power to make appointment and accordingly the appointment of the appellant alleged to have been made on May 1, 1981 was not valid. The High Court held that radiograms dated April 3, 1981 were invalid because they contained an express order of State Government which in discharge was not communicated to the Manager of the Institution. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) There is no merit in the submission because the letter dated May 1. 1981 which has been extracted hereinbefore clearly shows that on April 7. 1981 the order contained in the radiagram had suspended and withdrawn its powers. The appointment was otherwise valid though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the appellants. [980 G H] (2) The letter dated April 27 which has also been extracted above clearly shows the fact that on the date on which appellant was appoint ed as Principal the Committee had the power to appoint notwithstanding the fact, that its power to making appointment was suspended remained intact and therefore, the appointment was not invalid. [981 C D] (3) The order contained an executive order which is in conflict with the provisions of the Act and the scheme of Administration envisages the setting up of a Selection Committee for selecting candidates for appointment as Head of an Institution as provided in sec 16 F. The regulations confer power on the State government without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation as also make such other order consistent with the provision of the act as it deems necessary and in particular, may by such order modify or cancel or make any regulation in respect of any matter. [979 G H; 980 A B] (4) The appointment is otherwise valid, though ineffective, ineffective and not if it may be invalid. If appellant under orders of High Court functioned to discharge his duties as Principal discharged his functions and was pay paid, there would be no question for recovery of any amount paid by him to the institution.

The petitioners, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner". The petitioners state that the manufacturers of goods to whom they were sold "im Pregnate" the fabric which they sell in the market. They further contended that, since the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product", it was a question of fact and should have been decided by the High Court. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The view of the High court that there is no error apparent on the face of the record and that the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the "tyre cord fabric" is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or merely cord pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric, is not correct. [501 B] 2. The question whether the goods under consideration constitute a fabric which is a textile? is one which should decide the question. It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "Textile" and an evaluation of opinion of experts on the subject, to be able to decide the questions satisfactorily may also require some examination of commercial usage and terminology or the language of the market in goods of this type. [504 C D] 3. The meaning of the term "textiles", given in the Oxford Dictionary is: "A woven fabric; any kind of cloth". Apparently, it is more than that. It is, therefore, difficult to find fault with the view of High Court that there was no error on the record. [403 D] 4. The case of the Delhi Cloth Mills also is that the product is a. The use of the word "textile" in item 22 in the context of manufacturing of the goods would not make it clear that the products are more correctly described as "a textile". [502 F G] 5. The High Court was right in holding that there has been no error of law apparent on its face and that there had been no mistake apparent on record.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied work. The respondent No. 4 was a Senior Supervisor in the Company 's establishment at Dhanbad. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court Patna. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the management transferred the case to Labour court, Patna. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Dhanbad regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court Dhanbad and transfer the said proceeding to the Labour court Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of transfer on the ground that it was passed without jurisdiction as it was not passed by an authority subordinate to him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government was misled by the representation of the workman and transferring the case from the labour Court, etc. to Labour Courts, Patna should have given an opportunity to t he management. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the key question for consideration is whether the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workmen and transferring it from the Labour Courts Dhanbad to labour court should have afforded an opportunity of representing his views when any order to the prejudice of the normal procedure laid down in Section 64(1) and (2) of the Act is sought to be made against him, be it a transfer from one Income Tax Officer within the State to an Income Tax officer without it, except of course where the very object of the transfer would be frustrated if notice was given to the party affected. [295C D] 1.2 The Government was induced by the representations of the respond ent and without affording any opportunity of being heard to the appel lant. This takes us to the reasons given by the Government in support 'of the order transferring the cases from the Industrial Court, Patna to Labour courts, Patna, regu tered. Reference may also be made to a letter dated September 8, 1988 (Annexure D) from the Assistant Electrical Engineer in proof of the electricity supplied to the quarter occupied by the workman at Dhanbad and not seriously disputed the factum of his residence in the colony quarter at Dhanbad.[295C] 1:3 The order of transferring in that case was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee. This took us to 'the reasons given in support of the order dated August 8,1988 by which the Government of Bihar transferred the cases to Labour Cour t Court, Ranchi. In fact, in the counter affidavit he has not denied the documents annexed to the Special Leave Petition, and not adversely disputed the fact of his permanent residence in Dhanbad. [296D E] 1 :4 The order transferring in this case was quashing for not reasons to tho assessee. It took us through the letter dated Septem ber 8,88 (Annexure F) from Assistant Electrical Engi neer in proofof the electricity supply supplied to it at Dhanbad, and also the letter of the Headmaster of the School in which the children of the work man are studying.

The appellant, a hotel Workers ' Union, was an industrial dispute which was referred for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal referred the dispute to the Additional Industrial Tribunal, Delhi including the terms of reference. The Additional Industrial Commissioner, Delhi, held that the reference was incompetent and two grounds were urged in support of it; namely, (1) the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , (2) the Union could not make a party, and (3) the reference being vague, as it did not indicate how many of the workmen of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the words "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " which appear in the order of reference make it incompetent, inasmuch as the Union can not be said to have made a Party to the Reference under the . The fact that in the application for reference the words were added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not make the reference incompetent. The fact therefore that in this case the dispute was also about workmen to whom notice of dismissal had been given and in that connection the names of the workman concerned were mentioned in the orders of reference, and the names Of the workmen concerned were also mentioned in that order of Reference. The words " as represented by" in section 10(1) of the Act give power to the appropriate government where it is of opinion that an industrial Dispute exists or is apprehended to refer the dispute for adjudication. It cannot be denied on the facts of this case that there was a dispute between the hotel and its workmen and it went to this length that the hotel decided to dismiss a large number of workmen on October 7, 1955. The objection further is that even if the workman is entitled to be represented by an officer of a trade union of which he is a member, the reference in this Case does not mention any officer of the trade union but mentions the union itself. This in our opinion was a technicality upon technicality for the union not being a living person can only be served through some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will really represent the workmen before the Tribunal, and it was that officer which would really represent workmen before tho tribunal, and not that officer whom the dispute is of a Trade Union of which the workman was a member.

The appellant imported certain parts of the engine, such parts would be parts of engines, such part will get the benefit of exemption under the Notification. The appellant claimed that these parts were parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading No. 84.06 and Heading No 84.07. The Additional Collector of Customs rejected this claim on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit thereof in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the parts were classifiable under heading 84.09 and Heading 84.08 and Heading Nos. 8406 and 84.05 were not applicable to the facts of the case. The Customs authorities appealed to this Court. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 In order to avail of the benefit under the notification, it has to be proved that the part in respect thereof is parts of a internal combustionpon engines, as mentioned under Heading 84,06, such Parts will get exemption under Notification irrespective of the fact that they or any or some of them have already been included under Heading Nos 84.6 and 8406. [84F] 1.2 In the instant case, there is no material or evidence nor is there any finding of the Appellate Authority or Customs authorities that the bushes imported are parts of external combustion pists engines falling within Heading No . 84.04. The Notification does not, however, contain or refer to the Parts of internal Affection Piston engine engines, but also to 'parts thereof '. [85F] 2.1 The Notification exempts also parts of an engine, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, and also the parts thereof. [86G] 2:2 In order that exemption will be granted in respect Of parts of machinery mentioned under heading No. 8.06, it is necessary that the Parts mentioned under headings 8.07 to 8.08 should be all parts of such engines or engines. [87F] 3. The notification does not contain or refers to the parts of any of the parts mentioned under Chapter 84. The intention of the Notification is clear enough to provide that the goods specified in Heading No, 84.03 and 8.05 should get the exemption under that Notification irrespective irrespective of fact that there they or some or some others have already included under heading Nos. 807 to808. [88G H] 3:1 The words "parts of such engine or parts" are not used in the Notification, but only refer to internal combustion Pistons and not to 'Parts thereof". [87H; 88A] 3 :3 In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption would be granted if in respect to parts of machines mentioned under Item 8.09, such goods are parts or some parts thereof, it includes the parts which must he all the part constituting the engines or the engines, mentioned under item 8.10. [89B] 4:4 The Notification is not intended to confer a benefit on the parts covered by the Notification and in the absence thereof, the provisions of the notification will get that exemption as provided in the notification. [90F] 5:5 In the present case there is nothing on record to show that the Customs authorities have proceeded to take any action for the purpose of granting the exemption. The Collector of Central Excise, Bombay vs M/s. Pio Food Packers Ltd., ; , relied upon.

The appellants plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the right and management of the Dargah according to Muslim Law devolved on their two sons and one daughter, namely, Sayed Gastagir and Fathima Bee in proportion of 2:2 respectively. The defendants sent a reply stating that the plaintiffs claiming through female were not entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Dargah and even if they were entitled to claim any right of ownership, the same was barred by limi tation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the rights of Fathma Bee had become barred by limitation. The first appellate Court confirmed the decree. In second appeal, the High Court held that the defendants were not enti tled to any share in offerings in Dargah and that even if she had got any right, the said was lost as she did not claim any title till her death. Hence this appeal by the plaintiffs. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High court was right in holding that Fathimma Bee was a co sharer in the right of management and possession of the Wakf properties as well as the offerings. [529F] 1.2 There is no dispute now as regards the period of 27 days falling to the share of the plaintiffs and on the question that females are also entitled in the rights and management, or offerings of Dargah according t o Muslim Personal Law that title was denied, and she was expressly ousted out from the enjoyment of any share In the right, title was denial of Fatima Bee. [525G] 1:3 The only dispute now left is whether there was absolutely no evidence whatsoever to show at any point of time till her lifetime that Fafima Bee ever made a demand or asked for a share of Hundial collections as such it should be held that her rights had become extinguished by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathiman Bee had lost their right by ouster. [511B] 1 :4 There is nothing on record to show that any such question was raised or decided that females were not dis tinguished from the right or claim of any shares in the Wakf property. The only issue now left for be determined was whether the rights were expressly denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiff of Ftathima Sai Bee. This clearly goes to show, that relations between Fathyam Bee and her brothers were cordial and as a result thereof there was no question of any knowledge to Fathmatima Bee that she was being ousted from her right or share. [430C D] 1;5 The only question now left before the High Courts is whether they were claiming ouster on the basis of expressed denial of FAatima Saiyed from the fight or management of Dargah or any claim in the offering. [500D E] 2.1 There is also no controversy now as regard the period when 27 days fell to the shares of Fafma Bee. The plaintiffs were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under Muslim Law were not disentitled to any rights of management or posses sion in a Dargah and on that account they were pleading an ouster of Ffathima pair. Thus there was nothing on the record to indicate at any stage of time before her death in 1957 that Fatimma had ever made any demand or called for share of offerings as such, it should he held that she had asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of F.

The appellant was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the house rent allowances claimed by the 1st respondent came within the purview of the definition of "wages" contained in the Act. Held, that the rule which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplates that an employee posted at one of those places will cease to be entitled to the allowance if either the Government provides accommodation to the employee in question or the employee refuses to occupy the quarters so offered to him. The rules do not make the grant in such absolute terms. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases to be so entitled to his house rent and that allowance thus ceases to become "wages". The rule does not create any absolute right in the employee to the house Rent Allowance. It is equally clear that the rules which must include the rule quoted above are inconsistent with some of the terms Of the definition. That being so, there is no validity in the argument advanced on behalf of the 1 st respondent that rule 3(i) aforesaid is 1353 inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Act because it is no more payable under the terms contemplated by the contract between tile employer and employee contemplate that an employees posted at any one of these places will ceased to be "wages", within the meaning of the term in the definition in the , because it was no more than payable under tho terms of the contract.

The detenu was one Indru 's son, Ram Chand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 435 of 1980, the detenu is said to have purchased a diamonds from one Indu 's Ramchand Bharvani. On February 16, 1980, an order of detention was made by the State Government under section 3(1) of the (for short COFEPOSA) by which the detenu was served on the detenus. The detenu challenged the detention mainly on the ground that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the nature of the documents relied upon in the grounds of detention, and that the material relied upon by the detaining authorities in the ground of detention were more than sufficient to enable him to make an effective representation. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The supply of the earlier statements which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been with held could not, by any reckoning, expose those persons to any alarm or danger at the hands of the agents or partisans of the detenu. [353E] 2. There was unreasonable delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the detenus, of the material that had been relied upon or referred to in the "grounds" of detention. There were thus an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply of those portions of statements after satisfying itself that their disclosure would be against the public interest, the appropriate authority could, after due application of its own mind, make an order under clause (6) of Article 22 of the Constitution withholding the supply supply of these portions of the statements after satisfied itself that its disclosure would not be against public interest. [355H; 356A] 3. The delay of nearly a month, in supplying copies to detenus, was thus vitiated the detention. [356B] 4. There had been unreasonable delay in supplying them to the detenu, of these material facts and documents to the petitioners has vitiated the impugned detention. It is obvious that the supply supplied earlier statements were entirely different from those which were relied upon and referred to or referred in the 'grounds ' of detention.[355E F] 5. The detaining authority without applying its mind had to the circumstances of the case, mechanically refused as desired by the Collector, to supply the copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated February 14, 1980 which, in fact, was received by the detenus on April 3, 1980.

The respondents were tried jointly by the trial Court and the High Court. The High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A joint appeal is not maintainable under Cr. P.C. on the ground that it has been filed in the form of a petition in writing presented by the appellant and his counsel. The rule of law is that when the earlier decision of two judges of the same High Court in Beorajan 's case was cited before the learned Judges who heard the appeal, they took on themselves to say that the previous decision was wrong, instead of following the usual procedure in case of difference of opinion with an earlier decision. [415 D] (2) The Full Bench decision of the Gujarat High Court rightly distinguished and explained this decision. As observed earlier, once the judgment of the High court mainly proceeds merely to lay down the correct rule of the law, then there cannot be much difficult in upholding the maintainability. of a Joint appeal by a State against more than one accused persons. [416 E] (3) The High ' Court was wrong in holding the joint appeal not to be maintainable and in summarily rejecting the same. [414 G] (4) The decision of this Court in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's Case does not militate against the validity of a separate appeal by two sons convicted at one trial.

The appellant was a firm called O.R.M.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such is not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 Act but only receipt of the income in British India was assessed and it cannot therefore be held that the foreign business of the appellant was charged to tax under the 1918 Income tax. The High Court, however, allowed the assessee 's appeal holding (i) that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 25(3) in respect of interest on securities as well; (ii) that in view of the provisions of section 14(2) of 1918 Act the foreign income derived from business must be taken to be the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such discontinuance; and (iii) that there was no tax on the foreign company 's income. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Indian Income tax law did not permit the assessee to claim exemption under s 25(2), because, the assessee had only taxed on remittances received from the profits of the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. HELD : (i)(a) The exemption under S.25(3), is general and must be given effect to. [912 D] (b) The Indian Income Tax Act, 1918, was enacted with a view to provide for the levy of tax on income derived by an assessee in British territory. It was not intended that the income should be charged under the provisions Of the 1918 Acts. The exemption is general. The ratio of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held to be applicable to the case.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of the Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. The contractor received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department was a works contract. " The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a work contract. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a works Contract. The High court was wrong in answering the question against the assessee. [163F] 1.2 In Chandra Bhan Gosain`s case (supra) the contractor could not sell the bricks to third parties without previous permission of the company. In Chandra B Bhan Gosan`s Case this Court observed as follows: "lt may be presumed that it was understood in quote his rate for the bricks, the appellant would take into account the free supply of earth for making the bricks. The property in the bricks was entirely of the assesse. The essence of the contract was, therefore, the delivery of the bricks after manufacture. [164G H] 1:3 In Chandrabha Bhan Gosin`s ease this Court held that the contractor was bound to complete the work and to supply materials at the rates mentioned in the contract. The material shall remain at the contractor 's risk till the date of final delivery. in Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain vs State of Orissa, ; , followed.

The petitioner, a member of the Lok Sabha, was alleged to have committed an offence under section 3(1) read with section 5(2) of the Jammu and Kashmir Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988. The Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3rd December, 1971 by the President of India was either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation on 4th February, 1972. The petitioner contended that the duration of the House of People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2)of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd Dec., 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra rites the Constitution had no effect and consequently all Acts passed by the House during the extended period including the Finance Act 1976 were ultra vires. The respondents contended that in view of the provisions contained in Article 352 of the constitution, the President could not have validly extended the period of the Proclamation of Proclimations of emergency to a period not exceeding one year at a time. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The two Productions of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament until they were duly revoked by the two Houses of parliament. [475G] 1.2 The production of the Rajya Sabha Debates and of the Vidhan Sabha containing the proceedings of the two House of Parliament relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were passed in each of the said two Houses had not been published in the official Gazette. The period of five years (being the period for which the House may, under clause (4) of Article 83, continue from the date appointed for its first meeting in relation to the present House of the People shall, while the Proclamation issued on the 3rd day of December,1971 and on the 25th day of June,1975 are both in operation, be extended for a period of one year. [427C D] 1:3 The production and distribution of the papers relating to Emergency were retained by virtue Of the resolutions dated 27th March, 1977 passed by Parliament until it was duly revoked or revoked by two Houses. Since the two proclamions of Emergency had been duly published in official reports of the both Houses, the Proclamation dated 3th December, 1970 and the resolution of the Legislative Assembly approving the two resolutions have been duly approved by the Houses of the Parliament. [414D E] 1 :4 The production or distribution of papers relating thereto to Emergency was kept in operation by virtue virtue of its resolutions passed on the Houses by Parliament till they were fully revoked by both the Houses. [416E F] 2:5 The production, of the Gazette and the Rajya Assembly Debates containing the proceeding of the three Houses of Legislature relating to period between 1st April, 1971 and 26th August 1975 respectively had been kept in custody by virtue the resolutions of the Houses passed on that date. Since both Proclomations of Proclamation of 3rd March, 1976 and 25 th June, 1974 were in force when the House was passed its validity cannot be questioned. [420G H] 2.6 The production in the Lok Assembly Debates and the Lok assembly containing the Proceedings of the one Houses of India relating to periods between the date when the resolution was moved in each House of these two Houses have been kept In force by reason of the resolution passed by them approving the said Procluations of Pro Clamations. [411D E; 411A] 2 :7 The production that the Lok Committee Debates and Rajya Sabha Secretariat had approved the two resolution have been fully published in both the houses of Parliament.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the premises in question constituted a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. The said application was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High Court. He was therefore entitled to leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b). The respondents contended that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of the family and that it was alienable property and therefore capable of a valid transfer. HELD: (i) The question whether the property was a private or a public temple could have no market value and, therefore, was incapable of valuation. [157 E] (ii) The appellant 's case was that in execution of the decree in suit No. 650 of 1882 passed against the said Kuppaiyan the property belonged to and was an alienable private property. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on valuation made by him therefor. [158 G] (iii) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the subject ' matter of the dispute was the public temple or a private temple, it was incapable Of valuation. The appellant claimed that the property in question was a public Temple within the definition of Madras Madras Act 1 of 1951 and therefore incapable of value. [156 A] (iv) The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 656 of 1882. He did not claim any right or title to the property. The case of the respondents was that the said property belonged exclusively to the Thoguluva family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the Family.

The appellant, a retired employee of the respondent company, was re employed as a clerk in the appellant 's concern. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant and they urged that the practice started by the appel lant of re employing retired persons should be discontinued. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per day and the subordinate staff as. /6/ per month on all working days in lieu thereof should be allowed cash allowance to them. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellant ' s grievance against the direction in the award that it is not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the taffin of its employees. [572 E] (ii) The Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the respondent in re employing the retired personnel was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. When it appeared to the appe lant 's counsel that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant sympathetically and generously considered their request for re employment and that is, the basis on which some of the re employments have been made. [574 F] (iii) The fact that a re employed person has made an application before the Tribunal for relief under section 10(1)(c) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, cannot affect the validity of the said direction.

The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. The respondent filed a suit for attachment of the cheques lying with the Reserve Bank. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law, and (ii) the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". HELD : (i ) The money in the hands of the Reserve bank had ceased to be provident fund moneys and was liable to be attached. But the Union of India was a trustee for the subscriber of the money. When the amount lying with it was transferred by the Reserve to the Browne, the money remained at the disposal of the Railway Administration. [1213 F] (ii). The Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal of attachment. The order of attachment of 'the amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway Administra tration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . [1214 G] (iii) The Union of india was a Trustee for the respondent and it had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into sterling and to remit it to Browne.

The appellant, a pump manufacturing enterprise, issued a notice ending the employment and offering one month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing orders. The appellant offered one month"s pay to him as authorised by the Standing Orders. The Management accepted the offer and offered one months 's salary in lieu of notice. The management passed an order terminating the services of the appellant without any stigma attached to it. The Labour Court held that the motivation for the termination was the suspicion which lurked in the mind of the Regional Manager that information regarding tenders was being passed on by the workman '. In appeal, this Court, HELD : (1) The power of the court to go behind the form of the order is reaffirmed there. For instance Vaidialingam J., dissenting), that if the termination of service is a colourable exercise of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. It was not necessary for this Court to interfere with a finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point. [495 H] (2) The question whether or not the employer had lost confidence in the employee, was essentially one of fact aad this Court should not disturb the finding of facts recorded by that court on the ground of being colourable or mala fide or an act of victimisation. If the exercise of such power is challenged on the grounds Of being colourable and mala fide, or an action of victimisation, or unfair Labour practice practice, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [ 496 A B] (3) The management has passed the order of termination simpliciter and the order does not amount to one of dismissal as and by way of punishment. [498 C D] (4) The appellant did not even file a counter affidavit and the counsel for the Union agreed that the order was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. There is no evidence on record to show that the appellant had lost faith in the management, or that it was not bona fide.

The petitioners, who were the victims of serious breaches of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of 'eye camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines prescribed by the Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. The petitioners, whose names were mentioned in the Report of the Sub Divisional Magistrate, appropriate follow up action was contemplated by the State Government against persons concerned and that, indeed, a criminal case had been regis tered against Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team and also against officers of the Government who, according to allegations, committed serious breaches on duty in sanction permission for conducting the 'eya camp ' with effect from ensuring a high level of 0.5% of the total number of patients operated upon at Moradabad Camp. The State Government issued an order dated 9th February 1988 directing that the said Dr. As a result of the deliberations of the Committee and pursuant to its recommendations, the guidelines for conduct of eye camps earlier issued have been updated and revised. The Committee deliberated on the issue and its recommendations in regard to the norms for the conducting of eye camp ' and recommended its approval. The Union Government took up the matter with the Union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9.2.1988. However, some points made in the report and Recommendation of the expert sub committee of the Indian Medical Council may be consid ered by the Union Govern ment for incorporation In regard to this grievance, it was submitted before this Court that persuant to the results of the inquiries conducted by the Deputy Director (Eye treatment) and the Sub division Magistrate, proper follow up steps were contemplated by Government against those responsible for the tragedy. Disposing of the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The factual foundation laid before the Court and the limited scope of the proceedings no appeal could be made to the doctrine of State action. Shri Yogeshwar Prasad, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the State of Uttar Pradesh, submitted that the State would approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. He further contended that the state would certainly be willing to render help to the injured within the constraints of its resources. These matters would have to be gone into in the criminal and other proceedings that may be pending or in contemplation of the Govern ment. [256B C] 2. On humanitarian consideration, the victims should be afforded some monitary relief by the state Government. The amount shall be deposit ed, as was done in the matter of distribution of interim relief, with the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of the interim relief. [257E] 3. In addition to the sum of Rs.5,000 already paid by way of interim Relief, the State Govern ment shall pay a further sum of RS.5.000. The victims entitled to receive the additional payment shall be the same as those who had the benefit of the Interim relief of Rs 5,000.

The petitioner No. 1 was appointed as a temporary measure in the Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984. The said appointment was challenged by respondent No. 2 by way of a suit under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the action taken by the respond ent State Government under the Asom Rashtrabaha Pra Prachar Samiti Samiti ( taking over management and control) Act 1984 was an act done in violation of the provisions of Article 230 of the Constitu tion. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the petitioner No 1 had failed to establish that he had been appointed by a Board constituted under the Act and that the order passed by the Governor of Assam on January 15, 1984 was not in accordance with the Constitution. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that since the Act did not provide for temporary transfer of the management and Control of the affairs of the Samiti, it was a temporary measures continued at perpetuity and the Samiti was being run by nominated members and the rights of the members of the Board under Article 19 had not only been restricted but has been taken away. Hence this Writ Petition. Allowing the Writ Petition, HELD: 1.1 The Act and the noti fication issued under the said Act taking over the management of the Rashtra bhasha Samiti samiti Samiti could not be accepted to be in accordance wi th Constitution. [176G] 1.2 Even on the basis of the provi sion of the constitution Bench, the Act does not provide as to how when the temporary measures comes to an end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalika would be restored. It is apparent that since 1984 when this Act was passed and a notification appointing a Board was issued, the Government has not chosen to take any steps to restore the Society back to its elected authorities and office bearers inspite of the fact that they indicated and asked the counsel appearing for the State to let us know even if now the State is intending to restore it back to the Society but unfortunately it appears that with out considering the question and its constitutional aspects the reply came that the State has no desire to restore its Board back to their elected authorities, and therefore we are left with no option but to decide and upholding the Constitution and the right of association conferred under Article l(c) of the Consti tution. [177A B] 1:3 The Act does neither provide for nor is it apparent that because since 1984 the Act was made and a Notification appointing a board was issued the Government had not chosen t he to take steps to restoring the Society, but unfortunately the same was challenged in this Writ petition. It was also apparent that the Karyapala r and Byaburpika Samiti Sabha which were functioning in 1984 has come to an ac quired effect although from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. It appears that even after 1984 when the Act talks of a temporary arrangement in fact, the act does not provided for as to what how the temporary measure comes to any end the existing elected Byaabastha pika Sabha or Karyapalka would be restore within six months from the date of this Order will hold proper elections in accordance con sidering the Constitution to elect a Byabhavika Sabha.

The appellants, who were the reversioners of a Hindu widow made a gift of four houses at Asansol in favour of Kamala Devi on the 10th March 1940, a gift which she was not competent under the law to make. The deed of gift was registered on March 10, 1940, and possession of the houses was also given to her. After the marriage, however, Sumitra Devi felt ill and the deed of gifts was actually executed and registered on April 10, 1938, some two years after the marriage. On May 10, 1939, Sumitra 's father died in 1938 leaving behind his widow, a daughter and a son. The appellants filed a suit for possession of four house properties alleging that the gift was not bona fide but was made at the time of the marriage itself which was accepted by Nand Lal Sao on behalf of Kamala and the gift being later confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938 and possession was also delivered to her; soon after the death of Sumitra Devi, she felt ill. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed that decree. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellants were not entitled to the reliefs claimed by them. It is well settled that a promise made for such a gift for or at the place of the last marriage ceremony is binding on the reversioners. In the present case, the gift in the instant case was made on May 10 and the acceptance of the gift by the donor was for the spiritual benefit of the daughter and the son in law, and a gift made long after the contract was performed. The gift was binding on all the reversioners except the widow. It was open to Sumitra Devi to fulfil that promise as a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon her deceased husband, irrespective of the consideration whether she made a " sankalpa" at the date of the contract or not.

The appellant, a joint Hindu family, filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices detailed in the petition an(l) in the Statement of facts. Ruplal supported the appellant but Bhagat Puran Singh and Jagdish Chander did not put in appearance despite service and, therefore, the proceedings were taken ex parte against them. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej Singh have been clearly proved. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Ruplar, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej Singh would have gone to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [419D] 1.2 In view Of the very wide margin of vote (123), between Tej singh and Ru plal, a grave presumption and possibilities that the voters who would have voted for Ruplul would now cast their votes in favour. [416E F] 2.1 The effect of the posters was that all the voters were present at the instance of Tej Singh. As the margin of election was very small, viz. 123 votes, if such a misrepresentation was not made, in all probability, the votes would have go to the appellant (Avtar Singh) and, consequently, the result would be materially altered. [414B] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the poster by Tej singh was clearly established. It is also clear from the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties, that Tej Sing Singh was known to him. [413C] 2 :3 In view thereof, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Ram had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing by the posters. Tej Singh (R.W. 2) has not disputed that the payment of vouchers .(Ex. P 5 and P 6) was made by him and the vouchers were appended by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign, which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was alleged to have been a Forest Secretary in the State of Punjab. The Chief Minister of the State, after considering the application, affidavits and the submissions made on behalf of the parties, took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In the application for contempt, it was alleged by the appellant that one Shri Devinder Sharma was a Forest Officer in the Union Territory of Chandigarh and he had been convicted for criminal contempt of Court. The Single Judge of the High Court after considering all the affidavits and submissions made by the parties took the contrary view and held that there was no sufficient cause for the application of section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant: (i) that as no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High court in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt the section 19 (1) is inapplicable and the appeal is incompetent; (ii) that the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to punishfor contempt includes also the jurisdiction to dispose of the case either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has exercised its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt. When no punishment is imposed by theHigh Court, it is difficult to say that the High Courts have exercised their jurisdiction or powers as conferred upon it by article 215 of tile Constitution. [893F] 2. The jurisdiction of High Court is to punish. When an order or decision is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court, and "the right of appeal will be available under sub section (1), of Section 19 only against any decision or order of a High Court passed in the exercise of such jurisdiction to punishing for contempt". [894C] 3. When the High 'Court does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High Curt does not exercise its jurisdic tion or power to punish For contempt under Article 215, for such exercise will mean that the Supreme court should act in a particular manner, that is to say by imposing punishment for Contempt. [889D] 4. When a Court is conferred with the power or jurisdiction to act in any particular manner the exerciseof jurisdiction or the power will involve the acting in that particular manner and in no other. Article 215 confers jurisdiction or authority on the High COurt to punish, for contempt of court. The power or authority will be exercised by imposing sentence for contempt also. [879E] 5. When there is no punishment imposed by a High ' Court, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without any remedy. Even though no appeal is maintainable under Section 19( 1) of Act, the petition can move this Court under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. [869E F] 6. The aggrieved party under section 19 of the Act can only be the contemnor who has been punished for contempt in a contempt proceeding. [877G] 7. In such a case there would be no right of Appeal under Section19(1), as there is an exercise of jurisdiction or Power by the Supreme ' Court to punishingfor contempt, for Such exercise will include also the power to decide whether such punishment should be imposed or not and when the High `Court comes to the finding that such punishment shall not be imposed on it. [878G] 8. The appellant in such a situation can move the Court under article 136 of Constitution.

The appellant was the lessee of a plot of land in Poona. The lease was for a period of ten years and the lessor had to pay rent at the time of the lease. The lessor did not pay the rent but only paid the rent. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the notice was necessary before the lease could be terminated, and the trial court expressed the view that the provision in the rent note that on non payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end was a clause of nullity and not merely a clause Of forfeiture and that the lease was therefore determined under section 111 (b) and not under section III (g). The High Court held that this provision in sub section (g) of section 111 of the , was applicable, and that no notice as required by section 111(g) was necessary for terminating the lease in suit. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amendment made in 1929 to section 111 was merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and was not based upon any principle of equity, justice or good conscience and could not govern leases made prior to 1st April, 1930, and therefore, no notice under section II (g), was necessary. Held:(i) The provisions of section III of the Act are not intended to be exhaustive but must be construed in a broad way so as to advance the object of the legislation. It is only when statutory provisions were made to the contrary that rule would have been applicable and the court had no discretion. In the present case, the High Court was fully justified in refusing to grant relief against forfeiture. (ii) The rules laid down by the Master of Rolls in the present ease are useful maxims in general, and they reflect the point of view from which judges would regard (1) (2) A.I.R. 1929 Bom. 1, followed. (iii) The rule enunciated in sub s.(g) is not based on any principle or principle of justice, equity and good conscience, or whether it is merely a substantive and technical Rule introduced in 1929 and which still governs leases executed prior to the coming into force of the . or to leases executed after 1st March, 1930. (iv) The amendment made by 1929 to s 111(h) of the does not introduce any new principle of law or equity. The rule laid down in sub sections (g)(1) and (g ) is that if the sun has been required under the section for a certain period, it shall be presumed that such period was not intended for the purpose of the section. In this situation the High court was fully right in refusing relief against eviction.

The respondents were charged with having committed misconduct under section 3(1) (d) of the Madhya Pradesh Industrial Relations Act, 1960. The enquiry was held by an Arbitrator who gave his Award on 9th February 1970 whereby he came to the conclusion that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the Respondents of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17. The Arbitrator gave his award on 9rd February, 1970 whereby it came to conclusion that there was no second opportu nity for the Respondents to show cause against proposed punishment and therefore the finding that the inquiry was vitiated was set aside. The High Court confirmed the view of the Arbitrator and dismissed the writ petition filed by the Management. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that assuming that the Arbitrator had power to interfere with the punishment in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances he was not justified in setting aside the dismissal of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan especially on the ground that the conduct of Shri Emmanual and Mohd.
