Rauf was more grave than that of Rama Shanker and Barmaspradan while fomenting the strike; counsel urged that assuming para 3 of the Standing order No. RU.P. 17 provides for second opportunity being given to a workman to show his explanation, it contemplates giving of a second opportunity to the delinquent to showcause against the punishment of dismissal after he has been found guilty or the opportunity spoken of is the opportunity to meet the charges in the domestic inquiry; and that since the Arbitrator gave an opportunity to a person who had not been given such opportu tion was irrelevant. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether para 3 does not refer to the opportunity of meeting the charges but refers to the further opportunity being afforded to the Respondent to show defend himself against the action proposed to be taken by him and not the proposed penalty. [371E] 2.1 In the instant cases, the Arbitrator has undoubtedly taken the view that the opportunity spoke of by para 3 did not refer specifically to the opportu tal to meet charges but referring to the second opportunity which was given for the first time to the workman to give his explanation. The Court does not feel that the construction placed on Standing Order 17 is correct. [372F] 2:2 In the present case, the arbitrator had taken the decision that the second part of the standing order deals with several punishments and requires finding of guilt in respect of each one of them and this procedure is, therefore, different from that which has been contemplated in the last part of Standing Order and that last part deals only with the penalty of dismissal and for that punishment alone makes a special provision that no order awarding that punishment will be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity of hearing to a delinquent workman to offer his explanation.[372F G] 2 :3 The Court has also held in the case of Ram Kumar vs State of Haryana, [1971] Supp. SCR 840 that para 3 deals with two different stages concerning disciplinary proceedings against a delinquent, first holding of a 371 departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of natural justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to show causes has been provided for; but the plain reading of the paragraph does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore. the construction put on Standing order 17 is set aside and the matter remitted back to the Arbitrator for fresh disposal in accordance with law.

The appellants were tenants of certain lands in Malabar. They filed a petition under section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they had been in continuous possession of the land for more than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , or any law, custom or usage. The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants were not entitled to the protection of section 7 D of the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the respondents had been continuously in occupation of the lands for more years and (ii) the lease deed executed by them was a registered document which was unregistered and therefore could not be acted upon. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that section 7F of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 was applicable to the case. [112B] 2.1 In order to attract the applicability of section 6D it is necessary to show that the person who has paid amounts for occupation of land shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation on the 11th day of April, 1957, on the basis of that deed, notwithstanding the fact that the lease was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. [114C] 2:2 The expression "any other law" is used in contradistinction to any other law which may be applicable to a case where the provisions of the statute are silent. In order that section should be construed, it must be read as if the words "any law" were not defined in the Act and the definition of "tenant" has been given a wide meaning so as to include within its ambit any law which is inconsistent with the provisions contained in the statute. [116E F] 2 :3 The expression 'or other law ' occurring in section 7A(1) of the Madras Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1970 has been used in contrast to the expression "other law" and it cannot be said that the legislature intended that the definition should be given a wider meaning so that the statutory provisions would not be available to the statutory authorities. [117F G] 2.(a) The expression `or other person ' occurring under section 6A(2) of Act 1 of 1964 has been interpreted in a wide and comprehensive manner by this Court in several decisions. In the instant case, the respondents were tenants on the land in question for more or less than ten year to be held as deemed tenants. [118G H] 2(b) The definition of 'tenant ' contained in Section 2(g) of Kerala Land Reform Act, 1964 has a wide connotation and it includes within its sweep any law relating to tenancies. It is not possible to accept the contention that the expression `other law ' in section 6 A(2), as amended by Act 35 of 1969, has been construed in a wider sense so as not to include all other laws which may have been applicable to such cases. [119G H; 120A B] 2 (c) The word `or ' occurring therein means any law made by the legislature or by an authority within the meaning of the Constitution. It cannot be understood that the term `other person ' has been defined in section 2(h) of that Act and it is not necessary to refer to all other provisions of that statute. In fact, the definition contained in s.2(g), as it stood at the relevant time, has a wider connotation and its scope has been enlarged by the amendment made by Act 36 of 1969.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. He was prosecuted under section 135(b)(ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,000/ . The prosecution case against him was that he had kept the goods there, and that the portion of the room from which the goods were recovered was sublet to Dwarumal and Kishen who had kept them there. He also stated that the appellant had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 120B and sentenced him to six years rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) Section 106 read with section 114 of the Evidence Act was sufficient to enable the prosecution to ask the court to presume that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law; (2) that, the burden of proving that they are not smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession the goods are seized. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had failed to produce evidence to prove that the articles were legally brought into India. He could have succeeded in explaining satisfactorily how he was an innocent receiver of such goods without knowing that they were illegally imported or smuggled; and (3) that the prosecution had not produced evidence to establish that the appellants were legally bringing into India, [541 D] 2. Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act is a penal provision and it does not require any particular form of evidence to be adduced by the prosecution. It is only when the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed an offence punishable under section 138(b) or section 138, that the burden shifts on the prosecution in proving that he has been guilty of such offence shall be upon the person who asserts it. [541 E F] 3. Section 114 of Evidence Act provides that where any goods to which this section applies are seized under this Act in the reasonable belief that they have been imported or imported into the country without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory, the onus of proving the place from where they came, or when they were imported, was on the accused person. [542 G] 4. Section 116 of the Act provides for an exception to this rule and it is not necessary that the particular form should be given to the prosecution before a particular form is prescribed. It would apply only to goods seized under the Act. It does not say that the court must presume that it has been proved by evidence beyond reasonable doubt that the person in possession was concerned with the importation of the smuggled goods. [543 G H] 5. Section 112 read with s 114 of Indian Evidence is a substantive provision and its provisions are intended to be used for the purpose of enabling the prosecution of proving its case beyond any shadow of doubt. It provides that if any goods are confiscated under this section in the manner specified therein, the duty shall be paid on the persons from whose custody they were seized. [544 E F; 545 A B] 6. Section 113 of the is a procedural provision and does not confer any right on the appellant to claim that he was not concerned with any importation or exportation of goods. It only provides for the presumption that the onus shifts on proof of the existence of an offence. The burden of establishing that the offence has been committed by the accused must be on him who could have failed to discharge his burden. [545 B] 7. Section 118 of the does not create any right in the appellant '

The appellants, who were the President of a registered Association, filed a suit for accounts and for accounts. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal by the plaintiffs, the Judicial Commissioner reversed that finding and came to the conclusion that the other members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of goods sold by them. On further appeal by certificate, Held, that the suit was one for accounts of a dissolved firm, but for accounts relating to an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked. The suit before the Judicial Com missioner was not one for accounting of a dissolution of a partnership firm and it was not necessary that the partnership firm must be registered, though the disabilities consequent on non registration may be extremely inconvenient. The distinction between an illegal transaction and an illegal contract is that in order that illegality might be a defence, it must affect the contract on which the plaintiff is compelled to rely so as to make out his right to what he asks. Where a plaintiff comes to court on allegations which on the face of them show that the contract of partnership on which he sues is illegal, the only course for the courts to pursue is to say that he is not entitled, to any relief on the allegations made as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect of contracts which the law declares to be illegal (Senaji Kapurchand vs Pannaji Devichand ([1910] A.C.R. 435), referred to. The analogy does not really apply. As the preliminary objection was taken at a very late stage, it should be held that the appellants had a right to bring a suit on the ground of illegality It is enough to point out that under the , an unregistered firm is not illegal; there is no direct compulsion that a partnership Firm must be registration though the disability consequent upon non registration might be extremely difficult.

The respondents along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 1 of the compartment No 1 of compartment No I of compartment 1 of a compartment No 2 of the said compartment. The High Court was persuaded to the view that this was a case to which section 210(1) of Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 was attracted and that as an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the learned Magis trate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process against the accused. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The sub section referred to above excludes the jurisdiction of High Court only in cases where the acts alleged to constitute contempt of a subordinate court are punishable as contempt under specific provisions of the Indian Penal Code but not where these acts merely amount to offences of other description for which punishment has been provided for in the Indian penal Code. [463E] 2. The second ground on which the High Court came to quash the proceedings of the Magistrate, on the facts of this case is impermissible as an exercise under section 50(1), in its ingredients and content, is the same or substantially the same as Sec. 50(l) of the Act on the one hand and 9(1). [463F G] 3. The offence committed by the respondents falls within the overlapping areas of sec 42 IPC on the other and therefore constitutes the same offences apart from the fact that this argument does not serve to support the order of the High court in the present case, this argument is even on its theoretical possibilities, more attractive than sound. An act or an omission can amount to and constitute an offence under the IPC and at the same time constitute an ' offence '. [464G H] 4. The test is that taking the allegations and the complaint as they are without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High Courts will be justified in quashing the proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482 of the present Code. The third ground onwhich the High COurt came to quashed the proceedings is impermissible because an exercise of jurisdiction under section 48 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, in its essential ingredients and contents, is a matter which would be within the cognizance of a court subordinate to it where such contempt is an offence punishable under the Indian Indian Penal code. [465B C] 5.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Greater Bombay. The High Court dismissed his appeal holding that the petitioner 's bail application was not maintainable as he had been released on bail in a case where the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to grant bail. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Magistrate should have given him an opportunity to oppose the bail and (ii) the magistrate should have granted him an adequate opportunity to defend himself before releasing him on bail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the court to release a surety without bail or on his own recognizance is not a necessary element of the Criminal process and even if risk of monetary loss is a deterrent against fleeing from justice it is not the only deterrent and there are other factors which are sufficient deterrents against flight. [343E] 2. The object of bail covers both release on one 's own bond, with or without sureties. To read 'bail ' as including only cases of release with sureties will stultify the sub section; for then an accused released on his his own bond without bail, i.e., surety, cannot be conditioned to attend at the appointed place. [344G H] 3. The best guarantee of presence in court is the reach of the law, not the money tag. [345A B] 4. The socialist republic with social justice as its hallmark, monetary superstition, not other relevant considerations like family ties, roots in the community, membership of stable organizations, should prevail for bail bonds to ensure that the 'bailee ' does not fleeing justice. [346B C] 5. The most important guarantee of participation in court proceedings is the securing of the release of the accused on one "s own bonds with orwithout sureties. It cannot be said that an under trial is worse of than a convict or that the power of bail the Court to release increases when the guilt is established. [347C] 6. The only guarantee of residence in court was the reach and reach of law, no money tagged. [349D] 785 785 (i). A liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on another 's bond will stultifying the sub stitution. [348E] 786 (ii). The socialistic republic with Social justice as the hallmark of monetary superstitition, is brought out in the Report: "The evil of bail system is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. In one case the pooraccused is fleeced of his moneys by touts; professional sureties and sometimes have even to incur debts to make payment to them for securing their release; in the other he is deprived of his liberty without trial and conviction and this leads to grave consequences, namely, (1) though presumed innocent he is subjected to 343 the psychological and physical deprivations of jail life; (2) he has lost his job if he has one, and is deprived by an opportunity of work to support himself and his family with the result that burden of his detention falls heavily on the innocent members of the family, (3) he is prevented from contribution to the preparation of his defence; and (4) he was prevented from contributions to the prepare of his Defence. [350G H; 347A B].

The assessee, a newly established undertaking, had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills, hereinafter called 'the assessee '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee to include in the computation of capital so employed Rs. 2,21,,460 advanced to 'Castle '. On appeal by the Commissioner, the Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the assessee in the calculation of the capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15C. The High Court dismissed the petition of the Commissioner under section 66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal to state the case and refer it to the High Court was also dismissed. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Under the Income tax Act it is for the Tribunal, to decide all questions of fact; the High court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the Tribunal. Such a question may arise out of an order of a Tribunal and also if the Tribunal has misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. It must however appear that the Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at the conclusion. If the conclusion of the tribunal is based upon some evidence ignoring other important matters, it cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of 'Ctastle in the assessment of the assesses may have been a relevant circumstance, but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had relied. (ii) The Tribunal has therefore misdirected itself by law in reaching its finding and in refusing to require the Tribunal 'to state the Case and refer the matter to it, the High Courts were in error in interfering with the order.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was directed to file his personal affidavit. In the writ petition filed by him, Duggal respondent also challenged the validity of the later order of February 18, 1975. The High Court allowed the writ application and quashed the earlier seniority list. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The direction for impleading the Minister as a party was given by the High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of facts and circumstances of the case, it does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order of the High court adding the Minister. [972 B] 2. The directions for impleading Dugggal respondent as a Party were given by this Court with the view to inform the Minister about the allegations in the writ peti tion. [983 C] 3. Taking into consideration the totality and circumstances, it is not possible to interfere in the matter. [992 F] 4. The order of High Court directing that the Minister concerned should file his affidavit is set aside. [1004 B] 5. The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. [1015 C] 6. The Secretary of the Department shall file his Personal affidavit. [ 1016 E] 7. The Minister concerned shall file an affidavit in regard to the allegations contained in the amended petition and also raise a plea that looking to the facts of the cases, if the High Courts came to the conclusion that the minister was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in t he matter.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, on January 7, 1960 for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act (III of 1911) on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate ordered attachment and sale of the property. On appeal by the respondent, the Sessions Judge held that arrears of rents due under a lease cannot be recovered under section 260 of the Act. In revision to this Court it was contended that the words "rent on land and buildings" must equally be governed by the words 'recoverable by a Board etc." and therefore the provisions of section 259 could not be utilised for realisation Of arrears of land revenue on land or buildings provided such rent is claimable by the Board under the Act or the Property Rules or the Land Administration Rules but under the lease. HELD : (i) The words "claimable by" must also be construed in their widest sense and it cannot be said that they are not intended to cover all cases of arrears of any tax, water rate, rent etc. [347 C] (ii) Section 259 of Act does not confer a right on the Board to recover arrears of the rent due from the tenant under the provisions Of the Act nor does it confer a power on the Magistrate to recover the same. The words 'claimable" must be given their widest amplitude and they cannot be limited only to cases where the Act, or the Rules in terms make the rent on land. [346 D E] (iii) Section 258 of the , as it now stands runs thus: "Notwithstanding anything elsewhere contained in this Act, arrears of a tax, rent on lands and buildings shall be recoverable together with the cost of recovery (1) A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 936, followed. (iv) Any amount recovered from any occupier instead of from an owner under section 256 and it further provides that any amount recovered by any occupier out of the premises as such may be a charge on the property until paid; provided . . .

The appellant was employed as a Section Salesman in the respondent company. He was ap pointed as a section salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was employ ed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company 's product in his area. Neither the section salesmen nor the local salesmen or local sales men were employed by the company in order to canvass and promote the sales. The Tribunal held that the appel lant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Labour court had given findings in favour of the appe lant on the question whether the termination itself was illegal; (ii) the reference being incompetent, the award was not incompetent; and (iii) the Tribunal had given a finding in favour o the appeli lant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Labour Court has given findings on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before t he Labour Court. It is seen from the facts found that the respondent Company sells its product i.e. cigarettes manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in turn sell the product to various dealers appointed by the Company in the area. neither the section Salesmen nor local salesman or local travelling salesmen are employed in the shop of the wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell the products of the Company and to collect the amount of sale. The supervising work of other local sales man was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the areas of his operation. [475C D] 2.1 In the light of the finding that the termination of the services of the employee from service was illegal, the employee has to be under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the section i. e. manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a studyof the market condition. The supervision work of the other local salemen was part part of their work considered as only ancillary to his primary work of canvass and promotion. [476E F] 2:2 In the instant case, the appellant is employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company. The duty involve the suggest of ways & means to maintain the sales and a research of the market conditions. The supervise work of these other local Salesmen was integral part of the duties considered by t he Tribunal as also by the evidence produced on record before the Tribunal. It was not the duty of the respondent to procure orders for the Company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell their product in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company, but it was only incidental, to his principal function of canvassing & promoting the sale of the product in the four districts allotted to him. The appellant was required to supervise the work and of other Local salesmen appointed in the Area of his operations as well but it is only incidental on his main function of raising and improving the sales in this area. [477F G] 2 :3 In the absence of any finding that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage.

The appellant Company was a `pakka ' tenant. The land in question was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a `Pakka" tenant. On the question whether the Company had become an ordinary tenant under section 185 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act Samvat 2007, HELD: 1.1 The High Court had found in the earlier proceeding that the land in dispute was held as by the company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the Government for a public purpose of the State. [180B] 1.2 In terms of sub section (1) or sub section 2(i) of section 182, the Company is not a pakka tenant, as found by the High Court in the previous judgement, and therefore, it was, according to the said Act, an ordinary tenancy. The High court had found that the Company did not enjoy the status of a ` Gair Maurusi ' tenant and that it had never been an ordinary term as defined in the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue Act No. 66 of 1950. [181C] 1:3 In terms, of sub s.(1) of Section 182, if the Company has been holding the land from the State Government and it has never been a `a pakri ' tenant, the company has been held by that State when that came into force. The Company was in terms, under sub section(2)(i), of section 184 that the Additional Collector made his order for eviction of the Company. [182D] 1 :4 In the instant case, the High court found in its earlier proceeding, that the Land Revenue & Tenancy Act, Samvat, 2007 (Act No. 67 of 1950) which was the law in force until repealed by the M P. Land revenue and Tenancy Acts did not apply, since they were already held by State when the came into existence. The finding of the High COurt to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. The Orissa Land Reform (Amendment) Act, 1964, came into force on July 1, 1949. By a notification issued under section 1 (3) the State Government brought the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) into force, and referred cases of certain tax payers to the Commission appointed in that behalf. The petitioners contended that the Travancore Cochin Land Reforms (Amendment), Act, 1965 was not law in force until a notification was issued bringing into operation the provisions of section 1 of the Travancore Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1955, authorising the appointment of a Commission and referring the cases of tax payees to the commission, was invalid as it was inconsistent with or takes away orabridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. The respondents contended that (i) the Travancore Kerala Land Reforms and Acquisition of Land Reforms Ordinance, 1965, which received the President 's assent on October 16, 1960, was not a law in operation until a Notification was issued under Ch. IV of the Principal Act, and since the subsequent legislation sought to restrict the ceiling limit and vest the surplus land in the Government under section 45 as amended, there was compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus Land which is within the ceiling limits applicable to him under any law providing for the acquisition of such land, building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to the acquisition is provided for payment of compensation at a rate whichhall not be less than the market price thereof; and (ii) the provisions contained in Ch. III of Act 16 of 1960 were not applicable to the landholders under any laws for the time being in force which attracted the application of the second proviso to article 31 A. Held, that the Kerala Land Reform Act, 1950, was a law within the meaning of article 31A of the Constitu tion and since no notification was issue before Ch. 4 of the said Act, there could be no question of any inconsistency between the provisions in Ch., IV of Act 18 of 1960 and the provisions relating to compensation payable under the principal act. The Travancore Cochin Act, 19 of 1125 (M.)E.R. 1069, 1069 (M) E.R., 1070 (M). E. R. 1071 (M), 1072 (M.), 1073 (M.). 1074 (M,.E.), 1075 (M.,E.), 976 (M,E.), 1177 (M G.) and 1075 M.E. (MG.) vs State of Kerala, ; , referred to.

The widow 'was under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate and the consequent extinguish (1) I.L.R. , approved. Sreeramu vs Kristamma, I. L. R. , distinguished. Subbamnia vs Kristsamma, A.I.R., Mad. 946, disapproved. Subbiah Chettyar vs Subramania Iyer, I L.R . and Subbamannia Chettiar vs Subramani Pillai, IL. R,. , approved; Sreteramu 's case, (1876) 1. L .R. 50 I.A. 206, distinguished. Per MUKHERJEA J. The right of a Hindu widow to challenge the alienation made by her was not an absolute right and it could not be surrendered to the reversioner. The reversionary right to challenge it is no part of the widow 'Sreeranatha vs Savithri, I I.I,.L.J., dissenting) that the widow herself was in capable of disputing the title of the alienee or of the person who had acquired by adverse Possession against her, a like disability attaches to the reversioners also who could not have obtained the properties but for the surrender made by the widow. The appellants, a company registered under the U.P. Industrial Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958, were appointed as Directors of a Polytex Company in respect of ten lakhs shares held by the Cotton Mills Company for a period of six months with various powers specified therein and in particular to seize I lakh of shares of the Polytex company of the face value of Rs 10 lakhs held by it. The requisitionists of the meeting also asked the Polyestertex Company to treat the said notice as a special notice under section 284(2) and (5) read with section 190 of the Act for appointment of Sitaram Singhania, Rajaram Jaipuria and R.D. Gupta, Chairman of the Cotton Mill Company. The meeting also requested the Polylex Company to consider the question relating to the right of the cotton Mills Company to join as a requisitionist of a meeting under section 169 of the U . Thapar as a Director of the Company. On the same day, the requisitionists made an application before the Collector praying that the meeting be held in accordance with the order of the High Court notwithstanding any order of injunction etc. issued by any other court or authority in India or to be issued hereafter. The Collector rejected the application on the ground that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton mills Company had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the Collector of Kanpur in respect thereof. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the notice and also the order passed by the Collec tor under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act read with Section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertakings (Cues Recovery), Act,1958 appointing a Receiver in respect to the shares of Polytex Co. of the value of 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 lakhs holding by the cotton mills Company and also for a direction that the said meeting shall be held at accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the view that the order was an order in the nature of a charging order and the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares in question and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton mill Company had lost its right to the share shares. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The attachment of the shares under the Land revenue Act in respect whereof the shares were pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh also would not deprive the holder of the share holders whose name is entered in the Register of Members of the companies the right to vote at the meetings of the shareholders of the jute mills Company or to issue a notice under Section 169 of tho Act. [875E] 2. The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favor of the government of Uttar pradesh also would make no difference Sections 172 to 178 A of the deal with the contract of pledge. In view of the foregoing the pawnee in the instant case i. e. the Government had in this case rightly treated the registered holder i.e. the Cotton Spinners ' Association as the owner of the said shares and could exercise its rights under section 170 of the . [877F G] 3. The order of Collector being an order, in the form of a charge order, the Receiver has obtained an indefeasible right in them shares and can exercise their rights under Section 170 of that Act. The Receiver had also obtained an appropriate legal right in those shares and was entitled to exercise its powers under section 171 of the , for appointment or issue of a notice thereunder. [888B C] 4.

The petitioners were owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others. The Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit lands had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The petitioners filed a civil suit against the Panchayat and the Panchayat in the course of its written statement inter alia pleaded that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of the provisions of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 (Punjab Act No. 1 of 1961). The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the question involved in the case was simply one of title to the suit and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit Land was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat, it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In revision, the Additional Senior Sub Judge held that since a question involved was merely one of fact to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 read with section 13(A) of the Act and accordingly he held that the civil court had no jurisdic tion to try the suit, and dismissed the petition. The High Court in revision came to the conclusion that the issues involved in this case were not triable by a Civil Court by virtue Of section 11 of the East Punjab Village Panchayat Act, 1948 (Punjab act No. 2 of 1961) and accordingly dismissed the revision petition filed by the petitioners. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The civil court has jurisdiction to decide any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any land is or is not shamlat Deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act or to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act. [835E] 2. The Civil Court has jurisdiction under section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the , to decide such claim in such manner as may be prescribed. [889F G] 3. Section 13 of Punjab Village Panchayats Act, 1964 provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction to hear or adjudicate upon any question relating to any matter which the Commissioner is empowered by or under this act to determine. The contention of the Panchayat before the trial court was that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat mal and it had been vested with it. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was sham or not. The gram panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The plaintiff in that case had not claimed that the property belonged to him or that it did not belong to the Gram Panchayat. The trial Court had rightly dismissed the civil suit.

The appellant Board, in exercise of its power under Section 49(1) of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948, framed a general conditions for supply of electricity to the consumers. The Board was required to pay interest on the security deposit from the date of deposit till the date when it became due. The appellant Board filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of consumption security deposit and also the demand of payment of interest on delayed payment of the amount. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that there was no legal obligation to pay Interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms of Clause 20(a) & (c) of its General Conditions of Supply. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board: (1) The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumers in trust with the Electricity Board to secure the Board against default in payment of duty; and (2) The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposited has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The object of the deposit is to secure that the payment of consumption charges is not only a deposit in cash to safeguard recovery of electricity dues for the energy supplied to the consumer on credit but also a security towards payment or satisfaction of any money (For example, theft), which may become due and payable to the Board by the purchaser. The condition requiring a supply of a consumption Security deposit has a indirect bearing on its operations of Electricity Board which is to be performed in such manner as To ensure a deficit. [578D E] 2. The conditions of supply require a consumptionsecurity deposit has direct bearing upon the operations and of the Boards which are required to be conducting in such an manner as would ensure a shortfall. The nature of consumption Security deposits is such that it represents the moneys of the board. The impact of the obligation on the Board to pay the interest to the Electricity proceed on the assumption that the Board is keeping the security deposited and depriving the consumer of the use of money which is alleged to be earning interest with the Boards, is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. [579D E; 578A B] 3. The terms of supply providing for non payment of Interest are not so onerous as to affect the conscience or the integrity of the court. The restriction on the right to recover interest at the rate of 12% per annum is not unreasonable and it is reasonable. [577E F] 4. The obligation to make payment of interests to the purchaser proceed on assumption that it is keeping security deposit, has a directly bearing on this operations of Board which were to be held in such like manner as the Court may consider reasonable. The purpose of the deposits is to ensure that the intentions of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates somewhat harshly on a small section of the public, taken in conjunction with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) &(g) as imposing an unreasonable restraint. [576F G] 5. The scheme of the Act is that it does not contain any norm of guideline with regard to framing of terms and conditions for the supply of Electricity and in particular, the demand for payment of payment interest on amount due to the board by the petitioners similarly situated, the claims of the petitioners should similarly be dealt with by the Board.

The petitioners were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre. They were promoted to the post of Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.1.1973. The direct recruits to which category the peti tioners belong are not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is stated that the total number of officers who were thus getting Special Pay is of the order while only about 25 officers who are direct recruits working in the telecommuni cation Research Centre are not give Special Pay paid to the others holding the same posts. The petitioners, therefore, filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the denial of promotional opportunities to them on account of the irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the second relating to violation of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution by not grant ing them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who arc working in that centre with effectfrom 1. 1.1973, and discharging the same functions as the petitioners. The respondents contended that the petition ers (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to the Telecommuni tation Research Centres for a limited purpose are not entitled to any Special pay but the transferred officials had to be paid extra amount by way of special Pay in addition to their scale of pay which was the same as the scale of Pay of direct recruits because the transferred officers had to perform in the post which is not in their general line. Allowing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same As between direct recruits and the transferred official and that the transferred employees have to be pay able to discharge their duties. [1070E] 2. There is no justification to deny the Special Pay at the same rates to the direct recruits functioning in the Communication Research Centre.[1072F] 3. The petition ions (direct recruit ment) who were specifically recruited by the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition examination need to be given Special Pay. [ 1073G] 4. There was no justification for denying the Special pay at that rates to direct recruits Working in the communication Research Centre [1072H] 5. The discrimination between the direct recruit and the transfer officials regarding the payment of Special Pay was attempted to be justified by the Government in the Counter affidavit filed by Shri C.L. It was not the case of the Government that the petitioners are not competent and are not able to discharged their duties.[1073E] 6. There are no justification why the petitioners should not be denied the Special Leave Petitions on account Of the irregular operation of the Recruitment rules. All the direct ent recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Telephone Research Centre, [1074G H] 7. The Court is satisfied that there was no justi fication to deny promotional opportunities at the higher rates to them.

The appellant, an employee of an industry governed by the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, had not complied with the provisions of section 42(4) of the Act. The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Court for relief under section 7 8 (1) D. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: Under section 79(1) proceedings before a Labour Court in respect of disputes falling under clause (a) of paragraph A of sub section (1), must be commenced on an application made by any of the parties to the dispute etc. and under sub section(2) every application under sub s.(1) has to be made in the prescribed form from and manner. [737 B] In other words, effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect Of matters covered by section 42 of the . [738 C D] The scheme of section 7 (1 ) seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the labour court. In other cases effort must always first be done by the employers intending to affect any change of respect of matters covered in section 43(1).

The appellants were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The respondents filed an application before the Munsif claiming the right to contin ue in possession after 31. 7.1971 as tenants from month to month. The appellants ' application was allowed and an appeal therefrom filed by the respond ent was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi. The respondent moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction inter alia contending that the appellants ' applica tion under section 12 of the Act before the Civil Court was not maintain able. The learned Judge who heard the case held that in absence of a month 's notice under section12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsiff and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The Judicial Commissioner confined his decision to deciding the issues between the parties and granting one month ' s time to the respondents (appellants before him). The learned Single Judge who hearing the case found that in spite of a clear notice under Section 12(1), from the tenants, the appellants did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. The Division Bench held that the application was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the court by an application under section 10 or 12 is to be filed. In the instant case it is the Civil court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit for eviction under section 11 or making an application thereunder. The jurisdiction of the civil court is limited only where the matter is covered by section 12 and as we have made an assumption in favour of the respondents that section 12 has no application to the present case, there is no point in asking the appellants to file such an applica tions. [975D E] 2. The occasion for filing an applicat tion under Section 10 or 13 is to arise only where a matter is governed by section 18 and as it has been made an assumed that an application is not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the present ease, in our opinion, the proceeding has to be treated as a suit and the judgment of the learned Munsif as a decree therein. [980B C] 3. The case does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the first appellate court in favour o the appellants. The reason for filing such an application cannot arise only when the matter has been covered by Section 12, and as the question is whether the petition which was filed by them as an applican tion under s.12 should be treated to be a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. [981F G] 4. The High Court has rightly held that section 13 has no applica ble to the facts of the case. [978C D] 5. When a revision application was filed before the High court, it was held that it is for the appellants/tenants to choose which course to follow. [979D E; 980A] 6. The suit in question is the civil Court, Ranchi and the respondents are directed to restore peaceful possession of the premises in question to the appellants within one month from today failing which the appellants shall be entitled to execute the decree in accordance with law.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent for an immovable property through its Secretary, which was numbered as Suit No. 11 of 1973. The prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as the Secretary of the Society. According to the case of the appellant, one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. The trial court after holding that the appellant 's application filed under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Proce dure, was not maintainable proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the elected Secretary of Society entitled to prosecute or withdraw the same. The High Court agreed with the trial court that the application under section15 1 of t he Code of C.P.C., for restoration of the suit under its inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to it. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High Court by a petition under section 1 15 of the code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the trial Court was clearly wrong in dismissing the appellant s application as not maintainable. [237B] 1.2 The High court has rightly held that the only remedy of the appel lant is to file a fresh suit. If a party makes an applica tion before the Court for setting aside the decree, on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the order if it was satisfied that he had actually agreed to it.[237D E] 1:3 The High COurt should have inter vened in its revisional power on the assumption that it had no jurisdiction to do so. [238E F] C.W.P., Beyond pointing out that even according to the impugned order of the High court, the errors in the judgment of the trial Judge are serious, the High CO Court should have at least inter vented in its appellate power on a ground that the trial was vitiated by some error or omission apparent on the face of record. [239F] 1 :4 The main question which requires consideration is whether the trial commis sion court has jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting the withdrawal of the Suit under its revisional powers, if the Court is ultimately satis fied that the requisite consent as required by law was lacking. If the case is factually correct that Hari Narain Pandit was not its elected secretary and was, therefore, not authorised to withdraw t he suit, the prayer for withdrawal of ted suit was not made on behalf of the appellants at all and the High Courts should have gone back in its revision power on that ground.

The appellant was a Banker in the State of Bombay. On April 1, 1946, the Governor General promulgated an Ordinance called the Indian and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, which was to remain in force for six months from April 1. The Ordinance was repealed by the Indian Independence Act, 1947, and it was replaced by the Constitution (Seventilation of Emergency) Order, 1946. By section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, the words " for the space of not more than six months" were omitted from section 72 during the period specified in section 3 of that Act. The appellant was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate under section 7(1) (a) read with section 72 Of the 9 th Sch. Of the Government Of India Act. 1935, and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. Held, that the Ordinance was not in operation on July 11, 1953, when the emergency was declared to have ended on April 1,, 1946, by the India and Burma. The words "for the space" occurring in section 72 were not intended to be used as a substitute for the word "period". The words 'for the time being in force" in section 73 of the Indian Contract Act did not mean "the period of duration of the Ordinance in question" but meant "the date on which it was promulgated. The expression "for any space of less than six month from its promulgation " occurring in the opening part of section 72 was intended to cover a case where the Ordinance had been promulgated between June 27, 1940 and April 1 , 1946, and not when the Ordinance came into force.

The appellants were convicted for murder under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Amritsar. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence of death to life imprisonment. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the right to life is not a fundamental right; (2) the power to impose a sentence of imprisonment for life must be exercised in accordance with law and not arbitrarily, or capriciously; (3) the discretion vested in the court regarding the imposition of death penalty must relate not to the crime as such but to the criminal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to Life is not one of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution. It is a basic concept of life and personal liberty. [1070G] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure being satisfied that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354(3) of Cr. P.C. 1973, I would say that on the facts and circumstances of the case, it was neither feasible to define nor legally permissible for this Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special reasons ' occurring in section 354 (3). [1076H; 1077A] 2:2 The High court was justified by confirming the sentence passed under Section 368(b) of I. P .C., 1973, being satisfied on the evidence before it that there was "special reason" within that meaning and hence the death sentence imposed on them is not proper or uncalled for. [1177B] 2 :3 The High 's view that the award of death sentence to the two appellants was neither 'erroneous in principle nor was 'arbitrary or excessive ' or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion ', cannot be said to have been 'declared any law within the ambit of Article 141 so as to bind all Courts in the country. [ 1077C] 2(a). The High `s view is correct and must be upheld. [1007E] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, ; , followed. (b) In the great enthusiasm for doing so, the pendulum has swung to 1076 the other extreme and the guideline given is that the 'special reason ' must relate "not to the Crime as such But to the Criminal" for which there is no warrant in Section 354( 3) of Crl. Pc., 1973. [1017E F] 2.(a). In the very nature of things, it cannot be held that the sentence imposed by the High court on the two accused was neither "errentous in law nor was "arbitrary" or excessive or 'Indicative Of an improper exercised discretion '. Nor is it constitutionally permissible for the Supreme Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence awarded by the trial court was neither not 'errorally warranted by section 354, sub section (3), Cr.P., 1973 or "indicinal of an irregular exercise of power" nor "indics of an " improper exercise" of discretion". [1018G H; 1010A] 3:1. The Supreme Court has consistently held that in the matter of sentencing for murder, the court is enjoined with a duty to record special reasons ' in case the extreme penalty is awarded. But the question whether the death penalty should be awarded or not must depend upon the facts of the particular case and the law applicable. [1108B C] 2 (b).

The appellant was a Deputy Director of Investigation. He was suspended on 30th September, 1953 by the Commissioner of Income tax, Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry on allegations involving corruption and violation of service rules. The inquiry officer found that the Gautam Cycle Mart was started in 1942 and not in 1939, and that the appellant had been exonerated of the charges and imputations made against him on each occasion. He also pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. Inspecting Commissioner, and the appellant was exonerated of allegations and imputations. The Commissioner of Incometax, however, rejected the application for a certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. Unless such a point could be raised there could be no declaration that the departmental proceedings were null and void. There is also an application before this Court for revocation of special leave to appeal by this Court on the ground that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave. [585 C] (2) The question whether the appellant is given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It was for the appellant to satisfy the departmental authorities which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he suffered some injustice which to be set right.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The contracts between them related to the export and the sale was by the M.M.T.C. with their foreign buyer. The appellants contended that they were not the last purchaser but the M,M. T.C., who was the exporter and shipper of the goods. The High Court held that the contract between the appel lants and the M M. M.T.,C. indicated that the appellants ' contract of sale occasioned the export of the ore and that the contracts of the appe llants with the M/M.M T. C. were integrally connected with the contract entered into by the appellant with their Foreign buyer. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contract between M.S.T .C. and the foreign buyers are different contracts and it is the S.T.(C) which entered into independent contracts with their M.Ms. on F.O.B. basis. Under the contracts between the M em ployees and the S,T. C., the merchants were required to bring the goods F.o.B to the ship named by the S .T.c. to the Ship named by them. This was done in the course of export by the appellants. The sale is an independent one between the Corporation and their foreign buyers on F 'O 'B. contract basis. [444E G] 2.1 In the instant case, the contracts were inter connected with each other. The M.A.C.) entered into direct contract with their Indian buyers. There was no privity of contract between them and the Foreign buyers from the S,.T.E.C.; nor was there any privity of con tract between the two foreign buyers. [445F G] 3.1 The contracts were in the nature of contracts between M/s. Texports Ltd., and the appellant 's foreign buyer on FO 'C ' basis. The agreements between the S and their Foreign buyers are distinct and independent contracts of sale. Under these contracts between tho M.N.T,C. the merchants are required to bringing the goods free on board a ship to be named by their buyer. This Court in Serajuddin 's case has laid down that the mere mention of F.0.B., price or F. O.B ' delivery in contract between a merchant and the C.M.,T.S., which is an integral part of the sale, does not render these contracts either inte grated or the contract among the foreign buyer to the latter will not make the two contracts either in inte strument or the con tract of sale either int ernption or the ac cordingly between the merchant and S. T.,C., an F.I.R. [443D E] 4.2 The contracts are inter connected and it was the S t.T C. who was exporter and the shipper who was a consignee and shippers of the Goods. In the special leave petition, the appellants assailed the assumption made by the High Court to the effect that all contracts between tile merchants and the Corporation were integrated F.Os. with foreign buyer and, therefore, the purchase by the merchant from the mine owner was the last purchase in the State. The privity of the contract was between the appellant and the U.S.; but the actual exportation of the said goods was the contract both in the case of the M 'M.E.,C; and F.A., contracts with the foreign seller on F0 'B ' basis, because the export sale is independent one.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. The appellant filed an application before the Labour Court under section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act for reinstatement and compensation. The Labour Court held that termination of service of the appellant amounted to retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) of the Act and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25 F, termination was held invalid. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i) the termination of services of the respondent did not constitute retrenchment within section 2 (oo), and (ii) the Labour Appellate Tribunal had wrongly relied upon the decision in K.S. Jain vs Union of India, ; , where the termination was to be automatically effective by a certain date as set out in the order of appointment it would nonetheless be a retrenchment within that meaning section 2.(oo). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The termination of the service of appellant was ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits. [532C] (2) The respondent had worked for 240 days in a period of 12 months, it was not necessary that he should have been in the service for one whole year. Therefore, both on principle and on precedent it must be held that section 25B(2) comprehends a situation where a workman is not in employment for a period Of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be In continuous service for a periods of one year for the purpose of Chapter VA. [540D E] (3) The appellant had worked as a temporary employee for 240 day in a calendar month and was therefore deemed to have been continuously in service for 240 8 days within a period 12 months and indisputably, his case falls within section 25 B(2)(a). [533G H] (4) The retrenchment of the workman was ab legally void and ineffective and a declarations were made that the appellant continues to remain in service.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour and an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet but having failed to obtain relief, the appellant applied to the High Court for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution quashing the order dated March 17, 1965 on the ground inter alia that the order of dismissal was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order was at all given. The High Court held that the appellant was a temporary servant and had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant 's employment was termination of his services. Held, that the High Courts were in error in holding that the enquiry made by the Settlement officer was made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanor. The order passed by the High court is set aside and the order passed on March 17 is restored. Ram Narayan Das vs State of Bihar, ; , applied. State of West Bengal vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, A.I.R. 1958 S.C. 840, distinguished. State Of Bihar vs Gopi Kishor Prasad, [1958] S. C. R. 828 and Ram Narayan Dass 's case enquiry was made pursuant to Rules governing the conduct of public servants for ascertaining whether the probation of the public servant concerned should be continued in service or should be discharged under the terms of his employment, and to "a termination made pursuant thereto an enquiry into allegations of misconduct or inefficiency with a view, if they were found established to imposing punishment and not to an enquiry whether a probationer should be confirmed.

The appellant State Government made a number of selections to the posts of Professors in the colleges. The Commission recommended that the selection be made on the basis of seniority cum merit and that the candidates should be interviewed by the Selection Committee constituted under section 133(2)(b) of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1956. The State Government did not accept this recommendation and appointed a committee consisting of only one member to examine the suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors. The appellant challenged the validity of the selection on the ground that it was invalid because it was not made in accordance with the provisions of section 133 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kahmir University Act, 1956, which came into force on October 1, 1957. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Commission was consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers from one service to another, and that it had been specifically stated by the State Government that it consulted the Commission under section133 of the constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, they cannot advance their arguments with reference to article 16 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts erred in holding that section 133 was not correctly interpreted and whether the Public Service Commission for the State of Jammu & Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, has been consulted in accordance With its requirement. [875 D] (2) It is not provided by section 133 that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the candidate, or that it is not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee comprising only one of its members, so long as the commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [888 E] (3) The State Govern ment has in fact placed on record the minutes of the Com missioner dated July 22, 1969, which make it quite clear that the State Govern ments referred the selections to it, a committee was appointed by the Commission for that purpose, the Committee was presided over by a member of the commission, the report of the Committee is formally submitted to the Commission. The report of such committee is formally made available to the Government under section 134(2) (b).

The petitioner was the Chairman of a House of Commons of the United Kingdom. The question for determination in this case was whether the privileges and immunities of a house of Commons and its members and committees constituted by the Constitution were subject to the provisions of the Constitution and under article 19(1)(a) of the constitution, and that the petitioner 's fundamental right under article 14 was not infringed. Held, that the privileges conferred on the House of the Commons of a State and of the members and the committees thereof and its committees constituted under the Constitution are subject to their constitutional rights and they cannot be said to be subject to any restrictions imposed by the provisions Of the Constitution. The privilege conferred on Parliament of a state is subject to article 19 (1) (a), and therefore, if the House or Houses of Commons had the power or privilege to prevent the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect of the proceedings, it was not necessary for the Legislature to take any action in respect thereof. The privileges and powers of a member and the committee of a Houses of such Legislature are conferred by the latter part of article 105(3) on each House of Parliament and the members, and committees thereof. Article 194 (3) is not made subject to Article 19 of the Constitu tion and therefore if the house of the Legislature of a Province had the privilege to prohibit the publication or at any rate of the expunged portions of it, the Legislature would have no power to take action in regard to that publication. The House of Lords upon many occasions has declared the publication as a breach of privilege and the House has never formally rescinded the orders which from time to time it has made with regard to this subject.

The private college was taken over by the Government of Orissa on March 9, 1971 and a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the College and the Governor of the State. The management had to meet with financial crisis in the past and obtained financial help in the shape of liberal endowment under a trust deed from the then zamindar of Khallikote. The institution, it is stated, became one of the premier colleges in the town of Behram pur, Ganjam District, Orissa. The Government of Orrisa tion issued a Circular dated March 23, 1971 addressed to the Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa, which appears to supersede the earlier circulars on the subject. It was further clarified that at the time of reference to the P.S.C. for determina tion of suitability for appointment as Reader and later for consideration of their ap pointment by the Public Service Commission for appointment, cases of Lecturers of Government College eligible for appointment were also simultaneously referred to the Public Services Commission for consid eration of their ' suitability for appoint ment as Readers in the Government College. The Director of public Instructions ( Higher Education) issued a circular dated March 24, 1971, which stated that the teachers of Government Colleges who had been confirmed though drawing salary less than Rs.600/ were treated differently by the Govern ment from the eight Respondents on the sole ground that they were drawing as Reader 's salary of more than Rs,600/ . The appellants in Civil Appeal 1357/75 contended before this Court that although they had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Readers after the College had been taken over, their names were not referred to Public Service Commis sion for consideration. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The condition of draw ing of Rs. 600/ or more on the date of taking over, which has been laid down in the said circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment is arbitrary and discriminatory. [775C] 1.2 In the instant case, all the Respond ents are eligible to be referred to. the Public service Commission for the post of Reader. Whether they will be suitable for appointment Readers will be a matter entirely for due and proper consideration of the Public services Commission whose recommendations will be considered by the Gov ernment in the matter of final absorption. [777E] 1:3 The condition regarding draw ing Of Rs.6,600 or more is arbitrary, discriminatory and violative of Article 16 in the High Court as well as before us. The said circular took recognition of the service in the private college in the case of two (1) ; The only differentia was, therefore, the salary drawn by the Readers on the dates of take over; that action based on the salary aspect under the said Circular had to stand the test of Article 14 in the high Court as also before.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 A) of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 for plying their passenger vehicles on Khurjahatari Dabai Rajghat Ram whereon Parbatta route (route for short). The State Transport Authority rejected the applications on the ground that the scheme had been published in respect of the route in question and therefore an application for temporary permit was not made under section68 F(I A) the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of rejection of their applications. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal had no power to grant temporary permits to any one else, and that even though there were 7 vacancies and the Corporation applied for only 3 temporary permits once the Corporation made an application under section 66 F( 1 A) by the Corporation and granted no one else was entitled to obtain a temporary permit. The State 's appeal to this Court was against the High court 's order. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 68 F (1 C ) clearly envisaged a situation where application for a temporary or permanent permit is not made by the corporation. If the Corporation applies for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permits and section 68 E(1 C) would be squarely attracted. [985 D] (2) Section 69 F(l A) clearly envisaged the situation where applications for a permanent permit are not made in accordance with section 68F(1A). The Corporation will have to examine the application for permanent permits made by persons other than the Corporation, and if they are found to be competent eligible and qualified they may have to be granted permits for the benefit of the large travelling public. [986 E F] (3) Section68 F (l A ) clearly contemplated a situation when an application is made under Section 68F by the Commissioner or Regional Transport Authority as the case may be, for the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date when the approved or modified scheme is published. The Corporation would be entitled to all the temporary permit to the extent of the total strength fixed by the State Government under section 69 F (I A). [986 G H] (4) Section 67 F(2) clearly contemplated that even if there are 7 vacancies, and the corporation applied for all these permits, once the State transport Authority made an applica tion for the permanent permit not for the full strength but something short of it there was no power left in the State to grant permit to any person other than tho Corporation to operate vehicles on the route for which the scheme is framed till modified or approved scheme is notified. [987 A B] (5) Section 64 F(3) clearly envisages a situation wherein application for an temporary permit is made not under section 67F(I C).

The appellant, a son of the respondent, was born to him in 1933. He died leaving behind his widow and two daughters. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the property on the ground that the appellant had no ancestral property qua her own sons. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the respondents. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the property inherited by him from his maternal grandfather is not ancestral property and so it allowed the respondent 's suit. HELD : (i) The doctrine of stare decisis is in applicable and should present no obstacle in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench of the Punjab High Court were not correctly decided. [1001 D] (ii) It was not suggested that the custom differed from the Hindu law on the issue before their Lordships. The question as to whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather was ancestral property or not is a matter which can be agitated in a suit by a person who has no right to challenge his alienation of the said property. [1101 F] (iii) It is well settled that the doctrine ofsettling the law does not apply where there are two conflicting views on the question of law and one of them is that the principle of stare judicata should be applied in such a case. The doctrine is applicable only when there are conflicting decisions on the point of law. [1102 F] In the present case, the decision of the first Full Bench was wholly unsustainable as a decision on the points of the relevant custom.
