[1201 G] (iv) It would be difficult to say that the decision in Narotam Chand 's case should not be accepted as correct. The principle ofsettle the law is applicable and must present no hurdle in finding that the previous cases of that Full Bench were not properly decided.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them was sleeping in the Vermity of his house he inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. He sentenced the other three appellants to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and for two years under s 449 of the I.P.C. The first contention raised by the appellants was that there can be no conviction under section 450 of the Code unless murder has actually been committed. Held, that the words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 of tho Indian Penal code but also in two succeeding sections 450, 451 and 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Section 454 of the Cr. P.C., runs thus: "Whoever does any act with such intention or knowledge and under such circumstances that if he by that act caused death, he would be guilty of murder, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine." The words " in order to". have been employed by the Legislature not only must in section 448 of the IPC but also must in the two succeeding provisions. Section 451 makes punishable the commission of an offence of house trespass if it is committed "in pursuance of" the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act.

The appellant was a Sarswat Brahmin, resident of Pathankot in the district of Gurdaspur and the last male holder of the properties in suit. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable as there was no custom between the parties; (ii)that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial at all, (iii) that there was a custom according to which daughter was excluded from inheritance by the collaterals up to the fourth degree with respect to ancestral property of her father. Held, that the respondent had discharged this initial onus in two ways, namely (i), by producing the Riwaj i am of the Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and (ii). that irrespective of whether the properties were ancestral or self acquired the collateral 's in that case could not succeed to her father 's ancestral propertie 'section The appellant had discharged the initial onus by producing in evidence the Rwaj iam of 1913 and, consequently, the appellant must succeed. The appellant was entitled to succeed to his father 'S ancestral proper ties under section 4(1) (a) of the Indian Succession Act. The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collateral sarswatrahmin from succession to the self acquired property of his father, the initial burden, there fore must be on the collateral. The presumption as to the correctness of the Romaj i m ams of 1865 and 1893 was rebutted by the evidence adduced in the case.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. He executed two deeds in respect of certain properties in favour of the appellant and his wife, who were acting as Managing Agents of several companies registered under Indian Companies Acts. The deed provided that the respondent would pay to the appellant a sum of Rs. 1,000 per month on account of stamp duty payable by him. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract in respect Of certain properties and prayed for an injunction restraining the appellant from enforcing the agreement dated December 12, 1948, and also for an order restraining the respondent from enforcing it. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the instrument was not one of the five categories mentioned in the Schedule to the Indian Stamp Act and therefore the instrument could not be split up into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the executant were concerned. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the expression "distinct matter" must be construed in the setting in which it is used in the Indian context and not in isolation. It may be that in his turn he may be accountable to the beneficiaries for the due administration of the affairs of the trust but that does not mean that he, as trustee, is not entitled to exercise all these powers, the trust property having vested in him, and he being therefore in a position to exercise 856 all these rights in relation thereto. The fact however, that he may not be accountable under section 5 of the Indian , does not imply that he can exercise all those powers, but the trust properties having vested with him, he being a trustee, was not entitled, to exercise them, the Trust property having vests in him and he is therefore in an position to exercising all these functions in relation thereof.

The assessee was a Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two appeals. In respect of the assessment year 1949 50, the Income tax Officer deducted depreciation allowance from its actual cost of depreciation allowance under section 13(5)(b) of the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Income Tax Tribunal took a different view and held that this expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 was in force in the past" did not permit the Income 'tax Officer to make any deduction under section 66(1) of that Act. The High Court on reference answered the question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words which would be allowed to he assessee if the Income. tax Act had been in force and a claim had been made supported by prescribed particulars, that the words actually used were not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention; that the expression "any law relating to tax" would also have been omitted and this part of the paragraph would have read as "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating thereto tax on profits of business". HELD: The words "any laws relating to Income tax and Super tax or Any law relating To tax on profit of business" in para 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order are apt and sufficient to expressed the intention that if the income tax Act. 1922, which was not in force before the commencement of the Ordinance had been In force in that State, depreciation that would have be allowed if proper claim had actually been made should be deducted in ascertaining the written down value. [230 E] The words 'any law concerning tax on income of business ' are apt to express the intention by using these words in the Ordinance as "anylaw relating to taxation on profits" and so, depreciation actually allow under a law relating lo tax on Income tax would come within the first portion of the clause. [231 G] In the present case, the assessee had not claimed any deduction on the basis of the figures which were made by it in its written down values. The words used are apt, and sufficient enough to express their intention that the depreciation allowed under a laws which had been law in a component part of Part B States before it became included in the Part B state, it was unnecessary to add the words " or any Law relating to taxes on profits ' of business. [232 C] The expression "all the depreciation actually paid under any law or rules relating to Incometax and supertax or any tax on Profits of business shall be taken into account in computing the written off value under section 10(5) (b) as equivalent to which would had been allowable to him, if the Act had in fact been in existence.

The petitioner, a contractor in the State of Karnataka, was awarded contract for construction of a dam. The petitioner submitted his tender and the tender was accepted by the respondent Corporation on the ground that the petitioner had failed to fulfil certain prequal condi tions which under the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.T.), had to be ful filled even before the forms of tender could be supplied to any intending contractor. The Petitioner challenged the said decision before the High Court by way of a Writ Petition in the Karnataka High Court, contending that the pre conditions and the details called for in para V could be supply at any time before the final award of the contract, that the details asked for in Para V could he supplied at any point. The learned Single Judge dismissed the Writ Petition holding that there was no difference between the requirements in paras I and V and that only para I and not para V set out the pre condi tion of eligibility to submit a tender for the contract. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of para I is that before the tender books can be supplied, an intending ten derer should satisfy the K.P.C., by supplying such of the documents called for and are such material in assessing the fulfilment of the condition in para I, that he fulfills the three prequalifying requirements as stated in para 1. The more harmonious and practical way of construing the N.I .T. is by saying that, before the contract can be supplyed, an intended ten der should satisfy, the KP. C. by supplying those documents called on for in paras V as are material in assess ing the fulfilment o f the condition In para I. The other harmonious and legal way of interpreting the NI. T. is to say that, after the tender book can be furnished, an assis tive person should satisfy himself that the conditions set out in para l are material and that he fulfils the three conditions set forth in para 5(c) of the N .I.t. and that the information are only for information and are those which have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply of tender forms. It is for the K P.C. to assess the value of the certifi cates furnished in this regard and if the K p.C./appellant assessee fails to do so, the Court will decline relief. [237E F] 1.2 The more consistent and practical approach of interpretation should be by saying, that before a tender book could be issued, an appropriate intending tener should satisfied the K .P.S.C.; by supplying them such of those documents as are relevant in assessing its fulfilment of condition in Para I, and that they fulfil the three requirements set out therein. [238G H] 1:3 The more rational and practical course of construing a N.l.T. Notification is by stating that, at least some, if not all, of the document referred to in para VI are intended to verify the fulfilment Of the three Prequalifying condiments, that they fulfills the 3 prequal quali fied requirements of para l. The most harmonious and pragmatic way of interpretation is by doing that, namely, by saying "that", before the tenders can be supplies, an ' intending ten er should satisfy tho K.p.C." by supplying these documents called as material in assessment the fulfilment .of the condition. [239B C] 1 :4 The more literal and practical sense of interpretation would be to allow a party who has already supplied all the documents in time and sought no extension at all. If save for the delay in filing one of the relevant docu ments, M.C .C.

The appellant was the owner of certain evacuee properties. The Custodian General of Evacuee Property, in exercise of his revisional powers under section 27 of the Central Act XIV of 1947, revised an order of confirmation passed by the Additional Custodian of East Punjab on the 20th March, 1952. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the application for confirmation which was made by the appellant in 1948 and which remained pending until Act XXXI of 1950 came into force and superseded the earlier legislation in this behalf had to be disposed of in accordance with sections 5 A and 5 B of the East Punjab Act XIV Of 1947 as amended in 1948. Held, that the order under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian General under section 8 of the Act. The revisional power vested in him under section 38(4) of the , is not confined to matters ejusdem generis with clauses (a) and (b) but extends to matters which are expressly included in cls. (a), (b), (c) and, therefore, the application of the appellant for confirmation pending on the date when the Central Ordinance XXXI Of 1950 came in force had to he dealt with and disposed of under this Act and the order of confirmed in 1952 would clearly be subject to the revisional power of the CustodianGeneral under section 28 of the said Act. Held further, that having regard to the provisions of sections 5A and 5B of the West Bengal Act XIVof 1947 as it stood at the relevant time, the order passed by him was not open to appeal or revision but became final and conclusive.

The appellant company was a public limited company. Its main object was to provide for bonus based on custom or condition of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. " The appellant company challenged the validity of the Bonus Act on the ground that it was inconsistent with the provisions contained in section 32(2) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the claim for bonus for the relevant four years was founded on tradition or custom and did not fall within the provisions Of Bonus Act and that the exemption under section 32 excludes those employees from claiming bonus under the or such other Act is not correct. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that (i) the claim relating to customary bonus could be based either as a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees creating a term of employment for payment of Puja bonus; (ii) the exemption from claiming customary bonus or those based on conditions of service did not detract from the claim of customary bonus. HELD: (1) The Bonus Act is a complete Code and is exhaustive of the subject, whatever the species of bonus, there may be a bar, but it is quite conceivable that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which case other types of bonus are left untouched. [603 C] (2) The object and reasons of the bonus Act indicate that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of bonus based upon profit bonus ' or does the Bonus Acts speak on the topic of bonus of all species and, therefore, stands four square between a claim for Bonus and its grant unless it finds statutory expression in the provisions. [503 D] (3) The scheme of the Act shows that the object of the legislation is to provide bonus based not on any particular condition of services but on other considerations which are different from and unconnected with profit based bonus. It is true that if the Bonus Scheme is a valid piece of social reform, it would be subversive of the rule of res judicata. But it does not mean that the Court should go into the question whether customary or traditional bonus was claimed for the year 1965 and so, in later years, such a ground is barred by the general principles of resjudicata. [599 F] (4) The main object of section 32 is to prevent an invasion from the flank in that manner. If, therefore Parliament wanted to retain the right to claim bonus by way of industrial adjudication for those who are either excluded or exempted from the Act, it will have made an express provision saving provision to that effect as it has done for employees in Coal Mines.

The petitioners in the writ petitions were direct recruits to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana. They were appointed to the Higher Judicial Services of Punjab on or after December 31, 1976. The Rules governing seniority between direct recruits and promotees appointed to that service by promotion and by direct recruitment. Rule 12 governing seniority was amended by clause 6 in the same manner as in Punjab, that is to say, 1038 by providing that the seniority of members of the Service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation) and that the inter se seniority of the members of such service, whether directly recruited or appointed to any such post shall be fixed by the High Court according to the criterion of the dates of confirmation. The petitioners who were direct recruit to the higher Judicial Service filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of Rule 12 on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the rules governing seniority of judicial officers of the State are not violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitu tion inasmuch as they have been made by the Governor in exercise of his power under Article 235 of the Consti tution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the retrospective effect given to the rules from April 9, 1976 for the mere reason that on August 25, 1976 the High court had issued a notification fixing seniority of promotees and direct recruits appointed to posts in the Superior judicial Service of the Punjab and, therefore, it was not open to the High Courts to give an arbitrary date of confirmed to the promotees; (ii) the amendment made by clause (6) in the said manner is bad because the power of confirmation is a part of the control of the High ' Court which is vested in it by Article 235 and the power conferred upon the Governor by the proviso to article 309 is thus expressly, by the terms of that Article itself made subject to the law which the State Legislature may pass for regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed inter alia to the Judicial Service; (iii) the seniority list should be drawn by the Government on the basis of the respective dates of their confirmation without applying the rule or rotation; and (iv) the High COurt was not justified in applying the Rule of rotation at the time of confirmation so that, after every two promotees are confirmed one direct recruit has to be confirmed and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. Dismissing the writ Petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The retrospective effect was given to Rule 12 from April, 1976, for the merely reason that after August 25. 1976 the State Government had issued another notification fixing the seniority and direct recruit appointed to a post In the service on or before December 31.1976, on the footing of their length of service. [1055C D] 2. The effect of the retrospective operation was given only to the Rules from April 1, 1976 and not to the rule of rotation. [ 1056E F] 3. The seniority of all officers appointed or promoted to the superior Judicial Service, Punjab before December 30, 1976 will be determined on the dates when confirmation is made. [1001D E] 4.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, in this appeal filed R.P. No. 2403 of 1987, before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, challenging the order dated October 6, 1989 made in R.A. No . 2403/87. The Tribunal allowed the application holding that the State Government had no power to organise class or classes of posts in a civil service of or any class or class of civil posts under the State. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants for Adilabad and Warangal Divisions were illegal, contrary to order issued in G.O.Ms. No, 10 dated 25th January, 1987; (ii) the power given to the State Govern ment under proviso to paragraph 3(1) was only to organise a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts; and (iii) the constitution of a separate unit for purposes of recruitment, seniority or promotion etc., as the case may be. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The creation of division and maintain separate seniority are illegal contrary to orders issued in Government G. O.Ms No. 10 dated 15th January 1987. [569D] 2.1 In exercise of the power under proviso (i)(e) of paragraph 3 of the Order the State Gov ernment shall, within a period of twelve months from the date of commencement of the order, organise class and classes of civil post under the state into different local cadres for different parts of the State to make an order in that regard requiring the State Govt. to so organise it. [570E] 2:2 In exercise Of the power conferred under proviso paragraph 3 (1) of the Government of Andhra Pradesh hereby empowers ing the President, having regard to the requirements of the state as a whole for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts o f the State in the matter of public employment and in the matters of educa tion, and different provisions may be made for various parts of tho State to frame an order, in particular (a) require the State Gover nment to organise any class of posts within a zone; (b) require t he State Government to create a local cadre within a Zone; (c) appoint a separate seniority list in respect o f any category or classes or of civil services under the Government in respect thereof. [568D E] 2 :3 In exercise exercise of powers under proviso, paragraph 3, by an order require the state Govern ment whenever he considers it expedient so to do to have the power Under paragraph 3.(1) before the expiry of the period of 12 months prescribed in sub para (1), exercised. Thereby, it is clear that the creation and maintaining of separate seniority and Junior Assistants for Nirmalabad and warangal Divisions are illegal, contra viction of order issued by G.0.Ms, No. 101 dated 15.01.1987. [567F] 2;4 In exercise, of the powers under paragraph 3.1, it has been for the President notwithstanding the expiry period of the twelve months prescribed therein in sub paragraph (1). Thereby, the State 's power to organize class or Class or classes Of civil posts, and class or Classes of civil ary posts, under the Govern ment into different Local cadres should be exercised by the State government in accordance with para 3(i) before tho expiry of twelve month from October 20, 1975.

The appellant was the auction purchaser of a plot of land in which he had mortgaged his property to the respondent. The mortgage decree provided that the mortgagee would be entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants on the ground that the mortgagor had failed to pay the amount due under the mortgage and that the patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage, was binding on him. The appellant contended that he was subrogated to the position of the Bank, that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding the respondents, that he had got such power or not had to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management and that so long as nothing took place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. Held, that on the facts of this case it was clear that the appellant had no power to grant the permanent lease in question to the respondents. The fact that the plaintiff had no such power could not affect the rights of the appellant under section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act. The only relevant consideration was whether the mortgagor in possession had the authority to deal With the property, while dealing with the mortgaged property in a usual course, must rightly be deemed operative against the mortgagee. The true position has been stated in the following terms by,, Mukherjee, in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar (I.L.R. , and M/s. Banee Pershxd vs Beet Bhunjan Singh (I L.R . , referred to.

The petitioner entered into an agreement with the respondent for execution of certain works. The respondent sent a notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the petitioner for reference to arbitration. The petitioner filed his claim before the arbitrator. The contention of the petitioner was that Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the respondent, the respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator. On its failure it was open to him to approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Act for appointment or removal of the arbitration agreement. The claim was not put forward after the expiration of a specified number of years from the date on which the cause of action accrued, that is to say, from the dates when the claimant first acquired either a right of action or a right to require that an arbitration takes place upon the dispute concerned. The Court should exercise the power sparingly, cautiously and with circumspection to permit a party to the contract of a arbitration voluntarily entered into to relieve the party from dispute or difference and to order that the arbitration agree shall cease to have effect in respect of the dispute or differences. Clause 68 provides for the appointment of arbitrator and on its failure the Court may, on the application of any party to arbitration agreement, either (b)order that the Arbitration Agreement shall ceaseto have effect with respect to the difference referred. The Petitioner filed a petition under section 9 of the Arbitration Act before the High Court praying for an order restraining the respondent from implementing the arbitration clause and for an injunction restraining the petitioner from enforcing the arbitration award. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the period of limitation for commencing an arbitration runs from thedate on which cause of arbitration accrued, and that the Limitation Act applies to arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Courts and the making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration, does not prevent the statute of limitation being pleaded. In these special leave petitions it was contended for the petitioner that Clause 67 of the contract provides for an appointment of arbitrators and when a party has legally invoke clause 68, and issued notices to the respondents, the Court should have exercised its discretion sparingly, carefully and with caution to permit parties to the arbitration proceedings to relieve them from dispute. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Limitation Acts would apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary, cause of Arbitration for the purpose of limitation shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect thereof at the time when it should have accrued but for that term in a contract. [363D] 1.2 In the instant case, the proceedings before the arbitration are like civil proceedings before tho court within the meaning of section 14 of the . By consent the parties have substituted the arbitrator for a court of law to arbiter their disputes or differences and to orders that the Arbitrator shall cease with effect from the jurisdiction of the Court, by including an arbitration clause in the contracts providing that any arbitration under it must be commenced within a certain time or not at all. [362E F] 1:3 The provisions contained in sections 5 and 12(2) (b), are applicable to arbitrations. By consent, the parties had substituted the Arbitrator for a Court of law, to arbiters their disputes and differences. It is, therefore, open to the parties to plead in the proceedings that they have been given power in circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration Agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked.

The appellants, who were the mortgagees of certain lands in Bihar, applied to the Estate Officer for execution of a mortgage decree against the estate debtors. The objection was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds namely (1) that the objection as regards executability of the decree pleaded by the judgment debtors is barred by the principles of res judicata and (2) that it is 'so barred whereas according to the appellants as the Bakasht lands which form part of the mortgaged property had, not vested in the State. The executing court held that the objections were barred by res judicata. On appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the executing judge on two grounds namely : (1 ) that the plea was barred by principles of Res judicata and further that the bar of section 4(d) pleaded is not tenable. HELD: (i) In construing section 4 (d), it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the Act do not fall within the protection of the said Act and again at page 578 "Having regard to the said scheme, it is difficult to confine the application of section 5(d). [916 F G] (ii) The object of the legislation was to provide for the transference to the State of the interests in the proprietors and tenure holders in land and of the mortgagees and lessees of such interest. It would be reasonable to confine that operation of section 6 only to the claims made against the estates which have vested in it and no others. [917 F G; 918 A] (iii) The words "any suit or proceeding for the recovery of any money due from such proprietor" in section 4 are wide enough to include a claim as regards the debts due by the proprietors or tenure holders and so, it would be unreasonable to confine its application only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the Estate of the debtor. [936 B] (iv) The language of section 16 clearly indicates that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing section4(d), the Court would not only be right but would also confine the applicability of section 7A only to a execution proceedings.

The appellants who were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ' and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal and are within the permissible age limit and have succeeded are to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.S.,E.S Rules, 1971. The respondents who were allotted to the Indian Police Service Group 'B ' and were allocated in the year 1988 and 1989 under interim orders from the Tribunal for the Civil Services Examination in 1988 or1989 under the stay orders of this Court, have failed to join either of the services mentioned in Rule 17(i) of the Rules. The appellants who had been allocated to I. P.S./Central Services Group `A ' or I.I.P., Group 'C ' and whose names were included in the final list of candidates selected by the Commission, have filed these appeals after obtaining Special Leave from this Court. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the Tribunal has wrongly interpreted Rule 4(i)(a) of C.A.T. (Recruitment) Rules, 1954 as amended by the Central Civil Services (Amendment) Act, 1984 and has erroneously held that the amendment made in Rule 4 of the said Rules is not retrospective but only prospective. It was further contended that since the appellants had been allotted to I .P.C., Group `B ' or Central Service Group `C ', they were within the normal age limit as prescribed under Rule 17. Allowing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has rightly interpreted Rule 3(i), which is a statutory provision and has rightly held that it is only prospective in operation and not retrospective. [586B] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants have been allocated from I.T., IPS or Central Serv ices Group ' A ' to the CSCS. The Tribunal had rightly interpreted the said Rule as a whole and has wrongly held that there is no retrospective amendment in Rule 3 of the Recruitment Rules. [59D] 1:3 In the absence of any statutory provision, it cannot be said that the amended Rule was not retrospective in operation. It is only retrospective in effect and not retroactive. The amendment made by the Tribunal in 1984 is only clarificatory in nature and does not affect the validity of the amended rule. [60E F] 1 :4 The Tribunal was right in holding that the appellants were within their permissible age limits as prescribed by Rule 17, and that they were entitled to be considered for promotion to the post of Inspector General of Police. [61F G] 2.1 In view of the fact that the respondents have been allotted from I .T.,S.P./Central Service Group "A" to the Central Services, Group ' C ' and their names are included in final list, they will be given benefits of their successful success subject only to the condition that they must be within the per missible age limit without having to resign from the service to which they have been alloca ted. [62G H] 2:2 The Tribunal is right in taking a contrary view and has erred in holding the appellants guilty of contempt of court.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, had been dismissed. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the detenu 's request for assistance of a friend at the hearing and for the reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit was turned down. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have been better placed before the Advisory Board, and that he had sought the assistance of an advocate, and since the facts on which the ground is raised are not in dispute, the High court should have dismissed this contention. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The refusal by the Advisory board to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend was bad and continued detention of the Appellant became vitiated. [792C] 2.1 In the instant case, on 25th November 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise the detenu was denied the assistance. The denial of such assistance to the appellant was not justified. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the Appellant on account of such denial. [788E] 2:2 In the facts of the case, the Government merely informed the detenu that he has no statutory right to be represented by a lawyer. The Advisory Board had also stated in paragraph 2 that it was admitted by Mr. Sunderarajan before the Board that he is not a friend of the detenu and because of his professional experience he liked to help the detenu. [789F] 3:3 In the circumstances, two aspects have to be examined ( 1) whether the appellant 's refusal to permit him to be engaged by a legal practitioner or a legal adviser would be in breach of Article 14, if a similar facility is denied to the detenu; and (2) whether when the detaining Authority was assisted with a Deputy Commissioner and a superintendent of Central excise, was the request of the petitioner to be assist the detenu before the advisory Board. [781E] 4:4 In the present case, there is no dispute that on 25.11.1986 while the appellant is not afforded legal assistance, the detaining authorities were allowed to be represent by counsel. The failure of the detaining authori ty or the Government to appear before the detaining Board with the aid of a legal Practitioner or a Legal adviser will be in violation of Article 21 of the Constitution. [783F] 5:5 In the absence of any specific plea, it is not possible to accept the contention that if the detaining au thority or the Govern ment takes the aid o legal practitioner and a legal Adviser before the constituted Advisory Board the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the board through a legal lawyer. [784G] 6:7 In the premises indicated above, two questions have to he examined (1) whether on 25st November 1986 when the appellant had requested the Board to allow him the assistance o. a friend, namely, Mr. Sundararajan, in this view of the matter was perhaps a friend prepared to assist him before the Central Board; and and (ii) whether if the appellant wanted the assistance he would have if he was so minded, made a request to the Advisory Boards for permission to be heard by a counsel.

The appellants were the owners of certain jute mills. The mills were managed by a private limited company and were managed in accordance with the provisions of the , and the rules framed thereunder. The Government of India issued notices to the appellants under section 75 A (2) of the Bengal Jute Mills Act, 1923, for acquisition of the goods requisitioned and acquired. The appellants contended that the Government had no power to issue the notice on the owners as required by r. 75 A(2) Of the Rules. Held, that the order of requisition was valid service on the managing agents of the mills and was binding on the appellants. Rule 75 A contemplates that the orders of requisition must be brought to the knowledge of the person whose interests are being affected by it and that this was not done in this case for neither the holders of delivery orders nor the mills were apprised of the orders. The notice of acquisition in this ease was effective service on them as owners for the purpose of r. 74 A (3) would apply and the property in the goods passed to the Government of india on September 30, 1946. The order of requisitioning was effective only on September 15, 1946, and the appellants were not entitled to any compensation under section 18 Of the Act. Held further, that it is not correct to say that the notice of requisition is not properly served because the Government has no power under r. 76 A (1) to issue a notice on owners as contemplated by r . 75 A. The word "service" in section 18 of the Act means service of a notice and does not include service of notices of acquisition for the purposes of section 75A(2).

The assessee is a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, a notice was issued to the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Apprehending that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, the assessee set apart a sum of Rs. 4,50,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. Out of this amount an amount of Rs 2,02,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59 with the result that a sum Of Rs. 1,02.000 continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. At the same time the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section23A. Though it failed at the earlier stages, it succeeded ultimately in the Letters Patent Appeal filed by it in the East Punjab High Court. In the said appeal decided on May 24, 1965, it was held that no action can be taken against the assessee tinder Section 23 A. With this order all the orders passed and notices issued under the provisions prior to the date of the said judgment stood vacated. In its assessment relating to the assessment year 1963 64 under the 112 , the assessee contended that the said sum of RS. 4.50 lakhs is a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. By the date this appeal was taken up for hearing, another appeal preferred by the assessee relating to assessment year 1964 65 was also before the Tribunal. That appeal arose under the provision of the Companies Surtax Profits Act, 1964 which replaced the . The Tribunal first disposed of the appeal relating to that assessment year 1965 65. In so far as item in question is concerned it held that it was a reserve. Following the said decision, the appeal pertaining to the assess year 1963 65 was allowed. (It may be stated that the order of the Tribunal relating to assess year 1964 64 was subsequently rectified by an order dated February 15, 1972 and the said item was held to be a provision. But no such order was passed with respect to the said assessment year. Aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court, the Revenue obtained the aforesaid reference. The High Court answered the same in favour of Revenue and against the asses see. Hence this appeal by the Revenue. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding it to be an a provision and not a reserve [113C] 1.2 In Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, , it was stated in Vazir Sultan: "In other words the broad distinction between the two is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L. account, a reserve is in appropriation of profits, the asset or assets by which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. " [113D] 1:3 The High Courts were right in observing that the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision has been a charge upon the profits, to be take into account towards gross receipts against gross receipt in theP & L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand reserves are appropriations of profits. The assessee itself called it a provision; it did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve". [113E] 1 :4 In the circumstances of the case, the High court rightly held that the High Courts was right. [114G] Commissioner of Income Tax vs Metal Box Co.

The petitioners in these appeals were temporary Assistant Engineers (on a later point of time known as temporary Assistant Officers) appointed by the Railway Board pursuant to the authority given by the President of India on the recommendations of the Union Public Service Commission. The officers were informed that six of them would be absorbed into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class I) every year, this figure in the subsequent years was increased from time to time when in 1975, the figure as increased stood at 25 per year. The petitioners challenged the classification on the ground that Officers were appointed to temporary posts on the basis of competitive examinations and those recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Services Commission, terming it as arbitrary and not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the classification was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved, which mainly was efficiency of service, and that both the services had started separately and never became one. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State is prohibited to create separate channels of service and create discrimination by making one as an isolated one, and not providing for promotional avenues reasonably, fell to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's case (supra). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification made by the State Government on the recommendation of the Public Service Com missioner was neither arbitrary nor violative or violative of Article 14 and the High Court rightly dismissed the Writ Petitions of the petitioners before it on the view that it has nexus to its object sought for in view. [1027C] 1.2 The scheme at this point oftime to look for a substitution at our end, as that would unsettle a settled position, established more than a decade ago. It needs mentioning that the appeals being decided instantly are against the judgments and orders of the High Courts rejecting writ petitions of the petitioner before it. [ 1027D] 1:3 The scheme of the Railway Boards in lessening the Iona wait by giving them weightage of half of the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. Similarly when the dispute raised between the Officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented, in Katyani Dayal 's Case (supra), still it was a dispute raised before this Court which has been decided finally. A dispute now sought to he raised under Article 32 of the Constitu tion between the officers in a representatives capacity and Engineer Engineers across also in a Representative capacity must be held to be barred by principles of res judicata as also in the rule of constructive res judicata. [927E F] 1 :4 The distinction between, the two services was well marked in Katakyani 's cases (supra) and the important question of equality was once for all settled. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of one half of length of services subject to maximum of 5 years, it would otherwise be imprudent now, at this stage to dig up old issues. Similarly, when the disputed raised between officers in the representative capacity & Engineers notso represented, In Katyni Dayal ' 's ease (supra); still it is a dispute raising before this court which has already been decided earlier.

The appellant was tried by the Special Court constituted under the Saurashtra Ordinance, 1946. The trial court held that section 5 (1) of the Ordinance offended against article 14 Of the Constitution and quashed the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. On appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that sections 9 and 11 by empowering the State Government to establish a Special Court and to direct it to try under a special procedure such offences as may be notified by the Government in effect, authorise the Government to amend section 5 of the Criminal Procedure Code read with the Second Schedule (as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra), which provides that "all offences under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried or otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained", and that delegation of such power to the executive Government was beyond the competence of a legislature and was therefore void. Held, that section 11 of the Saurashtra Act in so far as it authorises the State Govern ment to direct "offences" to be tried by Special Courts does not offend against the equal protection clause of our Constitution and the notification issued thereunder contravenes article 14 of the Constitu tion. The word "offenses" is used in contradistinction to "offen cation". It is a well settled rule of construction that where two constructions are possible, one which must be reasonably connected with the object sought to be achieved by the statute should be preferred. In the present case the Legislature had left it to the Government and classify offences or classes of cases or classes thereof for the purpose of the Act, for the State Gov ernment was in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the State and the Court will not lightly interfere with the decision of the state Govern ment.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and section 396 of the Indian Penal Code, for having committed murder of one Mauji Lal and his wife Ram Shree (P.W.2) woke up on hearing some commotion when the miscreants who entered the eastern kotha of the house were breaking open the northern door P.W 2 raised the wick of the lantern material Exh. P. W. 1, and P. Ws. 1 to 7 raised the hick of lantern, material Exh P. P W. 8, but he was of the opinion that the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 7 could not be relied upon because they had used their influence in committing the murder of Mauji Ram. The Sessions Judge rejected the evidence on record holding that the prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubt and acquitted them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) P.w. 1 who had undoubtedly come near the scene of occurrence would have seen any of the culprits and could not identify them; (2) P,W. 2 had modulated her evidence to fit in with the case of prosecution and that the testimony of P W 2 by the learned Sessions Judge was not convincing; (3) P 's evidence was highly improbable and unreliable because it was admitted by P.S.I. that he had gone near the place of occurrence soon after the dacoits left the place; (4) P could not have been in a position to identify any of them; and (5) P had modulate her evidence with the help of lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers and she has received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the occurrence which had gone on for about 15 minutes. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The reasons given by the Sessions Judge for rejecting the evidence are not convincing. [955C] 2. The reason given by P 'W. 8 for rejecting her evidence is that she was in the eastern wall of the eastern door of the western kothakha where the main part of the incident has taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify with the aid of lantern so as to be in a situation to identify them. There was sufficient moon light at the time of the alleged occurrence and it is not improbable that these appellants were seen by P, W. 2 immediately after the culprits left the scene. Therefore, it could not reasonably be said that she had any "glimpse" of the miscreants so as not to be a 'doubtful ' whether P.M. 7 could have had a sufficient "gridpse". [956E F] 3. The evidence of the eye witnesses is corroborated by the evidence, and the other circumstances of the case namely that the door of eastern katha of house of the deceased was found broken open, that the dead body of Maui Lal was found lying in the verandah of the 'W 's house and that it was "douful" whether P, Ws. 7 and 8 had received injuries during that occurrence and had not mentioned the name of any of these accused to other villagers who entered their house soon after they left the spot. Therefore it could be safely inferred that the appellants were in the western wall of eastern door at the same time and it was not improbable or improbable that those appellants were known by P to them. [961F G] 4. The learned Sessions judge has rejected the prosecution evidence on the ground that no reliance could be placed on the evidence.

The respondent Corporation was created under the State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to the exclusion of its employees while on probation on ground of unsuitability and for non compliance with the provisions of section 25F of the . The employer Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation created under a State Act, entitled the transport corporation Act of 1950 ( 'Corporation Act ') for short) is in appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The termination of the service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as deemed retrenchment. [778C] 1.2 In the instant case, the services have been terminated on the ground of unsatisfactory service. The excepted or excluded cases are where termination is by way of punishment inflicted by way Of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman, retirement of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment. The exclusion of cases are, where termination of service by act of employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or termination of services of a probationer on the grounds of continued ill health. [788E F] 1:3 In the case of the employees who have been embodied in the definition, discharge from employment or termination would also be treated as 'deemed retrenchment '. The excluded cases were where termination was by way or punishment inflictedby way of disciplinary action voluntary retirement, voluntary resignation of the employee, retirement or termination or of service of probationer would further amount to disbanding surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to 'retrenchment '. [789E F; 788A] 1 :4 The excepted cases are Where termination is of service except those which have been incorporated in the defined definition, discharged from employment, or termination by way either disciplinary action or voluntary retirement. voluntary retirement would also come within the purview of section 2(oo) of the and not the excepted cases. [ 789C D] 1;5 The excepted categories are where retrenchment is by transfer or otherwise than as a punishment inflicted in lieu of disciplinary proceedings, voluntary re employment of the probationer would be treated to mean what they plainly say, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the expression 'ret retrenchment ' must include every termination of his service by an act of the employer. [ 788E F]. Union of India vs Hariprasad Shukla, ; , referred to.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied for registration as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act in respect of unconnected or unclaimed goods, and was accordingly registered. It submitted returns of sales effected by it of unclaimed & connected goods year after year and paid sales tax pursu ant to the assessments made by the Sales Tax Department. However, in assessment proceedings for the four quarters ending March 1959 the assessee applying to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Act. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act, and accordingly assessed under that Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Board of Revenue held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assesseee and that consequently a sale of goods took place. The High Court dismissed the revision application on 27 January, 1960 on the finding that the sales effected were sales under the provisions of the Bengal Sales Tax Act and that the assessee was a " dealer" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the said Act. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern railway was a 'dealer" for the purpose of the Indian Railways Act, 1941. [781E] 2. The assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Tax Offi cer & Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In the other case, the assessee Eastern railway disposed of waste and unserviceables lying with the Railway, and unserviceible material lying in it. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It appears to South Western Railway was a dealer" for tho purposes of the West Bengal Finance Act, 1942.

The appellant, a Director of the respondent Bank, was charged with offences under section 409 I.P.C., and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case against him was that he had taken part in the transactions of purchase or sale of securities and that he used to go to Dalmia on the day following the receipt of the advice for confirmation of the contract of purchase of securities. He denied having received any amount from Bhagwati Trading Company as a result of which he had not been authorised by the Chairman. The trial court acquitted him but convicted him under section 5 of the Act and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs. 500/ . On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the contract for purchase of these securities had taken place on September 16, 1955, and therefore the prosecution case was that the amount was received in cash and not through transfers which transactions had to be adjusted; (ii) the prosecution evidence showed that the amounts were paid in cash by the Bank to the Union Agencies through Bhagwati Trading Co., in contravention of the manner in which he was to deal with that money; (iii) the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act could not be drawn against the appellant as it had failed to prove that the transactions were made on account of securities sold to the Insurance Company, and (iv) the evidence showed the receipt from Bhagwati trading Company, but the prosecution did not lead any evidence in support of its case. Held:(i) The reasonable conclusion can be that they mentioned Bhagwati Trading company as that represented the true state of affairs and Chokhani had to inform the Delhi Office of the Bharat Union Agencies about the source of the money he was receiving for the Union Agency to meet its losses. (ii). It is really on the basis of his paying the money out of the Insurance Co., that Dalmia told him and Annadhanam on September 20, 1954, that be had no knowledge of the missing securities, that it appeared that the securities had either been sold or pledged and that the money had been paid to the Bank. (iii). The prosecution evidence was that a sum of Rs,. 10,000 was passed on to the appellant by Bhagwati Trading Corporation in contravention Of the manner prescribed by law. (iv). It was not possible to believe that the funds of the insurance company were either sold or mortgaged and that it had been made over to the Corporation which was the business which Bhagwati Trading Companies professed to do and, according to him, he knew that most of this amount was passed to the State Agencies. The mere fact that a person is not authorised by law to receive money out from his funds does not make any difference in the matter of payment of money to the person receiving it. (v). It would be unreasonable to think that the prosecution had failed in proving its case beyond reasonable doubt.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. By sub section (1) of section 115 it was provided that conditions of service applicable immediately before the appointed day to the case of any person allotted to another State shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the former Saurashtra and Kutch States Secretariats of the Part B State of Saurashtra and the State Government of Gujarat by an order dated August 19, 1966. By the proviso to sub section 7 it was further provided that "the conditions of services applicable immediately prior to the appointed date to the cases of any persons allotted to other states shall not he varied to their disadvantage except without the previous sanction of the appropriate Government". The appellants who were holding posts in subordinate offices of the ministerial staff moved a petition in the High Court for an order directing the State to treat its order dated September 19, 1965 as "illegal, void and of no effect" and to forbear from enforcing its order treating the persons whose names were specified in the annexure to the order as servants of the "Secretariat cadre". The High Court held that when the ministerial services of the erstwhile Saurashtra and Saurashtra States Secretarats were absorbed in the districts, integration of the service was complete and any transfer thereafter to the Secretariat could not and did not amount to absorption in equivalent posts. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants : (1 ) that the transfer of the latter Saurashtra and Gujarat State Secretariat personnel to the Gujarat Secretariat per se was not open to objection; (2) that the appellants were transferred to the subordinate offices and they were not absorbed in any equivalent post; (3) that there had riot been any equivalence established between the posts in, the Secretariatats. of the States of Saurashtra & Kutch and the posts In the absence of evidence to show that the previous approved of the Government was obtained, their right to be absorbed in equivalent post in the new State of Bombay and later in the State was not thereby affected; (4) that when ministerial service personnel in the former Gujarat State were posted and assigned duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Ahmedabad, there was no absorption under the Absorption Rules. HELD : (i) The High ' Court was right in deciding the case against the appellants. [519 E] (ii) The broad purpose underlying the proviso is to ensure that the conditions of Service shall not not be changed except with prior approval of Central Government, that is, before embarking on varying the conditions, of service, the State Governments should obtain the concurrence of the central Government. It is true that the ministerial servicemen in the States are posted and allotted duties in different districts in Gujarat and later In the instant case there has riot been anything equivalence established by the orders of theCentral Government, the States Reorganisation of Saurashtra or Kutch and that posts in tho new State were allotted. But in the absence Of evidence to establish that the prior approval was obtained the right to he absorbed in equal post in a particular department cannot be challenged. [525 E F] (iii) The ministerial service employees in the erstwhile Gujarat State and later thereafter in the state of Gujarat were posted, and assigned duty in various Districts in Saurashtra, and Kutch. But there is no evidence to indicate that the earlier approval was not obtained. There has been no equivalence established either between the post in Secretariat and the post of subordinate offices under the orders. [426 G] (iv) The contention that the order dated 9th September, 1965 was passed without jurisdiction because it was passed by a competent authority is untenable.

The petitioners who were dealers in cotton and other goods imported from outside the State of Madras, which was a declared goods under section 5(2)(a) (vi) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. The goods were sold by them to dealers in the course of inter state trade or commerce. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore void. It was contended for the petitioners that the tax was not levied on the purchase or sale inside the State but on the first purchaser in the case of imported goods and last sale in the cases of local goods, and that the discrimination was also between the first purchase in the Case of imported cotton and the last sale In the case Of imported goods, the stage of purchase is the sale of such goods by the last dealer liable to pay tax under this Act; and that in respect of the same item of declared goods, more than one person is made liable to tax and the tax is also levied at more than two stages. Held: (i) The classification made by the impugned Act was reasonable and did not offend article 14 Of the Constitution. (ii)The discrimination was only between the second purchase in tho case of import goods and the first sale in that case of local sales, and the third sale in those cases of imported imported goods. (iii)The tax was levied on a dealer who purchased cotton and sells it after the period provided for in section 5 (2)(b) (ii). The discrimination was not between the two sales in the present case and the other two sales.

The respondent mortgaged his property in the Court of the District Judge, East Tanjore for a sum of Rs. 3,215 and put in a petition under section 47 and Order 21, r. 2, Civil Procedure Code praying that as the amount so deposited together with the payments already made completely wiped off the amount due under the decree as scaled down by the High Court in favour of defendants 2 to 7, full satisfaction of the decree might be recorded exoner ating the mortgaged properties and also the defendant No. 1 in substance was entitled to have the debt scaled up in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The District Judge rejected this contention and held that defendants 2 and 7 were entitled to get the debts scaled aside under the terms of the compromise decree, but as no application had been made on behalf of defendant No, 1, the proposal which seems to have been accepted by the Receivers was that the amount payable by him under the decrees was to be settled at Rs. 2.215 and putting in a Petition under section47 and 297 Order 21 rule 2, C.P.C., praying for that as defendants 2, 3 to 7 were not entitled to claim the debt Scaled down in favour Of defendants 2 8 to 7 separately on payment of the amount directed to be paid by them under the compromise decrees, was rejected. The High Court also held that the amended decree directs that the said defendants do pay into court the sum of RS. 1,05,000 and odd and it is on payment thereof that redemption would be allowed of the mortgaged property. Held, that the view taken by the District judge was right and should not have been disturbed. The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant 's co debtor, and that of defendants 3 to7 separately on payments of certain specified amounts by 'them proceeds clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debt and the security had been split up.

The appellants were the tenants of the premises in question under the first defendant. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain and try the suit but dismissed the suit on the ground that there bad been no lawful subletting by the first plaintiff of the said premises to the second and third plaintiffs as the provisions of section 10 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. 1 Of 1947), were not applicable to them. The appellants filed a suit in the City Civil court raising a claim to the effect that the first appellant was a tenant of the defendants and was entitled to protection under the Act and that the second, and third plaintiff were lawful sub tenants of their premises. The trial Court dismissed the suits on the view that there had been no unlawful subletting by them of the suit premises to them and that they could not be evicted from the premises. On appeal the High Court held in favour of the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the City civil court had jurisdiction under section 28 Of the Bombay Rent Act, because the provisions Of section 28 of the Act were not attracted to a suit relating to possession of premises to which the provisions were applicable and (ii) the suit in question could not therefore be entertained by the City Court. Held:(i) The City civil Court was competent to try a suit under the Bombay Act. Section 28 clearly contemplates the filing of any suit relating lo possession of any premises to Which any of the provisions contained in Part 11 of the , apply and in that suit claims and questions arising out of the . Act or any of its provisions had to be dealt with. It authorises the court to deal with any claim or question arising out Of the Act or anything in such a suit. The provisions of the City of Bombay Rent Control Act on the other hand clearly indicate that all claims or questions arising from the Act, or any o its provisions, even though they may be in the nature of a title to the premises, were to be determined by the courts specified in section 28 and no other. (ii). The City of Civil Court could not decree the suit of the plaintiffs unless their claim to remain in possession was established under the , or any Of its provisions.

The appellant was the managing director of a private company. On May 26,1955, a private limited company was incorporated under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company. On July 7, 1955, the appellant transferred his business to the Company, and on July 7. 1955, he appointed another person as the managing directors to hold the office after his death. The appellant contended that the appointment of the appellant was void because (i) the appointment by a director of another in his place by act inter vivous be an assignment of the office of a director within section 312 and had only contended that such an appointment by will which is what has been done by Dadoba would not be an assign, and (ii) the appellant having conceded that an appointment was by a directors of another person in his office by act intra vivosous bean assignment of his office, he could not claim to have a say in the appointment. Held, that the word "assign" in section 312 of the new Act does not include "appointment". It would therefore be wrong to infer that by using the word 'his ' the Legislature indicated that an appoint by a Director to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment, was not to be included within the word`assign". The rule of construction on which the High Court relied in arriving at the view that it did, was put in these words: "It is a well established principle of construction that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of the section would have included the subject matter of the proviso. The rule would enable the court to hold in regard to section 86B at the most that an appointed of an alternate director by a partner, was an assignment or appointment of his successor, and it would not have used the word `assign '.

The appellants are the tenants against the respondent landlady. The respondent filed an eviction petition being H.R.C. No. 641 of 1975 in the Court of Small Causes, Madras against the appellants and one other partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart. The appellants raised a preliminary objection that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. It was further contended that the appel lants had unlawfully sublet the shop to the respondent landlord, and that the eviction petition was not filed at all. The Trial Court held that the ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respond ent. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The appellant then preferred a Civil Revision Petition being C.RP. No 44 of 1981 in the High Court against the decision of the Appellate Authority under Section 23 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. This revision petition was dismissed by the learned Chief Justice of the Madras High Court. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction peti tion was filed against the appe lants firm and one another partnership firm, M/S Adeshwar glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction Petition was not maintain able at all; that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the premises to the re sponding respondents or served them as partner and hence the eviction suit was not tenable at all and that it was only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. It is further contended on their behalf that the High Courts have erred in holding that the respondent had sublet the said shop to M/ s Adeshwar iron Mart without join ing any of its partners or serving the appellants as partners; that there was no evidence to show that M/M. Adeshwar Engineering Mart was carrying on any business at the said premises and that firm was carried on business for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the finding recorded by the Trial Court against all the partners was perverse and based on no evidence; that even if the findings were not sustainable, the High court should have dismissed the revision petition as it was filed without impleading the appellants; that in any event, the judgment of the High Curt is set aside. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that there is no substance in this contention. [420B] 2.1 In the instant case, there is evidence to indicate that M. Adivas Glass Mart was carried ing on business at a premises even for some period during which it had ceased lo carry on business there and that Firm was carried out business in that premises even after some time when the appellants were not impleaded as parties. [421C] 2:2 The respondent landlord has also produced evidence to prove that M, Adivas glass Mart was carry ing on his business at that premises and therefore, the finding against all of them is perverse. [416D E] 3.1 It is now well settled that a partnership firm can be sued by its own names without the partner being impleaded in the eviction proceedings. In the case before this Court no such objection has been raised at any stage till the stage of special leave and it is certainly not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years.

The Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Urban Areas (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land situate within the urban agglomerations referred to in section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Central Act. The Andhra Pradesh Act was repealed by the Andhra Pradesh Urban Areas Development Act, 1973 which came into force on 1st January 1975 and it was with reference to this date the surplus holding of land in excess of the ceiling area was required to be determined and if there was any surplus it was to be surrendered to the State Government. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Andhra Act by a writ petition in the High Court which held that the Andhra Legislature had no legislative competence to enact the impugned Act on the ground that it sought to impose ceiling on lands situate within these urban agglomeration and since the concept of agglomeration defined in section 3(f) of that Act was an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified to be an urban agglemy, the whole of the State of Andhra Pradesh was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the Legislature. The High Court also held that in view of the fact that the definition of family unit in section 4(f), the entire land including the land situate in all the other areas of the state of Andhra Nadu was not within the legislative competency of the Madras Legislature to provide that the whole or any part of such land should be treated as an urban area and that the Act would apply if and when the area in question was notified to he an urban commensatory Area under section 2 (n)(a) (ii) and there can be no doubt that so far as these urban Deccan Merchants are concerned, it was not beyond the legislative power of the Parliament to enact such a law. The State of Madras vs V.R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala, ; , referred to.

The workmen who were directed to be taken back in employment, reported for duty on October 2, 1953, and October 2. 1953, respectively, but failed to produce evidence satisfactory to the Company of their absence as required by the notice dated September 17, 1953. The management dismissed them from service without giving any reason. The workmen filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order directing that the employees who had turned up on or before October 2 '1953, must be taken to have been retrenched and the employer was not justified in refusing leave. The High Court held that the Industrial Tribunal had in each case considered the justification for absence without leave and in view of the circumstance that the men were in custody, the Company was not entitled to be take back as of right without any condition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the company having held a regular and proper enquiry in which Samar Sen had an opportunity of meeting the charges against him, it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the company unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. Held: (i) The Industrial Tribunal having held that no reasonable person could be appointed as a domestic enquiry in respect of any particular workman, it proceeded on the footing that the Company had decided to terminate the services of the employees and that deliberate 'slow down ' tactics and an incitement to other workmen to adopt such tactics both amount to misconduct. (ii) The Tribunal was right in holding that the workmen themselves tried to coerce the company by their own conduct, but it did not consider the justification of absence without Leave. If a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute, as in this case, the work of the Company will be paralysed if the company is forced to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period. The Tribunal had found that no such opportunity was given to the workmen and that was the reason why they were not taken back by the Company.

The appellant University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the U.P.
