Universities Act, 1974 was mentioned in the reserve list by the Selection Committee. Dr. Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserved list was appointed as Professor in a department of the Bot any. The appointment of Dr. Section 6 Procedure of Selection Committee (1) The quorum required for the meeting of a selection committee constituted under Section 5 shall not be less than five out of which at least two shall be the experts, if the selec tion to be made is for the posts of a lecturer or any other post of a teacher equivalent thereto. The appellant was appointed Professor in Botan and was kept in reserve list. Dr Nathawat on the ground that the Selection Commis sion was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve lists exhausted itself. Dr Urea met the appellant and made an application to the Syndicate for approval of his appointment as Professor. The Syndicate by its resolution dated 10th July, 1978 decided that the reserve List recommended by the selection committee shall be valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate which was subsequently extend ed to one year instead of six months in a resolution passed on 3.12.1983. The University by its Resolution dated 10.7.1978 resolved that the reserved List recommended for selection of employee be treated valid for one year, instead of 6 months in the resolution passed by the Syndicate dated 10 7.8.1978. The Vice Chancellor of the University by his order dated 4.9.1979 directed the appellant to prepare a fresh list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and to forward the main list alongwith its recommendations to the syndi cate. The appel lant filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said resolution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that once the selected person join the post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve s list is of no avail and becomes extinct. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The very purpose of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High court is accepted that once an selected person joining the post again selection made in the last decade from the reserve panel is exhausted, and the reserved lists are of no availed and becomes dis posed. There was no reason to think that the appellant intended to keep the reserve for a long period of one year. If Dr. Nathavithese was found suitable for the ap pointment to be appointed on a vacant post caused during the validity period of the reserve, then selection by the committee is exhausted. [421C D] 1.2 The very object of preparing the reserve ments would be frustrated if the views taken by High Court are accepted that when a person selected by the sele c tion committee has joined that post then selections made by it are exhausted and no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the Reserve list by Dr. section 6 Procedure is in vogue in all the universities of Rajasthan that a reserve List is used for the appointment on a post caused after the validity Period of one yea rs. If we examine the matter from another angle, it would be clear that according to the university such a procedure is in force in all universities of the Rajasthan that A reserve list is used in the appointment On a vacant vacancy caused during this period of One year, selection made on a vacancy caused after expiry of the term of the reserved post and several appointments had been made in last decade.

The petitioners, who were owners of certain lands in the development plan originally published on January 9, 1964, challenged the validity of sections 4 and 11(3) of the , as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed their petitions holding that sections 4 to 16 were not violative of articles 19(1)(f) and (g). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) section 17 was discriminatory, because it did not provide for any reservation of land for a public purpose; (ii) section 18 was discriminatory inasmuch as it did away with the power of revision conferred by section 17; (iii) section 19(3)(a) was violative of Article 14 of 'the Constitution. HELD: (i). The provisions of sections 3 to 16 are borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases there was little or no scope for the local authority acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the Act. [285 C] (ii). Section 17 which was attacked in these case provides that "At least once in every ten years from the date on which the last development plan came into force and where the plan is sanctioned in parts from the dates on which a development plan for any area or, as the case may be, the part of such plan has come into force shall, carry out a fresh survey of the area within its jurisdiction with a view to revising the existing development plan including all parts if sanctioned separately and the provisions of Sections 4 to16 (both inclusive) shall so far as they can be made applicable apply in respect of such revision of the development scheme. [286 E F] (iii). The preparation of the final development plan or the final Development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local author. If the provisions Of sections 4, 5 and 6 were borne in view and the rule framed thereunder compliance with the rules made thereunder complied therewith, as appeared to have had been done, there was no justification for the State Government acting arbitrarily. [287 C D] (iv) The preparation and the final state ment of a section of the Development plan or final development scheme was not anything which was at all left to its pleasure or liabili ty. If section 17 were borne In mind and rules framed under sections 4 & 11(1), it is difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. [288 E F].

The appellant, a resident of Kutch, was carrying on business in the erstwhile State of Kutch. The Saurashtra area of Kutch was within the territory of the State of Gujarat and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions. In 1948, the Government of India Act, 1935, came into force which provided for the acquisition by the Union of India or the extinguishment of any rights therein or in respect of any matter arising out of such employment. The appellant claimed that the territory was a part of India and had never been so declared as to be a part thereof. The Tribunal accepted the claim and held that the Great Rann of Kutch which formed part of the territory, was part of that territory and could not be enforced without the authority of an amendment modifying the boundary of the state of Gujarat in which is now included the Rann. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the area in question was a Part State and had been so treated as part of territory, and (2) the compensation awarded by the Tribunal was not adequate. HELD: (i) The area in dispute was an extension of the mainland of Sind and apart from the survey maps there was no evidence that it was part or part of Great Rn of Kutch and therefore, the claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of the International Tribunal an attempt is made to cede any part of tho territory which formed parts of the Union before 1948 or was in de facto occupation and in respect thereof which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maharao of Kutch could not operate as giving rise to an obligation to crede Indian territory. [301 C] (ii) The question whether a particular area is a part or a part is essentially a question of fact depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is well settled that in construing a statute, the Court has to ascertain the intention of the legislature and its policy. If the intention was to be gathered from the language used, it would have been possible to hold that the intention had been expressed by the Legislature. [302 C] The question as to whether a law should be interpreted in the light of the surrounding circumstances is one which must be determined on the facts of each particular case. In the present case, the evidence on record showed that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year for part of year it was water and for the remaining part it was land. [303 D] (iii) The contention that by the alignment of the boundary under the award, territory which was Indian is now declared foreign territory, had sovereign rights, acceptance of the award was not correct. It was not evidence of the fact that it Was territory over which the Mahamad of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger became Indian territory, were ceded under the sanction of a constitutional amendment. The evidence on which reliance was mainly placed in support of the claim was the conflicting alignments in the survey and other maps, the claims made by them were not accepted. [304 G H] (iv) The boundary between the two States was indefinite and by the award Of the Tribunal the true boundary of India was determined: the award did not purport to, nor does it operate as give rise to, an obligation tede Indian territories. The claim made in implementing the Award by the Indian citizens to exercise fundamental rights in respect o the territory in that Sector may be entertained only if it be established that the Territory is found to be originally governed by the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1950.

The mortgagor had leased 200 bighas of coal bearing land out of his holding in Mauza Bahaldih, eight annas share in Mauza Bansjora and Simitanritan and certain interest in Mauzas Bansjuna. The mortgagor had sold 200 bighas to the lessees for an annual royalty of Rs. 2,000 payable in two equal instalments, the first in the month of Aswin of the Vikram year and the second in the months of Chaitra. The mortgagee did not pay the amount due within twelve years from April 14, 1925, but filed a suit on July 12, 1946, in the Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad for a decree for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. The trial judge rejected the defence raised by the defendants and held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the covenant in the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922, a usufructuary mortgage was created on the mortgagor 's interest in Mauza Arshidabad and by the attornment made pursuant to paragraph 7 of the mortgage, the mortgagor must be deemed to be in possession till the mortgagor had parted with his interest in the mortgaged property; (ii) the suit to enforce the mortgage dated August 27, 1922 was barred under article 120 of the Limitation Act because the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit, she could still maintain the suit relying on the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 7, 1937 by the auction purchaser who purchased the mortgagors rights in Bahaldhih lands at the Court auction and that the sale of that property in enforcement of that decree was barred from limitation. HELD : (i)(a) The right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the security or where he is not secured in his possession of the hypothecated property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the claim maintainable by the mortgagee was one for compensation and the period Of limitation for a suit to recover the mortgage money is governed by article 120. [699 C] (b) The plaintiff 's claim to enforce that mortgage was within twelve year from April 7. This right to recover royalty in respect of Mauza BahaWih, and by virtue of the sale under the money decree passed against the mortgagor, a cause of action accrued to the mortgagee to enforce his mortgage and the plaintiff ' 's suit filed within 12 years from the date of dispossession was within time. [643 D] (c) The suit to obtain possession of Mauza Arshadpur was barred because the mortgages were partly simple. The right of the mortgagor to sue, where the mort gagee is deprived by virtue Of the sale or under the decree passed by a Civil Court constituted deprivation of thesecurity or disturbance of their possession by the creditors of the mortgagee, dispossession having taken place in 1937 the suit filed on July 10, 1946 was at the date when the mortgage amount was repayable.

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. The company was prepared to grant free transport facilities to the supervisory staff there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman, learned counsel for the appellants frankly conceded that in future no charges would be realised from the employees and they would he provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals of the appellants 5 978 SCI/78 362 as he felt bound by the judgment of the Bombay High Court which had held that the transport vehicle provided to the employees by the company would be a public service vehicle. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even if a nominal charge is realised from employees that would not make the transport a publicservice vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The term 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that too does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the enactment it indicates that vehicles which could not be termed as public service vehicles fell beyond the ambit of the taxing provisions of the . [362G H] 2. The word 'public ' has been used in the sense of a wide connotation and its dictionary meaning is to take in all kinds of services including transport facilities, whether private or public. It may also include any other type of services which may be carried on by persons who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. [362A B] 3. The expression 'public purpose vehicle ' is wide enough to take within its fold all types of services mentioned in section 2(7) of the , which include transport facilities and whether private. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are giving facilities notas members of public but also as holding special status. [361C D] 4. The transport service provided to employees by way of facilities not being as members, of the Public Service vehicles fell squarely within the ambit and scope of the charging provision. [363D E] 5. The Transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within section 2 (7) and 2(8) of Act. [364E F] 6. The appellants were not entitled to any exemption from tax for providing transport facilities. [365G] 7. The High Court was wrong in holding that transport vehicles provided to them by the appellants could be a Public service vehicle in any sense of the term.

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a no objection certificate for a quasi permanent cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under 795 Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants was dismissed in limine by a speaking order by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on 6th March 1978. The State Government appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 6 declares that the grant or no objection" certificate is without prejudice to the right of the licensing authority to refuse a cinema licence under rule 102. [897C] 2. Rule 7 declares that "no objection certificate shall be granted for the site on which the cinema house is to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence having been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a 'temporary ' licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Govern ment on being satisfied that there was not impediment to the granting of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same. [8897F] 3. Rule 8 declares that no objection Certificate for the sites on which cinema house was to be built but he is influenced by extraneous consideration can subsequently oppose the grant. The appellant cannot now be permitted to plead a right to oppose the granting or a no Objection certificate when that grant was under consideration can thereafter oppose the Grant of a "noobjection" certificate. [8797G] 4. Rule 9 declares that a "No objection Certificate" is without any prejudice to his right of appeal on a person who might have raised objections before the licensing authori ty against the grant o ' no objection certifi cates. The order granting the no objection is violative of the principles of natural justice and the order granting licence for quasi permanent Cinema by the State government is invalid. [877B] 5. Rule 10 declares that subject to the provisions of rule 101 and 102, the licensing Authority may grant a certificate to the applicant that there is no objection to the location of the cinema at the site proposed by the applicant. The appellants not being entitled to challenge the grant Of the "no Objection" certifi fates, they cannot now now be allowed to plead any right to resist the grant granted of a 'no objection Certificate.

The plaintiffs instituted a suit (O.S. No. 515 of 1957) against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated September 2, 1957 the defendant agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and for claiming specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that there was no concluded contract between the parties and that the plaintiffs accepted the offer by their plaint in O.S No. 46 of 1957 and that this acceptance was communicated to the defendant before November 6, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the suit was not an acceptance; (2) the contract was concluded on September 2. 1957 and (3) the earlier contract dated August 3, 1957 had no application for shares and the acceptance was made or communicated to him before November 1, 1957; (4) the High ' Court erred in holding that there could be no concluded contracts between the plaintiffs and the defendant. HELD : (i) The plaint in the present case was not a suit for specific performance but was an acceptance of the offer. [584 E] (ii) Under section 2(6), 3 & 7, Contract Act if it were to take shares was concluded by an oral application for share followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. The High Court erred on this ground.

The appellants were the purchasers of sugarcane purchased by them. The price of sugarcane was fixed at Rs. 1,000 per quintal and the sugar was sold to the appellants on the same date. The appellants filed a complaint before the police alleging that they had failed to pay the price of the sugarcane purchased within the time prescribed. No. 11 of 1966. The police investigated the case and after investigation submitted a charge sheet against them under section 3(3) read with section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence alleged and convicted them under sections 3(1)(b), 3(2)(c) and 7 of that Act. On appeal by the appellants to the High Court, it was contended that the investigation which is being carried on against the appellants under sub rule (3) of Rule 3 could not be validly made under section 5 of the Act. HELD: The Central Government had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture. [677 E] Ch. This Act was enacted by Parliament in exercise of its powers under Entry 33 of List III. Therefore, the power conferred on the Government under section 2 of the , cannot be challenged as invalid. The Central Govern ment was well within its powers in legislating in regard to sugarcane and the Central Government was also well within his powers in issuing the Sugarcane Control Order, 1955 in the manner it did because all this was in exercise ' the concurrent power of legislation under Entry33 of List 111. [67 C D] Ch . This Act is a piece of social legislation intended to bring within control the cultivation and sale of food crops. The regulation of the price at which any essential commodity may be bought or sold, and in addition to the Sugar Control Order 1955 which was issued by the Central Govern ment on 27th August, 1955 it also issued the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1956, on the similar date investing it with the power to fix the price for sugarcane and direct payment thereof as also the power of regulate movement of sugarcane. [676 E F] Ch.(1) The Parliament was well aware that the Central Legislature had no legislative competence to legislate in regard 'the control of sugar as that topic is within Entry 33 List III of the Constitution which empowers the Parliament to legislate with respect to production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs. That being so it was well beyond the competence of Parliament to enact the Act and hence the power confer ed on the Govern ment under section 4 of the Central Act cannot be questioned as invalid [676 G H] Ch., Ch. V. Sundararamier & Co. vs The State of Madras, ; , followed.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An Order No. CI 58 FMI 69 dated 30th June, 1969 was issued which recited that the Government had on 30th November 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. On 12th January 1977, the Government of India issued a further order which stated that the reasons for making the said order were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th September, 1969 when the order dated 12th June 1969 came into effect and before 949 the order of 12th May, 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concession constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said Order were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries was by way of refunds of sales Tax paid to the extent provided in the order, it could not he said to be an exemption or reduction as permitted by Section 8A. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory Estoppel is not applicable to the present facts and circumstances of the case because the benefit about sales tax was by itself a good law now in view of the recent decision of this Court in State of Bihar and Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC 430, which held that the said doctrine must be regarded as good law in view Of the recent decisions of this court in State 's case. [948G H; 949A B] 2. The plea on which it was submitted that the principle of Prom promissory estoppel was not available to the appellants because it is found by Government of Maharashtra that the concession granted under that order had given place for many type of misuse but such a recital by itself cannot establish that the benefits were, in fact, misused. [948C] 3. The second submission of the learned counsel for the appellants must also be rejected. Although at one stage a faint doubt was raised by learned counsel appearing for the appellant as to whether the doctrine should be regarded good law then he conceded that doctrine must he regarded asgood law now. Though the benefit relating to sales tax paid to new industries is by way Of refunds of Sales Tax paid, it is clear that in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax and reduction in the sales Tax liability to the amount stated in the Order. [947E F] State of Kerala & Anr.v. Usha Marrow Industries Ltd. , ; State of Orissa vs Usha martin Industries Limited, [1987], 65 STC, 430; State of West Bengal & Ors. vs Uma Martin Industry Ltd., ; State 'S.C.R. 430; and State of Gujarat & Anr., vs Usha Shantilal Shah, ; referred to.

The prosecution case was that the deceased and PW 3 were members of a group of persons. The accused party formed an unlawful assembly with deadly weapons, attacked the deceased with spears, A 2, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 with sticks. The deceased and PWs 1, 2, 3 and 4 were armed with spear and A 3 chopped of the fingers of left hand of the deceased. PW 3 was also injured. On the day of occurrence at about 7.00 A.M., when he was passing near the field of A 1, he was attacked by the accused party. The other unidentified persons were also attacked. The prosecution case against the appellants was that they caused the death of the de ceased and that they had been falsely implicated in the crime. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 141 I.P.C. deals with a combina tion of persons who become liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences. The non applicability of section i49 I. P.C is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants under 7 Section 302 read with Section 34 I.p.C., if the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of them all. [801E] 2.1 There is force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appellants that there was force in t he contention of th e appellants. The appellants being only three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 1.P .C. [889F] 2:2 There is substance in the plea of the appellants. It is in evidence that the complainant and the accused belonged to opposite factions and there was long standing enmity between the parties. The de ceased standing enmity was between the ac cused party. PW 1, the wife of the victim, and the deceased, and there were as many as 18 injuries on the person of the accused. On a day of occu sion at about 9.00 P.M. when he is passing near his field of PW 3, he is attacked by A 2 and A3 chopped off the fingers with knife. A 2 further gave blows to the deceased on his head. Thereafter, at the asking of A1, A 1 and A 2 dragged the dead body from the field. There were as several injuries on tho person of PW 2, the daughter of the ac countant. The fourth rib was broken and there is an injury to the lung. Keeping in view the manner of attack as disclosed by the eye witnesses and the number and nature of injuries, we have no hesitation in holding that the appellants made the mur derous attack on the deceasedand caused his instantaneous death.

The assessee, a company registered under the Travancore Cochin Income tax Act, 1922, was assessed to income tax on sub section (2) of section 52 and taking the view that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent that there should be under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of the transferred exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assessee. The Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax relying on section 52 sub section(2) and taking that view, he imposed a penalty of Rs 10,000 under section 114A of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. In further appeal, however, the Tribunal held that the assessee had not discharged its burden of proving that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains and that it was sufficient for invoking the provisions of section 114 A of the Indian Evidence Act. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The primary object of sub section 2(2)(b) is to provide a machinery for determining the true nature and effect of the transaction in question. It provides that where an assessee transfers a capital asset and in respect thereof two conditions are satisfied namely (i) the transferee is a person directly or indirectly connected with the assessee and (ii) the transfer is effected with a object of avoiding or reducing the liability to tax, on capital gain, the fair value of such consideration shall be taken to be the full market value for the transfer. [652C D] 1.2 The expression "transfer" in section 52(2), as it stood at the relevant time, is not defined in the Act but has been used in a wide sense and includes a transfer which is effected by a transfer of property in the course of trade or business. It is only when the transfer takes place that the transaction is effected. [643E F] 1:3 The expression 'transfer ' in section 54(2A) refers to a transfer made after the transfer has taken place and it includes a sale which is completed by the transferor. In other words, the transfer must be completed with the intention of transferring the property. It may be completed at any time before the transfer can take effect but that does not mean that the transferee should have been treated as an owner of the asset for purposes of assessment under section 24(2). [653F G] 1 :4 The expression `transfer ' is used in contradistinction to a sale made after it has taken effect. It would be an act which is complete at the time when the transferor takes over the property and there may be no completed transaction between the transferor and the transferee. [641C D; 647A B] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs M/s. Pestonji & Co., ; , referred to. In the instant case, the assessee was not a person who had taken over the asset but was merely a shareholder in the company. The transfer was made with the purpose of avoidance and reduction of liability of payment of income tax under section 52 of the Travancore Act. [651C E] Commissioner for Income tax vs Mask & Co.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated food. The prosecution case was that the appellant had purchased the quality of Til seeds from the shop and that he had sold them to the Food Inspector. The defence was that it was part of the prosecution case that the sale of the quality did not amount to "food" within the meaning of section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The trial court acquitted the appellant on the ground that the evidence of the complainant was more credible and that it could not be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the Food inspector that they can be used as food also. On appeal the High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused had committed an offence under section 2 (1)(a) and (b) of Act, 1955. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was not entitled to acquittal on the sole ground that he sold it in an adulterated condition. [331 B] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , followed. Bhagwan Das 's case, ; Bhagwan Das v Delhi Administration; , , distinguished. In the instant case, the evidence adduced by the prosecution was more reliable and the High court had rightly held that there was a tall; about the actual purpose for which the Til seeds were kept in the accused 's shop. [330 E] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Adminis tration, ; and Bhagwan Das V. Delhi Administration ; , referred to.

The plaintiff was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966 on the ground of limita tion. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismiss ment was bad and he continued to be in service. In the meantime, the Collector passed an order dismissing the appeal on 31.8.1966. The defendant preferred an application before the Divisional Commis sioner and that application was rejected on the plea of limitat tion. He filed a suit for declaration that his dismissal was bad as he had not been given any opportunity to defend himself. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff 'had failed to prove that he had been given an opportunity to cross examine the witnesses and that the suit was within time. The first appellate Court dismissed the appeal. In second appeal, the High Court held that the principle of merger applicable to decrees of courts would not apply to orders of departmental tribunals, and that in view of the special limitation, the order passed by the State Government had merged into the order in appeal therefrom and in the final order of revision was repelled by this Court on two grounds. Firstly, that the cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order was filed or representation was made, the right to sue shall first accrue; and secondly, that in the case of a service dispute that the original order merged in the appellate order of the State Govern ment and it is the appellate decision which subsisted and became opera tive in law and was capable of enforcement. The High Court also examined the question as to whether when the appeal of the appellate court affirming the decree of the trial court was made the original decree had ceased to be operative. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In every such case only when the appeals or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of actions shall first accrued and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from thedate when the Appeal was filed Or representation was submitted, the rights to sue would first accrue. [492C] 1.2 In every case only if the appeal or representation provides by law that it commences from the day of accrual of the cause o f action there is no get behind these words in spite of the apparent inequity of applying the same. The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, as far as Government serv ants are concerned Article 58 may not be invocable in view Of the special period. [482D E] 1:3 In every Such case only where the appeal/ representation provided or by law was disposed of , cause of provi sion shall first accrues and where there is an order made, though the remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from the dates when the causeo cation shall be take to have first arisen. [472D] 1 :4 In the instant case, since the claim has been dismissed on the view that the claim had been dismissed, on account of limitation and our conclusion is that the suits were within time, the judgment of the High court, the First Appellate Court and the High Courts are set aside and the matter is remitted to the trial Court for disposal in accordance with law.

The appellant filed a suit for the recovery of certain amounts due under an award made by the arbitrator. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court confirmed it in favour of the intending appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) If the appellate decree affirms the decree of the trial court it is a decree of affirmance and this position would not be affected even if the variation in question is to a very small extent and may be of very minor significance. [473 C] (ii) The word "decision" does not mean the whole of the decision but the decision on that part of the controversy between the parties which is brought to this court in appeal. It would thus be seen that if an appellate decree confirms the decision of the lower court, it is not a decree or of affirmence and this is not affected either by the extent of the variation made or by the fact that the variation is made in favour Of the intending appel lant and not against him. [474 E F] (iii) If an appellate Court confirms the judgment of the High court, the appellate judg ment of the Trial Court may be in favour o the intending applicant it is no part of that decision but a variation which has been obtained by parties by consent or a part of it is an integral part of its decision or the decree.

The appellant, a company registered under the U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1948, was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling motor vehicles. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 20,000/ as damages against the appellant. The appellant contended that the suit was not maintainable because they were not maintainable. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had failed to establish that the respondent had purchased the vehicle from the owner of the vehicle and that the vehicle was in its original form. The first appellate court also held that the amendment made in 1972 did not affect the jurisdiction of the District Court under section 115 Code of Civil Procedure. In revision, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court holding that it had exclusive jurisdiction under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act and that it was not open to the appellant to invoke the revisional power of the High court under section 114 of the Code. The High Court also held in favour of the respondent. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts had no jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code in respect of an order of a District Judge under section 24, Provincial Small Causes Courts Act, and that as the amendment did not effect the revisional jurisdiction of a subordinate court, the revision petition filed under section 116 of the Act was incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The revisional power conferred by section 115 of Code of civil Procedure by a District Court is not amenable to the revisional powers of the high Court under Section 114 of that Code. [36E] 2.1 In the instant case, the order passed under section25, Provincial, Small Cause courts Act by a subordinate Court is neither amenable to revision under section 35 of the U .P. Act nor can it be said that an order passed by a Subordinate Court is amenable to revisional jurisdiction. [37F G] 3. The revision petition under section115 of the C.P Act is not maintainable against a revisional order under section 38, the appeal and the associated special leave petitions must be dismissed. No. 2844 of 1979) that in case this Court is of the opinion that a revision petition against an order made by the District Judge is not tenable, the case should be remitted to the High Curt for consideration as a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution. [38G H] 4. The appeal and associated special Leave petitions must also be dismissed, but in the main, two questions arise : (1) Whether the High ' Court possesses revisional jurisdiction under s 115 Code in cases arising out of original suits or other proceedings of any valuation, decided by the district court, would be decided by that court as if the Amendment Act of 1978 were in force at all material times ; and (2) whether the High COurt had exclusive Jurisdiction under section 5 of the .

The respondents, who were owners of certain lands in Jaipur, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the Rajasthan High Court challenging the validity of the notification issued under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for the acquisi tion of certain land belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose namely for implementation of a development scheme viz. It was alleged that the respondents had failed to acquire the said land within the territorial jurisdiction of the State Government and were therefore entitled to file such a petition. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article226 of the Constitu tion in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon and the ad interim exparte prohibitory order secured by them on the basis of such petition from the learned Single Judge on March 13, 1984 when there was total lack of inherent jurisdiction on the part of (1) ; , 602 the Calcutta high Court to entertain such petition constitutes a flagrant abuse of the process of the court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification dated February 8 , 1984 issued under s 52(2) of Rajasthan Urban improvement Act, 1960 for the acquisition of the land under section52 (1 ) of the Act for the Urban improvement Trust ,, Jaipur is quashed and the proceedings before the Calcutta Bench are quashed. [605C D] 2. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition was within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the jurisdiction of Rajasthan High court at Jaipur. It is not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 53(2), for the grant of an appropriate writ , direction or order under article 227 of the constitution for quashing the notification dated 2 8 1984 issued by the State Govt. under s. 52 (1).

The appellant was the tenant of a building in suit. The respondent landlord purchased it from the society and, therefore, the appellant filed a suit for eviction of the appellant on the ground that the building had been constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the new Rent Act. The Additional District Judge dismissed the suit holding that the construction was not completed on 1st October, 1971 and therefore the new rent Act had no application to the building in question and the appellant could get any protection of the old Rent Act, and that the appellant cannot get any relief of the amended Rent Act because the building was constructed substantially in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the new tenancy Act had not been applied to the case and that there was no question of giving the benefit of section 39 of the Act to the appellant. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the buildings in question were constructed substantially from funds obtained by the co operative society and the landlord had purchased them from the Society and, consequently, the view taken by the High court that the house was not ten years old on the date of suit and was exempted from the operation of the newly added Rent Act was manifestly erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The building in dispute was subject to assessment therefore it will be deemed to have been completed on the dates of assessment which was 1st Oct. 1971. [343G] 2.1 In the case in hand the building admittedly was subject upto assessment therefore, it would be deemed that had been completed at the time when the revision came to be decided by the Court and, accordingly, there was nothing wrong in giving the benefits of section39 of the Rent Act to appellant. [344B C] 2:2 The question whether the appellant would be entitled to the benefit under section 39 as the building has not become ten years ' old on 1 st October 1971 is a question which will be decided after considering all the relevant facts and circumstances. [345G H] 2(a) Sub section (2) contemplates that the existing Rent Act will not apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. In the present case, the building is subject to assess therefore it would he deemed to be completed on 31st October 1971. The appellant could not get any benefit of the said new Rent Acts because the buildings had not become more than ten years ago on the day they were constructed. [346B C; 347A] 2.(b) Sub s.(2) envisages that the old rent Act will apply to the buildings during a periods of ten year from the dates on which completion thereof is reported to or otherwise recorded by the local authority having jurisdiction and in the case of a new building subject to Assessment the date, on which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and where the said dates are different, the earliest of the aforesaid dates, and in tact. [347C] 2 (c) Sub sec.(2), viz., the arrears of rent, if at the first hearing of the suit the tenant in default pays all arrears of land revenue to the landlord or deposit in court the entire amount of rent and damages for use and occupation of the building due from him such damages for using and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the plaintiff 's cost of the litigation in respect thereof after deducting therefrom any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section (1) of s.30, the court may pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction on that ground.

The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and stores at Ranchi, the first of them being contract No. 21 of 1942 dated November 5, 1942, and the other two being contracts Nos. 21 and 26 of 1942. The appellant filed an application under section 35 of the Stamp Act to set aside the award on the ground that it was a nullity and that no decree should be passed in terms thereof. The respondents contended that the agreement for reference to arbitration did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and that consequently it fell within item 12. Held, that the award was a valid one and could not be validated under article 372 of the Constitution. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated: That was held in The Rajah of Bobbili vs Inuganti China Sitaramasani Garu (I.L.R. , followed. The Court has to consider whether the award which was sent by the arbitrator to the court was the original instrument or a copy thereof. It is not necessary that the original document must be produced and, if it did not fall within that item, it must fail within item 2 and that accordingly secondary evidence of its contents cannot be given. Payment of penalty will not render secondary evidence admissible, for under the stamp law penalty is leviable only on an unstamped or insufficiently stamped document actually produced in Court and that law does not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents.

The respondent in Criminal Appeal No. 422/88 was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. It had been urged by him that Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules has been misinterpreted by the High Court in holding that the said rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said Rule and the said proviso cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo upon prosecution of such a government employee. The respondent in criminal appeal No. 423/88, was working in Public works Department in Punjab in 1979. He had been prosecuted for having committed offences under Sections 409, 465, 468 and 471 IPC read with Section 34 IPC. He was acquitted by the trial court on the ground that he had not been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before taking action against him. The High Court quashed the prosecution of Mangal Singh Minhas on one ground alone based on its earlier decision in Des Raj singhal and did not consider other grounds, if any, that may have been raised by him for quashing of the prosecution on grounds, however, other than those which had already been considered above. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 2, the said rules cannot be construed to be laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The third proviso to clause (b) of Rule2 cannot be read as laying down any absolute or General embargo on Prosecution of a Government servant if he is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause of actions which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the Supreme Court can be treated to be rule regulating the condition of service of such government servant. [920D] 1.2 The third Proviso to clause(b) is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule has been framed. This purpose can be achieved if the said provision by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to mean that even if a government Servant is prosecuted, punished in criminal proceedings instituted before him in respect thereof cause of Action which arose more than 4 years prior to such institution the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause (a) with regard to pension of such retired government servant contained in Clause (b). [921E F] 1:3 The third exception to clause 2.1 is in respect to a period prior to the institution of the departmental proceedings as against a person referred to therein for prosecution in respect for a cause of which arose and an event took place after such institution. [936F G] 1 :4 In view of what has been said above and keeping in mind the scope and purpose of rule making power under Article 309 and the purpose and object of Rule, 2.3, there is no doubt with regard regard to the interpretation of the said r.2. The third Explanation to clause 'b)of Rule 2 cannot be understood as laying it absolute or special embargo on prosecutions of a public servant if a Government employee is prosecuted & punished in Judicial proceedings instituted against him in connection with cause of his action which arose before such Institution, as had been held earlier by the Court in Desraj singhal.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913 to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 1,375, but preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares, with no right in the balance of the profits. The respondent company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order passed by the Income tax Officer under section 23 A of the Act on the ground that it was one in which the public were substantially interested and there fore the income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section23 A of Income tax Act for any of the three years. The High Court held that the respondent company did not fall within the definition of "company" in section 2(1) (a) of the Indian Income tax, 1922, and that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which, the public are substantially interested. The Commissioner of Income Tax appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "company " in section 23(A) of Act 2 of 1951 must be read as including not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power and that it could not be said that the definition was intended to cover a case where shares of the respondent carrying not less then 25% of the share capital were held by persons other than the controlling group. Held: (i) The expression " company " in sub section 1(1)(a) means a company which is substantially interested, having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one per cent or more of the votes power has been allotted unconditionally to, or is acquired unconditionally by or is beneficially held by the public. It is not necessary that there should be an express provision in the Act that the controlling interest must be exercised only by the or dinary shareholders, and not by shareholders entitleci to a fix rate of dividend. The Legislature by the Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares are not entitled to any fixed rate of dividends carrying not more than twentyfive per cent share of the vote power is allotted unconditionally, to or acquired unconditionally. It matters little to them whether the dividend is immediately distributed to the ordi nary shareholders or is accumulated, and therefore in assessing whether the twenty five% of shares are vested in persons other then the controlling members, the shares yielding a fixed rate Of dividend have to be ignored. The total voting power was 5,500 one vote, for each share, ordinary and preference alike and twenty five percent of that voting power is 1,376, but to invite the presumption under the Explanation this power must be exercisable only by shareholders,and not by shareholder entitlecio to a specified fixed rate. This, therefore, is a case in which shares not entitled lo a fixed dividends carrying less than 25% or more per cent Of the voting right are not shown to have been allotted partially to, and acquired unconditionally or held by public. The fact that there exists such a control ling interest does not make the company one in whom the public is substantially concerned.

The first appellant despatched 13 bales of cotton to the Mills on behalf of another quota holder. The goods were under the control of Dwarkadas Khetan & Company and were delivered to the same Dwarkadis Khetan & Co., and the first appellant sent a letter to the first respondent stating that he had been authorised to take delivery of the January quota on behalf Of another quota holders. The Mills did not deliver them to the appellants nor took possession of the goods. On the question whether the first two were liable to be convicted under section 7(1) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, HELD: (i) The entry in column 3 is not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but means what it says, namely, the person to whom delivered the name of Dwarakdas Khetan. [833 C] (ii) The entries in column 4 are not intended only to be restricted to quotaholders but means something more than what it means. It is clear that the entry in Column 3 is intended to cover all cases where physical possession has been made and the record amply bears it out, that this godown belonged to Dwarkadash Khetan & CO., and not taken back to the Mill. [883 F] (iii) The fact that the goods were left the Mills ' premises, the property in them had passed and when Dharsi Moolji refused to receive them they were handed over to Dwarkatas Khetan and not take back to their Mills. But the learned Magistrate did not have concerned himself with the question of actual physical possession because they say: "It would not be true to say, and the records amply bears this out, and that this account was incorrect.

The respondent was a lecturer in the College of Engineering and had been working as an Examiner of University. He was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he did not abuse his position as a public servant although the means employed were corrupt and illegal. On appeal by the State to the High Court it was contended that the ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code had no application because the offence under section 161 of the Act had been committed would cover the case of an officer who was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of a public duty, and that the word 'obtains ' on which much stress was laid did not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what was given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receivers one may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case, lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position in order to corrupt some other public servant without there being any question of his misconducting himself in the discharge of his own duty. HELD : (1)(a) The word 'subtains ' is not defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure but has been used in the sense in which it occurs. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that where two views are possible, one should be preferred and the other should be adopted. [728 B] (b) In the present case the High court proceeded on the basis that for the purpose of opening, Part of section 5 of the Corruption Act Dwivedi must be held to be a public officer. It was never the case that he had been guilty of any abuse by him of his position As a lecturer of the Government College. [700 C] (c) The use of the word "obtains" on which it could well be regarded as public duty and the use of these words showed that the clause was wider when it came to the case. [628 B D] (2)(a). It is true that in clauses (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) the abuse of position as public servant is clearly implied. The use by the word `obtains " on which a much stress has been laid does not eliminate, the idea that acceptance of whatever is given or offer to be offered, though the same connotes also element of efforts on the parts of the receiver one may accepts money, and if offered or solicit money, or exort the gratification by threat. in each cases lie obtains pecuniary advantage from abusing his office as a Public servant. [625 E F] (3)(a), The use in clause (d ) is not decisive of the question whether the remuneration by any of the fees or commission should be paid by the Government as is now necessary under subclause (a) of section 405 of the Penal Code.

The petitioners in each of these applications under Article 32 of the Constitution are a workman engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of Signal Unit in the Northern Railway. All the writ petitions having disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein are similar, and the petitioners have asked for a direction to treat them at par with maintenance workers and declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked For their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. One of the petitioners has been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave etc., they are now entitled to be treated as temporary servants and have prayed for their absorption In the Signal and Telecom Construction organisation under which the petitioners are working, according to the Railway Administration further privileges of being regularised in permanent service is affirded by giving them access to their regularisation against permanent vacancies which mostly occur in open line. For such purpose casual labour in open Line as well as willing project casual labour are combined for the purpose of screening and forming of panel on the basis of seniority depending upon the days of work put in. This Court changed the existing practice for reckoning seniority and directed that seniority of project casual workers should be combined and prepared departmentwise and category wise and in terms of the directions of this Court, steps have been taken. It has been further contended that by the time these writ petitions were filed, the Railway, Board ' 's order of 1st June, 1984 had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. Disposing of the Writ Petitions, this Court HELD: The Railway Administration to take prompt steps to screen such of the Petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purposes of regularising their service. [144E] In the instant case, casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railways and cannot be avoided. Several instructions issued by Railway Board and Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the Administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove such difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them.

The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of the power conferred on it by section 12 of the , issued a notification closing out all contracts of February 1956 and May 1956 Settlements at the rates mentioned in the said notification. The appellants who were members of the Association filed objections to the said bye law before the Central Government under section 12(1) of the Act, which was rejected on the ground that they had no power to make a bye law. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the provisions of sections 12 and 13 of the Forward Markets Act, 1951, were not ultra vires the powers conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 4(f) of that Act. The provisions of section 12 (1) did not confer any power on the Government to make bye law with retrospective effect and, therefore, the new bye law made on January 21, 1956, in so far as it purports to operate retrospectively was invalid. It could not, therefore be said that unless retrospective operation was given to the provisions Of section 12, the objects of the legislation would be defeated or the purposes for which the power was conferred could not be fulfilled. The object of the impugned bye law was to provide a machinery for the disposal of certain objections and to make provision for the better administration of the trade and commerce in the State. It did not, however, confer any such power on it as the Central Legislature had no competence to make the bye law without retrospective operation. The impugned bye laws were therefore valid. The contention that the new Bye law made by the Central legislature was beyond the powers of the Central government by section 3(f), must fail.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The shares of the company were held by the assessee as its consideration for grant of long term leases after 31st March, 1948. In respect of the assessment year 1358 B.S., Rs. 37,125/ and Rs. 21,822/ respectively for the year 1357 B. S. Rs. 28,125 for the assessment years 1358 A.S. Rs 37, 125/ 1952 53 1357B.S Rs. 20,470/ and for the subsequent years the assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the purpose of the year 1359 B.s were taxable as dividend and the remaining amount was not taxable since they were declared out of capital gains of the Company which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for granting long term mining leases after the 31st day March,1948. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of short term leases was not 'taxable ' since it was a receipt of income in the hands of the assessee and taxable as the income of the assesee from other sources. On further appeal, however, the Tribunal held that the entire sum for each year was income in its hands but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax ACt, 1922, was liable to be grosed up. In reference, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The High Court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain, and whether any part of that compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains. Prima facie, receipt of compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of fixed assets of a Company is of a capital nature: Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Assam, ; , but interest which is statutorily payable on compensation is income and is not capital gain. [737 B] (2) The question whether distribution of dividend out of profits was taxable must be decided on the basis of the form of questions, is more extensive. [750 C D] (3) In view of the language used in section 2 (6A), capital gains arising after 31th March, 1950 were not part of accumulated profits and if dividend be distributed to the shareholders out of those capital gains, to ' the extent of the distribution out of these capital gains the dividend must be deemed exempt from liability to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable to tax. [751 F] (4) The expression "income" in section 12(1) is wide enough to include all kinds of receipts which are expressly included in the definition of 'income '. [757 E] Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Mask & Co., ; , referred to.

The appellant, a Forest Range Officer, challenged the legality of the complaint holding that Sandal Wood Oil is not 'wood oil ' as defined in section 2(f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act. The learned Single Judge quashed the complaint on the ground that Sandali Wood Oil was not ' wood oil ' and held thatainst wood oil being the bye product derived commercially manufacturing process is not wood oil. He further held that tendu wood oil is a forest produce within the meaning of section 2 (f) of Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word 'wood ' used in the Act must receive its colour from its context and connotation and that the meaning should be excluded. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'enumerated items in clauses 1 and 11 'wood Oil ' is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary popular, popular and natural sense whenever that word would be properly applicable, but to enable the word as used in tho Act, when there is nothing in the context or the subject matter to the contrary, to be applied to some things to which it would not ordinarily be applicable. [164D E] 2.1 The expression being technical and being part of an inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner, it cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the principle object and purpose of the Act. [165E F] 2:2 In the instant case, there are several types of essential oils in India, the important being Sandalwood oil, agar wood oil, deodar oil and pine oil apart from oleo resin and wood oil derived from exudation from living trees in the forest area. An interpretation clause of the inclusive definition is not intended to prevent a word receiving their ordinary popular and technical sense whenever it that word will be properly applied, but in a exhaustive manner it cannot he restricted in so as To defeat the object and purposes of the statute. [166E F; 167A] 2 :3 The expression "enumerating items" in clause 11 's 'wood oils ' is defined in Section 2(k) which includes 'Sandal wood ', being a forest Produce, the oil extracted therefrom would also be within the definition of 'wood " oil". [167C D] 3.1 In Fatesang Gimba Vasava and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and ors., ; , this Court held that though bamboo is a Forest produce, the Bamboo chips of the specified description do not fall within the purview of the definition in section2(f)(i) of The Act. Therefore, it is a 'enologated item '. [167E F].

The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code but were acquitted. The High Court set aside the acquittal and convicted them on two grounds: (1) that there was no evidence against the appellants sufficient to warrant a conviction; and (2) that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Held, that the High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons for doing so. The judgment of the High court did not disclose any such reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial court. The evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn. The second point on which the judgment of acquittal was based was the lack of compelling reasons justifying interfering with the finding of the Trial Court. The third piece of evidence which the prosecution relied upon was the two dying declarations made by Shivlal to Gyaniram P. W. 1 and suffered from due material contradictions in their respective statements made at various stages of the case and which have been pointed out by the learned Sessions Judge who said about Gyani Ramram: Held, further, that there could be no doubt that the conviction of the appellants was not justified on the evidence in this case because the High Courts had not given any reasons for setting aside the judgment. The fact that the doctor was comparatively young and that his statement was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon, does not detract from his reliability that it would be dangerous to accept his testimony as being of any great value which is still more diminished by the finding as to the innocence of the accused.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it had two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur is an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the management and the workmen employed in that factory and represented by their union the Indoxco Labour Union made a joint application dated September 7, 1963 to the Government of Bihar for a reference under section 10(2) of the . The Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs, New Delhi, referred the dispute for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal found that the constitution of the said Indoxic Co Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the said purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and its workmen represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union did not materially affect the position that the dispute raised by the union is in respect of the employees of the Company wherever they may be stationed". The Tribunal further found that there was no evidence to show that the Indrasoxco workers Union had ever been granted special leave to attend the meetings of the executive committee of the union. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Tribunal 's conclusion, therefore, that the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6 or 21, 1963 or that, therefore the/ndian Oxygen Workers Union represented the workmen of the company 's factory at Ranchi came henceforth to be represented by Indian Oxygen workers ' Union which represented also workmen employed In the appellant 's other establishments, the reference extended to them also and the Tribunal ' 's award would cover them also. [554 B C] (2) The dispute referred to the Tribunal was only those set out in the agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian Gas Oxygen Workers union is erroneous and cannot be sustained.

The assessee was carrying on business in timber at Abdullapur. In 1939, the firm of Lala Hakam Mal Tani Mal and Jodha Mal were settled on March 31, 1939 and the business was taken over by the assessee. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the firm under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber business at Abdulapur. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 24(3), or in the alternative under section 26(4). The Tribunal also rejected the contention of the assessee that the firm was dissolved on March 1, 1939 after the Act 7 of 1939 was brought into force and that the partnership was not a changein the constitution of a partnership. On reference, the High Court held that as the assessee had commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution of the partnership, no tax could be payable by the first mentioned person in respect thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the firm having been dissolved on April 1, 1943, before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 Of 1939 came into force, and (ii) the assessee having commenced doing the business immediately thereafter, the business of the assesee continued till the midnight of March 31. 1939, and even if it be assumed that the business had been taken over after March 31 the assessee ceased to carry on business at the commencement of the Act. HELD : (i)(a) The assessee was constituted to carry On the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1. 1939. It must therefore be held that, the assessee commenced doing 'business immediately after its dissolution and immediately thereafter the business started. [653 C] (b) The partnership therefore came into being at the precise point of time at which the Indian income tax ( Amendment) Act 6 of 1939 came in force and it could not be said that the assesse was not carrying on any business at that commencement. [650 D] (c) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was entitled on the dissolution, of that firm in March 1943 to the benefit of section 25 (4), or under section 28(2)(b). [654 E] (d) The contention that the partners had become separate would imply that the partner who was at the date of dissolution of a firm cannot be accepted. It is well settled that a person who has been dissolved after April 1 cannot be said to carry out business at a time when he ceases to carry it.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the operation of the order of the State transport Appellate Tribunal. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order granting the permit, respondents 4 to 13 preferred appeals to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal against the order dated April 25, 1967. The appeal filed by the appellant to the High Court was dismissed holding that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules which was applicable to his case for the issue of a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the Regional transport Authority granting the permits. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order granting a permit is only a ministerial act necessarily following the grant of the permit. [181 E] 2. There is no dispute that section 64 of the Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant or of other matters with which we are not concerned here. There was, therefore, a clear error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunals in interfering with the grant granting of the permits to the appellant. [182 G H] 3. The High Court had rightly held that there is no question of any appeal provided for under section 64 against an order issuing a permit. Issuance of the said permit is merely a ministerial work necessarily following it the grant Of the permit and the appeals before the State Road Transport Appellate Tribu nal are, therefore not competent under section 65 of the .

The appellant was the sitting member of Parliament. The respondent was a sitting member. The appellant alleged that at the Hapur meeting respondent Prakash Vir Shastri and his supporters delivered inflammatory speeches against the appellant and thereafter the said respondent Shastri 's supporters entered the office of the Republican Party to which the appellant belonged, assaulted the workers of the appellant tore posters, abused the appellant 's workers. In support of the allegations the appellant relied on exhibit 28 the news report in the newspaper published on 8 February 1967 and also on Exhibit 23 the news item. The oral evidence was in support of rival contentions namely that the witnesses belonged to particular castes and sects. The High Court held that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February, 1967 and there was no attack on the office or the Republic ofan Party. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the publication of the pamphlet did not mention or refer at all to any meeting on behalf of respondent Prakashvir Shastri on 7 2 1967 at the Town Hall Maidan, Hapur; (2) there was rejection of evidence on consideration that the appellant had assaulted or chased and threatened his workers. HELD: (i) The news item in the newspapers ' Hindustan Times ' contained an attack on perception Elahi, a worker of the petitioner. The alleged incident at Chhajjupur is unacceptable because, first there was an assault on Shamshad Elahi a worker by respondent. The evidence on behalf the appellant was that the witness on behalf Of the respondent were D.W.
