The other allegations of the appellants were that on 2 February 1967 an election meeting was organised in support thereof and no election meeting held in support or against respondent Prakash Singh Vir Shastri was held in respect of respondent 's personal character and conduct of the appel lant. [895 F G] (ii) There is no evidence that the assault was by the workers on the appellant. The news items do not mention nor refer at any particular meeting on his behalf. The witnesses on behalf o the appellant were D,W. 2 and D.Ws. 3 and 4. The statements of these witnesses are corroborated by the oral evidence of PW 18. [884 A B] (iii) The alleged incidents at ChhaJjupur are unacceptable because there was a complaint by the appellant against the respondent. In the present case, annexure KK has not been established to be published with the consent of the respondent Prakash Chand or his election agent. The newspaper publication Exhibit 22 was an appeal on behalf 'of respondent Prakash.

The respondent auction purchaser purchased the property in question from the appellant auction purchaser. The sale was confirmed by the District Judge on December 12, 1980 holding that in view of Article 136 of the Constitution of India, an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code will be governed by Article 136 and that as held by the learned Single Judge of the High Court, Article 136 stood impliedly repealed by section 47 read with Article 136. The respondent auction sale purchaser filed an applica tion under order XXI Rule 90 of the Civil Procedure Code for delivery of possession of the property auctioned by him. The application was rejected on the ground that the application was within one year from July 21, 1979 and since the application for setting aside the sale was made within one month of the dismissal of the application, it should be held that the applica tions were barred by limitation. The appellant 's appeal to the Division Bench was dismissed in limine. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. Article 134 will apply to an application for execution of a decree for possession so as to apply 12 years ' period of limitation as prescribed by Article 137 of the . [361G] 2. The mere fact that the auction purchaser will be deemed to be a party in the suit in which the decree has been passed, as provided in clause (a) of Explanation II to section 47 of the C.P.C., and by virtue of clause (b) of explanation II all questions relating to delivery of posses sion of the immovable property shall be deemed t he questions relat ing to execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree within the meaning of section 47, an applic ation for setting it aside the auction sale may be made under Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the code. [361H; 362A] 3. The High Court was right in holding that after the amendment of Section 47 of C. P.C. by Section 20 of the Act, an appli cation for settingaside the sale can also be made within a period of 12 years from the date of decree irrespective of the date on which sale is absurd on the face of it. [362B] 4. The question whether an application filed under Order 21 Rule 95 or 91 would be governed under Article 136 will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [364C D] 5. In the instant case, the application made by the auctionpurchaser for setting t aside the sales on the grounds of fraud was made after the sale had been confirmed, and the Full Bench took the view that the period of Limitation under Article 180 of the old Limitation Act should be computed from the dates of the order disallowing the applic a tion to set aside the re spondent sale on the plea of fraud. [365E F] 6. The Full Bench was right. It is true that in spite of such settlement, the Full bench took the same view and held that after section 47(2) of the , an application would be barred by Article 134 of the Limitation Act. But after a sale becomes absolute on the sale of the applicatio n of the judgment debtor 's claim for setting up aside the Sale, another application for set aside t he sale by the judgment creditor is not maintainable and the period o limitation as provided under Article 137 will be computedfrom the date from the decree irrespective o the date when sale is vitiated. [366G H; 367A] 7. The view expressed by the Full Court in the case of Shri Ram & Ors.

The appellant was the successful candidate for election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14 and P 15, the first respondent, who was one of the defeated candidates filed an Election Petition challenging the election of the appellant to the State Assembly on the ground that the appellant had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (the Act '). The High Court recorded a finding that the wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the first res pondent. It also held that exhibit P 1 was not printed and pub lished only a day prior to the election. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the evidence of the witnesses who had stated that they had gathered the impression that the incident had taken place the previous day but he himself was of the view that the publication was meant to create such impression and did so; (ii) the first Respondent 's case that exhibit PW 1 was printed and Pub led only a days prior to his election, was not correct. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The contents of this poster directly named the first respond ent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the said poster was affixed prior to or after the election by the workers of the appellants with their knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practice under section 123 (4) read with section 123. [776E] 2. The appellant 's cross examination of this witness was directed to prove that he had not taken the photographs even on 25th and 26th March, 1987 but at a much later date and just prior to that date and no more.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel on the said land. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation, however, rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent No, 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner rejecting the plan submitted by the respondent 5 for the purpose of construction of an five star hotels. The respondent No 2 set up a fresh development plan on that land and submitted a revised development plan. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order granting sanction of the Plan submitted by it for the constructions of a hotel on that property. Being dissatisfied with the rejection, the Respondent No. 2 filed an appeal before the Minister of State for Urban Development, which was dismissed. In the special leave petition to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent had no authority to grant the permission for development of the land granted in favour of respondent No 5 as he had not been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before rejecting the application for approval of the proposed plan submitted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground has been adequately considered and taken into account by the High Court. [922D] 2. The ground for rejecting the Plan is no longer tenable, regard being had to the fact that the draft revised development scheme has since been published and the plan prepared by the Respondent 5 and conditioned by the appellant No. 1. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting sanction to the plan the respondent would be entitled to rely upon the same in rejecting the proposal submitted by respondent No . 5. [936C D] 3. The High Court was not justified in merely relying upon a proposal for the preparation of a draft revised plan. [946E] 4. The objection regarding the validity of the resolution is no more tenable, as regard being having to the facts and circumstances of the case, it will be improper to reject the plan. There is, accordingly, no substance in the appeal challenging the order dated 8th April 1984 granting exemption to the respondent. [948G] 5. The appellant No 2 directed sanction of a revised plan out of 44,820.49 sq. yds. belonging to the Respondent NO. 5. It was, therefore. apparent that there is no merit in this appeal challenging its order of exemption granted to the appellant.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of cloth and yarn. It filed two complaints before the Industrial Court under section 28 read with Items l(a), l(b) and 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 ( 'the Act ' for short). The respondents contended that the employees were guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out which under the law was illegal. The Industrial Court dismissed the complaints filed by the appellant union. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen are not being re employed. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The true test is that when it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure of industrial activity, the industrial court in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practice must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to determine the services of the workmen. [69D] 1.2 The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine its intention and bonafides. To accept the view taken by the Industrial court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted, to closure bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device to or pretence. [70E] 1:3 The true criterion is that while examining whether the employee has imposed a lockout or has closed down the business, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closing down of the industrial undertaking was a consequence of imposing lock out or the owner employer had decided to close down the industrial activities. [71G] 1 :4 The true principle is that whenever it is sought to be assured that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit, it must be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. Therefore the true test should be that when the employer refuses to continue to employ the workmen employed by him even though the business activity was not closed down. The duration may be an important fact to determining the intention and bona fides of the employer at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [72B] 1;5 In the instant case, the issue was whether the respondents had imposed a strike out or has closing down the industry. It is to be determined with accuracy whether the closing up of the Industrial activity was a result of imposing a lock Out or the owners employer had resolved to close the industrial establishment. [73G] 2. The true tests are that when there is a closure of the business itself permanent and irrevocable, the lockout must necessarily be temporary or permanent and the suspension of work or the refusal by an employer to continue cannot do so upon the painstaking off the industry, the Industrial Tribunal before which the action of the employers is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the stage of closure decide and determine whether it was a bonafide one or was a design or pretence for determining the services. [74H; 75A] 3.1 In case of a lock down there is only closure of that place of business where as in case of closure there is no closure of business itself Permanent and irrevocable. The continuity of the activity may be relevant to determine tho intention and the bonafides of the employee at the date of closure, but isnot decisive of whether the closed down of industrial undertaking is a consequence or not.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. Clause 2,000 was the value of shares of the Loyal Mills. The assessee company claimed to be a dealer or an investor according as it incurred losses or made profits and therefore the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties of the assessee company could be taxed as business profits. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee was a dealer in investments and properties and not merely an investor. On appeal by the assessee to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, the Tribunal held that in the case of the asses see company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was remanded to the High Court for directing the Appellate Tribunal to state a case on the aforesaid questions of law under section 66(1) of the Income tax Act. The High Court held that the question as to what were the characteristics of the business of dealing in shares or that of an investor was a mixed question of fact and law and what was the legal effect of the facts found by the Appellate tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question as regards whether the profits or losses arising on the sale Of shares, security and immovable property of the assesses company can be taxed is a mixed questions of fact, and law. [679 E] (2) The final conclusion of the Tribunal can, therefore, be challenged on the grounds that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the Tribunal in reaching its decision on the point; and such a challenge is open under section 67(1).

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On June 19, 1950, he was deputed to enquire into these charges and after making an elaborate enquiry in which several witnesses including the appellant were examined, he sent a report on October 20, 1953, that the charge of corruption was made out, and he concluded as follows: " The Government shall, subject to the provisions of rule 5, refer the following cases to the Tribu nal, namely : (a) Cases relating to Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above in respect of matters involving corruption on the part of such Government servants in the discharge of their official duties and (b) All appeals or petitions to the Government against orders passed on charges of corruption and all disciplinary cases in which the Government propose to revise the original orders passed by such officers. " The appellant filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds that (i) the enquiry into the conduct of the Government servants was without jurisdiction; (ii) the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion and was therefore bad. Held, that under r. 4(1)(a) of the Madras Civil Services Rules, the enquiry against the appellant was started by a Tribunal to which the Govern ment might refer the same; (iii) the Government could dismiss or remove him from service only if it considered necessary to do so in public interest; and (iv) the High Court had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally.

The appellant, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co. a private Limited Company with its registered office in Bombay died on May 13, 1945 having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The obligation to pay the tax on the dividend so deemed to be distributed was of the shareholder and the general provision in section 24B for enforcement of liability against the legal representative of a deceased person to pay tax which would have been payable if such person had not died, had a limited application. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant 's income as having been received by him before his death and included it in the assessable income of the company. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment but the Tribunal held that the income received by the appellant before his retirement became liable to be taxed in the hands of the legal representatives and that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 24 B because he had not been made a party to the proceedings. On appeal, the High Court held that even if after the expiry of the year of account receipts which were received by a legal representative who would have died could still be taxed as his income in the assessee 's hands and therefore they were not liable to tax in the appellant company for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that even assuming that after the expiration of the accounting year receipts which are deemed to have been received would have become his income, ceased to be liable to assessment as income of a person who died and therefore the income could not be taxed under section 23B(4) of the Act. HELD: (i) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952 means a person by whom income tax or any other similar tax is payable and in the absence of appropriate provisions for collecting tax from the estate of a dead person in the Act, the claim of the Income tax officer to make an assessment under section23(4), must fail. [503 D] (ii) The Legislature not having made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the estate or of the deceased person, the expression "any tax which will have been paid by him" cannot be deemed to had supplied the machinery for taxation of income received on by a deceased assessee and therefore it was not liable for be taxed. [525 E] (iii) The legislature not having provided that the Income ' tax Officer shall make an assessment under section 22(4)(a), the expression 'any tax payable" which would, but for the death of the erstwhile shareholder, have been receive by such deceased person is to be regarded for the purposes of assessment as the personal income of legal representative is to charge tax not in accordance with the provisions of the law.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a Ruler and was recognised by the President as the successor of his princely State. The appellant 's petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that it was for the appellant to establish that the villages in question had never been assessed to land revenue but no evidence had been led to this effect. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the expression "maufidar" in section 2(m) of the Act had not been used in any narrow or technical sense and therefore a Ruler could not conceivably be a maufidar. The question whether the villages mentioned in Schedules A and B of the petition under article 226 and the petition were not so recognised was one which arose out of the definition of the word "proprietor" in the Act. The High Court rightly held that the appellant was an ex Ruler and as he was also a moufifidar he fell within the definition Of the word 'proprietor ' in the ,of the Constitution. The fact that the village in question was not assessed to rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages does not make him a Ruler for the purposes of the privy purse guaranteed by article 366(22) of tile Constitution. In the present case the appellant had given no evidence to establish this fact. The only inference which could be drawn against him was that he had given any evidence to prove that the lands in question were not assessed or land revenue.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, (Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of India). The guidelines contained in Government of india O.M. dated 3.4.1986 were not kept in mind while ordering his transfer. tie complained that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong for a longer period, have been allowed to continue at Shillong. The learned Single Member of the Central Administrative Tribunal quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: (1) The guidelines issued by the Government are not followed; (2) The administrative instructions contained in the administrative instructions issued 430 by the Central Government are neither followed nor with which finding we shall deal later. The guidelines say that as far as possible, husband and wife must be posted at the same place. The jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 of the constitution of India in service matters. (We find it all the more surprising that the learned Single Judge who passed the impugned order is a former Judge of the Supreme Court and is thus aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdiction.) The Administrative Tribunal is not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. In this case, the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the orderof transfer. The order of the Tribunal reads as if it were sitting in appeal over the order dated 3rd April, 1986 made by the senior Administrative Officer (competent authority). Shri Goswami, learned counsel for the respondent relies upon the decision of this Court in Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 rendered by a Bench of which one of us (J.S. Negi and M.L. Sharma, JJ.) was a former judge of the Delhi High Court and was thus aware that the guidelines issued are not applicable to the case of the respondent. The judgment also does not support the Respondents ' contention that if such an order is questioned in a court or Tribunal, the authority is obliged to justify the transfer by adducing reasons therefor. (emphasis added) The said observations in fact tend to negative the Respondent 's contentions instead of supporting them. The Administrative Tribunals are not appellate authorities sitting in judgments over the administrative orders of transfers. In the case in all India services, the hardship resulting from the two being posted at different stations may be unavoidable at times particularly when they belong to different services and one of them cannot be transferred to the place of the other 's posting. While choosing the career and a particular service, the couple have to bear in mind this factor and be prepared to face such a hardship if the administrative needs and transfer policy do not permit the posting of both at one place without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employees. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any place in India, subordinating the need of the couple living together at one station, 'they cannot as of right claim to be relieved of the ordinary incidents of all India Service and avoid transfer to a different place on the ground that the spouses thereby would be posted At different places. (6) The Tribunal is thus not an appellate authority sitting in Judgment over the Orders of transfer; (7) The Administrative Tribu nal has exceeded its jurisdic tion in interfering in the order passed by transfer. (8) The order does not suffer from any mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does say so merely because certain guidelines issued were not followed, with which findings we shall dealt later.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. The prosecution case was that Al, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A 6 armed with lathis, A1 to A6 attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2,8, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them came within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I.P.C. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while consid ering the nature of offence observed that as under the circumstances of this case the 3 offence committed was proved beyond doubt. [312B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the intention of appellants was only to cause hurt and not to cause simple and grievous injuries to him. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused persons could have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient, in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, it is not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. [412C D] 2:2 The intention was to causing grievous hurt, and as su ch the offence com prised by them comes within the ambit of Section 324 read with section 34, IPC. Thirten external in Juries were held on the death of Jawahar, out of those 12 were on the lower legs. Out Of these 11 were only on lower side and arms, the weapons were found to be on the upper side and arm. The injuries were found by the doctor who conducted the post mortem examination. Out otheu dents 11 were of on lower leg and arms and arms respectively. The appellants were convicted under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for five years. This appeal by A1 is against the judgment of the High court. While granting special leave to appeal this Court by its order dated August 10, 1979 allowed bail to the appel lants.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1969 was promulgated by the Governor on May 1, 1970. Section 3(27)(a) of the Act provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, `special Indian law ' means a law enacted by the British Parliament specially for India. The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of the amount decreed by it and for an injunction restraining them from enforcing its rights under the Ordinance. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the provisions of the Ordinance were not applicable to the appellant Bank and, therefore, there was no question of scaling down the debt due to the Bank by the respondents. In appeal, the High Court held that the words `special law ' in section 4(e) of Act would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian law, whether it is created in pursuance of or by or under the special Indian Law. The Division Bench also took the view that the expression `special laws ' refers or relates to a special law enacted under the law and not by the law itself in order to come within the purview of section 4 (e) and that the phrase `formed in pursuance thereof ' in Section 4(d) of Ordinance VIII of 1969 would not apply inasmuch as the appellant bank was not formed in pursuance to any `specialIndian law ', but by orunder a `special ' Indian law. The Bank appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of section 3(28)(a), 4(b) and 4(c) of Banking Companies Ordinance, 1949 are not applicable in the instant case. [969C] 1.2 In Krishna Murthy 's case (supra), it has been held by the Division Bench that the word `special English law ' refers to a law made by the Indian Legislature and not to a legislation enacted by any legislature of our country. The intention of the Legislature is very clear in that the provision of section4(e)(a). It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by or Under a specialIndian law and, not in pursuance Of such a law, it will not come within its purview of Section 4 (d) and (e). [968D E] 1:3 The words `any special Indian laws ' refer and relate to a statute enacted by an Act of British Parliament for India, would not be applicable to corporations formed or created by any special Indianlaw which, in the face of the provision, has not meant that the corporation in question should be formed by a third party in pursuance with the law. [964E F] Krishna Murthy vs Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, A.I.R. 1961 S.C. 969; Krishna Murthy & Ors. vs Andhra Praxam Parishad, A I.R., 1962 S.T.C., 972; Krishna Kumar vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to.

The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned notification on two grounds, namely (1) that the impugned Act was beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and clause 5 of the Order; (2) that it authorises the Central Govern ment to fix ex factory prices and is bad as it cannot possibly subserve the purposes of the , ensuring equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a fair price; and (3) that even if ex factory price can be Axed under the Act, and the Order, the impugned Notification was still bad as there was no reasonable safeguard against the abuse of power and no provision for a check by way of appeal or otherwise. Held, that though in form prices are fixed for factories only in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, in effect they are fixed at the level at which they were at the end of May 1958, once the production of these three regions is controlled, there is no reason why the Government should go on also to fix wholesale or retail price. The object of the legislation is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of general public so that the prices may be maintained or increased, their equitable distribution secured and they may be available to the general public at fair prices. The impugned notification merely fixes ex factory rates and is not bad as its validity cannot be challenged on the ground that it violates article 14 of the Constitution. The fixation of price in these three areas is not arbitrary and does not take into account the cost of production.

The workmen of the appellant company were employed in the respondent company. The previous award made by the Tribunal between the same parties on April 26, 1951 and confirmed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal by its order dated August 30, 1951 had not been terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act and therefore the reference was bad in law. On appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated under section 19 (6) because the previous award did not contain any provision for transfer of pending proceedings before a Tribunal constituted under the Act before the 10th day of March, 1957; and (ii) the reference having been made to the Labour Court by the State Government under section 7A of the , it was bad. HELD: (i)(a) The expression "any proceeding" in section 33B inserted in the Act by the Amending Act was not intended to be a continuation of proceedings pending before a tribunal constituted under that Act and, therefore, the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of living index in the year 1957. [149 C] (b) The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the state Statistical Bureau, West Bengal for ascertaining the working classes cost of working index since August 1954 up to March 1957. The Tribunal rightly held that the working Class cost of the living index stood at 344.1 in August 1954 and it rose to 4006 in May 1957 with the result that there was a rise of 56 points, a substantial rise in the cost of live index by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the ground that the Government had the power to transfer them from that date to any other tribunal. [150 D E] (c) The contention that the Tribunal wrongly relying upon Exhibit 2, corrected the figure relating to working class menials and the corresponding entries in regard to the working category cost of labour index did not hold good.

The appellant was a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The said Mutt was situated at Uravakonda in the district of Anantapur. It appears that on the 6th September, 1939, the Board of Hindu Religious Endowments constituted under the Madras Act 11 of 1927 framed a scheme under section 63 of the said Act for the proper administration of the Mutt and its endowments. The management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under the scheme made no difference to the actual administration of it. It was no doubt urged before the learned Judge that the appellant 's writ petition should not be entertained because he had a definite adequate alternative remedy under the latter Act, but this plea was rejected by the learned judge with the observation that where the fundamental right is clearly infringed, it is the duty of the Court to interfere in favour of the citizen unless there are reasons of policy which make it inexpedient to do so. Held, further, that the scheme having been framed as early as 1939 under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act which was valid when it was enacted, could not be challenged on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed to the appellant under article 19(1)(f) and as such invalid. The right of the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the grounds that it deprives him of his fundamental right under article 14 is a valuable right which he has not been deprived of by the impugned orders and it was in respect of such invalid orders that the Court held that the petitioner was entitled to seek the protection of article 19.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He remained absent from duty for a long time. On the basis of an enquiry held by the managing body, the appellant was removed from service. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12, 1982. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appellant is not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State of Orissa will do well to consider the cases of all those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December 31, 1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services. An appointment on 89 day basis with one day breaks which deprives a teacher of his salary for the period of summer vacation and other service benefits is wholly arbitrary and suffers from the vice of discrimination. [901C] 2. The validation Act has been enacted by the Orissa legislature with the obvious object of granting relief to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping them in short spell appointments like 89 day appointment as here with one month break and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other services benefits. An appoint on 89 days basis with a one day strike which deprives another teacher of salary for that period is wholly unjustified and suffersfrom the vice vice of discriminatory discrimination. The Court, therefore, set aside the judgment of the High Court and direct the respondents to treat the appellant as the regularly appointed Hindi teacher in the school alongwith the salary for summer vacations and other breaks which must be taken as non est, from the date of his regular appointment i.e. the date from which he was removed.

There shall be paid to the Chairman, Vice Chairman and Members, mileage allowance for journeys performed for any official work outside the district. (a) Chairman, Panchayat Samiti Rs. 100/ as a consolidated amount in lieu of the travelling allowance, daily allowance or any other allowances to which he might have been entitled in order to compensate him for expenses incurred in connection with the discharge of his official duties. " The appellant was declared elected and respondent No. 1 was declared duly elected. Respondent No. 2 filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground inter alia that the appellant had failed to establish that the allowances payable under rules 3, to 7 were not in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have incurred for the purpose of performing the journeys in order that to discharge his official duty. The High Court held that the allowance paid under rules 2 to 7 was in addition to the payment of the consolidated monthly allowance under r. 5 and that the Chairman must be making gain out of the payment to him of daily allowance. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the allowances paid under rr. 3 to 6 made the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samiti an office of profit, and the second was whether the office was an office under the State Government; (ii) the payment was in excess Of the amount which he had to incur for 'the purpose of discharging his official functions; and (iii) the appellant must be made gain out from the payment. HELD : (i). The High court came to a correct conclusion in holding that the amounts paid under rs 3 to7 were not convert the office into an office or of profit. [635 C] (ii). In the course of his submissions, the appellant has failed to prove that out Of the amounts received as travelling allowance the appellant will in fact invariably make a say, it could not be held to have made gain to him so as not to make his office an Office of profit.[635 D] (iii). The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents filed a suit for eviction against the appel lant on the ground that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, it further held that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respond ent but the tin sheds marked with letters C DGH had been built by the appell lant without respondents ' consent which materially altered the accommodation and on that findings the trial court decreed the suit. The first appellate Court reversed the decree of the trial Court, holding that the Partition wall did neither constitute material alterations nor was there any evidence to show that the appellant had constructed any sub stantial change either in the form or structure of the building. In second appeal the High Court held that temporary construction made by a tenant in the shape of kitchen and bathroom did not con sidered material alteration as the constructions were temporary in nature, did not make any sub letting ment of the premises. The High Court also observed that the fact that a construc tion was permanent or temporary in character did not affect the question as to whether the constructions materially alter the accommodation or not. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the disputed construction even though temporary in form, which could be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation, would fail within the mischief of material alteration ' and that the High court committed error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alterations. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Legislature intended that only those constructions which bring about substantial change in the front and structure of tho building should provide a ground for tenant 's eviction, it took care to use the word 'materially altered the accommo dation. [975D] 2.1 In determining the question of 'material alteration ' the Court must address itself to the nature, character of the constructions and the extent to which they make changes in the rear and structure o f the accommodation. The legislature intended that merely those constructionswhich bring about a substantial changein the front or structure should provide an ground for eviction. It took care, to use word ' materially altered ' the accom modation. The essential element which needs consideration is as to Whether the constructions are sub staltial in nature and they alter, the form, front and t structure of tile accommodation. [979E F] 2:2 In determining whether the construction is sub sta ntial in character and they alteration, the Court has to consider whether the construc es have been made with the con stan cy of material alterations.[975G H] 3.1 The Legislature wanted that only such constructions which brought about substantial changes in front andt structure of t he building should provided a groundfor eviction. [978A B] 2(a) In determining this question the Court should address itself, to the character, character or extent of the construction and the amount to which it makes changes in tho front and the structure of that accommodation having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out. The Court must examine itself to consider the nature and character of constructions and if so, whether those constructions are of such substantial nature which make material alterations in the accommodation.[978C D] 3:2 The Legislature has intended that all constructions which brings about substantial altera tions in the back and structure should provided an ground.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Trial Court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. The High Court allowed the revision set aside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of the ex parte order. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that since Navlakha was an employee of the Company sitting in its registered office in Calcutta the summons will be deemed to have been duly served upon the company within the meaning of the first part of clause (b) of Order 29, Rule 2 of the Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1032C] 2. The meaning of clause(b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. [ 1033D] 3. Rule 17 of Order 5 would include Managing agents and the appellant under the orders of the Court had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. The respondent was not a person who is entitled to be served on behalf of the company in accordance with sub clause (c) of rule 2 of Order 9, Rule 13 C.P.C. [1134E] 4. The expression "Principal officer" in Clause (a), has got meaning to be interpreted in the context of the provision of the Civil Procedure Code in order 5 which was meant for issuance and service. In Rule 17, it has been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the notice on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. [934F G] 5. The appellant under orders of Court had given bank guarantee to the decretal dues. The Bank guarantee furnished by the respondent is Annexure B to the counter affidavit filed by the appellant company under Order 9 Rule 13 of the C. P.C., which contains a statement that the Bank guarantee was not in dispute and it was left at the registered office of the appellant Company.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The respondents filed a written statement before the Magistrate on the basis of a police report. After passing a preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 (wherein the Magistrate had recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed, the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145 the Magistrate passed the final order in favour of the appellant. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) there was no finding by the Magistrate that there was an apprehension of breach of peace; (ii) there had been an apprehension that breach of a peace existed even in 94 the final orders, and (iii) there could be no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under sub section (5) of section 145. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Magistrate was not justified in holding that the final decision of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach existed at the time when the preliminary order was passed. [952D] 2.1 In Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , this Court held that once a Magistrate finds that there is a breach or of peace it is not necessary that the dispute should continue to exist at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the disputed land has ceased to exist so as not to bring the case within the ambit of sub section(5) Of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [962E] 2:2 The High court was right in holding (i ) that the Magistrate could under sub s.(1) of Section 145, Criminal Procedure Code assume jurisdiction only if he is satisfied that at the date of passing the preliminary Order a dispute likely to cause a breach Of the peace exists concerning any land etc. At that time he had not to record a finding again about the existence of a dispute which likely to create a breach in the final decree passed by the magistrate so it was not necessary for him to repeat what he had said in the preliminary decree in the earlier proceedings; and (ii). The enquiry under section 145 is limited to the question whether there was a breach on the part of the Magis trate or not. [942G H] 2 :3 In the instant case, the High Court was right that once the Magistrate has given a finding to the effect that there has been a breach it is no necessary that he should pass a preliminary ord under sub sec.(5) and thereafter to make an enquiry under sub Section (4) and pass a final order under section Sub section (4). [943A B] 2(a) The High ' Court was wrong in holding the final deci sion of the High court that there could not be any question of sufficiency of material which had satisfied the Magistrate 's satisfaction. [972C D] 3:1 In the present case, there was nothing to show in the instant ease that any prejudice was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court. The enquiry was limited to a question whether the apprehension of violation of peace existed and such a finding was implicit in thefinal order passed by Magistrate so it is neither necessary that at this time he has not recorded a finding earlier about the factum of breach or the existence thereof. [982E F] 2.(b) The Magistrate had no jurisdiction to issue a notice under section 146(1) Cr.

The appellant, a non resident company, was assessed to income tax for the years 1941 42, 1942 43 and 1943 44. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the appellant that it was not liable as it had not been treated as profits by the assessee and the decisions in St. Pericon Ltd. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay, ; , applied. The Appellate Tribunal held that section 14(2)(c) applied only to non residents and that the profits could be taxed only if they were remitted to British India. In reference under section 66(1), the High Court held that sections 42(1) and 42(3) applied both to nonresidents and consequently declined to refer the question to the court under section 64(1). The appellant came up in appeal by special leave against the decision of the High court. Held, that the finding of the Commissioner was correct and it was open to review under section 67(1); but that the decision in St . Perican vs Commissioner Of Income tax Bombay, , relied on. The question whether a particular amount is assessable as profits or not depends upon the facts found and circumstances of each case. The inference from facts would be a question of law. The ultimate finding on the issue must, therefore, be an inference to be drawn from the facts proved on the application of the proper principles of law and it will be correct to say in such cases that an inference from other facts is a question Of law. Commissioner of Incometax vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., , distinguished.

The appellant assessee was a private limited company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee paid a sum of Rs. 75,465 as commission to the General Manager, the appellant 's father, who by his order dated October 31, 1949 found that Rs. 70,465 paid to the general manager was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business and therefore the commission paid to him was not really paid wholly for the purposes of carrying on business. The Income Tax Officer determined a sum Of Rs. 71,465 which had been disallowed by the Income tax Appellate Tribunal. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the amount of Rs 75,467 paid to it was an allowable deduction and that the allowance was restricted to half of the amount claimed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that the entire amount of RS. 75.465 paid by the respondent was an expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for purposes of the assessee 's business. [532 D] (ii) In the circumstances established by the asses see, the entire sum of RS 75,463 paid to a private company was an allowance laid out entirely and exclusively laid out for the purpose of business. It was open to the Appellate Tribunal to come to a conclusion either that the alleged payment is not real or that it is not incurred by the assesses in the character of a trader or it is laid out solely and exclusively within the purpose for which the expenditure has been incurred.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. The Secretary of the Union made an application to the Patna High Court on March 13, 1957, praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957 by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of Union and thereafter in making an award on the basis of the reference. The appellant filed his application to this Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying for a direction on the Tribunal not to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 's case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. Held, that the Tribunal committed an error in rejecting the appellant his prayer to be represented by a representative of his choice in preference to the sum of Rs. 1,000 which the company had agreed to pay as a term of settlement. The scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act does not contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act, when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen. The necessary corollary to this is that the individual workman is at no stage a party to the industrial dispute independently of the union.

The appellants were the tenants in a joint Hindu family. The suit for ejectment was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent against defendant No. 1. On appeal by defendant No, 553 At the hearing of the appeal of the surviving appellants, the only point which was urged before the Court was that the surviving appellant was competent to continue the appeal in view of O.XXII, r. 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the nine appellants constituted a joint family and the surviving plaintiffs could continue the appeals even after the death of Kedar Nath and the abatement of the appeals so far as he was concerned, that the Court could have reversed or varied the whole decree in favour of all the original plaintiffs and could have granted relief with respect to the rights and interests of Kedarnath as well. Held, that it is not proved that Kedar Nath, deceased and the other appellants constituted joint Hindu Family that the right to appeal survived to the surviving respondents alone and that they could have continued their appeal in spite of O .XXII r. 33 of the Civil Procedure Code. The provisions of 0. XLI, r, C.P.C., enable one of the plaintiffs or one of them to file an appeal against the entire decree in certain circumstances. Once an appeal has been filed by all the plaintiffs the provisions of O,.XXII apply to the stage when an appeal is filed and empowers one of its plaintiffs or defendants to file appeals against the whole judgment in certain circum stances. Once the appeal has abated, as all the appellants had a common right and interest in getting a decree of ejectment against defendant no. 2 and such decree could have been on a ground common to all of them. The respondent cannot be ejected from the premises when he has a right to remain in occupation of the premises on the basis of the decree holding that Kedarnath, one of his heirs, had a joint interest in letting out the property could not have ejected him. It is not possible for the respondent to continue as tenant of one of landlords and not as a tenant of others when all of they had a separate right to eject him or to have him as their tenant.

The appellant landlord sought to break through these defences by urging that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed and further that forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise can be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g). The Rent Controller dismissed the application. In appeal, the Appellate Authority held that the provisions of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 did not apply to the lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience applied did not desiderate the technical requirement of a valid notice in writing of an intention to determine the lease. On further appeal by the tenant, the High Court held that this provision in sub section (g) of section 111 was not based upon any principle of justice and equity and therefore, it could not be said that no notice under section 112 was needed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The legal position as to the interpretation of a statutory provision is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 does not, ipso facto, extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine his lease by giving notice in that behalf. [920D] 1.2 The statutory law as it now stands is that a happening of an event specified in Section 111(h) does not ipso facto extinguish the tenancy but only merely exposes lessee to risk of forfeiting and clothes clothes the lessee with the power, if any, to determined the lease by give notice in this behalf. The statutory Law, as it then stood, however, is that tho happening of a event specified therein does not either ipso facto or extinguish the leased lease but merely exudes the lessee 's right, If he so chose, to decide the lease, by giving notices in that respect. [936E F] 1:3 The legal fiction created by section 112 of the Transfer of Property Act is that "the happening of such events specified therein do not, even ipso facto extinguished the lease". It is a fitting finale to this part of the argument that in the High Courts arguments proceeded on the footing that the Supreme Court has ruled in Namdeo Lokman Lodhi vsPIL Bai & Ors. the provisions in section 106 and 111 of the . [936F G] 1 :4 The legal presumption under section 113 of the is that such a statutory presumption is rebutted by proof of the existence of an express term or condition regarding sub letting in terms of a particular provision of law, equity or good conscience and would not govern the bases made prior to the coming into force of theTP Act or to a lease executed prior to its coming into operation. [946G H] 1 5. The legal presumptions under section 114 of the are: (i) that the tenant has been given notice in the writing of intention to determined, the lease being for a period of five years from the date on which the tenancy was terminated; (ii) that he has received the notice in question in the manner prescribed by law and (iii) that such notice is not required because the tenant had received the same in the ordinary course of business. [948A B] 1 6. The provisions of sections 106 and 112 of Transfer of property Act do not apply in the present case as there was no express provision in the Act or the rules framed thereunder which would govern the matter as could be held to be consistent with the rules of equity, justice and good law.

The Governor of Assam, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub clause (c) of section 3 of the , delegated his power under cl. (2) of article 311 of the Constitution to the Governor of the State. The Governor was satisfied that in the interest of the security of the state it was not expedient to give him an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. He therefore, passed an order dismissing him from service. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that the Governor had no power under sub cl. 2 of article 310 to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank until he was given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and where it was proposed after such inquiry, to impose on him any such penalty, until he had been given a proper opportunity of making representation against the proposed action. The High Court held that the satisfaction under the unamended provision was not sufficient to sustain the order of dismissal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The satisfaction under sub clause 2 of Article 311 is not conclusive and it must be based on some evidence which would have influenced the mind of the authority in passing the order. [488 E] (ii) The Governor has to arrive at his satisfaction that in view of the provisions contained in article 311(2), he had arrived at a decision which was not reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry. If the Government servant is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the basis of any evidence adduced during such inquiry it would be difficult to sustain an order of punishment under sub el. 2, of article 31. [489 F G] (iii) The expression "any other sufficient reason" used in clause (2), is not capable of being construed as meaning "other sufficient reasons". The satisfaction contemplated by the unamended clause cannot be said to be conclusive and must be founded on some material which would influence the mind or the authority passing it. [490 G H] (iv) The order of removal passed against the appellant was therefore bad in law.

[1108C D] 2:2 The earlier decisions of this court in Civil appeal No. 941 of1976 did not recorded any decision or decision on merits, but the court took the same view that they should be directed to relegated to the civil suit On the assumption, it is a clear case of an existing or established entitlement of Shiana Waqfs to perform religious ceremonies, practices observances, ceremonies and function minus the recitation and utterance of Tabarra (detailed in the Writ petition) over the Plots and structures in question and respondents 6 and 7 and the Sunni community of Mohalla Doshipura are permanently restrain by an order from interfering With the exercise Of such rights in the manner they have been permitted to perform. [1040E F; 1041A] 2 4. The earlier Judgment of this High Court in C.A. No. 9941/76 did not set out any decision of the rights on merits and it took the contrary view that proper adjudication would not be possible without impleading the two Boards (Shia Central Wakf Board and Sunni Central Waqf Board). [1141C D; 1042E] 5. The subsequent judgment of the Allahabad Court in CA No. 931/75 did not contain any decision by this Court on merits. It was one of the contentions of Shib Muslim community that before the U.

The assessee, a public limited company, filed its return showing the loss as capital loss and the Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment year 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital gains. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim of set off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income Tax Officer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. In a reference under section 256(1) of Income Tax Act, 1961, the High Court held that there were no genuine losses; it held that the loss had not been determined as required under Section24(3), and that there had been no genuine Loss; it rejected the assessee 's claim of carry forward and set off of loss on the ground that loss had been not determined as contemplated under Section 25(3). In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the Revenue that the benefit conferred under Section 23 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the said claim could not be set off in accordance with the provisions of that sub section. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The benefit conferred by Section 24 of 1922 is continued to remain given effect only under the 1922 act and notwithstanding anything contained in this Chapter, no loss which has not been deter mined in pursuance of a return filed under Section 139 shall be carried forward under this Section for more than eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment Year for which the loss is first computed under the Act or as the case may be. [1164C D] 2. The word 'capital gains ' used in section 24(1)(b) and Section 80 together, is not defined in the 1922 Acts. It is a well settled rule of interpretation that where there is no express provision in the Income Act for the purpose of giving effect to any provisions of the Act, it would be permissible to interpret the words in their widest amplitude so as to give them an extended meaning and to take into account all the relevant provisions of law including those relating to the subject matter of the tax. [1064E F] 3. The expression 'capital gain ' is not used in the 1961 Acts. The definition of capital gains ' in section 2(22) of 1922 Acts includes any loss which is not determined in pursuance thereof. It has been defined in Section 2(28) as including any loss arising out of business, profession or vocation. [1264C E] 4. The provisions of Section 74(1), (b) & (c) are clear and unambiguous. They do not contemplate any ambiguity in the language used by them. [1364D] 5. The claim of the assessee that set off was admissible in its entirety, had to he notified by an Order in writing and there was nothing more to show that it was a notional capital loss. [1464E] 6. The High Court was clearly in error in holding that the assessee had filed its Return showing the losses and the income tax Officer neither computed the loss nor passed an adverse order, the IncomeTax Officer was not entitled to take advantage of his own failure and reject the assessee"s claim for setting off of losses on the grounds that loss has not be determined as requi site under Section 22(3)(a) or (b). [1465E] 7. The view taken by the High Courts is correct. [1564F] 8. The Tribunal was right in holding, that the relief granted to the asses see had been given effect tO under the provisions 1961 Act.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. All, the service conditions of the persons working in the three units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. When the trifurcation was made, the Service Rules governing the three unit had a common Rule which was Rule 12 in DAQAS and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DQSAS, Rule 13 provided that other conditions of service shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect of the serv ices, be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. The respondent was appointed as a Junior Scientific Officer in the DQ & P. at the relevant time, on October 13, 1966. He continued in service upto the age of 60 years and was not liable to be retired at the alleged superannuation age of 58 years. The Respondent filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal challenging the validity of the aforesaid order dated October 10, 1987 passed by the Central Adminis tration Tribunal contending that he was entitled to remain in service up to the superannu al age of sixty years and that he should be retired from the date of his superannuation at the age Of 58 years, and that the respondent was not enti tled to any benefit. The Tribunal held that the Respondent was not entitled to the said benefit. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants Union of India that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of serv ers for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age was increased, it could not be held that he respondent who belonged to another unit, viz DAQAAS was entitled ted the said benefits. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid and there is no substance in the present appeal. [85F] 1.2 In spite of the decision of this Court in Union of lndia vs Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei & Ors., , it was not held that respondent who belongs to another concern, viz, DAQAs, was entitled lo the said bene fit. The question involved in the instant appeal is, however, not whether the Government has such power. [86H; 87A] 1:3 In spite Of the decision by this Court and even pending the appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of india retired the respondent at the time of his re instatement in service as if he had not been retired. The denial of the benefit of enhanced superannuation age to the members of one 24 unit while the same is granted to the member of another unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [87D] 1 :4 In the instant case, the denial of benefit of the enhanced superannuation ages to the employees of one24 unit while tho same is grant ed to the other members of the other unit amounts tO discrimination, violation of Article 14 of the Constitu tion. The decision by the Tribunal was both proper, and valid, and there was no substance In the present case. [88E F] 1;5 The respondent had retired at that age.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The counting of votes took place with regard to Ward No. 1, Ward No 2 and Ward No 3. On that date the Court adjourned the hearing of the case for 969 recording the evidence of these two witnesses in respect of whom an application had been made by the election petitioner on the previous day. The appellant presented an application to the High Court under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution for quashing the order of the Judge. The High Court dismissed the petition in limine on the ground that there was no fair trial of the petition to the prejudice of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that having rejected the application, it was not open to the Judge to examine these two persons as court witnesses and this was a serious irregularity which the High court should have set right by quasbing the order based on the evidence Of these witnesses. HELD: (i) The trial judge examined two witnesses as Court witnesses and it is quite clear that but for the evidence, of these witnesses it would have been very difficult if not impossible, for the Judge, to have come to the conclusion he did and find the appellant guilty of corrupt practice. [975 D] (ii) There was no evidence on which the Judge could have come in the conclusion that Hakim Abdul Rahiman Shaik was not a person whose veracity could not be depended upon. There was also a charge in that pamphlet that he had turned the Kabarasthan into a brothel and was trading in illicit liquor for which was alleged to have been convicted. [936 C] (iii) The first publication having taken place on the 8th June, 1967 the limit of ten days fixed under section 21 sub section (1) of the Act began to run from that date and the petition which was filed on the 24th June was beyond time and should not have been entertained. If the point had been canvassed before the trial Judge, he would certainly have gone into the matter and found out why there were two Gazette Publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21(1) (i).

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that it was ultra vires as it was not saved by the new Act. It was contended for the petitioner that (i) the words "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of this Act" in section 3 must, in their setting, be read as qualifying the word, "notifications" and not the word "sections", and (ii) the Validation Act was not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under Entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively. Held:(i) The Validation Act is intra vires and the impugned notification is not ultra rites. It is intra constitutional and does not infringe article 14 of the constitution. The Validation act is not a law which the State Legislature was competent to enact and it is therefore a nullity. (ii).The Validation Act, in so far as it imposed a sales tax on the supply of materials in a contract for the construction of works simpliciter on the footing of a sale was held to be intra vires. The impugned notification was not therefore ultra vires. Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur, ; , followed. (iii)The Validation act was not a valid law and it was beyond the competence of the Legislature under Entry 52, for, the reason, that it operated retrospectively.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court, Punjab. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A four year term of rigorous imprisonment more hardening than habilitative, even though we deplore the sex violence the young appellant has inflicted on his cousin 's wife snatching a tricky opportunity. Even so, the incriminating company of lifers and others for long may be counter productive, and in this perspective, it is blend deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [790B C] 2. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, restray molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexually victimised. It may be marginally extenuatory to mention that modern Indian conditions are drifting into societal permissiic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [788E F] Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration, ; Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart from being deterrent. The current efforts of Governments, Central and State, to reform jail regimen, we hope, will give a better deal to the caged community. For these reasons, in this case, the Court deem it desirable to superadd to the sentence of imprisonment a few directives to ensure that the carceral period reforms the convict. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appel lant turns a newlic leaf of normal life. [789H; 789A B] Sunil Kumar Batra vs State of Punjab, ; ; Sunil Kumar Jain vs Delhi Adminis tration, ; and Sunil Batra (s) case and another vs State, ; , referred to.

The assessee, a limited company dealing in land. It maintained its accounts on the mercantile system. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator. This represented the difference between the sum of RS.7,37,190 payable to it in terms of the award dated July 29, 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum Of Rs.12,276 out of that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesseee on the date of the Award. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesee, and therefore, was a receipt of revenue nature liable to tax, and accordingly, a receipt was of revenue character liable to be assessed. The High Court rejected the second contention and upheld the view taken by the Income Tax officer. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The legal position is explained in further detail by the Gujarat High Court in Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, [1962] 1 SCR 676 that the award made by the Collector was merely an offer or tender of the compensation determined by the Collec tor to the onwer of the property on the acquisition, the High Court was right in the view it took. [395C D] 1.2 The legal fiction is explained by the Gujrat High Court, in Tomandas Kundanlalmal vs The Deputy Land Acquisition officer & Anr., [1962 ] 1 SCR 678 and Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Dy Land Acquisition Offi cer, ; , referred to. In the instant case, though the award was made by an Arbitrator on July 29. 1955 enhancing the amount of compensation payable, it was only that amount that had accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact paid or not. As has been stated earlier, a mere claim by the claimant, after taking possession, at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation.
