It must not be forgotten that even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by the Government to the High Courts and the High court may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [396E F] Topalal Kundanmal & Sons vs Commissioner Of Income tax Gujarat, , referred tOere: Whether the offer made by Land Acquisition Officers was inadequate and the claimant is entitled to an additional compensation and if yes, at what rate is in flux till the question is set at rest finally, we do not think that any enforceable right to a particular amount of compensa tion arises. [397F] 1:3 The legal situation was explained in detail by this Court in Harish Chandraraj Singh vs Deputy Land Acquisi tion Officer & Anr. , [1962) 1 SCR 677 and Harishchandra Raj Singh 's case ; , followed.

The appellants landlords filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the tenants on the ground that they were in arrears of rent. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the compromise under consideration in that case was lawful, (2) the suit was barred by limitation; and (3) the relief for possession was not barred by time. HELD: The suit was clearly within the meaning of section 12(1)(f) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. [882 D] In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Act the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". The protection is inherent In the language used in the section as a whole and remembering the beneficial object of the statute for the protection of a tenant based upon public policy. [888 E F] Nagindas Ramdas vs Dalpatram, ; , referred to. In order recording the compromise the Court said: "On a perusal of the joint compromise it was found that the same is legal and is within the purview of the plaint". The averment in the plaint was, therefore, accepted and the case was decreed.

The appellant company was carrying on business in shares and securities. The managing agency of the company was terminated by the Income tax Officer under section 23A(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax officer held that the loss incurred by the company related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the purpose of acquiring the managing agency. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In further appeal the Tribunal referred the question whether the loss was a capital loss and held that in view of the capital loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ suffered by the assessee on account of depreciation in the value of shares held by the Company in Elphinstone Mills Ltd., the loss of the value was not reasonable to expect the appellant company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view Of the capital gains incurred and he accordingly cancelled the orders of the Incometax Officer under s 23A (1). The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal by certificate, HELD : The form of the word used no doubt lends itself to the suggestion than regard should be paid only to the two matters mentioned, but it is impossible to arrive at a conclusion as to reasonableness by considering the two matter mentioned isolated from other relevant factors. Moreover, the Statute does not say 'having regard only to losses previously incurred by a company and to the smallness of the profits made. Their Lordships are of the opinion that the statute by the words used while making sure that "losses and smallness" of profit" are never lost sight of require all matters relevant to the question of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established is one of them.

The appellants filed a petition under section 39 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, for modifying the award and for setting aside the order of the Civil Judge. The District Judge allowed the petition on the ground that an appeal lay under section 37 of the Act against the order passed by the Civil judge. On appeal to the District Judge, a preliminary objection was raised that no appeal lay (1) I.L.R. [1959] 1 All. 65, followed. (2) section 15 of the did not apply because the appellants had apparently applied under section 15 Of the Act to the Court to modify the award made by the Consolidation Officer and they had succeeded in getting an order modifying the same in their favour. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the orders of the District judge and the Civil Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1)(a) Section 37 of U.P. Consolidation of Holding Act, 1953, does not apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37 Of the U. P. Consolidation Of Holdings Act. [935 A] (b) The effect of section 37 is that all the provisions of the except sub sections (1), (2), (3) and (4) apply to arbitration under the Consolidation of holdings Act. In the present case, the effect of sections 46 and 47 of the , read with sections 46 & 47 of U .P. was inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of U,.P. to the proceedings under the Act. The effect is that section 37 applies to arbitrations under the consolidation Act. Therefore, the result of section 36 is that the effect Of section 37 must be inter aliato applied sections 15 & 39 of Uttar Pradesh to the proceeding under the . [934 C D] (c) Section 12(6) must be read with section 37 and if it is so read it is quite clear that what is made final is the decision of the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings, if any, have been taken under the provisions Of the . The effect would be to apply only to sections 15, 16 and 39.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This resolution was also not a regulation made under the said section 64. However, since respondent No.2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. It is this promotion which was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post as superintending engineer, since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. Hence this special leave petition by the Corporation. Allowing the special leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [75B] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner has been a degreeholder Junior Engineer and diploma holder Junior Engineers. Hence, the observation are per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice followed till 1988 nor the resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Act. It was a case where the writ petitioners wanted such a classification to be made. It may be observed that it was not a case of the direct recruits and promotees integrated into one cadre. The Court then concluded: "We are therefore of the opinion that though persons appointed directly and by promotion were integrated into a common class of Assistant Engineers, they could, for purposes of promotion, be classified on the ground of educational qualification. The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to tho exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution and must be upheld. [76H; 77A] 1:3 In the absence o rule or regulations the authority cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was taken till the years 1988 and was also sought sought to been done since1988 by the respondent corporation in 1988 nor resolution passed by the Respondent Corporation in 1988 or the resolution issued in accordance 9.

The petitioners in the writ petition were appointed as Judges of the Supreme Court on May 13, 1987. The Chief Justice of India recommended that a time frame must be set for the response of the constitutional authority in the State and if there was no response forthcoming within the time, the Union of India should be in a position to proceed with the recommendation of the Chief Justice. On January 25, 1988, the Chief Judge withdrew the objection regarding this Court 's jurisdiction and made a statement that he was of the view that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union Government to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of public interest and the writ petitions requiring a direction to the Union o. India to fill up the vacancies were maintainable. The petitioners in their writ petition challenged the validity of the said statement on the ground that it violated Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it did not contain any provision for appointment of Judges of High Courts. The respondents contended that the Chief Justices of the High Court and the Chief Minister of the State had no personal or personal capacity to appoint Judges in the High Courts and the failure, if at all, was an infringement of their fundamental right under Article 14. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Constitution has been enacted with a view to provide for the establishment of high level judicial commission to be called the National Judicial Commission for the ap pointment of Judges in certain States and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. It is not necessary that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. [460G H] 1.2 The Constitution is a social welfare legislation intended to provide speedy justice between the people and the Union Territories. It has been designed to protect the independence of judiciary from being subjected to exploitation by the State or its instrumentalities. It was enacted with the object of providing for the appointment of judges in certain specified States. [461A B] 1:3 The Constitution, as it stands today, is a welfare legislation aimed at securing the independence and integrity of the people. It seeks to protect and improve the independence, integrity and harmony of the society by ensuring that the independence is not abused or misused. It also provides for the constitution of an independent judiciary in the country. [462C D] 1 :4 The Constitution envisages a high level Judicial commission which consists of three Judges, one of whom must be appointed as Chairman of the judicial system and the other of the Judges of such High Courts who are to be appointed by the Chief justice of the States. The appointment of a Judge has nothing personal either to the Chief Judges of that High Court or the Chief Ministers of the state concerned. If in a given case the ChiefJustice of the high Court has recommended and the name has been considered by the Governor so as to reach the hands of the chief Justice of theHigh Courts, there cannot ordinari ly be any justification for reopening the matter merely because there has been a change in the personnel of the District Judge or the High Judges of those High Courts or the Supreme court. [463E F] 1;5 The constitutional purpose and process it becomes imperative that the role of the institution of the Judge of India be recognised as of crucial importance in the matter of appointments to the Supreme Courts and, therefore, it becomes obligatory that the roles of the establishment should be recognised by a larger bench. If the recommendation is to emanate di rectly from a source other than that of the Governor of the .State, the two questions indicated above which are of vital importance to the efficient functioning of the Judicial system in the Country require consideration and there is an element of immediacy in the matters of appointments, to the High courts and, the Supreme. Court.

The respondent was appointed as an Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's order dated January 9, 1979. He did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon as an official of the bank. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order contending that since the impugned order of discharge got merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the Single Judge on the ground that 'as the original order was without jurisdiction or competence, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm '. The Division Bench allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of punishment and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. It is for this reason that the High Courts were right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment but having regard to the special facts and circumstances pointed out earlier, it should not have ordered payment of 'all consequential bene fits ' flowing from the declaration that the impugned orde r was bad in law. [519D] 1.2. The High Court was right in directing payment of all consequential reliefs. [525E] 1:3. In the instant case, the order imposing punishment has to be quashed not because the merits of the case so demand but because the technical plea of incompetence suc ceeds. [500F] Pulin 's case concluded that the acts of the Market Committee de facto performed within the scope of its assumed official authority, in the interest of the public or third persons and not for his own benefit are generally as valid and binding as if they were performed by a de jure committee. It, therefore, should not be ordered payment Of 'all ' consequential benefits flowing from tho declaration that 'the impugned order was bad In law. The fact however remains that the said impugned order has to he quashed not since the merits o f the case, so demand and because the Technical plea of lack of jurisdiction or incompetence are generally considered as valid. [511F G] Pulinshah vs State of Orissa & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant, a Zonal Development Plan for Delhi, submitted a plan in respect of certain areas including Chawri Bazar, which were to be divided into two parts. The Master Plan was prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Act and it came into operation under section 11 in the area concerned. The building operation proposed by the respondents as per the plans submitted by them did not contravene any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of rejection on the ground that the Commissioner had no jurisdiction to reject the plan submitted by the respondent and that the order rejecting the sanction was legal and justified by the provisions, of cl. (1) of sub s.(2) Of section 336. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Master Plan had been prepared under s.7 of the Act and therefore it had come into operation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Master plan has been prepared in accordance with the provisions contained in section 7. [168A] (ii) The scheme of the Development Act is that if any particular and definite use of land is indicated in a Master Plan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted. Similarly, if a Zonal development Plan provides for a particular use of any land or building in that zone, it cannot be put to a different user. If neither of the plans provide for the particular use by any land nor of the building in the Area or Zone, section 14 will have no application whatsoever. [169B C] (iii) The respondents ' lands are not in any manner indicated as being taken up by any part of the proposed road, mentioned in the Master plan and, if that is so, there is no violation of section 14 of the development Act.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No, a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No 1 was one of the members of the Assembly of India. He was a member Of the Legislative Council of the United States of America. He had been a member in the Legislative Chamber of Commerce and was also a member thereof. In connection with the election to the Legislative assembly of the States of Vindhya, the appellant was declared elected by the Governor General on August 8, 1949, and he was declared duly elected. The respondent No. I filed an application before the Special Judge under section 164(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code for his discharge from service. The Special judge rejected the application holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. On appeal by the State, the High Court held that the appellant had failed in establishing the falsity of the allegation made by him and that he had brought these moneys from his home and handed over them to the appellant 's person who was not a member but a member and that the evidence showed that the money was given to the respondent No 1 for the purpose of giving bribe or illegal gratification. The State appealed to this Court. Held, that the statements made by the appellant to him were admissible in evidence and he could not be proved orally by him. The statement made by appellant No., 1 to them and the fact that they were recorded under section 161 was inadmissible in evidence. The statements made to them were admissible under section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as it stood at the relevant time. The offence of taking bribe or unlawful gratification is a crime against public confidence and it is of the essence of that public confidence in the independence of the judiciary that public faith in the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of Constitution must be maintained. It is not necessary that there should be a particular act which would have been committed if the gratification was given or demanded for any other purpose. The question whether the gratification should be given or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case, the statements were made by both the parties to the effect that they had come to an end and that they did not know what the money had been received from the appellant. The fact that the notes were handed over to the appellants was not sufficient to establish the falsity or falsity of allegation made in the statement. The High Court erred in holding that it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove the falsity. The mere fact that a person is a member does not make him an accused and his conviction cannot be sustained unless he proves that there was no evidence to show that he has brought the money from his house or that he received any gratification as alleged by the prosecution.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the appellant was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was acquitted by the trial court. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the ground that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High court in the manner it has been done. [826G] 2. Rule 16 is intended to ensure that a Police officer judicially convicted to rigorous imprison ment exceeding one year shall be dismiss ed, and this provision of law must be strictly complied with before any person can be punished for an offence under the Act. The authority was also permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. [825A B] 3. Rule 17.1(2)(a) of Punjab Police rules, 1934 stipulates that a constable judicially sentenced shall be dismissal and this requirement is mandatory. The order of dismissal passed against the respondent was therefore illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. [827B C] 4. Rule 18.2 (2)(b) of Rules, 1955 mandates that a public officer judicially ordered to be dismissed shall be dis criminated and this provi sions of law should not be ignored. The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [828C D] 5. In the instant case, the question involved was a new one. It has been asserted on oath before this Court and not denied by the respondent that the aforesaid Kahan singh had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order of his dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and that later he was again dismissed. [829E F] 6. The appeal is accordingly allowed. There will be no order as to costs.

The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In fact the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were not speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that these transactions were speculative transactions and consequently the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh (I.L.R. [1957] All. 971, referred to. In the present case the question is covered by the decision of this court in Raghunath Prasad Poddar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Calcutta, , and D. C. Mehta vs Commissioner Of Income tax (Central), Calcutta, ; , on which the Tribunal 's decision was based. The High Court held that transactions were neither speculative nor speculative transactions but were merely speculative transactions. In view of the decision in Raghunath P. Poddar vs Commis sioner of Income Tax, Calcutta and D . C. Jain vs Commissioner for Income tax [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R., this question was also referred to a larger Bench. The appellant contended that the transaction was not speculative but was merely speculative transaction and consequently it should be held that loss should have been treated as trading loss relying upon two decisions in D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner, of Income ' tax, [1959], Supp. 2 S.T.C., and Dhandiram vs Commissioner , of Income. tax, Bombay City vs Commissioner (Central) Calcutta, [1961] 1 S C.R,. 971. The respondent contended that it was not necessary to prove that the said transactions were either speculative or speculative transactions which were not completed by actual delivery of the goods to the transferee and therefore the loss suffered by the appellant in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the respondent 's non speculative business High Court on reference following its earlier decisions in Raghunath Prashad Poddar vs The Commissioner of Incometax, Calcutta [1961 ] 1 S,.C. R. 972, referred tO.

The appellant was the candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The constituency was a double member constituency, one seat being general and the other reserved for a Scheduled Caste. Section 33(1) of the Act requires each candidate to "deliver to the Returning Officer". a nomination paper completed in the prescribed form and subscribed by the candidate himself as assenting to the nomination and by two persons referred to in sub section (2) as proposer and seconder. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the validity of the election on the ground that it was not signed by the proposers and seconders in the usual way by writing their names, and that the Returning officer had omitted the attestation because of some slip on his part and it could be proved that he was satisfied at the proper time, the matter might be different because the element of his satisfaction at the time, which is of the substance, would be there and the omission formally to record the satisfaction could probably, in a case like that, be regarded as an unsubstantial technicality. Held, that the word "subscribe" in section 33(i) of ' Subscribes" does not include both signing, writing and the making of a mark as the Act itself does in the definition of "sign". The words " subscribe to" and "subscribing" are used in different senses and they have not been signed " by the proposer or seconder. In the present case the nomination papers were not " signed " either in one way or the other, but only " subscribe " as the act set out in the second schedule.

The appellants, workmen of the Company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given by the company. The appellants were dismissed by the Company on September 7, 1972 and their names had been struck off from the rolls of the company from that date. On September 26, 1972, the appellants wrote to the Company returning the cheques sent by the appellants and stating that its letter dated September 7 was received by them on September 20, 1972. The Company 's reply to the said letter was that it had reached them only on September 21, 1972; that they were interested in the service of the workmen and had neither voluntarily abandoned the service nor did they wish to do so, and that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off by their union. The company 's stand that the letter dated 9th September, 1972 had reached the appellants only on Sept. 20,1972, that they had not abandoned the services of the appellant and did not want to continue in service of that Company and had totally abandoned the Company ' 's service, that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the appellants standing orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the Company was justified in removing them from its rolls. The Labour Court held that the action of the respondent company in removing the names of the appel lants from its roll on the presumption that they have abandoned service would constitute a change in the conditions of service of appellants during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. The High Court also held that there was no abandonment of service on the part of the employees concerned, that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned their service and had thus abandoned the company ' ' 'service" their names were struck off. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the impugned action of respondent No. 1 in removing their names from its muster rolls on the plea that they did not intend to abandon the service, amounted to a change of the conditions Of service of workmen during the disputed pendency of industrial dispute and that the termination could only he in terms thereof, be in term of the agreement between the parties and since there was nothing in the surrounding circumstances or conduct of the parties indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knot or link which holds one to the office and the obligations and privileges that go with it Their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed as voluntary abandonment by them of the service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The action of Respondent No. I in removing appellants from its Roll on the presumed presumption that their names have been struck out from the muster rolls of respondent company on the said presumption was illegal and arbitrary. [616C] 2.1 In the instant case, there was neither any allegation nor any evidence to show that the workmen concerned had voluntarily accepted the service or had abandoned the employment of the respondents in the aforesaid circumstances. The impugned action on the appellants ' part amounted to an change in condition of service during the period admitted pendency. [625E F] 2:2 It is not possible for the respondent No 1 to contend that the workers concerned have been employed elsewhere during this period, still they are no provision in the certified standing orders by virtue of which the Company would have terminated the services. The workmen concerned have thus voluntarily abandoned service and have abandoned the respondents ' service.

The respondents were trustees of a public trust styled "Shri Tricumraiji". The trustees sold the mortgaged property to one Saheba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. An action instituted by the mortgagee against the trustees to enforce the mortgage was compromised and it was decreed that the trustees do pay Rs. 3,910 due under the mortgage by monthly instalments of Rs . 89 of 0. Raju, J. The respondents filed an application for execution of the mortgage. The trial court held that sale of the mortgaged properties which belonged to a public Trust was without the sanction of the Charity Commissioner and on that account a sale in execution of a decree held without the previous sanction of Charity Commissioner must be deemed invalid. On appeal by the trustees, the High Court set aside the sale holding that sale in the execution of decree held with regard to the property which belonged exclusively to a private trust was invalid and on this view remanded the case to the District Court for decision on all the points correctly arising out of the matter. The District Court held that the expression "sale" in section 36(a) includes a sale of immovable property in execution 'of a decree for sale of mortgaged property, enables any person either owning such property or holding an interest therein by virtue of a title to apply to have the sale set aside on his depositing in court, (a) for payment to the purchaser, a sum equal to five per cent. of the purchase money and (b) for pay to the decree holder, the amount specified in the proclamation of sale as that for the recovery of which the sale was ordered less any amount which may since the date of such proclamation of sales have been received by the decreeholder. The High Court also held that even though there is a judgment of a Single Judge of the High 'Court, he is not bound to follow that precedent because by following the precedent the Judge would act contrary to section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act and would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution; and (2) that a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court in Pijare Karimbhai 's case was binding on Raju J., if the Full Bench judgment is given on a reference made on a question of law arising in a matter before a single Judge or a Division Bench, or aBench. The appellant came to this Court after obtaining special leave from this Court. HELD : (i) In view of the decision of the Full bench of the Bombay High Court that a Single judge hearing a matter is inclined to take the view that the earlier decisions of the Supreme Court, whether of a Division or a Bench of a single Judges need to be re considered, he should not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a single judge but should refer the matter 'to a Division bench for decision. [461 F] (ii) The judgment of the Single Judge was binding upon Raju J. If the Full Court judgment is overruled by a Division Judge or Bench of that High Court, he would be bound to comply with it and the District Judge would be entitled to constitute a larger Bench to examine the question.

The respondent joined the post and Telegraph Department as a clerk on June 4, 1935. The Government had the absolute right under Rule 56(j) of Fundamental Rules to prematurely retire a servant in 'Public Interest ' after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service by giving him three months ' notice or pay in lieu of such notice. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said rule and also the order passed by the Government on February 8, 1956. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules is ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of Rule 2 (2)of the Libera lised Pension Rules may also be to weed out unsuitable employees. This will be in addition to the provisions already contained in rule 2(3) of Pension Rules. [899G H] 1.2 The object and purpose of Rule 2046 has been achieved by amending Rule 2.1 of the Pension Rules, 1950. Para 620 of the Manual being executive instructions, it is a statutory rule. There is thus no legal or equitable ground to interfer with the judgment of the High court. [889B] 1:3 The object underlying Rule 2 is to provide an incentive to the Government to retire a Government servant at any time after he had completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice. This would be in consonance with the statutory rule and the rules framed under Article 77(1) of Constitution of india. [879C] 1 :4 The object is to give unguided discretion to the Govern ment to retire an officer at any place after he is attained the age of 55 years. Any Government servant who has completed thirty years of service can be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule. [869D] 1;5 The Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8 1956 are in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article77(1), of the Constitu tion. Para 623 of the Railway Pension Manual being 'Public interest ', the railway employees are only goverted by the said Rule and para 620 is void and inoperative. This Court while setting aside the judgment dated January 21, 1973 in Special Appeal No. 60/72, held as under: "Thus the areas of operation of Para 620 are different from that of clause (h) and (k) of Rule 2946 of the Rules. The said para which has been framed by the Union Government in exer cise of its executive powers under Article 73 of the constitution should be given due effect since there is no statutory provisions or a rule framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Consti tution which is inconsistent with it. Para 619 of the manual being executive instruction, para 620 of Railway Pension Rules 1950 has no parity with Rule 2.(2) and pension rules.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1946. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. The Excess Profits Tax Officer did not set off the said deficiency of profits that accrued in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending on 31st December, 1941 and 31st January, 1944 respectively. He, therefore, confirmed that there were no profits and losses during the chargeable year ending on 30th May, 1941 to 31.3. 1943. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In appeal, the assessee had urged that deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable period from October 1940 to 31 st March, 1942 should be allowed a set off in computing the excess profits for purposes of consideration. The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to a setoff of the deficiency only for the relevant accounting period ending on31st March,, 1941 and that it could not be said that there was any deficiency of profit during those periods. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The method of computation under section 7 of the Act must be on the basis of 'accounting period ' and after that the deficiency in profit for that period should be computed on that basis and after set off carried forward to be set off during the relevant chargeable accounting year. [690C] 1.2 In the instant case, the chargeable account ing periods ending 31st Decem ber 1941 and 30th January 1944 were occupied with manufacturing activity alone and there were sales, therefore no part of the profit realised upon the sales could be apportioned to those chargeable accounting years and consequently that it was not possible to apportion the deficiency of income tax for the assessment year 1940 41. [643D] 1:3 The method under section 6 of the Excess Profits tax Act must he on the principle of apportionment of profits to which it had adverted to, the profits earned upon sales effected during the taxable accounting period ended 31st march, 1944 and the deficiency worked out on that footing in respect thereof. [625E F] 2.1 In the present case, there was no sale or purchase of any raw material or finished product. The assessee carried on business at Raichur and accused or arose at Raichur. There was no sales, however, in their mills at Raichur, accused or arisen at Raichur which took place in Bombay, the question was whether the activity which the assessee carried carried on at Raichur was part of their business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. [650F G] 2:2 The method adopted by the authorities under the Act for computation of the excess profit for the purposes of computing the chargeable profits for chargeable accounting is on the footing that the profits of a part of business, the manufacturing of oil in their mill at Raichur accused or arise at Raichur are liable to be computed only when they are actually sold and not when they actually sold. [526G] 2 :3 The High Courts were right in holding that the principle laid down by this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. Shaw Wallace & Co., Ltd., ; , applied to the facts of the instant ease, was applicable to the instant cases.

The petitioner, a Mechanical Engineering degree holder in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the KPSC, was appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer on a regular basis. He had qualified in Civil engineering and answered questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified for Mechanical Engineering and answered the questions in category II on the other. The Public Service Commission invited applications from candidates who had appeared in the written test conducted by the K PSC and there after in an interview held by it. After the written examination and interview, but before a common rank list was prepared by the Public Service Com missioner, the petitioner filed Writ Petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the selection and preparation of separate rank lists of selected applicants holding Civil and Mechanical Engineering degrees. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petitions and directed the Government to prepare two separate seniority lists, namely one for the Civil Bench and other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Services Commission is directed to prepare a common list, namely, one for Civil Bench & the other for Mechanical Branch. The Kerala Government and the K.PSC accepted the directions given by the learned Single judge and proceeded to take steps for the implementation thereof. However, some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petitions filed appeals before the Division Bench of the High court. The appeals were ultimately dismissed, in view of the fact that the KPsSC faced difficulties in giving effect to the directions issued by the High Courts. Hence these special leave petitions. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In pursuance of the directions made by the Division Judge in his judgment dated 23rd April 1980 quoted above, the State Government and Public Service Commissions of Kerala proceeded to prepare separate lists. But facing difficulties, in the view of this Court 's order dated 23th April 1980, it is necessary to clarify the position and give necessary directions. As stated earlier, the KPWSC faced difficulty in giving effective effect to these directions given in his Judgment and order dated 11th November, 1980 has been subsequently recalled by this Court by its order dated 7th April, 1981 and we do not find any valid ground to reverse the judgments of the learned single Judge. [749E F] 1.2 In view of difficulties faced by the Kerala Government or the K PWSC, it was necessary to clarified the position that the petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list prepared by Public Service commission.

The respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, was incorporated in 1979 and the plaintiff respondent No 1 had been appointed as a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The partnership deed provided that the profits of the partnership business would be computed on the basis of the valuation made by the assessee. The Income Tax Department valued the suit at Rs.150 being the sum of Rs.50 for declaration, Rs. 50 for profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. The plaintiff respondent filed a suit for dissolution of the firm and accounts valuing at Rs 150 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint. The defendant No.1 contested the suit contending that it was not maintainable under section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act, and that it is manifest that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the plaintiff in the suit. The trial court rejected the objection of the defendant No 1 that it could be tentatively valued at Rs 50 only. On appeal, the High Court held that the valuation put by the appellant on the plaint was arbitrary and unreasonable and set aside the valuation given by the respondent on the relief claimed in the plaint and directed the trial court to pass a fresh order after considering the statement in the written statement filed by the defendant. The High Court also observed that when a plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate". It was further held that when the valuation fixed by the Income tax Department appears to be arbitrary and irrational the court may reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The interpretation put by this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. It is true that in a suit of accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849, this court while taking note of the appellant 's right to give a tentative value on the suit but he was not permitted either to choose any unreasonable and arbitrarily figure for the same purpose. [901C D] 2. In a suit under section 10(1)(d) of Income Tax Act, the plaintiff must state the valuation which would have resulted after taking into all the account and he can put a final valuation upon it. The case of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be incorrectly decided. [992C D; 903A] 3. In Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1934 Allahabad 848, this Supreme Court while taking into consideration the plaintiff 's rights to give an arbitrary valuation in the Plaint, and observed that if the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [962C] 4. In such a case it is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valuation. The cases of some High Courts who have taken the different view should be held wrongly decided. The learned counsel for the parties have placed before this Court the materials on the record at considerable length and we do not have any hesitation in holding that the value put by respondent No1 on the plaintiff (respondent before us)

The respondents in these two matters and the petitioners in the other five Special Leave Petitions are concerns in M.P. assess able to sales tax (for short, the assesses '). The State Government exempted the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who have set up industry in any of the districts of Madhya Pradesh specified in the annexure to this notification and have commenced production after 1st April 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in Column (2), subject to the restrictions and conditions specified in columns (3) and (4). The respondents filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the exemption granted by the State Government. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that the industries run by them were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption under the notification and that the Director of Industries should have granted them a certificate to this effect. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification under it can be prospective or retrospective only only prospective operation can be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. [608C] 1.2 In view of the clear language of section 12 of the Act and the notification thereunder, the assessee claim that they are eligible for the exemption under notification and not on the basis of any further requirements not so set out. No.1 is in any way inconsistent with the statutory instruments in this case. [613D] 1:3 The Notification does not set out the conditions on which, and the procedure in accordance with which the Director o/s Industries has to issue the eligibility certificate. It merely sets out the condi tions for exemption from the provisions of the scheme providing for the grant of incentives for setting up the new industri al Units; "tra conditionalities" are not included in the notification. [625E] 1 :4 The Notification is clear that while a notification under it could be prospective, only prospective opera tion can be granted to a Notification rescinding the exemption already granted earlier.[608F] 2.1 In view thereof, the 1987 amendment has the effect of rescinding its exemption granted in respect of the industries mentioned by it. [509G] 2:2 The 1987 amendment had the effect effect of reviving the exemption given by the 1981 notification in respect o f the industries covered by it and section 12 is clear from that, while a Notification under the same can be retrospective or retrospective, only retrospective operation can he given to the notification resc overruling an exemption already made earlier. It may also be pointed out that even if it could not be said that two interpretations of the notification were equally plausible, the asses see cannot invoke the doctrine of promissory estoppel.

The petitioners in the writ petition were appointed to temporary posts in the Delhi Judicial Service on the recommendation of the High Court. The appointments were made by the Administrator on the recommendations of the Full Court of the Delhi High Court and appointments were also made on merit cum seniority basis so much so, the direct recruits who had been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in a temporary capacity to substantive vacancies in the Service. The petitioners contended that the appointments were not by way of promotion but by wayof relaxation and that the appointment was made on seniority cum seniority cum merit basis so long as the direct recruit had completed ten years of service in the cadre post, he could be considered for promotion to the next higher grade. The High Court rejected the contention and held that the petitioners were appointed regularly in accordance with qualifications laid down under Rule 7(a) and (b) of the Rules. In the writ petitions filed by them, it was contended on behalf of the direct recruitment to the Delhi Higher Judicial Service that the posts in question were temporary posts and not by promotion but on seniority basis, that the direct appointments were only by way or by way and that they could be appointed only after a regular selection from amongst the members of the service. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that appointments to temporary vacancies in accordance With qualifications laid under Rule 6(a), namely, by selection and after completion of ten years judicial service, must be made according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed. [397E] 1.2 In the instant case, for example, an appointee to a temporary post of Additional District & Sessions Judge can only hold that post in a substantive capacity if he has completed not less than 10 years of Service in the State Judicial Service as required by Rule 7 (a), and if he was appointed on the basis of selection from among the members, of the Union of India as envisaged by rule 16(1) and if his appointment is made after a member of the Punjab Judicial Service in consultation with the High court as enjoined by Rule 5(1), quota rule assuming that there is any, cannot apply to such appointments. [398F G] 1:3 The observations of this Court in A. In re A. V. Rangaswamy & Ors., ; , followed. 1.4 The observations made by this Court are not intended to operate as res judicata or bar the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to entertain and decide any question relating to seniority. [399G] 1 :5 The observations in A, in the case of A.V. Rangaswami vs Union of lndia & Ors. , ; , relied on by the respondents are not applicable to the facts of the instant cases because the appointments made under Rules 16 and 17 were made on merits cum seniority based on meritcum seniority basis. [435B] 1 6. The observations regarding seniority in A was not intended as a matter of course, but only an observation that a candidate 's position may be placed in such a way that by legal fiction he will be placed as senior to a person as a District and Sessions Judge by national placement at a time when he did not even reach the age at which he or she would have become eligible for appointment. [400C] 1 7. The observation of this court in A V Rangaswamy vs Union Of India & Ors, ; , is not intended merely to operate on the assumption that the rules of continuous officiation in the Cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a period of 10 years judicial experience, are applicable to temporary appointments made by way, or by promotion and such appointments must be held to be valid and binding on the parties. [402D E] 8.

The assessee, a member of the Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1960 61 and 1961 62. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment in the status of "an association of persons". In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income in the hands of Debi ParII be deleted. The Tribunal confirmed the orders of the Income tax officer and directed the Income Tax Officer to assess the income as "the income of the family of Debi parshad". In appeal by the Commissioner, the High Court set aside that order. In appeals to this Court, HELD: (1) Where the income tax Officer assesss the income of an association of individuals under section 31(3)(b), the Appellate Tribunal is competent to set aside such assessment and direct the Income. tax Officer to make the direction with regard to the assessment of the income, provided the assessment was not barred by the law of limitation. [392 D] (2) Where as the result of an appeal, any change in, the assessment or re assessment of a firm or association of ' persons is ordered to be made, the Incometax Officer may authorise the Income_ tax Officer, to amend accordingly any assessment made on any partner of the firm or any member of such association. The power of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner to make such direction is not and could not be referred to the High court. [391 E] (3) Where an order of the appellate Assistant Commissioner is set aside by the Income ' tax Officer in revision, the order can be made even after the expiry of four years.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share in the plaint. The valuation was fixed at Rs. 15,00,000 and it was not open to him to value his relief on the memorandum of appeal under section 7(iv)(b) without an amendment of the valuation made in the suit. Held, that the suit fell under section 6(iv) (b) of the Indian , and the court fee had to be paid either under section 8(iv). The Court fees payable in suits covered by the several sub sections of section 7 were not mentioned in the Code of Civil Procedure. The provisions of article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act did not apply to suits falling under section 9 of the Suits Valuation Act and the valuation for jurisdiction purposes alone was mentioned. Held further, that where the plaintiff seeks to pay the fixed court fee as required by the said article, he and his advisers are apt to take the view that it is unnecessary to state the amount for which relief is sought to be claimed for the purpose of Court fees and the value for jurisdiction alone was, therefore, mentioned. The suit fell within section 7 (iv)(c) of Act and it could not be reopened at this stage. Held also, further, in a case falling under sub section (iv), a departure has been made and liberty has been given to the plaintiff to amend his valuation for the payment of court fees not only on the plaint but also on the suit and the memorandum or appeal. The Court fee had therefore to be deposited either under s 7(v) (c) or under section 10 of the Code.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) seeks special leave to appeal against the order of the High Court dated 28.4.1989, of the NDMC in a writ petition filed by Respondent No. 1 and its Managing Director, Respondents 2 and 3 respec tively, on the ground that the structural nature and basis of its calculation of the extent of these "Refuge Areas" are dealt with by Bye law 16.4,8.1 and 16.2.8. 1 which provides for refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metre per person on each floor at the rate of 1 sq. m. per person. The appellant 's case was that the plan providing for refuge area in the proportion of one Sq. metre to one sqm. metre, per person, on each floors was considered by the Chief Fire Officer as a better and more reliable fire safety measures than those envisaged by the bye laws and the Chief fire Officer preferred to accept them. As regards the requirement of bye law 16, it was urged that the clearance from the Chief Levi dation Officer envisaged by Bye laws 17.1 is in addition to the requirements of bye laws 16.8, and 16,4.8 and that in appropriate cases, where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measure which, in judgment of the Court of the Delhi High Court, are considered to provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure than those contemplated by the Bye laws 16, 4.8 etc., the NDMC would not be precluded from accepting them. The respondents filed a counter affidavit contending that the application was barred by time and that the appellant had failed to establish any legal right to the property. It was further contended that the applicant had no locus standi to file the writ petition as he had not been impleaded as a party to the proceedings. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the objections raised were not bona fide. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of Bye law 15.4 is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the DDA to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for sufficient fire safety in accordance wi th Bye laws or, in a proper measure. [610C] 1.2 In appropriate cases where the plan and designs incorporated fire safety meas ure 16.1 are considered, to provide an inflexible, rigid standard and whether the location and distribution of refuge areas therein is violative of the Bye law. The only way in which, perhaps, the zonal developmental requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and prob lems inherent in the insistence upon construction of such pedestrian walk way in an isolated case, could be reconciled is to direct the NDMC, in the event of its ap proving the plans otherwise, to keep the requirement in abeyance for the present subject to a written undertaking to be lodged with it by the respondent 1 and 2 to the effect that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmental requirements in that behalf is finally decided upon, the respondent I and 2 would undertake to put up such a pedestrian path way and Podium. [613D E] 1:3 The only course open to the NDMC to commence the construction work according to the plans submitted by them, on t he condi tions that they file a written Undertaking before the NDMC that the construction would be at the risk of the Respond ents 1 & 2 and it would not progress beyond a height of 15 metres and in the case of an ultimate rejection of the plan, they would have no claim against the NDMC for any loss occasioned to respondent 1 or 2.

The plaintiff, who was the owner of a motor cycle shop in Bombay, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of his business from April 1, 1946, that the motor business was still joint family business and that he had a right to ask for accounts of that business subsequent to March 31, 1946. The trial court decreed the plaintiff 's claim on the ground that the cause of action in the two suits was identical and not separate and distinct and that the suit was barred by res judicata or by Order II, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal, the High Court held that the relief claimed by the plaintiff was different from the one which was sought to be enforced in the previous suit and that it was barred both by the principle of res judicata and by order 11, rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The compromise closed once for all the controversy about taking any account of the joint family businesses including the motor cycle business after the 31st March 1946, and the plaintiff is bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decree following upon it. [102 D] (ii) It was not as if there had been an oversight on the part of the parties but the parties knew that the businesses might go on afterwards; but if they were carried on, they did not particularly care for providing by the compromise decree for accounts for those businesses being taken after the 1st of April, 1946 and the appellant is bound to honour the terms. [103 E] (iii) The suit embraced the entire property without any reservation and was compromised, the plaintiff having abandoned his claim to account in respect of 108 the motor shop subsequent to that date. If the plaintiff really intended that accounts of the motor businesses or indeed of all other businesses were to be taken up to the date of the final decree, there was no point in mentioning the 31th March, 1946; but, if they Were carried on after the31st March, 1945, they could not possibly have been done.

The appellant was employed as a factory of salt works situate at Wadala, Bombay without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the . The Salt Works were converted into salt by the process of treatment and adaptation of sea water into salt. The appellant contended that the various provisions of the Act cannot be applicable to salt works where the process was carried on in the open air and not in building, was not held to be "a factory" on that account. Held, that the Salt Works would come within the definition of the word 'factory ' and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within the purview of the definition. The word " premises " is not restricted in scope to buildings alone of course, the building referred to in this clause is the building which is referred to In section 93 of the Indian Factories Act. The use of the words " any other purpose" in the definition indicates that the word "premises " is used in relation to a factory and would include something more than a mere temporary shed or a temporary shed. The process carried out in the Salt works and described above, come within this definition of manufacturing process ' in el. (k) of section 2 of the , and the appellant has been rightly convicted of the offence of working the factory without obtaining the licence. Held further, that where a statute uses words which are not capable of being construed as statutes, they must be construed in their ordinary sense and not by any technical or scientific meaning. The definition of " manufacturing process " is wide enough to include within its scope all buildings and things which can be used for the purpose of manufacturing processes.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, three occupational Institutes (Polytechnics) at Hassan, Devangere and Chintamani were started in the State. The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangore as Instructor. One Shri K. Chetty was far junior to the respondent in service. He continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Shri K, Narayanaswamy Chetty, whose case was identical in all respects, and six other officers who were similarly situated, were absorbed permanently in the Departments of Technical education with effectfrom the initial date of joining duty on deputation". The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of absorption. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the Respondent in the Depart ment Department of Technical Educational be given effect from 11th November, 1949 when he initially resumed duty on his deputation to the Polytechnics at Devagere. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed as tailoring Instructor from a particular anterior date, or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in that Department. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the State Government dated February 19, 1964, directing the absorption in the departments of Technical Development was not ordered owing to any fault of the appellant. It is not the appellant 's contention that this principle whereby the absorption was related back to the date of his appointment as such, was ever departed from except in the case of the respondents. [262 E] 2. The question whether a person was deputed to the Department or not has to be decided on its own facts and circumstances. In the instant case, seven employees had come on deputation with other Departments to the De partment of Technical Training Institute at Devengere as Instructor and were absorbed temporarily in the Commis sioner and appointed as Tailoring Instructor under the rules then in force, and as his reversion at this distance of time for no fault of his would cause a great hardship to him. [263 D E] 3. The appellant 'reversion was not directed owing to some fault of Shri. K. Narayanaswamy Chettiar, who was admittedly junior to him in the parent Department. That he was, in all material respects, in the same situation as K. This so called reversion to the parent department for a short period in 1955 56 could not by any reckoning be treated as a break in his service, this period having been treated as leave. [264 E F] 4. The case of Shri B. Narayanaswami Chetty was identical with that of Narayanaswamy Naidu because there was a break between him and the respondent. This being the case, the High ' Court was right in holding that the State Govern ment had evolved a principle "that if a person is deputed to a Department of technical Education from another department and he stay on in that other department for reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to that date irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions.

The petitioner in the writ petition challenged the constitutional validity of section 8(1) (a) and (b) of the , on the ground that it violated Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The petitioner contended that the impugned section was violative of Article 14 of the constitution as it violated articles 14,19(1), (2) and 22(5) of Part III of the Constitu tion inasmuch as it contravened article 14 of 'the Constitution. It was further submitted that the provisions of the Act were not violative of Articles 19(i)(g) and 21 of the Consti tution and that the Act violated articles 19(6), 21, 22 and 23 of the Con stitution. The Court held that the restrictions imposed by section 8 (1) were reasonable and did not violate article 14. It further held that it was not necessary to examine the question whether the foreigner will be a suitable adoptive parent for the child and the child will be able to get warm and affection of family life as also moral and material stability and security and whether it would be in the interest of the child to be taken in adoption by the foreigner. The court further held, that the foreigner was not entitled to any protection under Article 19(5), 21 or 22 of Part 111 of the Indian Constitution. In the writ peti tion filed by the petitioner, it was contended that section 8 of the was violative and violative of article 14 inasmuch as the impugned Act violated Articles 19 (1)(f) and 31 of the ' Constitution inasmuch as they contravened articles 14 and 19(2) of part III of Part 11 of the . The Court also held that there were no reasonable grounds for holding that the detention of the petitioner was not justified. In support of the petition, it had been contended on behalf of the respondent State that the Foreign Adoptions Act, 1973 was violative as it offended articles 14 or 19(4) of that Part III and that section was void because it violated article 22(6) of ' the Constitution inasmuch that it contravened Articles 14 and 31. Dismissing the writ Petition, HELD: 1. The impugned Act is not violative or violative of any provisions of Part Ill of the and is therefore void. [847C] 2.1 The Foreign Adoption (Regulation and Development) Act, 1974 was enacted to provide for the regulation and development of foreign exchange in the country. It has been enacted with a view to ensure that the children are not deprived of their fundamental rights guaranteed by Part III or any other law. It is an economic activity which is carried on by the foreign parent in India. The foreign parents who have taken a child in adoption would normally have the child study report with them before they select the child for adoption and in case they do not have the children study report, the same should be supplied to them by the recognised social or child welfare agency processing the application for guardianship and from the child Study Report, they would be able for gather information as to who are the biological parents of the children, if the biological parent is known. Social status and family background.

The appellant, Indian Cable Company Ltd. was a company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn. It had its head office at Calcutta. The workmen employed at Calcutta were paid bonus for the accounting year 1965 66. The company claimed that the allocable surplus should be calculated by first working out the gross profits for calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found payable had to be calculated and 60% of the rebate has to be added back as allocable. The Tribunal rejected this claim of the company. On appeal, the High Court held that the nationalc tax liability was to be worked out by first making working out its gross profits and deducting therefrom the prior charges under section 6, but not the bonus payable to the employees. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal was not justified in allowing deduction of certain items from the grossprofits for purposes of computing the available and allocable and allocables; that the High court was wrong in disallowing the claim of Unions. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. [14 F] (ii) The claim made by the Unions that after distribution of bonus at 20% for the year 1964 65, there must have been a surplus and it should have been set on for the next year, namely, 1965 66 was an expense allowable under s 37(i) of Income tax. [15 G H] (iii) The contention that the amount of Rs. 65,764 has not been accepted by the Tribunal is without substance. It follows that recomputation of the available surplus allocable available and the percentage of bonus for The accounting year 1966 66 on the basis of our judgment will be as follows: Rs. Rs.65,76 4. (i). Rs. 5,75,760.00 (ii). Rs 2,50,000.00. (iii).

The appellant, a Commercial Tax officer in the State of Tamil Nadu was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1962. He was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax Officer it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner that the charges should be dropped. The Government accepted the report of the Deputy Director and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. Charges were framed against the appellant in respect of allegations substantiated, obtained his explanation and sent its report thereon. The Full Board of Revenue then reported that the charge may be dropped". In 1969 the Government accepted his report and dropped charges making it the following Order on 2911 1974: (i) As the preliminary inquiry disclosed a Prima facie case, of corruption a detailed inquiry was taken into by the Director of Vigilance & Anti Corruption; (ii) The Government considered that there was a primafacie case in respect thereof. On appeal by the appellant, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Government and directed the Government to frame charges afresh as for major penalty against the respondent. In the writ petition filed before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the respondent including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 The State of Madras had no power to retire a Government servant in public interest after he attained the age of SO years or after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant will be reinstated in service and paid the arrears of salary due to him under the rules. He is entitled to his costs. [78G] 1.2 In the face of the promotion of the appel lant just a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is indeed odd to retire the appellant from service. The appellant would be an asset to the Department. One curious feature of the case is that while the 1969 entry noted that an enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against the appe lant, the ultimate result of the enquiry which was that the allegations should be dropping was nowhere noted in the personal file of the Appellant. The basis of the entry was knocked out by the order dated November 29, 1974 of the A Government and the effect of the entries was blotted out by promotion of appellant as Deputy Commis sioner. After his promotion as Deputy commissioner there was no entry in the service book to his discredit or hinting even remotely that he had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But, with nothing of the sort, it was indeed odd, to retire an appellant a few month after promoting him to a Selection post. [79H; 80A B] 1:3 The previous history of a Government employee should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the Promotion, we see no justification for needless digging into the past. No. 1112 dated September 19, 1975 Commercial Taxes Religious Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Pradesh is quashed. The order of November 29 1974 of Government was to grant absolution to the appellant from service and pay the arrears due to it under the Rules. He will be entitled to payment of his salary due under the rule.

The appellants, who were the owners of two buses, filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of Rule 5(1) of the Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Rules, 1962, on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the draft scheme was not a separate scheme and therefore the schemes framed and approved were fully in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Rule 5 is repugnant to section 68 E which provides that any scheme published under sub section (3) of section68 D may at any time be cancelled or modified by the State Transport Undertaking and the procedure laid down in section 68C shall, so far as it can be made applicable be followed in every case where the scheme is proposed to be modified as if the modifications proposed were a separate Scheme. [368 C] (2) The scheme framed under sub s.(3) is not one of the matters that was raised for consideration by this Court in Dosa Satyanaraya namurty etc. vs The Andhra Pradesh state Road Transport Corpora tion, ; , followed. (3)(i) The schemes are vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 69 C and the Rules made thereunder. [369 E] (ii) Rule 6 is not ultra vires because it does not contravene article 14 inasmuch as it contravenes article 19(1)(f). It is open to the State Government to issue a permit in respect of any route or routes which may be notified by the appropriate Government under section 68F(1). [368 G] (iii) The draft scheme framed and sanctioned by the Corporation could not be assailed as not in conformity within the requirements Of section 68 F(1), because, it is open for the State to issue permits by reason of section 5F(i).

The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii), the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The assessee made various attempts to get duplicate forms of declarations from the dealers but, on account of circumstances over which it had no control and because of the unhelpful and hostile attitude of the Commercial Tax Officer within whose jurisdiction the said dealers functioned, it was not able to furnish the duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the claim of the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the furnishing of the declaration forms by the purchasing dealer was a condition for claiming the exemption thereunder. In further appeal, however, the Tribunal held that section 5 (2)(b) of the Act in effect exempts from taxable turnover all sales to a registered dealer of goods of the class or classes specified in the certificate of registration of the dealer as being intended for the purposes mentioned therein. The High Court on a reference under section 66(1), held that since the assessee had not furnished the required declaration forms, the furnishing was a breach of the condition and therefore, the imposition of penalty was illegal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "for the purposes" in section 5 are wide enough to include all sales made by a dealer for the purpose mentioned therein; (ii) the proviso to the said sub clause imposes a condition on a dealer who claims the exemption and therefore the furnishing must be held to be directory and, therefore, it would be enough and if it was substantially compiled with.
