HELD: (i)(a) The words "as being intended" in the proviso are wide and not restricted to sales made for the pur pose of resale by a registered dealers of goods other than those mentioned therein, but do not furnish any help for construing them. [628 B] (b) The object of section 5 is self evident. Therefore, presumably to achieve the twofold object namely prevention of fraud and ' facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the benefit shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. That decision was concerned with section 5.(2)(A) of tho Act in question, but there was no proviso to that section in the Orissa Act similar to the one found in the present section. [ 630 C] (c) The construction suggested by the learned ' counsel introduces an incongruity which shall be avoided. The object is self apparent. Therefore presumably to achieving the two fold object namely, prevention of fraudulent and collusive attitude of a dealer, the exempted provision given is enacted subject to the condition that it imposes the condition. [625 E F] (d) Section 5(1)(a), as amended by Act VI of 1956, enjoins on a registered person not to accept and on the purchasing dealers not to give a declaration except in the form prescribed. That proviso imposes the conditions. The proviso to this sub clause prescribes in effect that the declaration form is to be furnished by the dealer and r. 27A with those of section 6(2) (a)(i) of Act, whereas the construction suggested introduces an apparent incongruitywhich shall be ignored.

The petitioners were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. They challenged their conviction by writ petitions before the High Court which dismissed them on the ground that they had not been produced before the Magistrates in compliance with the proviso to section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The petitioners contended that the requirement of the proviso was complied with and since the petitioners were released on bail, they could not be convicted under sections 395 and 396 of the Penal Code. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 Under trial prisoners whose names and particulars are given in the list filed by Mrs. It is not uncommon to find that under trial prisoners who are produced before Magistrates are unaware of their right to obtain release on bail and on account of their poverty they are unable to engage a lawyer who would apprise them of their rights to apply for bail and help them to secure release on jail by making a proper application to the Magistrate in that behalf. [529F] 1.2 The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It would, therefore, direct the State of Bihar to furnish to the Court the dates on which these under trial prisoner were remanded to judicial custody from time to time by the Magistrates so that we can satisfy himself in regard to compliance with section 167 (2) and we would, accordingly direct that on the next remand dates when the under trial Prisoners, charged with bailable offences, are produced, before the Magistrate or the Sessions Courts, the State Government should provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application for bail, provided that no objection is raised to such lawyer on their behalf and if any application for interim bail is made, the Magistrates should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad outlines set by us in our judgment dated 12th February, 1979. [540C D] 1:3 The State of West Bengal will furnish to this Court within three weeks from today particulars as to the location of the courts of magistrates and Courts of sessions in the State along with the total number of cases pending in each of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 giving yearwise breakup of such pending cases and also explaining why it has not been possible to dispose of such of those cases as have been pending for more than six months.

The appellant was the landlord and the respondent a protected tenant. The tenancy had been terminated by notice dated December 31, 1951, under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (Bombay Act LXVII of 1948). The appellant filed an application on April 7, 1953, under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court and contended that the provision of section 34 was not taken into consideration by the Revenue Courts in deciding the application of the landlord under section 29(2) and that the revenue courts were wrong in the view they had taken that sub section did not apply to the present proceedings. The High Court allowed the application relying on its previous Full Bench decision in Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (I.L.R. , held that as the tenancy had (1) L.R, I.A. 206, followed and (2) the right to terminate the tenancy was extinguished by the notice given to terminate it. Held, that the view taken by the High court is correct and sub section (2 A) would apply to all cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy has not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Act. The right to obtain possession had accrued when the notice was given, the law to be applied, in case of notices given before the Amending Acts came into force. Durlabhbhai Fakhabhai vs Jhawanji Bhikabhai, (1923) L R. 75 I. A. 206 and Durlababhai Fkhbhaibhai vs J. N. Sinha, (1868) L .R. 70 I.T.R., referred to.

The petitioners, who were evacuees and their properties, challenged the order of the Custodian declaring two houses to be evacuee property. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the custodian. Held, that the petitioners ' interest in the house could not have vested in the Custodian. The acts of the respondents in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. It was well established and not disputed that no property of any person can be declared to be an evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act. The act of the respondent in declaring two house to be evacueees and their property could not, therefore, vest in the custodian without due notice to him. The orders of January 10, 1952, were without jurisdiction so far it affected the rights of the petitioners in the properties concerned. The action taken under the Act was without jurisdiction as no notice had been issued to the petitioners under section7 of the , their interest in them could not be upheld; and the acts of Custodian in so much as they deprived the petitioners from their property were not upheld. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, ; , 702. 752 was not a patty to the proceeding in which the order in dispute had been made. The Act only affects the rights and interest of an evacuee which the petitioners, on the admitted facts, are not. It only affects rights of an evacue which the petitioner, on admitted facts were not.

The assessee company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool and (2) for weaving of yarn. The agents agreed to a deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the assessee Company from their remuneration. The case of the assessee was that the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by it in order to earn profits and would, therefore, fall within the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922 hereafter referred to as 'the Act '. The assessee company contended that the payments were not legally deductible under section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax, 1922 as it was not incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The Tribunal held that the agreement amounted to a joint venture and therefore the amount paid to agents could not be claimed by the assesse Company as a deduction under 191 section 10 of the Act. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court reversed the order of the Tribunal mainly relying on certain materials which were not at all found by the Tribunal in its order nor were those materials mentioned in the statement of case. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the High court that the payment in question was not legally allowable under section10(2) (xv) was correct. [192 D] 2.1 In the instant case, on the facts found the Court held that there was a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of share profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible. It was on the peculiar facts of the Dharamvir Dhir 's case that this Court observed as follows: ron the facts proved in the present case, the trust agreed to finance the business of the appellant on the terms set out in the agreement and there is nothing to show that he could have made any better arrangements or would not have last the contract if he had failed to enter into the agreement, i.e., the agreement to pay the amounts in dispute. [195 F G] 2:2 The High Court was right in holding that the cumulative effect of the interpretation of the various clauses of the agreement dated October 20, 1955 unequivocally revealed that in the garb of an agency the parties entered into a joint partnership for distributing the net profits after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agree ment by which the agents agreed that share losses would be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. [196 E] 2 :3 The High court had exceeded its jurisdiction in travelling beyond the agreed statement of the case framed by the tribunal and had relied on certain material which were neither at all considered nor those materials were found by it to be those materials. [197 G H] 4.1 It is open to the Appellate Tribunal to come to a conclusion either that the alleged payment was not real or that it was incurred by, the assessee in the character of trader or it is not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the Business of the assesee and to disallow it. [198 G] 4:2 In the present ease on the materials found the court held that payments were in excess of the reasonable return as contemplated under the Act and disallowed it. The High ' Court was, therefore. right in its view that the amounts paid to selling agents were not expenses incurred for earning profit.

The assessee company was a limited company. The loans were advanced to the assessee company in respect of certain shares held by it. In the assessment year 1958 59, the assessee claimed that the accumulated profits should be included in its income for the purpose of section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected this claim holding that the amounts earned by the company during the year in which the loans were raised to the asses see 's company could not be regarded as included within the accumulated profit of the company. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the amount was not liable to tax under section 2 (6A) of Income Tax and accordingly directed the inclusion of the said sum in its taxable income for purposes of section 1(6 A)(e). The High Court on a reference made by it answered the first question in the affirmative and the second question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Appellate Tribunal was not competent to refer the second questions, and the reference to that extent must be considered void. [951 F] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs M. V. The Revenue, Madras II vs G. TheRevenue, Madras, ; , applied. (2) The expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 of the Act includes profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current profit would mean the profits of the accounting years in a given case. [950 A B] Commissioner for Income tax Madras vs G M. Badiani, , followed.

The respondents were the successors in interest of one of the predecessors in title of the appellant. The lands were settled on the plaintiff by the Maharaja of Burdwan to the Rajgunj Asthal, and that the defendants were not liable to pay any rent for a period of time. The defendants claimed that they held them under a Lakheraj grant made prior to the permanent settlement, that neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them, and the entry in the record of rights published during the settlement in 1931 was correct. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the District Judge reversed the decision of the trial court and held that the documents on which the defendants claimed to have dealt with the properties as owners under assertion of an adverse title were not proved to relate to the suit lands, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that as there had been no determination of tenancy, no decree in ejectment could be passed but that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent and that they were not entitled to assess the rent. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that a strong presumption should be made in favour of the correctness of the entry because it was made in the ordinary course of business, and as there was no determination Of tenancy, any decree in eviction could be made but that such grant had been lost. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The documents relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they hold under a permanent Lakheaj grant are not shown to relate only to the suits lands. [1170 E] (a) The plea of adverse possession was not made the subject of an issue and there is no discussion of it in the judgments of the Courts below. [1107 F] (b) The documents on record did not show that the respondents claimed to hold under the rent free grant to the knowledge of the plaintiff prior to 1931, and therefore, they were all trespassers.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of contract. The trial court held that it being an incidental issue in a suit, which the Civil Court had jurisdiction to try, it will also have jurisdiction to decide the incidental or subsidiary issue and recorded a finding that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist. On appeal by the respondent defendant, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and remanded the matter to the trial Court for deciding the question whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist within the meaning of the Tenancy Act. The appellant filed a Letters Patent Appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 85A bars the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts to decide or deal with any question which arises under the Tenancy Acts and if section 85A imposes an obligation on the civil court to refer such issue to the competent authority under the Act, it would be no answer to the provisions to say that the issue is an incidental or ancillary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of the said Tenancy Act, the jurisdiction would not be ousted because the issue was not required to be decided or dealt with under the Land Revenue Code. [589F G] 1.2 The High Court was of the view that the jurisdiction conferred on the Civil court to settle, decide or dispose of any suit in a properly constituted civil suit before a civil court having jurisdiction to entertain the same would not he ousted because it is not required that to be settled or dealt by the competent authorities under the Revenue Act. [588C] 1:3 The High 'Court was right in holding that if an issue arises in a proper properly constituted Civil suit which the civil Court is competent to entertain, an incidental and subsidiary issue which might arise with referral to provisions contained in section 85 A would also be barred and it will have to be referred to the appropriate authority under that Act. If there is an issue which had to be settle, decided or deal dealt with by a competent authority, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arose in a duly constituted civil Suit cognizable by the Civil Judge, it is incumbent upon the Civil courts to refer the issue to a competent Authority under the said Act and the civil Courts will have jurisdiction. [587C D] 1 :4 The High court was right. It was not correct to say, that where in a plaint for specific relief an issue has arisen whether the defendant is an agricultural or not, would the Civil suit be barred because the issues are not required by the Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1964. [591D E] 2:1 In the instant case, the plaintiff sued for specific sale of agricultural land governed by the provisions of Tenancy Act in the Civil Suit and the defendant appeared and raised a contention that in view of the provisions contained under section 63 of the Land Reforms Act, he being not an agricultural agriculturist he is barred from purchasing the land. Such an issue being within the exclusive jurisdiction of Mamlatdar, it was incumbent upon him to refer to the Civil Authority under Tenancy Act and to decide it on the reference being answered back, to dispose of the suit in accordance with the decision of the competent Authority. [592D E; 590E] 2.2 In view of section 85(A) of the Bombay Tenancy Act the civil courts would be competent to settle the issue or the Civil Tribunal has no jurisdiction to deal with the same.

The two appeals relate to two assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 (calendar year 1957) and 195960 (calender year 1958). The two industrial undertakings were formed by the reconstruction of the business already in existence. The two undertakings were divided into three parts, namely, (1) the Steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division; (2) the Jute Mills Division; and (3) the jute mill Division. The assessee 's main business was that of heavy engineering. The iron Foundry & Jute Mill division was set up by the assessee company in its steel Foundry, and the jute Mill Division set up in the said two undertakings was a new industrial undertaking to which section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 applied. The three original undertakings were converted into two parts, one being the Steel Strips and the other being the Jute mill Division, and both these original undertakings had been formed by reconstruction of its business already there in existence, namely the business of heavy Engineering. The new industrial undertakings which were later on converted into a new Industrial undertaking were also amalgamated with the assessee 'S subsidiary company. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the steel Foundries Division setup by the asses see company were formed out of the old business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15 C of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that they were constituted by reconstruction and reconstruction of their business already as existing and therefore the assessee could not be said to be an indus trial undertaking to set up a new new industrial unit on account of which exemption of tax under section15C may be claimed. The High Court in reference upheld the view taken by the Income tax officer and dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that (1 ) the two undertakings are not entitled only to exemption but also to one part of it, namely whether the industrial undertakings, Steel Foundries and the Cotton Mill Division, are formed by a reconstruction of business already In existence; (ii) the two new undertakings cannot be said not forming out of reconstruction of any business already exist in existence; and that the articles produced by the two companies are used by the Boiler Division of the assessee. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The fact that an assessee by establishment of a new concern expands his existing business, which he certainly does, would not, on that score, deprive him of the benefit under section 14C simply because it goes to expand the general business of the asses sees. [776E] 2.1 In order that the new undertaking can be said "to be not formed out" of the already existing business that undertaking will not be denied the benefit of section 15D simply because the same goes to expanded the general industry of the assesses on some directions. The facts in the instant case are entirely different from those in the present case. The inamdars were granted to the temple for the performance of services connected therewith. The inamdars had been paying remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the purview of section 44 B(2)(a)(i). But there could be no doubt that section 44B (2) (a) (i) allows a resumption of the inam where there has been an alienation of the Inam either before or after 1934. The inams in the present case are resumable under section 44 A(2) and are resusable under s 44 B (2)(b). The inamdar had made an exchange, gift, sale or mortgage of the inams either before and after 1934 but these were not regranted to the Government under whom the inamdars held the inam lands. The Inamdars were in possession of the lands under the lease. They were also lessees of the land under the inamdar. During the continuance of the tenancy, their possession was not adverse to the inamholders. A fortiori, their actual possession was neither adverse nor adverse to Government under which they held the inams. The plaintiffs claimed title to the lands on a permanent lease and the inams were resumrable under section44 B (1) and (2). The Inamdar 's claim was negatived by the District Judge who held that the right to resume an inam could not be extinguished by adverse possession, and that in any event, the claim of adverse possession was established. On appeal by the State, HELD : (i)(a) The inams were originally granted to office holders as remuneration for service to be performed by them, and were outside the purview Of section 44 C. [545 B] (b) The inam lands were resimable under sections 44 B and 44 B. But there can be no dispute that section44B (1). was attracted if the holder of the grant had made a exchange, gifts, sale etc., of the properties or has granted a lease of it for a term exceeding five years. No. The District Collector held that these inams were personal inams burdened with services and the order of resumption was therefore illegal and a nullity. [544 E F] (c) The plaintiffs ' claim to be permanent alienees of the Lands was not established. The grant was within the scope of section44 C.P.C.

The appellant was the owner of certain houses situated in Indore City. Prior to January 26, 1954 the Indore Municipality was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909 and the Indore municipality imposed the tax on houses at the rate of 7% of their gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The appellant challenged the validity of the resolution on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual rent less 10%. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant Corporation that the Corporation was entitled to levy the house tax at the rates of 7%, of its gross annual rental value and that it was not bound to deduct the 10% allowance provided by sec. 2(c) and therefore the rate Of 7% was saved and secondly, that under sec. 79(1) of the 1954 act the Corporation need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year, that it has to prepare a new assessment list only once in every 4 years, that the Municipality can go on adopting the assessment list prepared in an earlier year and the owner or the occupier of the building would be deprived of the right to object to the valuation or the annual lettingvalue or the tax assessed thereon for at least 4 years even though the valuation may have decreased for one reason or the other. HELD: (i) The appellant Corporation was not entitled to demand the tax as it was inconsistent with sec. 73 of the Act and had to be adjusted in the light of the provisions of section 73 of that Act. [132 D] (ii) The resolution passed by the Municipality to levy tax at 7% on the gross annual value is obviously inconsistent with the provisions Of section 73. Therefore, to the extent that it is inconsistent with section 73 it is neither saved nor deemed to have been made under the Act, and has to be adjustment in the context of the provision of sec.73. [133 E] (iii) The Municipal tax levied on the buildings or lands or both in any official year in which such list is in force. The Municipal taxes are an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and assessment list on the base of which the tax is assessed is for each such official year. Therefore it was neither saved or deemed to be made under section 73, that is, if it was assessed on net and not the grossannual letting value after deducting 10% Statutory allowance in respect of repairs and any other accounts whatsoever.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. The Deputy Commissioner of Income tax, however, relying on the Memorandum of Association allowed the assessee Company to manufacture and sell chemicals and on the Directors report held that the assessee company was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 1,15,259. An appeal was then filed before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal at Trivandrum and the assessee 's contention was that a stock in trade could only be that which was the subject of trade, and that the stock of raw materials along with the business, including machinery, plant and premises was not sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a reali sation sale after the Company had been wound up. The Tribunal found that the business had not completely ceased to exist, since the assessee was carrying on manufacturing, on behalf of the purchaser, and the sale could not be regarded as a realisation sale after tho company was wound up, but had the characteristics of a trading sale. On appeal by the Department, HELD : (i) The transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business. It was a winding up sale with a view to realising the capital assets of the assessee. [966 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that by the sale no business was done, and therefore the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. [963 E] (iii) The sales were not in the ordinary course of trade but were part of the realisation of the trading stock and winding up of the company. There was, in fact, no identifiable price for the chemicals and raw materials except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals, and raw material and the price with them. From that alone, however it was impossible to infer that the chemicals or raw materials were sold in a particular way, because the agreement clearly indicated that the, assessee Company was keeping the factory going not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf.
